In the old model when print textbooks were acquired more frequently, students had to figure out how to return them, get a refund, and exchange it for another textbook. With digital content being embedded in Canvas, course content is automatically available to students as quickly as they can add and drop courses.

Jason LorganExecutive Director of Student Affairs

body.heading: The Solution
body.text: Equitable Access is a flat-rate course material program that was created by UC Davis staff in partnership with VitalSource, an eTextbook provider, and Canvas, the institution’s comprehensive learning management system. The program was created to be "the Spotify of textbooks," enabling all undergraduate students to access all the textbooks they need for one fee of $199 per quarter. Once registered, all digital textbooks are available to students in their Canvas account on the first day of class, ensuring they have the resources they need to succeed from day one. The concept for this program parallels that of student health insurance: It’s mandatory to have insurance if you’re a student at UC Davis, but costs can be unpredictable. To offset this, students are pooled together with the expectation that some students will require more care and others will require less care, but the cost is equal for everyone. To create this structure, the UC Davis and VitalSource team downloaded an entire academic year of student schedules. They then cross-referenced those schedules with their textbook adoption database to calculate the cost for each student to obtain their textbooks. From there, they negotiated textbook prices with publishers to lay the foundation for a subscription plan. The nature of the Equitable Access program seeks to address the principal-agent problem with textbooks: Although educators are choosing the books, students are expected to pay for them. Because the program is digital by default, it provides students with the option to opt out up until the add/drop date and removes the burden of returning and acquiring physical textbooks. “In the old model when print textbooks were acquired more frequently, students had to figure out how to return them, get a refund, and exchange it for another textbook. With digital content being embedded in Canvas, course content is automatically available to students as quickly as they can add and drop courses.” -Jason Lorgan, Executive Director of Student Affairs

body.heading: The Results
body.text: “What’s great about Equitable Access and its integration with Canvas is that it reflects both digital and physical content that has been assigned to students. As the central digital hub for learning, Canvas brings the most essential aspects of what students need for assignments and course study into one environment so everything is fully integrated.” -Ryan Petersen, Vice President of General Management at VitalSource This seamless integration within Canvas has simplified the textbook acquisition process for students. This was apparent in a recent student survey: 68% of students said the Equitable Access program made them feel more free to choose classes without worrying about textbook prices. 70% of students reported that acquiring textbooks through the Equitable Access program was easier than shopping for textbooks on their own. Through regular communication with the university library, the UC Davis team found 55 titles faculty had adopted as textbooks were titles to which the library already owned an unlimited number of licenses for simultaneous users. These library resources are now linked directly from the course content in Canvas and no longer have to be purchased separately by the bookstore for student access. “Our goal is to decrease the Equitable Access subscription price over time. We currently only have one term’s worth of data, but we are on track to meeting that goal.” -Jason Lorgan, Executive Director of Student Affairs

title: Creating Consistency for Every Learner: Independence School District
snippet: Learn how Independence School District chose Canvas LMS to positively impact and
intro: Learn how Independence School District chose Canvas LMS to positively impact and create consistency for every learner.

body.text: Independence School District , or ISD, ensures “each learner will achieve the skills…to be successful in an ever-changing world.” Recently, ISD’s technology coach, Sage Arnote, and virtual learning coordinator, Becky Herl, spoke on the district wide adoption of Canvas for Elementary.
body.html: Independence School District, or ISD, ensures “each learner will achieve the skills…to be successful in an ever-changing world.” Recently, ISD’s technology coach, Sage Arnote, and virtual learning coordinator, Becky Herl, spoke on the district wide adoption of Canvas for Elementary.

body.heading: The Challenge
body.text: At Independence School District, transitioning their young learners to a virtual environment came with its challenges. To make an informed decision about how to best tackle these challenges, ISD reached out to both neighboring districts and their own stakeholders to identify common pain points surrounding user experience in their virtual learning environments. What started as a conversation about improving the elementary virtual learning experience, turned into a broader discussion about how to set all students, guardians, teachers, and support staff in the district up for success with a consistent Canvas LMS experience. “We surveyed districts around us to learn what was the biggest complaint from their patrons. The largest grievance was different course expectations [in Canvas]. We have tried to be uniform in our K-12 practices using Canvas LMS. Because we want to offer our families ease of navigation and course consistency, our secondary schools have also adopted Canvas for Elementary,” Herl said. Making this district wide transition to Canvas for Elementary was a strategic change that came with many benefits.

At Independence School District, transitioning their young learners to a virtual environment came with its challenges. To make an informed decision about how to best tackle these challenges, ISD reached out to both neighboring districts and their own stakeholders to identify common pain points surrounding user experience in their virtual learning environments.

What started as a conversation about improving the elementary virtual learning experience, turned into a broader discussion about how to set all students, guardians, teachers, and support staff in the district up for success with a consistent Canvas LMS experience.

“We surveyed districts around us to learn what was the biggest complaint from their patrons. The largest grievance was different course expectations [in Canvas]. We have tried to be uniform in our K-12 practices using Canvas LMS. Because we want to offer our families ease of navigation and course consistency, our secondary schools have also adopted Canvas for Elementary,” Herl said.

Making this district wide transition to Canvas for Elementary was a strategic change that came with many benefits.

body.heading: Key Insights
body.text: Implementing Canvas for Elementary for all levels across K-12 resulted in a more consistent virtual learning experience for teachers, students, and guardians. Canvas for Elementary’s clean navigation gives teachers the option to customize where to place important student information like Homeroom, Schedule, Grades, and Resources. Guardians of both primary and secondary students can nickname and easily toggle between their students’ courses. Creating an implementation plan complete with onboarding and ongoing support for all stakeholders results in higher buy in and a smoother adoption.

• Implementing Canvas for Elementary for all levels across K-12 resulted in a more consistent virtual learning experience for teachers, students, and guardians.
  • Canvas for Elementary’s clean navigation gives teachers the option to customize where to place important student information like Homeroom, Schedule, Grades, and Resources.
  • Guardians of both primary and secondary students can nickname and easily toggle between their students’ courses.
  • Creating an implementation plan complete with onboarding and ongoing support for all stakeholders results in higher buy in and a smoother adoption.

body.heading: The Solution
body.text: After identifying Canvas for Elementary as the solution, ISD prepared for implementation. To provide the smoothest transition for the whole district, ISD developed a timeline for implementation, surveyed their own stakeholders, trained staff, students, and families, and created a system of continued support for ongoing enrollment. “We…have support to help our parents in the form of an email and phone number that they can reach out to our staff to assist with questions,” Arnote said.

Sage Arnote, Technology Coach at ISD

body.heading: Ongoing and Onboarding Support
body.text: As part of their implementation plan and to ensure that all educators would be ready for the change, instructional and virtual learning coaches planned summer PD opportunities to bring teachers together and introduce them to Canvas for Elementary ahead of the upcoming school year, according to Arnote. When asked how students, and guardians were trained, Herl outlined how Canvas for Elementary was introduced before the school year began at back to school night. The idea was to introduce Canvas for Elementary early at the same time as orientation and Chromebook distribution so that all students and their guardians would get a glimpse of the new, consistent virtual learning experience for themselves. Virtual learning handbooks for both the elementary and secondary levels were also created and distributed at this time. In addition to the summer onboarding, additional ongoing training opportunities were presented throughout the year to support teachers with any questions they had along the way. This included the creation of a virtual help desk called ISDHelpMe and training videos. “‘We did provide as instructional coaches ongoing training and we had optional meetings that teachers could attend if they wanted. We also put together a checklist at the start of any semester that went through all the things that were required of a teacher with regards to their Canvas courses,” Arnote said.

title: What Professional Associations Should Expect from Their LMS
snippet: Most LMS platforms track completion and call it done. This guide covers what
intro: Most LMS platforms track completion and call it done. This guide covers what professional associations actually need — member engagement, credible credentials, and programs that scale.

title: The Future of Edtech: Building Better AI for Education
snippet: This report explains what purposeful AI use looks like in education, and
intro: This report explains what purposeful AI use looks like in education, and includes an audit to help leaders assess whether the use of AI across their institution is a help or hindrance to academic integrity.

body.text: Just a few years ago, the conversation about AI in higher education was mostly about detection: catching it, blocking it, keeping it out of student work. Now, more than 90% of students and educators now use AI, and it's moved into the cognitive core of learning, where students summarize, analyze, and reason with it every day. The strategy for AI in higher ed hasn't followed usage trends. In 2024, only 20% of US institutions had published an AI policy, even as 92% of provosts reported faculty and staff asking for guidance. The result is AI adopted feature by feature, department by department, with no shared standard for what good looks like. This report gives leaders a way to close that gap. It lays out an institutional audit built around the five risks that surface when AI runs without academic context, the questions to ask in each case, and the characteristics of AI worth adopting. What's inside: The audit examines five risk areas. More output, less learning : When students submit polished work without doing the thinking behind it. Poor teaching quality: When generic AI produces content that doesn't match learning outcomes. Equity and accessibility gaps : When AI helps confident users most and widens the distance for multilingual students and those with accessibility needs. Weak data transparency : When no one can see what data an AI system uses or where human oversight sits. Ad hoc adoption : When isolated features pile up without a long-term plan. For each risk, you get the questions to ask your team and a description of what context-aware AI does differently, including how Canvas by Instructure and IgniteAI approach each one.

title: Choosing a Learning Management System for Skills-based Learning
snippet: Transitioning to skills-based learning requires the right technology. Learn how
intro: Transitioning to skills-based learning requires the right technology. Learn how to evaluate an LMS that prioritizes mastery and career readiness.

body.text: As the modern workforce shifts its focus from traditional degrees to demonstrable competencies, educational institutions must adapt by adopting a skills-based learning model. This transition requires more than just a change in curriculum; it demands a robust Learning Management System (LMS) designed to track granular progress and certify mastery. This guide serves as a roadmap for leaders to evaluate whether their current technology supports a "skills-first" ecosystem or if it's holding students back from professional readiness. To successfully implement skills-based learning, an LMS must move beyond simple gradebooks to offer deep visibility into student achievement. The document identifies several critical pillars for a successful transition: Competency Mapping: The ability to align every assignment, discussion, and assessment to specific learning outcomes or professional standards. Evidence-Based Portfolios: Moving beyond "pass/fail" by allowing students to curate a digital record of their work that proves their proficiency to future employers. Flexible Learning Pathways: Supporting non-linear progress where students can test out of known concepts and spend more time mastering challenging new skills. Actionable Data Analytics: Providing instructors with real-time dashboards to identify which students are struggling with specific competencies before they fall behind. Interoperability and Open Standards: Ensuring the LMS integrates seamlessly with external credentialing tools and labor market data to keep skills relevant.

title: Breaking Barriers: How Accessibility Transforms K-12 Education
snippet: Learn how digital accessibility in K-12 education drives student equity and
intro: Learn how digital accessibility in K-12 education drives student equity and success by removing barriers for all learners through inclusive design.

body.text: Accessibility is for everyone. Because student needs are nuanced, teachers' technology and strategies in the classroom should meet students where they are and lessen the barriers to equal learning opportunities. Discover the barriers to accessibility and how today's educators can remove them so that every student can succeed. Accessibility in K-12 education is more than a compliance requirement; it is a fundamental driver of student equity and success. By removing barriers to digital content, districts empower every learner—including those with disabilities, English language learners, and students in rural areas—to engage deeply with their curriculum. This document outlines how a proactive approach to accessibility creates a "curb-cut effect," where inclusive design choices like high-contrast visuals, closed captioning, and mobile-friendly layouts ultimately benefit the entire student body and their families. Transforming the educational experience requires reliable tools that simplify the creation of accessible materials for busy educators. When accessibility is integrated directly into the learning management system, teachers can focus on pedagogy rather than technical troubleshooting. By prioritizing easy-to-use checkers and automated formatting, schools can foster a culture of inclusivity that builds student confidence and independence. Investing in these digital foundations ensures that no student is left behind, regardless of how or where they access their education.

body.text: When students are engaged, they are more confident, ask more questions, make connections, and take ownership of their learning. So how can educators increase engagement? We asked education professionals from our community to share their unique perspectives on student engagement, as well as their strategies to boost meaningful involvement. Download our crowd-sourced collection of engagement strategies below. Student engagement is a multidimensional challenge that requires a holistic approach to bridge the gap between learner expectations and institutional delivery. This report, based on global research conducted with Hanover Research, explores the current state of higher education through the dual lenses of faculty and students. The findings reveal that while academic performance remains a key metric, "soft" factors—such as a sense of belonging, mental health support, and the flexibility of learning environments—are becoming the primary drivers of long-term student success and persistence. To cultivate a truly engaging experience, institutions must harmonize their digital strategies with human-centered needs. Educators are increasingly looking for tools that provide actionable data, allowing them to intervene early and personalize support for struggling students. By prioritizing digital equity and streamlining the instructional workflow, universities can remove technical friction and refocus on what matters most: the relationship between teacher and learner. The future of higher education engagement lies in creating a seamless, inclusive ecosystem that supports the "whole student" throughout their entire academic journey. "Through the Eyes of Educators: Insights into Student Engagement" is a research-driven report that explores the shifting landscape of classroom engagement from the perspective of frontline teachers. title: Driving the Learning Journey with Actionable Assessment
snippet: Learn how to turn assessment data into a roadmap for student success. Discover
intro: Learn how to turn assessment data into a roadmap for student success. Discover how actionable insights and continuous feedback drive growth in this K-12 guide.

body.text: Actionable assessment is the fuel that drives the educational journey, transforming raw data into a roadmap for student success. This guide explores how shifting from high-stakes testing to a continuous, student-centered assessment model allows educators to identify learning gaps in real time. By focusing on "assessment for learning" rather than just "of learning," teachers can provide targeted interventions that ensure every student—regardless of their starting point—stays on the path to mastery. The document highlights the synergy between Canvas LMS and MasteryConnect, which work together to make assessment data both visible and useful. It provides a strategic framework for reframing assessment in the classroom: using formative data to adjust daily instruction, empowering students through self-reflection, and utilizing predictive benchmarks to ensure state-test readiness. By making assessment an integral, ongoing part of the learning process, districts can create a more equitable environment where data serves as a bridge to deeper understanding and personalized academic growth. "Driving the Learning Journey With Actionable Assessment" is a strategic guide for K-12 leaders that advocates for a shift from "high-stakes" testing to a more continuous, "high-growth" assessment model. The guide argues that assessments should not merely be endpoints but vital checkpoints that provide the real-time data needed to personalize instruction. By utilizing the Mastery by Instructure suite—specifically Mastery Connect—districts can transform assessment data from a retrospective report into a proactive "GPS" for learning, ensuring every student stays on the path to mastery. The guide outlines a framework for building an assessment strategy that truly impacts student outcomes: Assessment for Learning: Moving toward formative assessments that provide immediate feedback, allowing teachers to adjust their instruction "in the moment" rather than waiting for end-of-year results. Visualizing Mastery: Leveraging standards-based gradebooks and dashboards to give teachers, students, and parents a clear, visual representation of which concepts have been mastered and where learning gaps exist. Empowering Professional Learning Communities (PLCs): Using shared, actionable data to foster collaboration among educators, allowing them to identify successful instructional strategies and scale them across the district. Student-Centered Growth: Encouraging students to take ownership of their learning by providing them with clear goals and a transparent view of their progress toward specific standards. Ultimately, this guide reflects Instructure’s authoritative yet supportive brand voice. It frames assessment as a powerful tool for equity, ensuring that every student receives the targeted support they need exactly when they need it. By integrating assessment deeply into the daily learning workflow, Instructure helps districts build a more resilient, data-informed culture focused on continuous improvement and individual student success.

title: Reimagining K-12 Education: Insights for the Future
snippet: Move beyond the basics. Discover the critical shifts in K-12 education, from
intro: Move beyond the basics. Discover the critical shifts in K-12 education, from hybrid learning and SEL to data-driven equity, in this future-focused research brief.

body.text: To better understand the future of teaching and learning, we sat down with seven K-12 leaders who shared the changes they witnessed in education in 2021--and what they hope to see moving forward. Moderated by Richard Culatta, chief executive officer of ISTE, the discussion focused on quality instruction, investment in technology to foster connection, reimagining assessment strategies, and more. "Reimagining K-12 Education: Insights for the Future" is a forward-looking research brief that synthesizes data from Instructure’s global studies to outline a new trajectory for primary and secondary education. The document argues that the post-pandemic era requires more than just a return to "normal"; it demands a fundamental reimagining of the classroom where technology is an invisible but essential driver of equity, engagement, and efficiency. It positions the Instructure Learning Platform (Canvas, Mastery, and Elevate) as the foundational ecosystem for this transformation. The brief identifies several "critical shifts" for the future of K-12: The Hybrid Habit: Highlighting that digital tools are no longer emergency measures but permanent fixtures that facilitate personalized learning and allow students to engage with content at their own pace. Prioritizing Student Well-being: A move toward holistic success metrics, recognizing that social-emotional learning (SEL) and mental health are as vital to student growth as academic test scores. Data as a Tool for Equity: Using learning analytics not for high-stakes accountability, but as a "real-time compass" to identify and support students who are falling behind, particularly those in underserved communities. Empowering Teachers through Integration: Addressing teacher burnout by advocating for a "single pane of glass" approach, where instruction, assessment, and communication happen in one unified platform. Strengthening the Home-School Connection: Emphasizing the need for transparent, mobile-friendly communication tools that empower parents to become active partners in their child's learning journey. The document showcases Instructure’s visionary, supportive, and advocate-driven brand voice. It highlights the challenges of the modern classroom as opportunities to build a more resilient and inclusive education system that prepares every student for a digital-first world.

title: Imagining a New Future for Higher Education
snippet: Move beyond emergency response. Discover how to intentionally design the future
intro: Move beyond emergency response. Discover how to intentionally design the future of higher education with a focus on hybridity, equity, and student well-being.

body.text: Uncertainty can catalyze learning. But how? And what does the future of higher education look like after years of uncertainty? To better understand how disruption drives innovation today and tomorrow, we sat down with eight higher ed leaders who share how colleges and universities can continue to build resilient, thriving communities. Explore the vision to prepare for the future below. "Imagining a New Future for Higher Education" is a forward-looking research report based on Instructure’s global State of Higher Education study. It serves as a call to action for university leaders to move past "emergency response" modes and begin intentionally designing the future of learning. The document argues that the pandemic accelerated a shift in student expectations that cannot be reversed, positioning the Instructure Learning Platform (Canvas) as the foundational infrastructure for this more flexible, inclusive, and student-centered future. Data-Driven Agility: Encouraging the use of real-time analytics to make the institution more responsive to student needs and to identify systemic barriers to success. This guide reflects Instructure’s visionary, authoritative, and provocative brand voice. It frames the current era not as a period of recovery, but as a unique opportunity to dismantle legacy structures and imagine a more equitable and impactful higher education experience.

title: From Student-Focused to Student-Centric: Your Guide to Strengthening the Student Experience
snippet: Strengthen the student experience by putting learners at the center. Discover
intro: Strengthen the student experience by putting learners at the center. Discover strategies for driving engagement, well-being, and success in this Higher Ed guide.

body.text: In the professional world, a Learning Management System is a strategic engine for compliance, talent retention, and operational excellence. This guide is specifically designed for business and government leaders who need a platform that is as secure as it is scalable. We move past basic training delivery to explore how a modern LMS can support complex workflows, from onboarding new hires to managing high-stakes certifications. The focus here is on reliability and a user experience that mirrors the consumer apps your employees already use, ensuring high adoption rates across the organization. Technical accuracy and data security are non-negotiable for public and private sector entities. We detail how an open-cloud architecture and robust API capabilities allow the LMS to sit at the center of your tech stack, communicating effortlessly with HRIS and CRM systems. By prioritizing a platform that offers deep analytics and mobile-first accessibility, you can ensure your workforce remains agile, compliant, and continuously developing, regardless of where they are working. "Student-Focused, Student-Centric: Your Guide to Strengthening the Student Experience" is a strategic roadmap for higher education leaders looking to modernize their institutional approach to learner success. The guide argues that in an increasingly competitive and digital landscape, universities must move beyond simply providing "access" to education and instead design a seamless, holistic "Ed-cosystem" that centers on the individual needs, well-being, and career aspirations of the student. It positions the Instructure Learning Platform (Canvas) as the essential infrastructure for delivering this personalized experience at scale. The guide outlines several core strategies for building a student-centric institution: Creating a Frictionless Journey: Emphasizing the need for a unified digital experience where students can easily navigate course materials, support services, and communication without technical barriers. Prioritizing Holistic Well-being: Recognizing that academic success is inextricably linked to mental health and a sense of belonging, urging institutions to integrate support resources directly into the learning workflow. Fostering Active Engagement: Moving away from passive content consumption toward interactive, collaborative learning experiences that keep students motivated and connected to their peers and instructors. Empowering Through Agency and Flexibility: Providing students with mobile-first tools and self-paced learning pathways that respect the demands of non-traditional and working learners. Closing the Feedback Loop: Using real-time learning analytics to identify when a student is struggling and providing immediate, personalized interventions that demonstrate the institution’s commitment to their success. Instructure’s visionary, empathetic, and partner-oriented brand voice is also a highlight in this guide. It posits the shift toward student-centricity not as a luxury, but as a survival mandate for modern institutions aiming to improve retention, equity, and long-term student outcomes.

title: A District Leader's Guide to Using Assessment Data
snippet: Empower your district with a smarter assessment strategy. Learn how to turn
intro: Empower your district with a smarter assessment strategy. Learn how to turn assessment data into actionable insights to drive student mastery and instructional growth.

body.text: K-12 schools have no shortage of data. With all this data, educators need to know how to use it to elevate student outcomes and make a meaningful impact. Assessment data remains critical for district leaders to make informed decisions. Find out how to turn assessments into insights that can improve teaching and learning in your district below. The "District Leader’s Guide to Using Assessment Data" serves as a strategic roadmap for K–12 administrators to move beyond merely collecting data to actively using it to drive institutional growth. Central to this guide is the philosophy that data should empower, not overwhelm. By utilizing the Mastery by Instructure suite—specifically Mastery Connect—district leaders can transform fragmented assessment results into a visual, standards-based "map" of student learning. This shift allows for a more proactive approach to education, where interventions are targeted, curriculum is evaluated for effectiveness, and every instructional decision is backed by real-time evidence. The guide outlines how to build a smarter assessment strategy through three core pillars: Driving Actionable Insights: Moving from complex spreadsheets to intuitive, visual dashboards that show exactly which students have mastered specific standards and which need immediate support. Strengthening Admin-Teacher Partnerships: Fostering a collaborative culture where Professional Learning Communities (PLCs) use shared data to align teaching practices and scale successful strategies across the district. Supporting Equitable Outcomes: Leveraging holistic data from tools like Elevate K-12 Analytics to identify systemic gaps, ensuring that resources and professional development are directed where they will have the greatest impact on student success. Ultimately, this guide is an authoritative yet supportive resource for leaders committed to continuous improvement. It reinforces Instructure’s mission of building an "Ed-cosystem" where technology clarifies the path forward, helping districts cultivate an environment where teachers can teach more effectively and every student has the opportunity to thrive.

title: Your Higher Education Guide to Choosing a Learning Management System
snippet: Choose the right LMS for your institution. Explore key evaluation criteria—from
intro: Choose the right LMS for your institution. Explore key evaluation criteria—from ease of use and integration to reliability—in this comprehensive guide.

body.text: Choosing a Learning Management System is about more than just checking boxes on a technical checklist; it’s about finding a partner that helps you create a truly connected learning ecosystem. This guide simplifies the complex evaluation process by focusing on the pillars of a modern LMS: reliability, open integration, and a mobile-first design. We know that technology should never get in the way of teaching, so we’ve outlined how to identify a platform that is intuitive enough for every user while being robust enough to handle the demands of a growing institution. The guide provides a clear roadmap for stakeholders to assess how an LMS can drive student success and institutional efficiency. By prioritizing features like cloud-native hosting for 99.9% uptime and a wide array of LTI-compliant integrations, you can ensure your digital tools work together seamlessly. Whether you’re looking to boost engagement through video-based learning or simplify grading for busy educators, the goal is to choose a solution that empowers your community to focus on what matters most: the learning experience. "Your Guide to Choosing a Learning Management System (LMS)" serves as a strategic roadmap for educational leaders to evaluate and select a platform that aligns with their institutional mission and long-term goals. The guide argues that a modern LMS should be more than just a digital file cabinet; it must be a dynamic, open ecosystem that fosters engagement, ensures accessibility, and provides the scalability needed for future growth. By following this framework, institutions can choose a partner like Canvas that provides the flexibility, security, and community-driven innovation required to thrive in a digital-first world.

title: Canvas Studio Guide: Higher Ed Edition
snippet: Move beyond passive watching. Discover how Canvas Studio transforms video into
intro: Move beyond passive watching. Discover how Canvas Studio transforms video into an interactive, data-driven learning experience for Higher Education.

body.text: Canvas Studio reimagines video as an active, collaborative learning tool specifically built for the higher education landscape. By moving away from passive consumption, this platform integrates media directly into the Canvas LMS, allowing students and instructors to engage through threaded discussions and interactive video quizzes. This approach transforms a standard lecture or demonstration into a vibrant dialogue, fostering a more connected digital campus where every student has a voice and every video becomes a powerful opportunity for critical thinking. The platform provides faculty with a streamlined media lifecycle, from effortless screen recording and webcam capture to automatic captioning for enhanced accessibility. Most importantly, Canvas Studio offers precise, real-time analytics that give instructors deep insights into how students are interacting with content—identifying exactly where engagement peaks or drops. By empowering students to also act as creators through video assignments, Studio helps institutions scale personalized instruction and ensure that digital media serves as a meaningful bridge to student success and academic mastery. "The Canvas Studio Guide (Higher Ed Edition)" is a comprehensive guide designed for colleges and universities to maximize the pedagogical potential of video. It moves beyond treating video as a passive medium, positioning Canvas Studio as a core component of the "Ed-cosystem" that facilitates active learning and two-way communication. The document argues that in a modern Higher Ed environment, video should be a collaborative space where students and instructors engage deeply with content and each other. Key pillars of the guide include: Active Video Engagement: Highlighting the platform's ability to allow students and instructors to comment, discuss, and ask questions directly on the video timeline, turning content into a conversation. Integrated Formative Assessments: Detailing how embedded quizzes and knowledge checks within videos help instructors measure student comprehension in real-time and provide immediate feedback. Powerful Analytics for Educators: Showcasing how instructors can use viewer data to see exactly how students are interacting with content—identifying which parts are being watched, skipped, or re-watched to inform future teaching. Student Content Creation: Encouraging students to move from consumers to creators by using Studio’s intuitive recording tools for video assignments, demonstrations, and peer reviews. Accessibility and Scalability: Emphasizing features like automatic captioning and a mobile-friendly interface to ensure that high-quality video learning is inclusive and accessible to all students, regardless of device or ability.

body.text: Student success is more than just a resume. This e-book shows the importance of giving higher ed students the tools to showcase their skills and competencies in a digital portfolio. No longer are students bound by a one page resume; they can showcase all they've acquired in the language future employers are looking for. The "Roadmap to Student Success" is a strategic white paper that outlines a comprehensive framework for higher education institutions to redefine and achieve student success in a digital-first era. The document argues that student success is no longer defined solely by graduation rates, but by a holistic journey encompassing academic achievement, personal well-being, and career readiness. It positions the Instructure Learning Platform (Canvas) as the central "Ed-cosystem" that enables institutions to guide students through this complex roadmap. With Instructure, we're taking that to the next level and getting an SS certification to be able to show that this is third party verified, that this works as a program for students achieving their goals. We've been looking at different studies different ways of getting third party as a certification. And that's one of the reasons why we were really excited to partner with Instructure on this. Today, evidence based research is becoming more and more of a requirement. And while we've been focused in doing these sort of studies internally and sharing them with our customers, partnering with Instructure allows us to give a new level of credibility, a new level of academic rigor to those impact studies. And that's really exciting for a lot of our customers. One of the really exciting things about partnering with Instructure is that you get an entire organization working for you. So I've been on a call with up to four people with advanced degrees, thinking about my data and the problems that we're trying to solve and how to properly represent, the data to in a study, and that's really exciting. That's a lot of, hiring and management overhead that we wouldn't be able to afford. So partnering with Instructure just takes away a lot of overhead in that sense. So we're really reducing the iteration time here, the feedback loop to teachers and educators on efficacy from decades to days. The value of getting ESSA validation is taking things to a level of peer review and of academic rigor that a private company by itself cannot do. Partnering with and renewing some of the largest districts in the country is something we've been able to do because of the focus on evidence based research, because we're able to tie impact directly to platform usage. What I'm most excited about for the future of Chalk Talk is enabling teachers, enabling educators to do less of the work that code and computers and robots do really well and do more of that irreplaceable work that is the human connection. body.text: The North Carolina state constitution requires the benefits of public higher education to be extended to the people of the state — all of them. To truly fulfill this duty, the University of North Carolina (UNC) public university system must more fully adapt to the needs of today’s learners and the changing labor market. For working adults especially, accessing higher education and relevant training can be challenging due to time, cost, a bewildering array of options, and uncertain connections to a clear career path. With the goal of more easily unlocking access to adult education, Project Kitty Hawk (opens in a new tab) teamed up with Canvas and Amazon Web Services (AWS) to deliver workforce-aligned online programs to upskill North Carolinians. This effort will help contribute to an ambitious statewide goal to close the educational attainment gap in North Carolina, ensuring that 2 million North Carolinians have a high-quality credential or postsecondary degree by 2030. Hear how this project was built and what they hope to achieve with this new, agile business model that will leverage best practices from the private sector, lessons from other state system initiatives, and proven strategies from leading online institutions.

title: Navigating the Future of Education: Embracing Innovation and Disruption
snippet: Education faces unprecedented challenges and opportunities in an era
intro: Education faces unprecedented challenges and opportunities in an era characterised by rapid technological advancements and evolving workforce demands. This keynote speech by Professor Martin Bean CBE from InstructureCon 2024 explores the transformative trends reshaping the landscape of higher education, emphasising the need for a connected system approach that integrates education, work, and skills. The session also highlights the emergence of shorter, more flexible credentials and the growing value placed on skills-based learning and assessment by both learners and employers.

body.text: Education faces unprecedented challenges and opportunities in an era characterised by rapid technological advancements and evolving workforce demands. This keynote speech by Professor Martin Bean CBE from InstructureCon 2024 explores the transformative trends reshaping the landscape of higher education, emphasising the need for a connected system approach that integrates education, work, and skills. The session also highlights the emergence of shorter, more flexible credentials and the growing value placed on skills-based learning and assessment by both learners and employers. A key focus is on the importance of digital skills wallets, which provide a 360-degree view of the learner. These digital tools enable the seamless tracking and showcasing of skills, competencies, and achievements, bridging the gap between education and employment. The speech also considers the shift from traditional degree-based hiring to skills-based hiring, underscoring the importance of continuous learning and reskilling in today's dynamic job market. It delves into the implications of generative AI on education, examining its potential to enhance learning experiences, streamline administrative processes, and optimise student success. Watch to better understand how education can harness the power of innovative approaches to meet the demands of the future and empower learners to thrive in an ever-changing global landscape.

title: Headlamp: Aligning Academia and Employers by Shifting Towards a Skills-First Mindset
snippet: Ever noticed how often you need to upgrade your smartphone to keep up with the
intro: Ever noticed how often you need to upgrade your smartphone to keep up with the latest tech? Similarly, as the job market shifts due to emerging skills and AI disruption, we need to evolve our education and talent development structures to keep up with this rapidly changing world. Together with our partners, we’ve pioneered a skills-based platform that aligns educational institutions, employers, and learners around today's in-demand skills. Hear from the University of Utah about their approach to skills-based education. Learn how companies like Mission Cloud hire using a skills-based approach. On Headlamp, employers can use skill-based portfolios and prioritize candidates who have upskilled and demonstrated their proficiency. Headlamp uses coursework and transforms it into dynamic job-ready portfolios that employers can evaluate to find and develop the right talent. It’s time for our education and hiring systems to evolve together, continuously updating to meet current needs. Join us to explore how Headlamp’s skills-first approach bridges the gap between education and industry. Discover how our cutting-edge collaboration tools and modern, AI-driven LMS capabilities support the development of a continuously evolving, highly skilled workforce, ensuring long-term success for both learners and employers.

The courses could be anywhere from two weeks long to six weeks long, and they award a credential or certificate when it's complete. title: FGCU: The Power of Micro-Credentials
snippet: Hear how FGCU created a university-wide badging program.
intro: Hear how FGCU created a university-wide badging program.

media.transcript: Micro credentialing is possibility. Micro credentialing is endless possibility, really. As long as you have purpose, as long as you have quality, then you're going to be able to provide opportunities to people that they wouldn't otherwise have. And I think that's really what higher education should be doing. We really got started on micro credentials at FGCU by recognizing the issue. Right? One of the things that, really drove it was just recognizing that increasingly there's a desire on the part of employers to have something besides a degree or a major that signals somebody's readiness for their career. Micro credentials, because of their short term application and credentials as a short credentials as a short term program of study that is intended to be done quickly. It's flexible, it's nimble, and it's something that is competency based. Creating a university wide digital badging initiative here at Florida Gulf Coast University has really allowed us to open the doors for learners of all ages and stages across the region. At FGCU, we have three different types of micro credentials that lead to the award of a digital badge. Industry specific, transferable skills, and continuing education and skills academy. These categories are all aimed at different populations and with a different purpose. One of the goals of badging is to signal some of the strengths that students have that maybe aren't directly signaled by their resume. Some of the work that we've done in the transferable skill badging arena has really helped to make students, I think, more aware themselves of what their strengths are in terms of the skills that employers really care about. We're developing these programs in partnership with leading employers across the region and the nation. All of our partners are telling us things that they're looking for, and these micro really been an has really been an instrumental partner in allowing us to use micro credentials effectively and addressing some of these skill gaps in the work force. When we are learning new things together with a partner, it's really nice to see that the partner is equally invested in changing these platforms to meet the needs of future learners. One of the things I really like about Canvas Credential, it's it's really designed to be flexible for you to create the badging program that works for you. Seeing the micro credential revolution has been meaningful. We are listening to what is really needed for success and and those skills that are needed, and we're finding a way to provide it to our students without compromising, what that degree stands for. We really have designed our micro credentials to not only make it transparent for students to articulate their value to employers, but also for students to actually be able to see what the connections are between what they're doing in their undergraduate experiences to that workforce. All college education is general, but all jobs are specific. So I really the rule view the role of micro credentials. It's not to replace college education. It's to supplement it. This is our region, and we care about the success of our economy, of our workforce, of the well-being of people in this area, and this is our contribution. It's about always needing to transform the way that we educate people in our community so that they can realize potential.

body.text: Micro-credentials at Florida Gulf Coast University provide flexible, competency-based programs that signal readiness for careers beyond traditional degrees. The digital badging initiative aims to recognize and signal strengths not directly shown on resumes, helping students become more aware of their valuable skills. FGCU is developing programs in partnership with leading employers to address skill gaps in the workforce, contributing to the success of the regional economy. Micro-credentials are designed to supplement, not replace, college education, providing skills needed for success without compromising the value of a degree. body.text: The Online Learning Consortium (OLC) is a global community of education professionals dedicated to advancing the quality and impact of digital learning. In 2022, OLC migrated its professional development offerings to Canvas, and in 2023 moved to Canvas Credentials to award micro-credentials. This presentation will explore how OLC leveraged the LMS transition and features of Canvas to create more engaging and effective professional development experiences for our community. We will also share our findings on the use of Canvas Credentials to showcase personas and pathways of offerings instead of just topics and tools.

title: Minutes are the Wrong Measure
intro: Screen time laws now reach into classrooms in a growing number of states. See why minute caps miss what matters and what districts should measure instead.

body.text: Across the nation's schools, a debate is underway regarding the negative impacts of student screen time, prompting action from numerous state legislatures . Utah now bars screen use in kindergarten through third grade, with narrow exceptions. Iowa caps digital instruction at 60 minutes a school day through fifth grade. Alabama set screen standards and teacher training for prekindergarten. Tennessee makes every K-5 district adopt a policy to cut unnecessary screen time. Kansas, Kentucky, Missouri, and Oklahoma all saw bills this session proposing daily caps or flat bans in elementary grades. Los Angeles Unified went past all of them , prohibiting instructional screen time through first grade and setting limits by grade band above it. These laws reach directly into the instructional tools a district chose, paid for, trained teachers on, and wrote into its curriculum. Whatever you make of them, these laws are regulating teaching. If you manage a classroom, a school, or a state agency, chances are you will have to defend your teaching approach, often to those who have already formed their opinions. Though you can defend it, your position shouldn’t be on time spent; it should be on results. Why the minutes don't tell you anything Start with what the research being cited actually studied. Ask a researcher what counts as excessive screen use in the literature, and the answer is usually five or six hours a day of passive entertainment . The key here is “passive entertainment,” which isn’t related to learning moments. It says nothing about a third grader spending 20 minutes in an adaptive reading program, and it shouldn't be used as if it did. There's also a problem with the measurement itself. Screen time research often relies on people estimating their own usage, and researchers who have checked those estimates against what devices actually logged keep finding the two don't match. That shouldn't surprise anyone. Most of us would guess wrong about our own screen time, and we're the ones holding the device. It's a shaky foundation on which many of the laws are being leveraged to get fast-tracked through the local legislature. Then there's the lumping of mixed use. Most instruments roll every kind of screen into one number, so 20 minutes of live feedback on decoding, 20 minutes of video, and 20 minutes of scrolling all land in the same column. A study built that way can tell you a correlation exists. What it fails to tell you is which activity produced it, and it certainly can't soundly inform a legislature which one to cap. A minutes target also does predictable damage once it lands. What gets measured gets managed, so a district handed a quantitative number starts managing to the number instead of the qualitative outcome. The first programs cut are the adaptive reading and math tools, because the tools students actually stay in are the ones that clock the most time. To their credit, most of these bills carve out students with IEPs and 504 plans. But an exception is still an exception. When the rule is that screens go away and a few students keep their devices open, the accommodation becomes visible in a way it wasn't before. Assistive technology works best when it's unremarkable, one more thing on the desk. A cap with a carve-out turns it into a marker, and it singles out the students the exception was written to protect. The carve-out also doesn't reach everyone who depends on these tools, including multilingual learners and students who don't have a device at home. What to measure instead So, what do we do? There’s a way to reframe the discussion to put the emphasis on where it belongs, and steer away from the generalization that all screentime is bad. When someone says children shouldn't be parked in front of screens all day, agree with them. That's the right instinct, and it's the same standard good schools already apply. The point that needs to be emphasized is whether the student is actually doing something vs whether if the screen is just on. Purposeful technology prompts, responds, and adapts. It asks students to make things, solve problems, and work with each other, and a teacher can tell you what it's for and when to stop using it. A student parked in front of a screen that just plays at them is doing something else entirely, and a minutes count cannot tell those two apart. We have to put trust in the teacher that when they invite technology into their classroom, it’s to the benefit of the student, and used responsibly to help enrich the learning experience. That distinction gives you a real answer instead of a defensive one. In August, the U.S. Department of Education put it about as well as I've seen . Instructional technologies, the guidance says, "should be judged by their impact on learning, not simply whether they happen on a screen." The same letter lists five questions any product should be able to answer: what learning problem does it solve, when should it be used, for whom, for how long, and what evidence shows it improves learning. Those questions travel. A teacher can ask them about a tool she's considering for Tuesday. A curriculum director can ask them before a renewal. A legislator can ask them instead of writing a cap. Social media, AI, and instructional software are three different problems Much of the current pressure comes from a pile-up of multiple concerns about technology. Worry about social media, unease about AI, and questions about classroom software have collapsed into one conversation, and screen time is the phrase carrying all three. Each is worthy of a much broader discussion, and requires separate answers. Social media is designed to hold attention and its financial model is built on engagement, so that worry is well founded. Classroom AI is evolving faster than the research supporting it. Being transparent about this limitation builds more trust than making unsubstantiated claims. Instructional software is a third issue, chosen by adults, tied to standards, and answerable for whether students learn. Run them together and you regulate the easiest target instead of the real one. The vetted math program is easy to cap. The algorithm running on a student's own device at 11 p.m. is not. What edtech owes you That standard points squarely at my own industry, and it should. For years, vendors asked districts to take software effectiveness on faith, based on usage metrics alone.Real partnership requires working directly with districts to deliver practical support, overcome implementation challenges and drive measurable outcomes for both students and educators. The 2026 Evidence Report reviewed 150 widely used classroom technologies. The value of purpose-built edtech vastly outperformed consumer tools, with 40% carrying an identifiable ESSA evidence level against 2% of consumer technology. Three in five purpose-built tools have no identifiable evidence level at all, and among the ones that do, the largest group sits at Level IV, which means a logic model. A logic model is a well-argued case for why a tool ought to work. It isn't a finding. Ask for efficacy studies on students who look like yours. Ask what happened in the districts where it didn't work. Ask vendors to publish null results instead of burying them. A vendor that can't answer the five questions isn’t ready for your needs, and the ones that are will get better because you asked. Novelty was never a reason to buy anything. Districts have the scars to prove it. Say yes with confidence Once a tool clears that bar, use it and say so without apologizing. Let the outcomes and student success be the tangible proof that responsible tech has its place in classrooms. Hedging about technology that's working teaches your community that all of it is suspect. The most credible thing a leader can say in a public meeting isn't a claim about edtech in general. It's four sentences about their own decisions. Here's what we adopted and why. Here's how we checked. Here's what we cut. Here's what we're watching. The third sentence does the most work, because no vendor can say it. You can. And keep the last point in view, because it's the one that gets lost. Technology isn't automatically better. It also isn't automatically worse. Great lessons run on devices and great lessons never touch one, and there are dismal versions of both. A worksheet doesn't beat an adaptive reading program just because it has no screen. Instruction comes first and the tool follows. Sometimes the right tool is a device. Sometimes it's a book, or a teacher reading the room and throwing out the plan. Teachers make that call all day long, and they make it well when they understand what a tool does, what it doesn't, and who it's for. That judgment is the thing worth protecting. A minutes cap replaces it with a number, and students are the ones who pay for the shortcut.

Los Angeles Unified went past all of them, prohibiting instructional screen time through first grade and setting limits by grade band above it.

These laws reach directly into the instructional tools a district chose, paid for, trained teachers on, and wrote into its curriculum. Whatever you make of them, these laws are regulating teaching.

If you manage a classroom, a school, or a state agency, chances are you will have to defend your teaching approach, often to those who have already formed their opinions. Though you can defend it, your position shouldn’t be on time spent; it should be on results. 

 

Why the minutes don't tell you anything

Start with what the research being cited actually studied.

Ask a researcher what counts as excessive screen use in the literature, and the answer is usually five or six hours a day of passive entertainment. The key here is “passive entertainment,” which isn’t related to learning moments. It says nothing about a third grader spending 20 minutes in an adaptive reading program, and it shouldn't be used as if it did.

There's also a problem with the measurement itself. Screen time research often relies on people estimating their own usage, and researchers who have checked those estimates against what devices actually logged keep finding the two don't match. That shouldn't surprise anyone. Most of us would guess wrong about our own screen time, and we're the ones holding the device. It's a shaky foundation on which many of the laws are being leveraged to get fast-tracked through the local legislature. 

Then there's the lumping of mixed use. Most instruments roll every kind of screen into one number, so 20 minutes of live feedback on decoding, 20 minutes of video, and 20 minutes of scrolling all land in the same column. A study built that way can tell you a correlation exists. What it fails to tell you is which activity produced it, and it certainly can't soundly inform a legislature which one to cap.

A minutes target also does predictable damage once it lands. What gets measured gets managed, so a district handed a quantitative number starts managing to the number instead of the qualitative outcome. The first programs cut are the adaptive reading and math tools, because the tools students actually stay in are the ones that clock the most time.

To their credit, most of these bills carve out students with IEPs and 504 plans. But an exception is still an exception. When the rule is that screens go away and a few students keep their devices open, the accommodation becomes visible in a way it wasn't before. Assistive technology works best when it's unremarkable, one more thing on the desk. A cap with a carve-out turns it into a marker, and it singles out the students the exception was written to protect. The carve-out also doesn't reach everyone who depends on these tools, including multilingual learners and students who don't have a device at home.

 

What to measure instead

So, what do we do? There’s a way to reframe the discussion to put the emphasis on where it belongs, and steer away from the generalization that all screentime is bad.

When someone says children shouldn't be parked in front of screens all day, agree with them. That's the right instinct, and it's the same standard good schools already apply. The point that needs to be emphasized is whether the student is actually doing something vs whether if the screen is just on. 

Purposeful technology prompts, responds, and adapts. It asks students to make things, solve problems, and work with each other, and a teacher can tell you what it's for and when to stop using it. A student parked in front of a screen that just plays at them is doing something else entirely, and a minutes count cannot tell those two apart. We have to put trust in the teacher that when they invite technology into their classroom, it’s to the benefit of the student, and used responsibly to help enrich the learning experience.

That distinction gives you a real answer instead of a defensive one. In August, the U.S. Department of Education put it about as well as I've seen. Instructional technologies, the guidance says, "should be judged by their impact on learning, not simply whether they happen on a screen." The same letter lists five questions any product should be able to answer: what learning problem does it solve, when should it be used, for whom, for how long, and what evidence shows it improves learning.

Those questions travel. A teacher can ask them about a tool she's considering for Tuesday. A curriculum director can ask them before a renewal. A legislator can ask them instead of writing a cap.

 

Social media, AI, and instructional software are three different problems

Much of the current pressure comes from a pile-up of multiple concerns about technology. Worry about social media, unease about AI, and questions about classroom software have collapsed into one conversation, and screen time is the phrase carrying all three.

Each is worthy of a much broader discussion, and requires separate answers. Social media is designed to hold attention and its financial model is built on engagement, so that worry is well founded. Classroom AI is evolving faster than the research supporting it. Being transparent about this limitation builds more trust than making unsubstantiated claims. Instructional software is a third issue, chosen by adults, tied to standards, and answerable for whether students learn.

Run them together and you regulate the easiest target instead of the real one. The vetted math program is easy to cap. The algorithm running on a student's own device at 11 p.m. is not.

 

What edtech owes you

That standard points squarely at my own industry, and it should.

For years, vendors asked districts to take software effectiveness on faith, based on usage metrics alone.Real partnership requires working directly with districts to deliver practical support, overcome implementation challenges and drive measurable outcomes for both students and educators. 

The 2026 Evidence Report reviewed 150 widely used classroom technologies. The value of purpose-built edtech vastly outperformed consumer tools, with 40% carrying an identifiable ESSA evidence level against 2% of consumer technology. Three in five purpose-built tools have no identifiable evidence level at all, and among the ones that do, the largest group sits at Level IV, which means a logic model. A logic model is a well-argued case for why a tool ought to work. It isn't a finding.

Ask for efficacy studies on students who look like yours. Ask what happened in the districts where it didn't work. Ask vendors to publish null results instead of burying them. A vendor that can't answer the five questions isn’t ready for your needs, and the ones that are will get better because you asked.

Novelty was never a reason to buy anything. Districts have the scars to prove it.

 

Say yes with confidence

Once a tool clears that bar, use it and say so without apologizing. Let the outcomes and student success be the tangible proof that responsible tech has its place in classrooms. Hedging about technology that's working teaches your community that all of it is suspect.

The most credible thing a leader can say in a public meeting isn't a claim about edtech in general. It's four sentences about their own decisions. Here's what we adopted and why. Here's how we checked. Here's what we cut. Here's what we're watching. The third sentence does the most work, because no vendor can say it. You can.

And keep the last point in view, because it's the one that gets lost. Technology isn't automatically better. It also isn't automatically worse. Great lessons run on devices and great lessons never touch one, and there are dismal versions of both. A worksheet doesn't beat an adaptive reading program just because it has no screen.

Instruction comes first and the tool follows. Sometimes the right tool is a device. Sometimes it's a book, or a teacher reading the room and throwing out the plan. Teachers make that call all day long, and they make it well when they understand what a tool does, what it doesn't, and who it's for. That judgment is the thing worth protecting. A minutes cap replaces it with a number, and students are the ones who pay for the shortcut.

title: 5 Lessons For Modern Public Safety Training: How to Sequence a Program and Prove What It Delivered
intro: Discover 5 key lessons for modern public safety training: sequence academy programs, unify practical and course records, and automate certification tracking.

body.text: In December 2024, the Massachusetts State Auditor published a review of the Municipal Police Training Committee, the agency that holds training records for more than 23,000 police officers and related personnel. Auditors found no access log for the locked records room and no formal filing and retrieval system, just records stacked on metal cabinets. Files they requested were often "missing, not readily available, not properly filed." The same audit found that academies did not consistently deliver the standardized recruit officer curriculum, and that not every recruit course was taught by a certified instructor. This is not how modern public safety programs set out to run their training, but it happens the way most program problems happen: a curriculum grows across years, ownership moves between people, the record of what was actually taught lives in three places, and no one holds the whole picture until an auditor asks for it. Long-running training programs outside law enforcement have already worked through the same problems, and one of the clearest examples was presented publicly this summer by the team behind a multi-phase government program: sequenced phases, a required body of knowledge, live practical components, coaching, and a standing structure for keeping the whole thing current. That program trains contracting professionals rather than officers, so the analogy has limits worth naming out loud. 1. Sequence the program first, then count the hours It's January, and the training sergeant is building next year's academy calendar. She's working from a spreadsheet of blocks and a list of which instructors can take which weeks. Firearms goes early, because the range is booked solid after March. The legal block on when force is authorized lands in week 11, three weeks after defensive tactics. By Friday, the calendar is done. Only one block was placed for what recruits needed to learn first. The rest followed the range calendar and when three instructors had leave approved. US basic law enforcement academies required an average of 806 hours of basic training in 2022, against an average state or statutory minimum of 620 hours. A companion BJS report from June 2025 breaks that out by who runs the academy, from 681 hours at state POST academies to 1,015 at county police departments. That 334 hours is the clearest evidence available that standardized training is not yet standardized. Nearly 90% of academies also required field training afterward, averaging another 503 hours. So the hour count is a floor a state sets, but the curriculum built to hit that number tends to become a list of topics in whatever order somebody added them. What that looks like when a program gets it right: the order comes from the job. Each phase covers the work someone actually does at that stage, and it opens only once the phase before it closes. The academy version is to define, for every phase, what a recruit must demonstrate before moving forward, and to write it where instructors and recruits can both see it. The syllabus and the calendar ultimately carry the design. 2. Put the practical work in the same record as the coursework Thursday afternoon, 24 recruits cycle through a simulated traffic stop while two instructors score them on paper rubrics. The scores get totaled. The sheets go into a folder in the training office, and the folder goes into a drawer. Five months later, a field training officer wants to know how her rookie handled that scenario, because he's freezing on stops. She can pull his written exam score in about 10 seconds, but the scenario rubric takes two phone calls to find which cabinet the folder went into. The exam score and the rubric answer different questions. One says the recruit knows what the law allows during a stop. The other says what he did when a driver wouldn't take his hands off the wheel. Academies have been moving toward the kind of training that produces the second document, and the systems holding the record haven't kept pace. The Police Executive Research Forum reported that lecture still consumed 57% of academy instruction time, with practical applications and scenarios at 31%. PERF's first guiding principle puts critical thinking and values-based decision making at the center of recruit training; that judgment is the thing rubrics capture. Both pieces need to live in the same place; the practical work should be built as graded assignments inside the program, scored against the judgment calls the job actually requires. A recruit's performance on a scenario then sits in the same record as the exam score, where a field training officer can find it. 3. Give the live program a standing owner In March, the state POST issues an updated bulletin on vehicle pursuits. The academy's legal instructor rewrites the block in April, and the May cohort learns the new standard. In September, a rookie from that cohort terminates a pursuit the new way and his FTO writes him up, because the field training manual still describes the old policy and nobody told the field the block had changed. This knowledge gap is common enough that PERF's 2022 report found that only 57% of agencies said field training officers receive periodic training on changes to the academy curriculum. So roughly four in 10 FTO programs are correcting recruits against a version of the curriculum that no longer exists. Part of the issue is who is responsible for teaching. The 2022 BJS census counted 31,446 part-time academy instructors against 10,652 full-time, about three to one. Any change to a block has to reach a teaching staff that is only in the classroom part-time. The fix: a governance team that meets on a set cadence, with a fixed agenda covering cohort setup, learner support, content updates, and version control. Every content change goes through that team, and it leaves with a date attached and the name of whoever tells the field. 4. Put the renewal clock where the record lives One lieutenant maintains the department's certification spreadsheet. It runs 240 rows, one per officer, with a column for each mandated topic and cells that turn yellow at 60 days out and red past due. She built it, and she's the only one who really understands it. When she takes three weeks of leave in July, the yellow cells keep turning red in a file nobody else opens. In April 2026, the Washington State Auditor reported that only about 16% of veteran officers had finished the state's required 40 hours of violence de-escalation and mental health training, and only about 14% of new officers met their deadlines. On patrol tactics training, the state's best single year between 2020 and 2024 trained 1,273 officers against an estimated 2,700 needed annually, and the auditor projected that roughly half of all officers could be out of compliance by 2028. The same audit found agencies hitting barriers when they tried to track compliance in the state commission's data system, and reports going to the Legislature that carried inaccuracies and omissions. Compliance failures add to an already existing staffing problem. Agencies responding to the IACP's 2024 recruitment and retention survey were operating at roughly 91% of authorized sworn strength, so every officer who falls out of compliance is capacity the agency already doesn't have. Recertification runs every year, and a requirement tracked in a spreadsheet is a requirement someone has to remember; the renewal clock belongs in the system that already holds the training record, with notifications sent directly to recruits and officers. 5. Assume you'll have to prove all of it Three years after a cohort graduates, a records request arrives from a plaintiff's attorney. It asks for one officer's academy training on de-escalation: the hours, the dates, the curriculum used, and whether the instructor was certified to teach it at the time. The training director who ran that cohort now works in another county. Since then the curriculum has been revised twice, and the instructor who taught the block retired last spring. IADLEST model minimum standards call for documenting curriculum and keeping historical records for each basic training class for at least 20 years, and for retaining student records at least as long as state law requires. The stakes have gotten more concrete. IADLEST reported in 2024 that its National Decertification Index holds more than 53,500 records of officers whose certification was revoked, contributed by 49 POST agencies. A background investigation on a lateral hire and a civil filing three years after the fact both come looking for the same academy records, and a CALEA or state accreditation review asks on a published schedule. The test is simple, but not necessarily easy: Can you produce, on demand, who completed what, on what date, taught by which certified instructor, against which version of the curriculum? Where Canvas Career fits Canvas Career by Instructure puts cadet training, certification tracking, and readiness reporting in one system. Enrollment by role and team routes the right content to the right recruits, and practical assessments land in the same learner record as coursework, so the scenario rubric ends up next to the exam score. Certification pathways carry their own reminders. That takes the renewal clock off one lieutenant's spreadsheet and puts it somewhere command staff can see it, alongside a current view of who is trained and what is due. Find out how Canvas Career gives police academies one platform to manage cadet training, automate certification tracking, and report on officer readiness.
