title: What I Learned Taping Our First Episode of Learning While Leading
intro: Education leadership is lonelier than it looks. Dr. Marina Aminy on steering 116 colleges by influence, not mandate, on our podcast. Hear the first episode.

body.text: We noticed that Instructure talks with incredible leaders every day, but had never given them a place to talk honestly and share with an audience about how hard it actually is to lead in education. And so, the Learning while Leading podcast was born. With our first episode of Learning while Leading (recorded live at InstructureCon 2026 in Louisville, in front of a live audience), I wanted to share some thoughts on how it went and why I think it’s important that leaders share their stories with other leaders. My co-host Justin Stone and I only had one name on the list for our first guest: Dr. Marina Aminy, executive director of the California Virtual Campus (CVC), who works at the system level of the California Community Colleges. Marina's been a customer of ours for years, and getting to know her as a leader over that time is a big part of why I wanted her first. For context on what she's actually running: 116 colleges, roughly 2.3 million students a year, all with real independence from each other. If I were going to test a new show on someone, I would want a guest who has spent a career getting a large, decentralized system to move together. Marina was it. The icebreaker gave her away We ask every guest the same question to open the show: what's your dream class, who's teaching it, and who's sitting next to you? Marina didn't hesitate. Muhammad Ali. She has a black belt in taekwondo, her father boxed for the Afghan national team and taught school in Kabul, and she wanted pointers on form as much as she wanted to hear Ali talk about growing into who he was in public. Her answer told me a lot about how she leads: fighter and teacher, at the same time, by inheritance.That instinct showed up for the rest of our conversation. A system built so no one has to ask permission twice The story Marina told about course sharing is the kind of thing that sounds simple until you learn how long it actually takes to pull off. A student at a remote college, one that doesn't offer the single class they need to transfer, used to be stuck. No seat, no workaround. So the CVC built a way for students anywhere in the 116-college system to take a course from another campus without a new application, a new email, or a new ID. It took seven or eight years to get the technology right. It now runs on an Instructure platform, and last year, about 60,000 students used it, enrolling in a couple of minutes instead of waiting in a queue. Marina used real examples and cases to help sell through her vision. For instance, she highlighted Lake Tahoe Community College, small and remote, picked up thousands of enrollments it never would have reached on its own. "It's not a zero-sum game," she told us. Colleges bracing to lose students to the shared platform found the opposite happening. Steering 116 colleges Marina’s role is more of influence than mandate. She can't tell any of those 116 college presidents what to do, so I asked how she gets anything done at all. Her answer, paraphrased only slightly: stop micromanaging, trust your team and your partners, and let the work speak for itself. She'd also rather put faculty, researchers, and students in front of the people who need convincing than herself. And it works to her advantage. In fact, some of her loudest advocates showed up on their own, with no campaign behind them: students posting TikToks about how easy CVC made enrollment. Her own son found the program before she'd mentioned it at home, which made me laugh, because my daughter Sophie does the exact same thing to me with Canvas. But persuasion has limits, and Marina knows when to stop being diplomatic. One college shortened its drop-for-nonpayment window from 14 days to three, giving students almost no time to scrape together tuition before losing their seats. She got in a room with that college's leadership and made it personal to their own values: you've built equity into your strategic plan, and this policy contradicts it. Not a lecture. A mirror. What it actually costs her I asked what keeps her going when the win takes years, and the road is full of colleges telling her no. Her answer, without missing a beat: "a lot of chocolate." Then, more seriously, honest conversations with peers when something falls apart, and a habit of picking apart her own missteps afterward instead of just moving on. That part of the conversation got personal for me, too. I've found that the higher I've risen in my own career, the lonelier it's gotten, and it was a relief to hear Marina name that out loud instead of pretending leadership always looks put-together. She talked about how mentorship gets harder to find the further you rise, and how it looks different at every stage of a career. As a woman, an immigrant, and a Muslim over 50, she's had to keep finding new mentors as her old ones stopped being the right fit. Her advice to women coming up in education leadership: find other women, ask for help before you think you need it, and bring an ally into the room before a high-stakes meeting, not during it. Her advice to the men in the room: give credit out loud, and repeat a woman's point back with her name on it when you notice it got skipped over the first time. She uses AI like a colleague she doesn't fully trust yet Marina's view on AI in her role is mostly used to save time, and she holds it at arm's length everywhere else. The clearest example: students using course sharing sometimes need a prerequisite manually verified before they can enroll, and that human review is slow enough that her colleges dropped between 3,000 and 5,000 students last year who simply ran out of time waiting on it. That's the kind of bottleneck she wants AI to help close. Where she won't use it: her own writing. "I read it and I'm like, this just doesn't sound like me at all," she told me, and she'd rather sound like herself than sound polished. She's also wary of letting AI run analysis on research data, after a colleague pointed out that bias baked into one AI-assisted analysis can quietly spread into everything that cites it afterward. On policy, she wants guardrails, not a script: guidance on security, privacy, accessibility, and FERPA, and then room to actually do her job without someone unfamiliar with the daily work telling her how. Sharing the voice of leadership I encourage you all to listen to Marina’s story, as I believe many of the challenges she faces resonate across the desks of so many leaders in education. She was a terrific first guest and an even more inspiring person. Thank you, Marina. This is exactly why we felt it was important to create this podcast: leaders running the business side of learning need an outlet to voice their challenges, their solutions, and even just ask for help. Learning while Leading is a monthly podcast. Please listen, follow, and give feedback on what you’d like us to discuss! And if you have an idea for a great guest to be featured on the program, please share it at LearningWhileLeading@instructure.com. Listen to the full conversation: Episode 1: Making it work: The business of leading

For instance, she highlighted Lake Tahoe Community College, small and remote, picked up thousands of enrollments it never would have reached on its own. "It's not a zero-sum game," she told us. Colleges bracing to lose students to the shared platform found the opposite happening.

 

Steering 116 colleges

Marina’s role is more of influence than mandate. She can't tell any of those 116 college presidents what to do, so I asked how she gets anything done at all. Her answer, paraphrased only slightly: stop micromanaging, trust your team and your partners, and let the work speak for itself.

She'd also rather put faculty, researchers, and students in front of the people who need convincing than herself. And it works to her advantage. In fact, some of her loudest advocates showed up on their own, with no campaign behind them: students posting TikToks about how easy CVC made enrollment. Her own son found the program before she'd mentioned it at home, which made me laugh, because my daughter Sophie does the exact same thing to me with Canvas.

But persuasion has limits, and Marina knows when to stop being diplomatic. One college shortened its drop-for-nonpayment window from 14 days to three, giving students almost no time to scrape together tuition before losing their seats. She got in a room with that college's leadership and made it personal to their own values: you've built equity into your strategic plan, and this policy contradicts it. Not a lecture. A mirror.

 

What it actually costs her

I asked what keeps her going when the win takes years, and the road is full of colleges telling her no. Her answer, without missing a beat: "a lot of chocolate." Then, more seriously, honest conversations with peers when something falls apart, and a habit of picking apart her own missteps afterward instead of just moving on.

That part of the conversation got personal for me, too. I've found that the higher I've risen in my own career, the lonelier it's gotten, and it was a relief to hear Marina name that out loud instead of pretending leadership always looks put-together. She talked about how mentorship gets harder to find the further you rise, and how it looks different at every stage of a career. As a woman, an immigrant, and a Muslim over 50, she's had to keep finding new mentors as her old ones stopped being the right fit. 

Her advice to women coming up in education leadership: find other women, ask for help before you think you need it, and bring an ally into the room before a high-stakes meeting, not during it. Her advice to the men in the room: give credit out loud, and repeat a woman's point back with her name on it when you notice it got skipped over the first time.

 

She uses AI like a colleague she doesn't fully trust yet

Marina's view on AI in her role is mostly used to save time, and she holds it at arm's length everywhere else. The clearest example: students using course sharing sometimes need a prerequisite manually verified before they can enroll, and that human review is slow enough that her colleges dropped between 3,000 and 5,000 students last year who simply ran out of time waiting on it. That's the kind of bottleneck she wants AI to help close.

Where she won't use it: her own writing. "I read it and I'm like, this just doesn't sound like me at all," she told me, and she'd rather sound like herself than sound polished. She's also wary of letting AI run analysis on research data, after a colleague pointed out that bias baked into one AI-assisted analysis can quietly spread into everything that cites it afterward.

On policy, she wants guardrails, not a script: guidance on security, privacy, accessibility, and FERPA, and then room to actually do her job without someone unfamiliar with the daily work telling her how.

 

Sharing the voice of leadership

I encourage you all to listen to Marina’s story, as I believe many of the challenges she faces resonate across the desks of so many leaders in education. She was a terrific first guest and an even more inspiring person. Thank you, Marina. 

This is exactly why we felt it was important to create this podcast: leaders running the business side of learning need an outlet to voice their challenges, their solutions, and even just ask for help. 

Learning while Leading is a monthly podcast. Please listen, follow, and give feedback on what you’d like us to discuss! And if you have an idea for a great guest to be featured on the program, please share it at LearningWhileLeading@instructure.com.

title: The Essential Features of a Higher Education LMS
intro: Selecting a higher ed LMS is more than just checking off features. Learn what truly matters—from integration architecture to mastery-based pathways—for your institution’s teaching and learning goals.

body.text: Colleges and universities looking for a learning management system aren’t going down a checklist so much as putting together an elaborate tech puzzle. All the people at the platform decision table need to know how the edtech pieces connect to each other, what happens when something breaks in week 12, and whether the system can represent how your institution actually teaches. Here’s what to look for in a higher ed LMS so it can work for your whole institution. Start with the higher education LMS features faculty touch every day The daily user experience of any LMS is the most important part of evaluating one. Adoption and usage on the platform will make a much bigger impact on your tech investment ROI than a feature list. So it needs to work for how instructors and students will actually use it every day. Watch an instructor build a module, sequence it with prerequisites, and copy it into next term. Watch what the rich content editor does with pasted text; an editor that buries content in inline styles produces pages that fall apart on a phone and fight a screen reader. Departments usually want to standardize the shell of a course without freezing the parts faculty need to change, and the mechanism for that can vary a lot between platforms. (Canvas by Instructure handles it through Blueprint Courses, which push a template's structure out to linked sections while leaving specified pieces editable.) The gradebook deserves its own scrutiny. Weighted assignment groups and late policies applied by rule are the baseline. What matters more is control over when grades post, so an instructor can grade across a week and release everything at once, and a change history showing who altered a grade, when, and from what. The Canvas gradebook keeps a grade change log alongside per-assignment posting policies. Check the phone. Students read, submit, and check grades on mobile, and plenty of instructors grade there too. Consider a test on a mid-range Android over a weak connection instead, and get specific about what works offline . Integration sets the ceiling on everything else Your LMS is the front door to a stack that includes a student information system, a video platform, library discovery, proctoring, tutoring, e-portfolios, publisher courseware, and other tools. Whether those pieces work together comes down to standards. The short list worth writing into an RFP: LTI 1.3 and LTI Advantage , including Deep Linking, Names and Role Provisioning Services, and Assignment and Grade Services. SIS integration in both directions , enrollment and section data in, final grades out. Ask whether that's a supported connector, a flat-file import, or a services project with its own line item. OneRoster matters here too, if your SIS speaks it. Common Cartridge and QTI for content and assessment portability, which determine how expensive it is to leave a platform later. Caliper Analytics or an equivalent event stream, plus a documented REST API with published rate limits and single sign-on through SAML or OIDC. One move to start: 1EdTech publishes a public directory of certified products and applications to verify the integration features of edtech product. Ensuring accessibility for every student Roughly one in five undergraduates reports a disability, per the National Center for Education Statistics, and an LMS needs to work for those students just as much as anyone else. Section 508 and the ADA already applied, and the Department of Justice's April 2024 Title II rule set WCAG 2.1 Level AA as the standard for public colleges, with compliance deadlines in 2026 and 2027 depending on institution size. But the benefits go beyond compliance. Captions help students studying in a loud dorm or working in a second language, clear heading structure helps anyone skimming a module on a phone, and accessible design tends to be better design for everyone. Institutions that treat accessibility as a course-design habit and check on content as it’s built instead of after a complaint spend less time on remediation. One important distinction for accessibility in LMS conversations. Platform accessibility covers the interface the vendor builds: navigation, the gradebook, the quiz player, the mobile app. Content accessibility covers what faculty upload, which is where most real barriers come from. A platform can conform to WCAG and still host thousands of untagged PDFs, so the useful question is what the system does about the second problem, and whether it flags issues while an instructor is authoring, offers students alternate formats, and reports status at the course and department level so someone can act on it. Bring disability services into LMS conversations early and see what’s possible on any platform you’re considering. Put a screen reader on the platform, navigate a quiz with the keyboard only, and have a student who uses assistive technology submit an assignment from a phone. Find out more about navigating accessibility and inclusivity in higher education LMS platforms. Analytics that everyone can act on Every platform will show you a dashboard, but does the data work for everyone? Predictive analytics can help faculty and advisors identify at-risk students, which is an important retention tool, so learning analytics in the LMS need to be cross-functional and relevant across the institution. A few key features to think about to get better outcomes from LMS analytics. Data and timing. The underlying data is fairly consistent across vendors: participation and page views, submission timing, quiz item performance, grade trends, login gaps. That's enough to notice a student drifting in week three, which is early enough to matter. Flagging logic. Rules-based flags, like two missed assignments or no login in seven days, are transparent and easy to defend. Predictive models can catch more and carry more risk, so ask what the model was trained on, which variables it uses, whether prior-performance or demographic proxies are among them, and how the vendor tests for bias across student groups. Alert routing. A flag sitting in an instructor dashboard reaches one person who might be teaching 200 students that term. What you want to know is whether alerts reach advisors, push into your student success platform, create a case with an owner and a due date, and leave a record of whether the outreach actually happened. Find out more about the capabilities that make early alerting systems work . Support for mastery-based and self-paced programs Most systems are built around a course, a term, and a grade. In a competency-based program, a student moves forward by demonstrating a specific skill rather than by sitting through a set number of weeks. Not every LMS can be configured to handle both. Here’s how Design and assessment. A platform needs to hold competency definitions at the program level, attach performance standards to each one as a rubric with an explicit mastery threshold, and capture the range of evidence a program will accept as proof, whether it’s a written exam or a clinical observation or prior work experience. Timing. Non-term and self-paced structures are the norm in CBE, so the LMS needs to support enrollments with individual start and end dates, progression that triggers on demonstrated mastery instead of a calendar rollover, and an instructor view that shows progress instead of just due dates. Prior and portable learning . When a student arrives with a portfolio or an industry certification, the system should record it as evidence against a competency, with a named assessor and a date, in a form that survives an audit. The record should also be able to leave, so look at support for the Comprehensive Learner Record and Open Badges from 1EdTech if you want mastery data to travel with the student. Read more about how to build and scale competency-based education programs and flexible pathways. The evaluation table At a glance, here’s how to position your questions around specific LMS features and functions when starting conversations with a vendor. Criterion What to ask What a good answer sounds like Evidence to request Accessibility conformance What version and level does your ACR claim, when was it evaluated, and by whom? A specific standard, a date within the last 18 months, and a named evaluator The full ACR, not a summary page Integration architecture Do you support LTI 1.3 and all three LTI Advantage services? How are tool permissions scoped? Yes to all three services, with a described permission model and a stated position on legacy 1.1 1EdTech certification records; a written migration path Learning analytics Who receives the alert, and what happens next? Advisors and named staff roles, with the intervention described Documentation of the alert routing; subgroup error-rate reporting Competency-based pathways Can the gradebook express mastery? Can a program run on direct assessment? A described mastery model and named institutions running one Documentation of the credit-hour equivalency reporting Security and privacy What is the scope of the SOC 2 report, and who are the subprocessors? A scope statement naming systems, plus a current subprocessor list The report scope section; the subprocessor list in writing Course design tools What does onboarding look like for an adjunct hired three weeks out? A specific program with a time commitment attached Training materials; adoption data from a comparable institution Mobile and access equity What degrades on mobile, and what happens on a dropped connection? A candid list of limitations Documentation on confirmed offline capabilities See how these capabilities come together to support learning, teaching, and growth across your entire institution or find out why more schools choose Canvas as their higher ed LMS than any other. Frequently asked questions What features should a higher education LMS have? The criteria that come up consistently in institutional evaluations includ: accessibility conformance backed by a current ACR, LTI 1.3 integration with LTI Advantage services, learning analytics routed to advisors, support for competency-based and flexible pathways, documented security and privacy compliance, course design tools faculty are trained to use, and mobile access that matches the desktop experience. What is the difference between an LMS for K-12 and higher education? Higher education platforms have to handle credit-hour and direct assessment program structures, federal Title IV reporting requirements, faculty course ownership, and integration with an SIS that manages registration and degree audit. K-12 platforms are built around parent access, standards-aligned reporting, and district-level content control. Should an LMS support LTI 1.3? Yes. 1EdTech ended support for LTI 1.1 on June 30, 2022. LTI 1.3 changes how tools authenticate and how permissions are scoped, and the LTI Advantage services built on it cover roster provisioning, deep linking, and grade passback.

title: The Bridges We Haven't Built: Why Skills Still Can't Travel Between Education and…
intro: Explore why skills struggle to travel between education and employment with Sean Murphy from the Bipartisan Policy Center, and discover how to bridge the gap.

body.text: Learning means a lot of things, and plenty of it happens outside of a traditional classroom. Someone can teach themselves to fix a car from videos, run a volunteer project that demands more real management than a management course, or learn more from an internship than any class in their last semester. How much of that makes it to an academic record or is easily translated for an employer looking for those skills? Sean Murphy works in that gap. He's the director of workforce and post-secondary pathways at the Bipartisan Policy Center ; he came to it from a local workforce board placing veterans and justice-involved youth, staff jobs for a US senator and a governor, and corporate philanthropy at Walmart. Most people working on this problem talk about breaking down silos, but Sean thinks silos naturally occur in all systems. He says, "That's just the reality of people, right? And that's okay. We just need to figure out how do we build better bridges." The four parts of a talent system that works Sean's version of the system covers everything, meaning the public workforce system, education, and employers together over any one of them alone. It has four moving parts. Someone has to understand what the job demand actually is. The system has to recognize what skills people already have. It has to tell them clearly where their gaps are and how to fill them. It has to match them to opportunity. There’s not a single-partner solution for solving every part. Education has to be at the table. Employers have to be transparent, which means rewriting job descriptions so they spell out the tasks and skills a role actually requires. Then they have to articulate, either through industry associations or on their own, what they'll need in three to five years. Training providers carry a piece of it too. Any talent system built to last and serve everyone within it needs to sustain these four parts, even when disruption shows up, whether from a national shift due to innovation, a plant opening or closing in one town, or one person's career screeching to a halt due to layoffs. Running underneath all four is data. Why data built for compliance fails the people it's meant to serve "Data is not always sexy to most people," Sean said. "I get excited by it, but it's just not. It's the boring stuff behind the cool AI. It's the boring stuff behind big policy decisions." Most of the workforce data we have was built for compliance. It reports upward, feeding research and informing government decision-making, but it was never designed to serve the worker or the employer trying to use it. Sean saw that gap up close in the public workforce system, watching counselors do remarkable work with individuals while lacking the tools to reach more of them or to personalize what they offered. At Walmart, Sean sat on the data work group for the commission behind BPC's report, A Nation at Risk to a Nation at Work . He's proud of how much of the final report centers on data, and equally clear that the next round has to go deeper, specifically by putting workers and employers at the center of the data work, not just treating them as its subjects. There's also a discipline problem he runs into. "There's a lot of dialogue that I'm in where everyone just says, well, we need more data." His response is one question: for what? Until you can say who you're serving, what data serves them, and what tools can realistically produce it inside the systems you already have, more data isn't a plan. Nobody gets to turn off the lights on the old system and switch on a new one tomorrow, so any answer has to work inside what exists while it evolves and changes. What digital credentials still leave out Sean's senior year of college was, by his description, a dream. One quarter in DC interning for a US senator. One quarter in Olympia at the state legislature. One quarter abroad. His transcript says 15 credits a quarter. "It doesn't talk about really those internships. It doesn't really talk about what I learned in being abroad for a quarter," he said. "It doesn't tell an accurate story." The institution handed him the experiences that launched his career, then handed him a document that mentions none of them and left the explaining, the connecting the dots, to him. Digital badges were supposed to close that gap; a badge can carry a lot of information. In practice, Sean said, most carry three things: the name of the school, the name of the program, and the date you finished. This tends to mean that the value tracks the reputation of the institution rather than anything you learned while there. Sean has a couple of well-known schools on his own record and no complaints about them, but as he said, “just because I went there doesn't mean I know more than somebody else.” People tell him they're running a badging program. "First of all, it's not a badging program. A badge is merely the format in which you share the information. It's not the actual program. You can have a credential without a badge. You cannot have a badge without a credential." His test is whether the credential connects to anything. A badge has to flow into the systems where decisions get made: HR platforms for job applications, student information systems for admission to the next program, career navigation platforms, and state talent marketplaces people use to find work. Without that, he said, a digital badge is "really no different than the credential that you printed off and you put on your mom's fridge." That's the work he engaged in at Walmart starting in 2019, after the American Workforce Policy Advisory Board turned attention toward learning and employment records. The list of organizations he backed in his work managing grant portfolios runs long, including the US Chamber Foundation, 1EdTech, Credential Engine, the Competency-Based Education Network, and the Digital Credentials Consortium. Philanthropy could test ideas that government money can't. The catch, as he puts it, is that philanthropy struggles to spread what works, which is part of why he's back in policy . Why the skills-based hiring headlines outpaced the hiring For a while, the headlines were everywhere. Major employers were pulling degree requirements off job postings. Then the hiring practice came in well behind what the announcements implied. Sean's explanation is that a degree is a proxy for skills, and it's the one that's legally defensible. He pointed to a framing Society for Human Resource Management (SHRM) has used. Hire someone with a degree and they don't work out, and nobody blames you. Hire someone without one, on the strength of their skills, and they don't work out, and maybe that's on you. "We've got to realize that everyone's been skills-based forever," Sean said. Hiring has always been about skills. What's new is validated skills, and a wider set of proxies, from short-term credentials up through degrees, that can carry that validation. Degrees stay central, but what changes is everything around them; people are learning across more modalities, teaching themselves in ways that didn't exist a decade ago, learning on the job, and needing new skills more often as innovation picks up speed. Skills also can't be discussed generically across every part of hiring. The people doing workforce planning need to talk about them differently from the people doing the hiring, with real overlap between the two. Skills are "a language of learning, employment, and service." A way to communicate what you've learned so that it transfers to someone else. He is emphatic that this doesn't replace the degree, and equally emphatic that adopting it means real change management across every system involved, not just swapping one for another. The people in the middle BPC's goal is that every adult gets the skills and credentials they need, but “every adult” is a very different population from every 18-year-old. Here's how he describes where the money goes. We spend a lot preparing people to learn how to learn, across K-12 and post-secondary. We spend a decent amount on people who are out of work. Between those two states, he said, "we leave it up to chance for everybody in the middle." Everyone in that middle is left to explain for themselves what they can do, what they've done, and what they think they could do next. Some of that will always fall to the individual. But a lot gets lost in translation, and a lot of people never get connected to the right job or the right training when it would have mattered. His alternative is that institutions stay in the relationship. Some of that is direct teaching, online or in a classroom. Some of it is validating learning that happened somewhere else , like a volunteer project, and translating that into experience that an employer can defend It also opens post-secondary institutions to a new set of dollars, and Sean floated a version he clearly enjoys: instead of asking him for alumni money after he already paid a great deal of it, sell him a subscription to keep learning and to keep having his skills validated. What institutions can start now instead of waiting on legislation Federal legislation does not move quickly. So what does a registrar's office or a single CTE program do this semester? Sean's answer starts with the recognition that there’s no blueprint and no silver bullet. Some recommendations become federal legislation. Some become agency implementation. Some are simply things partners in the community can go do without waiting for anyone. He named places where the work is already happening. AACRAO has been pulling registrars together around data and comprehensive learning records. ACE is deep in credit for prior learning , an area where multiple organizations are working without shared definitions yet. Credential Engine is building out credential registries , which will need robust, collaborative data to work. Ten states have federal funding to build talent marketplaces, and others that weren't selected or didn't apply are building anyway, California among them . body.html:
Learning means a lot of things, and plenty of it happens outside of a traditional classroom. Someone can teach themselves to fix a car from videos, run a volunteer project that demands more real management than a management course, or learn more from an internship than any class in their last semester. How much of that makes it to an academic record or is easily translated for an employer looking for those skills?

Sean Murphy works in that gap. He's the director of workforce and post-secondary pathways at the Bipartisan Policy Center; he came to it from a local workforce board placing veterans and justice-involved youth, staff jobs for a US senator and a governor, and corporate philanthropy at Walmart. Most people working on this problem talk about breaking down silos, but Sean thinks silos naturally occur in all systems. He says, "That's just the reality of people, right? And that's okay. We just need to figure out how do we build better bridges."

The four parts of a talent system that works

Sean's version of the system covers everything, meaning the public workforce system, education, and employers together over any one of them alone. It has four moving parts.

  1. Someone has to understand what the job demand actually is. 
  2. The system has to recognize what skills people already have. 
  3. It has to tell them clearly where their gaps are and how to fill them. 
  4. It has to match them to opportunity.

There’s not a single-partner solution for solving every part. Education has to be at the table. Employers have to be transparent, which means rewriting job descriptions so they spell out the tasks and skills a role actually requires. Then they have to articulate, either through industry associations or on their own, what they'll need in three to five years. Training providers carry a piece of it too.

Any talent system built to last and serve everyone within it needs to sustain these four parts, even when disruption shows up, whether from a national shift due to innovation, a plant opening or closing in one town, or one person's career screeching to a halt due to layoffs. 

Running underneath all four is data. 

Why data built for compliance fails the people it's meant to serve

"Data is not always sexy to most people," Sean said. "I get excited by it, but it's just not. It's the boring stuff behind the cool AI. It's the boring stuff behind big policy decisions."

Most of the workforce data we have was built for compliance. It reports upward, feeding research and informing government decision-making, but it was never designed to serve the worker or the employer trying to use it. Sean saw that gap up close in the public workforce system, watching counselors do remarkable work with individuals while lacking the tools to reach more of them or to personalize what they offered.

At Walmart, Sean sat on the data work group for the commission behind BPC's report, A Nation at Risk to a Nation at Work. He's proud of how much of the final report centers on data, and equally clear that the next round has to go deeper, specifically by putting workers and employers at the center of the data work, not just treating them as its subjects.

There's also a discipline problem he runs into. "There's a lot of dialogue that I'm in where everyone just says, well, we need more data." His response is one question: for what? Until you can say who you're serving, what data serves them, and what tools can realistically produce it inside the systems you already have, more data isn't a plan. Nobody gets to turn off the lights on the old system and switch on a new one tomorrow, so any answer has to work inside what exists while it evolves and changes.

What digital credentials still leave out

Sean's senior year of college was, by his description, a dream. One quarter in DC interning for a US senator. One quarter in Olympia at the state legislature. One quarter abroad.

His transcript says 15 credits a quarter.

"It doesn't talk about really those internships. It doesn't really talk about what I learned in being abroad for a quarter," he said. "It doesn't tell an accurate story." The institution handed him the experiences that launched his career, then handed him a document that mentions none of them and left the explaining, the connecting the dots, to him.

Digital badges were supposed to close that gap; a badge can carry a lot of information. In practice, Sean said, most carry three things: the name of the school, the name of the program, and the date you finished. This tends to mean that the value tracks the reputation of the institution rather than anything you learned while there. Sean has a couple of well-known schools on his own record and no complaints about them, but as he said, “just because I went there doesn't mean I know more than somebody else.”

People tell him they're running a badging program. "First of all, it's not a badging program. A badge is merely the format in which you share the information. It's not the actual program. You can have a credential without a badge. You cannot have a badge without a credential."

His test is whether the credential connects to anything. A badge has to flow into the systems where decisions get made: HR platforms for job applications, student information systems for admission to the next program, career navigation platforms, and state talent marketplaces people use to find work. Without that, he said, a digital badge is "really no different than the credential that you printed off and you put on your mom's fridge."

That's the work he engaged in at Walmart starting in 2019, after the American Workforce Policy Advisory Board turned attention toward learning and employment records. The list of organizations he backed in his work managing grant portfolios runs long, including the US Chamber Foundation, 1EdTech, Credential Engine, the Competency-Based Education Network, and the Digital Credentials Consortium. Philanthropy could test ideas that government money can't. The catch, as he puts it, is that philanthropy struggles to spread what works, which is part of why he's back in policy.

Why the skills-based hiring headlines outpaced the hiring

For a while, the headlines were everywhere. Major employers were pulling degree requirements off job postings. Then the hiring practice came in well behind what the announcements implied.

Sean's explanation is that a degree is a proxy for skills, and it's the one that's legally defensible. He pointed to a framing Society for Human Resource Management (SHRM) has used. Hire someone with a degree and they don't work out, and nobody blames you. Hire someone without one, on the strength of their skills, and they don't work out, and maybe that's on you.

 "We've got to realize that everyone's been skills-based forever," Sean said. Hiring has always been about skills. What's new is validated skills, and a wider set of proxies, from short-term credentials up through degrees, that can carry that validation.

Degrees stay central, but what changes is everything around them; people are learning across more modalities, teaching themselves in ways that didn't exist a decade ago, learning on the job, and needing new skills more often as innovation picks up speed. Skills also can't be discussed generically across every part of hiring. The people doing workforce planning need to talk about them differently from the people doing the hiring, with real overlap between the two.

Skills are "a language of learning, employment, and service." A way to communicate what you've learned so that it transfers to someone else. He is emphatic that this doesn't replace the degree, and equally emphatic that adopting it means real change management across every system involved, not just swapping one for another.

The people in the middle

BPC's goal is that every adult gets the skills and credentials they need, but “every adult” is a very different population from every 18-year-old.

Here's how he describes where the money goes. We spend a lot preparing people to learn how to learn, across K-12 and post-secondary. We spend a decent amount on people who are out of work. Between those two states, he said, "we leave it up to chance for everybody in the middle." Everyone in that middle is left to explain for themselves what they can do, what they've done, and what they think they could do next.

Some of that will always fall to the individual. But a lot gets lost in translation, and a lot of people never get connected to the right job or the right training when it would have mattered.

His alternative is that institutions stay in the relationship. Some of that is direct teaching, online or in a classroom. Some of it is validating learning that happened somewhere else, like a volunteer project, and translating that into experience that an employer can defend 

It also opens post-secondary institutions to a new set of dollars, and Sean floated a version he clearly enjoys: instead of asking him for alumni money after he already paid a great deal of it, sell him a subscription to keep learning and to keep having his skills validated.

What institutions can start now instead of waiting on legislation

Federal legislation does not move quickly. So what does a registrar's office or a single CTE program do this semester?

Sean's answer starts with the recognition that there’s no blueprint and no silver bullet. Some recommendations become federal legislation. Some become agency implementation. Some are simply things partners in the community can go do without waiting for anyone.

He named places where the work is already happening. 

  • AACRAO has been pulling registrars together around data and comprehensive learning records. 
  • ACE is deep in credit for prior learning, an area where multiple organizations are working without shared definitions yet. 
  • Credential Engine is building out credential registries, which will need robust, collaborative data to work. 
  • Ten states have federal funding to build talent marketplaces, and others that weren't selected or didn't apply are building anyway, California among them.

But his advice for people who want to be involved in this work is just to start: look outward at who's already doing the work, then ask what you need to examine internally and build into your strategy. Who are the stakeholders inside your institution? This isn't the registrar's job alone.  Are you issuing digital records that carry a deeper, richer set of information about students? Are you doing it in a way that's interoperable across systems, using the right data standards? 

The politics of policy

Sean believes everyone in a leadership position wants to see people succeed, and that the real divisions in workforce policy run rural to urban and east to west at least as often as left to right. When something stalls, he thinks the cause is usually process rather than opposition.

He points to evidence like the short-term Pell passing after genuine party disagreement about how it should work. The MATCH Act was passed with overwhelming support from committee.

What moves things, he argues, is clarity. Know who you're serving. Say what problem you're solving. Back it with proven models where they exist and promising ones where they don't, then show the path from here to there.

title: Say Hello to Canvas Lite
intro: Free Canvas access is here for independent educators. Canvas Lite by Instructure lets you build a course, invite students, and start teaching right away.

body.text: Whether you're teaching homeschool, tutoring, running community workshops, or piloting a new course, Canvas Lite is for you. We know how much independent educators care about giving their students a great learning experience, and how frustrating it is when technical barriers get in the way. Canvas Lite gives you real, no-cost access to the Canvas platform, without waiting on IT setup or district approval. Build a course, invite students, and start teaching on the same platform schools, colleges, and universities around the world rely on every day. This feels a lot like Free for Teacher, and that's on purpose Free for Teacher was a hit because it handed individual educators something they rarely got: real access to Canvas, with zero procurement and zero red tape. Teachers didn't have to wait on a district decision to try a tool that actually worked for them and their students. Canvas Lite is the next phase of that idea. It's the same Canvas experience, but it comes with a few upgrades that reflect what we've learned from the original offering, including identity verification for every teacher who signs up (using a government-issued ID and a selfie, through our verification partner, Veriff) and its own dedicated domain, separate from the Canvas environments institutional customers use. Students invited into a course don't go through that verification step, so getting a class up and running still feels quick and simple. What's actually in Canvas Lite You're getting the tools teachers reach for the most, including: Building modules and pages with rich content Collecting file, text, and URL assignment submissions Running quizzes and applying rubrics SpeedGrader, with annotations, audio and video feedback, and grade exports Built-in messaging, discussions, and course announcements Course-level integrations with tools like Google Drive, Zoom, and Microsoft Teams The Canvas Teacher and Canvas Student mobile apps Where Canvas Lite fits alongside Canvas Think of Canvas Lite as a useful way for individual educators to sample the Canvas ecosystem: the tutor with a handful of students, the homeschool parent teaching a semester-long unit, the instructor looking for a more streamlined way to deliver a course before asking their institution to adopt it more broadly. It comes with a cap of 5 courses with 50 learners per course and a 500 MB storage limit per course. And if a teacher outgrows that or needs administrative features, AI tools, course analytics, attendance tracking, or API access tokens, we're happy to talk anytime about a full Canvas license. There's a nice side effect here too. As Melissa Loble, our chief learning officer, said: "A learner who works in Canvas Lite this year will recognize Canvas when they walk into a high school, a college or a training program down the road." That familiarity matters more than people give it credit for. Try it starting September 30 Canvas Lite goes live worldwide on September 30, 2026, at canvaslite.instructure.com. We'll publish self-serve guides and resources in the Instructure Community to help you get started. We built Canvas Lite because individual educators have been part of the Canvas story since the beginning, and we wanted a better way to keep showing up for them. If that's you, we'd love for you to give it a try. Learn more when canvaslite.instructure.com goes live later this month!

title: Five Qualities to Look for in a K–12 Records Platform
intro: Choosing a K–12 student records platform? See the five qualities that separate systems built for districts from document tools stretched to fit schools.

body.text: You've made the call that paper records have to go. Whether you got here from a near-miss deadline, too many afternoons spent hunting for a specific record, or it’s time to protect records from potential physical harm, the question you face has changed. Now, it's, “What do we replace paper with ?” Not every records platform is built for the K–12 space. Plenty started as higher education tools or general document storage, then got stretched to fit schools that run on state compliance rules and graduation timelines. But why swap paper problems for software problems? Before you book a demo, it helps to know how to identify a records platform built for your context. Let’s look at five qualities that matter most, and what each reveals about a system. Start with what the research says to prioritize A good checklist grounds itself in what districts actually experience once they switch to digital records. So before we get to what to look for, it's worth knowing where they come from. In spring 2025, 278 K–12 administrators across 208 institutions were interviewed and revealed a pattern that mattered most for records offices: time, and how much of it a modern system hands back. Among districts using records management tools, over half (54%) of K–12 Cumulative Folders users said they saved a lot or a great deal of time just locating student records. Nearly two-thirds (62%) of Document Management users reported the same when pulling alumni or staff files. Diploma Services told a similar story, as 52% of users saved significant time issuing diplomas, and only 9% saw no savings at all. Note that consistency. Across record types, administrators kept reporting that the right platform gives staff their hours back. That's the lens for the following qualities. The five qualities that matter Each quality comes with the question to put to any vendor, and the proof that Parchment clears the bar. 1. Speed and turnaround How fast does a request reach the requester? A modern records platform turns around requests in minutes, and confirms delivery. Districts that have switched already see it, like United Independent School District in Texas. UISD went from a two week window to fulfilling requests in two minutes. 2. Value and ROI Modernizing should pay for itself in numbers you can put in a budget line. Ask what a district actually saves when it switches. Columbus City Schools saved more than $28,000 after moving to Parchment—over $16,000 in postage and $12,000 in printing and copying. 3. Scale and reliability Just because a tool works for one school in a pilot doesn’t mean it’ll work for an entire district. Ask for example districts that are close to your size. For example, Columbus manages records for 46,000 students across 113 schools on a single system. If a platform can’t work at scale, you'll feel it in peak seasons. 4. Built for K-12 Plenty of platforms handle documents; far fewer are built for K–12. Ask whether a system knows your specific rules, like compliance with state requirements like Ohio's three-business-day response window. And if you’re a charter or virtual, what kind of experience and support do they offer? It should also protect what's already on file, like FERPA-compliant policies, SOC 2 Type II certifications, and audit logs that show who accessed a record and when. If a records room holds decades of paper, the right platform has a path for that too, including legacy formats like microfiche and microfilm, with the option to shred or return the originals after they're digitized. 5. Reach and delivery A digitized record is good, but it still has to reach the college, employer, or agency that asked for it. Ask a vendor how far their network reaches, and whether you get confirmation of delivery. Parchment connects districts with over 6,100 higher-education institutions and 7,300 receivers, then confirms delivery so you know when the transcript arrives. Questions to ask vendors Here’s how to turn those qualities into questions for your next demo. Quality Question to ask Speed What's your average turnaround on a records request, and how does the requester know it was delivered? Value What do districts my size typically save on postage, printing, and staff hours in the first year? Scale Can one system run every school we have, and what happens to turnaround during our busiest weeks? K–12 fit How do you meet our state's compliance rules, and do you support charters and virtual programs the same way you support traditional schools? Reach How many receiving institutions are in your network, and how does my office confirm a record was delivered? If a vendor answers those with real numbers and named districts, you're probably looking at a platform built for the job. Vague answers, on the other hand, tell you something, too. For a full evaluation framework, including the questions that get into contracts and data migration, check out our guide to choosing a K-12 records and lifecycle platform .

title: Scaling Healthcare Training: Moving Beyond Completion Records Without Admin Burden
intro: Healthcare accreditors want proof of clinical competency, not just attendance. Discover how to streamline documentation and scale training without the growing administrative burden.

body.text: More often, health systems and accreditors are asking healthcare training academies what their programs produced. Not just how many people are completing training, but what competencies the trainings are producing. Joint Commission standard HR.01.06.01 requires hospitals to document staff competence during orientation and reassess it at least once every three years, with the assessment done by someone qualified in the skill under review. Every program a hospital buys either adds to that record or leaves the hospital to build it again in-house. What it costs an academy When a healthcare system asks a training academy what its programs produced, the academy sends completion records, because that's the easiest and fastest thing to pull together and report on. The buyer walks into a contract review holding a list of finished courses, and she makes the case for renewal with what she has. To produce a fuller record that not just attendance but clinical ability takes time and resources, usually pulling it away from something else. Staff spend the weeks before a review pulling records, and that time comes out of program development. Each new placement site, state, or contract adds admin work, and that work grows faster than revenue. An academy that can produce that evidence on request has something to sell that most of its competitors can't put together. Why the evidence is hard to produce The Accreditation Council for Continuing Medical Education (ACCME) asks accredited continuing medical education providers to report what each activity measured . An activity is any educational offering: a course, a conference session, a webinar, a simulation, or a journal-based program. Here is the 2025 picture across all 242,511 of them. What the activity measured (light) Outcome measured Activities Share Learner competence 231,122 95% Learner knowledge 180,326 74% Learner performance 94,861 39% Patient health 29,217 12% Community or population health 17,378 7% Nearly every activity measures competence. Fewer than four in 10 measure what the learner did afterward in practice, and about one in eight reaches patient health. But those three words — knowledge, competence, performance — get used interchangeably, and they mean different things. Knowledge is what a clinician can recall. Competence is what she can demonstrate in a controlled setting. Performance is what she does back on the unit. In clinical training, those happen in different buildings owned by different organizations. A nurse completes a central line dressing change correctly in a skills lab. She has demonstrated competence, in a room the academy runs, and an instructor the academy employs scored her doing it. Whether she does it the same way on a night shift eight weeks later is performance, and it happens in a hospital. The evidence exists. Somebody just has to capture it while it's happening. The preceptor is the way in. Placement-site preceptors already watch learners work inside the hospital, so an academy that gives them a fast way to score what they see gets performance evidence added to the record. Overall, one learner record has to hold things that arrive from four directions. A clinical instructor scores a skills check-off in the lab. A preceptor at a placement site, who works for someone else, writes an evaluation. An exam returns a result. A state board or certifying body asks about a credential months later. At every one of those handoffs, somebody moves data between systems, matches it against a roster, and keeps it attached to the right person. An academy solves that by deciding what to capture, capturing it where the learner already is, and keeping it in one record. A report somebody builds at the end can only show what they managed to collect. Who carries the work In Training magazine's 2025 Training Industry Report , 41% of respondents named lack of resources or personnel as their single biggest training challenge. The accredited provider population is shrinking at the same time. The number of accredited CME providers has fallen 37% since 2006, from 2,413 down to 1,518, and the count has dropped every year in between. Those 1,518 organizations still delivered all the learning activities in 2025. Whatever documentation each activity requires, there are fewer overall trainers, practitioners, and organizations producing all of it. This all shapes what buyers want. In a 2021 study of 398 hospitals and health systems, the Association for Nursing Professional Development found a median of one nursing professional development practitioner for every 70 registered nurses. That practitioner is responsible for competency documentation across all 70. Training that arrives with the evidence attached saves her work. Training that arrives as a completion list makes more of it. Healthcare training grows in ways that each add records to keep: A new clinical placement site means a new set of preceptors submitting evaluations. A new state means a different set of continuing education requirements to track against. A new health system contract usually means the agreement includes quarterly reporting. Every one of those means somebody collects and reconciles another set of records. How Canvas Career handles it Most platforms can store completions, but can’t always carry competence evidence Canvas Career by Instructure is a skills-based learning platform for adult learners and continuing education. The problem / What Canvas Career does (light) The problem What Canvas Career does Evidence arrives from a lab, a preceptor, an exam, and a credential body, and lands in four places Progress tracks against skills, so a scored demonstration and a finished module sit in the same learner record Somebody builds the buyer's report manually The admin dashboard shows engagement and skill data live, with drill-down by learner, cohort, or program Every instructor and every site runs the program a little differently Role-based pathways define the program once, so every cohort gets the same thing A protocol changes and somebody rebuilds the content IgniteAI can help draft lessons, modules, and assessments, so a change becomes a revision Rosters drift apart between systems Integrations can run to HRIS and CRM systems Find out more about Canvas Career by Instructure, a skills-based LMS for workforce and continuing education, and see how healthcare training academies run credentialed programs on one platform.

More often, health systems and accreditors are asking healthcare training academies what their programs produced. Not just how many people are completing training, but what competencies the trainings are producing. 

Joint Commission standard HR.01.06.01 requires hospitals to document staff competence during orientation and reassess it at least once every three years, with the assessment done by someone qualified in the skill under review. Every program a hospital buys either adds to that record or leaves the hospital to build it again in-house.

What it costs an academy

When a healthcare system asks a training academy what its programs produced, the academy sends completion records, because that's the easiest and fastest thing to pull together and report on. The buyer walks into a contract review holding a list of finished courses, and she makes the case for renewal with what she has.

To produce a fuller record that not just attendance but clinical ability takes time and resources, usually pulling it away from something else. Staff spend the weeks before a review pulling records, and that time comes out of program development. Each new placement site, state, or contract adds admin work, and that work grows faster than revenue. 

An academy that can produce that evidence on request has something to sell that most of its competitors can't put together.

Why the evidence is hard to produce

The Accreditation Council for Continuing Medical Education (ACCME) asks accredited continuing medical education providers to report what each activity measured. An activity is any educational offering: a course, a conference session, a webinar, a simulation, or a journal-based program. Here is the 2025 picture across all 242,511 of them. What the activity measured (light) 

Outcome measured

Activities

Share

Learner competence

231,122

95%

Learner knowledge

180,326

74%

Learner performance

94,861

39%

Patient health

29,217

12%

Community or population health

17,378

7%

 

Nearly every activity measures competence. Fewer than four in 10 measure what the learner did afterward in practice, and about one in eight reaches patient health.

But those three words — knowledge, competence, performance —  get used interchangeably, and they mean different things. Knowledge is what a clinician can recall. Competence is what she can demonstrate in a controlled setting. Performance is what she does back on the unit.

In clinical training, those happen in different buildings owned by different organizations. A nurse completes a central line dressing change correctly in a skills lab. She has demonstrated competence, in a room the academy runs, and an instructor the academy employs scored her doing it. Whether she does it the same way on a night shift eight weeks later is performance, and it happens in a hospital. The evidence exists. Somebody just has to capture it while it's happening.

The preceptor is the way in. Placement-site preceptors already watch learners work inside the hospital, so an academy that gives them a fast way to score what they see gets performance evidence added to the record. 

Overall, one learner record has to hold things that arrive from four directions. 

  1. A clinical instructor scores a skills check-off in the lab. 
  2. A preceptor at a placement site, who works for someone else, writes an evaluation. 
  3. An exam returns a result. 
  4. A state board or certifying body asks about a credential months later.

At every one of those handoffs, somebody moves data between systems, matches it against a roster, and keeps it attached to the right person. An academy solves that by deciding what to capture, capturing it where the learner already is, and keeping it in one record. A report somebody builds at the end can only show what they managed to collect.

Who carries the work

In Training magazine's 2025 Training Industry Report, 41% of respondents named lack of resources or personnel as their single biggest training challenge. The accredited provider population is shrinking at the same time. The number of accredited CME providers has fallen 37% since 2006, from 2,413 down to 1,518, and the count has dropped every year in between. Those 1,518 organizations still delivered all the learning activities in 2025. Whatever documentation each activity requires, there are fewer overall trainers, practitioners, and organizations producing all of it.

This all shapes what buyers want. In a 2021 study of 398 hospitals and health systems, the Association for Nursing Professional Development found a median of one nursing professional development practitioner for every 70 registered nurses. That practitioner is responsible for competency documentation across all 70. Training that arrives with the evidence attached saves her work. Training that arrives as a completion list makes more of it.

Healthcare training grows in ways that each add records to keep:

  • A new clinical placement site means a new set of preceptors submitting evaluations. 
  • A new state means a different set of continuing education requirements to track against. 
  • A new health system contract usually means the agreement includes quarterly reporting.

Every one of those means somebody collects and reconciles another set of records.

How Canvas Career handles it

Most platforms can store completions, but can’t always carry competence evidence Canvas Career by Instructure is a skills-based learning platform for adult learners and continuing education. The problem / What Canvas Career does (light) 

The problem

What Canvas Career does

Progress tracks against skills, so a scored demonstration and a finished module sit in the same learner record

Somebody builds the buyer's report manually

Find out more about Canvas Career by Instructure, a skills-based LMS for workforce and continuing education, and see how healthcare training academies run credentialed programs on one platform.

title: Designing for Every Learner: Accessibility and Inclusivity in Higher Education LMS Platforms
intro: Navigate accessibility and inclusivity in higher ed LMS platforms. Learn how to meet ADA Title II compliance and prioritize inclusive design for all students.

body.text: Frostburg State University has two people in its Instructional Design and Technology department. Between them, they support hundreds of courses. Rita M. Thomas, Ed.D. manages the department and spoke about accessibility work in higher education at the most recent InstructureCon: "Faculty and staff are expected to produce accessible content ... but they usually build and revise that content outside business hours, when our central accessibility office is offline." Her response was to build a custom AI assistant, grounded only in sources Frostburg State already endorses (not the open internet), that answers faculty questions about alt text, heading structure, color contrast, and accessible tables whenever questions come up. It walks users through remediation in Word, PowerPoint, PDF, and Canvas by Instructure, explains why each recommendation exists by tying it back to Universal Design for Learning and the Quality Matters rubric, and hands off to a human instructional designer when a question falls outside its scope. Every institution has an obligation to accessibility, but the work falls to every instructor who uploads a PDF, and the support model most campuses have was built for a smaller volume of content than they now produce. The deadline moved by a year On April 20, 2026, the Department of Justice published an interim final rule pushing back the compliance dates in its ADA Title II web accessibility rule. Public entities serving populations of 50,000 or more now have until April 26, 2027. What did not change is the standard itself. WCAG 2.1 Level AA still applies to websites, mobile apps, and digital course materials, and every underlying ADA obligation stayed in force. The extension bought schools time, but didn’t change any of the work required . Unfortunately, progress has been well under where it should be. WebAIM tested the top one million home pages in 2026 and found detectable WCAG failures on 95.9% of them, up from 94.8% the year before, which reversed six straight years of slow improvement. The average page carried 56.1 errors, a 10 percent jump in 12 months. Six failure types account for 96% of everything detected: low contrast text, missing image alt text, missing form labels, empty links, empty buttons, and missing document language. Education sites performed better than average at 48.9 errors per page, which is still lagging behind where it should be. There is no average student Regulatory pressure explains why higher education needs to prioritize accessibility, but not what good design looks like once you're doing it. Aimee Stork of Joni and Friends, while speaking about designing for neurodiversity, put the design problem this way: "For decades, design and education have chased the ghost of the 'average user.' We build interfaces, write curricula, and create digital modules for a mythical, standardized mind that simply does not exist in nature." Her framing moves the conversation past compliance checkboxes and into interface decisions. Stork describes the first thing a neurodivergent student meets in an unfamiliar course as structural anxiety: "They are asking themselves, Where am I? What is expected of me? How do I navigate this?" A course with unpredictable navigation charges every student a tax before any learning happens. "When a user doesn't have to waste finite mental energy trying to decode the interface, they can dedicate 100% of their cognitive capacity to processing the actual content." That principle produces concrete design choices: Clear module organization and learning objectives stated upfront. A spiral structure that reintroduces foundational concepts at predictable intervals instead of sealing each topic in its own box. Accordions, expanding tabs, and flip cards so students unpack dense material at their own pace rather than facing a wall of text. Interactive transcripts that run alongside video, synchronized and clickable, so a student can read, listen, or jump to a timestamp. Designed for some students, used by most Students with disabilities don’t make up the majority of students, but the majority of students benefit from accessibility features. In 2019–20, 21% of undergraduates and 11% of postbaccalaureate students reported having a disability , according to the National Center for Education Statistics. An Oregon State University Ecampus Research Unit study surveyed 2,124 students across 15 public and private universities. Among students who used captions, 98.6% found them helpful. Across all respondents, 75% used captions as a study aid in both face-to-face and online classes, and 85% used transcripts the same way. Only 13% of those respondents had registered with disability services, but reported ways that accessibility features like captions helped them, including with focus, retaining information, and getting past bad audio. This is the whole case for building an inclusive learning management system rather than a compliant one. If your accessibility strategy activates only when a student files paperwork, it reaches a small fraction of the students who benefit. Stork's notes, "What is necessary for some is often beneficial for all." What to look for in an accessible LMS Platform capability sets the ceiling on what any instructional designer can accomplish. These four questions can help you build an accessibility program and meet the federal deadline. Ask for the Voluntary Product Accessibility Template. Canvas documents conformance against W3C Web Accessibility Initiative guidance, Section 508, EN 301 549, and WCAG in its VPAT, and Instructure has published its ongoing work toward full WCAG 2.1 AA conformance in areas including color contrast, ARIA roles, focus handling, and keyboard operability. Ask which screen readers get tested and how often . Canvas testing covers JAWS, NVDA, VoiceOver, and TalkBack across supported browser combinations. Ask what authors get at the point of creation . The Canvas Rich Content Editor includes an accessibility checker that catches common errors, along with alt text fields, caption management for video, and table header designation. Checking at authoring time is what keeps remediation from becoming a semester-end project. Ask what students can change themselves. In Canvas, that includes a high contrast interface setting, underlined links, keyboard shortcuts throughout, an agenda list view of the calendar, font sizing that survives browser zoom, and the option to turn off alert timeouts and animations. Institutions can also enable the Microsoft Immersive Reader button, which strips visual distraction, adjusts spacing and fonts, isolates lines of text, and reads content aloud. Accessibility is more than just a document you produce for auditors. Our guide, Accessibility in Higher Education: Building a Better Student Experience , covers Universal Design for Learning in course design, the platform features that carry the most weight, and how to set institutional standards faculty will follow. Get the guide here . Frequently asked questions What makes an LMS accessible? Two things have to be true at once. The platform must conform to WCAG 2.1 Level AA, documented in a current Accessibility Conformance Report. The course content built inside it must also meet the standard, which is the institution's responsibility rather than the vendor's. What is WCAG 2.1 Level AA? WCAG 2.1 is the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines version incorporated by the Department of Justice ADA Title II rule. Level AA is the middle of three conformance levels and the one used as the legal benchmark in US enforcement. What changed in WCAG 2.2? WCAG 2.2 became a W3C Recommendation on October 5, 2023, revised December 12, 2024. It adds nine success criteria and removes one, 4.1.1 Parsing. Four of the nine additions are Level AA: Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), Dragging Movements, Target Size (Minimum), and Accessible Authentication (Minimum). What is the difference between a VPAT and an ACR? A VPAT is the blank template published by the Information Technology Industry Council. An Accessibility Conformance Report is the completed document containing actual evaluation results. Who is responsible for accessibility in online courses? In a 2025 survey of 78 US educators published in Open Praxis , 50.67% named faculty, 36% said faculty and staff share responsibility, 9.33% named distance education staff, 2.67% disability resources, and 1.33% IT. Legally, the obligation sits with the institution.
