title: Breaking Up With Paper Records Is Easier Than You Think
intro: Paperless student records cut transcript turnaround from weeks to minutes. See how four districts made the switch, one process at a time.

body.text: If people loved paper records, you’d hear registrars defending the filing cabinet like it’s their favorite coffee order. But they don't. Ask any records office why they haven't switched, and you'll usually get something along the lines of “It's not that paper works better, but the switch feels like a project nobody has time to start.” Change is hard. And when your records system touches everything from transcripts to transfers and graduation, ripping it out and replacing it can understandably sound like a six-month nightmare IT initiative no one has the capacity for. But take heart, because plenty of districts have already made the switch. And they didn't do it as one sweeping change. They did it one process at a time, and most of them were surprised by how quickly the "after" showed up. So let's look at a paper vs. paperless day and a few stories from those who broke up with paper. A day with paper vs. a day without it In the past, someone called or emailed asking for a transcript. You write it down, then walk to the records room. You find the right drawer, then the right folder, then the right year. You pull the file, make a copy, stick it in an envelope, and mail it. Now, picture the same request at a district that broke up with paper. It comes online. You verify it, click send, and it's confirmed delivered, often in minutes. Notice what's missing from the second version? There’s not a huge learning curve with the new system. No extra software stacked on top of the old way of doing things. Just less standing between the request and the record. Here's what it looked like for four districts that already made the switch. The break-up can be faster than you'd think Start with United Independent School District in Texas. A turnaround that used to take two weeks now takes two minutes. Joe Almazan, their Director of Admissions, tells the story of an alumnus who needed his transcript late one night to hit a midnight college application deadline. Almazan went into the office, pulled it up, and sent it. That could never happen in a paper-bound process. Helena Public Schools in Montana saw a similar jump. A record that once took up to three weeks now sends in about 10 minutes. Students use a self-serve station and get confirmation that their transcript went out, and staff can see when a university actually downloads the file. Not wondering whether it arrived sounds pretty nice. Virtual Learning Academy Charter School in New Hampshire went digital with diplomas. The team estimates they save 90% of the time they used to spend on manual issuance. Kristin Jones, a program assistant there, said, "What used to take me 30 minutes now takes me one minute." (Worth noting this works for charters and virtual schools too, not just traditional districts!) Then there's Durham Public Schools in North Carolina, running records across 53 campuses. Schools verify and send the same day now. As their records team describes it, once a request is verified, they can upload and send the records right away. Four districts and schools of different sizes in different states show this isn't a fluke that worked once under perfect conditions. It's what happens when you take the paper out of the process. (Insert your favorite break-up song here.) Signs you're ready to move on Not one of those districts fixed everything at once. They picked one painful process, moved it, and built from there. So before you picture a huge rollout, run through a shorter list first. Here’s a quick checklist to help you get started—pick one or all to gather different data points and help start your internal conversations. Name your most painful record type. Which one generates the most calls or scrambles? ☐ Count a month’s worth of requests. Tally them for 30 days. Most offices are surprised by how fast the number climbs once they actually look. ☐ Map who touches a record. From the moment a request comes in to the moment it's delivered, how many hands and how many steps are involved? ☐ Pick one process to move first. The district stories all started with a single win. ☐ Set a "confirmed sent" standard. Decide what "done" should look like, like a delivery confirmation. ☐ If you worked through that list and already have a process in mind, you're more ready than you think. You can’t start with a master plan of changing a dozen processes. Instead, build a better way for one process, learn along the way, and keep building. You don't have to figure it out alone Every district that breaks up with paper starts with a records room, a stack of requests, an overwhelmed staff, and the nagging sense that there had to be a better way. Modernizing records isn't a do-it-yourself gamble where you're inventing the map as you go. It's a route plenty of schools have already walked, which means the potholes are marked, and the shortcuts are known. You get to learn from what worked at Helena, Durham, VLACS, and United ISD (and so many more), instead of guessing. Students get transcripts faster. And your staff get hours back to focus on bigger and better initiatives. Maybe this break-up wouldn’t be as messy as you think. If it’s time to get into the details, check out what to look for in a records management platform .

title: The Digital Skills Exchange: The Alchemy of Turning Skills into Opportunities
intro: Money can now flow into skills, and skills into money. See why individual learning wallets are the biggest shift in education finance in years.

body.text: Across half a dozen jurisdictions, governments are quietly converging on a new financial instrument. The names vary. Singapore calls it SkillsFuture. France calls it the Compete Personnel de Formation, the UK calls it the Lifelong Learning Entitlement, and the US, as of May 2026, calls it a Skill Savings Account. The mechanics differ, the architecture doesn’t. Each one puts money into an individual wallet that can only be spent on learning. That sounds technical. It’s the most interesting shift in education finance in a generation. To see why, look again at the wallet. The standard description is too small. A wallet is storage. A safer place for degrees, badges, and certifications. That misses what’s happening on the other side of it. Medieval alchemists chased a philosopher’s stone, a substance that could turn one thing into another. The credentials and skills field works on similar conversions: credentials into opportunities, skills into jobs, policy into tools, incentives into outcomes. Wallets are where these conversions happen, or fail to. A folder doesn’t do conversions. A conversion engine does. Two currencies, one floor There are two currencies in play here. Skills are one. Dollars, pounds, and euros are the other. Most of working life is spent converting between them, and most of education policy is about making that conversion easier. The wallet is becoming the foreign-exchange desk where the conversion happens, in both directions. The first direction is familiar. Skills become credentials, credentials open jobs, and jobs pay salaries. Drawn as an arrow: Skills → Credentials → Job → Salary. What’s new is the second direction. The policy instruments listed above all do one quietly radical thing. They drop cash, or cash-like credits, into a person’s wallet, ring-fenced for learning. Across half a dozen jurisdictions, governments are quietly converging on a new financial instrument. The names vary. Singapore calls it SkillsFuture. France calls it the Compete Personnel de Formation, the UK calls it the Lifelong Learning Entitlement, and the US, as of May 2026, calls it a Skill Savings Account. The mechanics differ, the architecture doesn’t. Each one puts money into an individual wallet that can only be spent on learning.

That sounds technical. It’s the most interesting shift in education finance in a generation.

To see why, look again at the wallet. The standard description is too small. A wallet is storage. A safer place for degrees, badges, and certifications. That misses what’s happening on the other side of it.

Medieval alchemists chased a philosopher’s stone, a substance that could turn one thing into another. The credentials and skills field works on similar conversions: credentials into opportunities, skills into jobs, policy into tools, incentives into outcomes. Wallets are where these conversions happen, or fail to.

A folder doesn’t do conversions. A conversion engine does.

 

Two currencies, one floor

There are two currencies in play here. Skills are one. Dollars, pounds, and euros are the other. Most of working life is spent converting between them, and most of education policy is about making that conversion easier. The wallet is becoming the foreign-exchange desk where the conversion happens, in both directions.

The first direction is familiar. Skills become credentials, credentials open jobs, and jobs pay salaries. Drawn as an arrow:

Skills → Credentials → Job → Salary.

What’s new is the second direction. The policy instruments listed above all do one quietly radical thing. They drop cash, or cash-like credits, into a person’s wallet, ring-fenced for learning. They let people turn money back into skills.

Cash → Wallet → Learning → Skills.

Run both arrows at once, and the wallet looks less like a folder and more like a trading floor. That’s a Skills Exchange. Not a new platform. A marketplace where these two currencies trade against each other continuously over a working life.

 

What the new instruments actually do

The instruments differ in their mechanics. The architecture is shared.

SkillsFuture in Singapore deposits state credits into citizen accounts, renewed periodically. France’s CPF accrues euros over time worked, drawable for accredited learning. The UK’s Lifelong Learning Entitlement gives publicly funded learners a four-year tuition account they can spend across providers and modules. The US version takes a different route. Introduced in May 2026 as the Skill Savings Account Act, it’s a tax-advantaged savings vehicle: employees can contribute up to $10,000 pre-tax annually, employers up to $5,250, and qualified education withdrawals are tax-free.

Different vehicles, one shared logic. Each creates a pool of capital that an individual controls and spends on learning over time.

In financial terms, these are liquidity injections into a market that didn’t have much of one. Front-loaded public investment at age 18 doesn’t move. Credits in a wallet, available across a 50-year working life, do.

 

The market problem

A new currency invites the usual problems. Fraud, mis-selling, hype. Skills are no exception. The Netherlands learned this when its Individual Learning Account scheme collapsed under headlines about wine-tasting courses and tourist experiences sold as training.

The regulatory reflex is familiar. Narrow eligibility, pre-approve content, and ration learner choice. Some of that discipline is sensible when public money or tax-favored dollars are involved. The risk on the other side is also real: a Skills Exchange that’s legally lifelong but practically still operates on the old one-shot, one-format, one-path logic.

The design question is how to trust learners with more agency without abandoning them to pure commercial logic. That requires information about outcomes, not just inputs. It requires quality assurance that’s substantive rather than cosmetic. And it requires a definition of value that runs longer than next month’s wage uplift. Left to platforms and employer data alone, that definition will collapse to short-term ROI. Established institutions are among the few actors with the standing to argue for something richer, provided they’re willing to name, assess, and stand behind what richer means.

 

What this means for education institutions

Education institutions have spent decades operating as credential issuers. They mint the currency, others decide what it’s worth.

On an exchange, that role inverts. Credentials start behaving like assets. They get bought, held, combined, and sometimes ignored. The institution stops being the floor and becomes one of many actors trading on someone else’s.

When a learner can point LLE funding, a Skill Savings Account balance, or SkillsFuture credit at a university, a college, a private provider, or an online platform, the established institution is no longer the default choice. Habit and history don’t carry on an exchange floor. Visible value does.

One is legibility. Institutional offerings have to fit the new units of trade. Smaller chunks of capability that can be stacked and recombined, priced, and compared against alternatives. The three-year degree remains one product among many. It’s no longer the unit of account.

The other is evidence. A wallet-funded learner shopping between a module, a micro-credential, and a master’s needs more than brand reputation to decide. There has to be traceable proof that the offering moves people into better work or broader capability. Without that, the exchange will price the offering on its cover.

The floor is tilting and a new digital alchemy for recognition is taking shape.

The wallet is the conversion engine. Money and skills move in both directions through it. SkillsFuture, the CPF, the LLE, the US Skill Savings Account, and the others coming behind them are pumping liquidity onto the floor. Providers compete, or collaborate, to turn that liquidity into capability.

The medieval alchemists chased lead into gold. They never found their stone. The conversion worth chasing was always learning into opportunities. That stone might just be a digital wallet.

title: Competency-Based Education and Flexible Pathways: What They Require From Your LMS
intro: Explore the benefits of competency-based education for adult learners and discover the essential LMS features needed to support flexible learning pathways.

title: Is Your District’s Relationship with Paper Records Getting Complicated?
intro: Paper records slow down transcript requests, drain staff time, and put decades of student history at risk. See why registrars are breaking up with paper.

body.text: If registrars had a relationship status with paper, most would probably describe it as, “ It's complicated. ” An anxious parent calls fifteen minutes before you lock up. Her son has a job offer that expires Monday, and the employer needs his final transcript today. You pull up the request—not with a digital record to check, just your own memory of where things live. This file predates the current system, so it's in the records room, in a banker's box, filed by graduation year rather than name. Twenty minutes later, you're back at your desk. You found the transcript, stamped it, and faxed it over. Does the system work? Only because it depends on your memory, time, and occasionally staying late or improvising. Maybe you haven’t faced this exact scenario, but the time searching for physical files adds up. Staff locate, copy, and fax transcripts or forms, and demand grows during peak seasons. Alumni wait days for a transcript, and families call to check in on the progress of their request. There’s got to be a better way. (Spoiler: there is.) You're not alone If your registrar's office runs on paper, you're the rule rather than the exception. Legacy systems are tough to leave behind. Staff work at capacity, and for some districts and schools, the idea of overhauling long-standing processes halts conversations about digitizing records. Sixty-eight percent of registrars say they manage records on paper always or often. And yet, because only 48% of non-registrars think that's true. That's a 20-point gap for two people to disagree over the same job. It can feel like leadership doesn't care, but they're not the ones scrambling in the records room fifteen minutes before it’s time to go home, so they don’t always know. When your team works from two different perspectives on how inefficient a process is, things are bound to get complicated. Stacks of records and costs you can’t count The relationship doesn't stay contained to transcript requests. We have to go back to day one of a student’s time in your institution. Thirty-eight percent of districts say enrollment is often or always paper-based. Before a student has sat down in a new classroom, office staff have stacks of forms to get into three different systems. From there, every request is its own manual hunt of finding the file, printing it, mailing it, logging it, etc. Do that a hundred times a semester, and you've got a part-time job nobody budgeted for. And some of it never even gets used. One district printed more than 15,000 transcripts in a year, and a good chunk were never picked up. Paper piles up with too little of it moving fast enough when someone needs it, and then too much of it sitting there when nobody does. Where paper shows up What it costs you Transcripts Each one means a manual hunt. You find the file, print it, mail it, and log it. Printing You print hundreds or thousands of records—how many aren’t even picked up? Staff time The budget doesn’t account for time, but tasks get pushed back when you’re physically managing records. Families and alumni A transcript that takes days instead of minutes can mean a missed deadline or blocked opportunity. Physical risk A fire or natural disaster can wipe out decades of records. Nobody line-items "staff time spent hunting for a file." But it's there, buried in every other task that got pushed to next week because paper ate the afternoon. Families and alumni feel it when a transcript that takes days instead of minutes can mean a missed deadline or a stalled application. And there's the risk that physical records face. One fire or natural disaster can wipe out decades of records. Let’s un-complicate this, shall we? Paper records feel familiar, but they bring complications, many of which aren’t necessary in a digital world. Is it time to redefine the relationship? Find out if paper records are holding your district back and see how you can break up with paper with our quick and free quiz !

Maybe you haven’t faced this exact scenario, but the time searching for physical files adds up. Staff locate, copy, and fax transcripts or forms, and demand grows during peak seasons. Alumni wait days for a transcript, and families call to check in on the progress of their request.

There’s got to be a better way. (Spoiler: there is.)

 

You're not alone

If your registrar's office runs on paper, you're the rule rather than the exception. Legacy systems are tough to leave behind. Staff work at capacity, and for some districts and schools, the idea of overhauling long-standing processes halts conversations about digitizing records.

Sixty-eight percent of registrars say they manage records on paper always or often. And yet, because only 48% of non-registrars think that's true. That's a 20-point gap for two people to disagree over the same job. It can feel like leadership doesn't care, but they're not the ones scrambling in the records room fifteen minutes before it’s time to go home, so they don’t always know.

When your team works from two different perspectives on how inefficient a process is, things are bound to get complicated.

 

Stacks of records and costs you can’t count

The relationship doesn't stay contained to transcript requests. We have to go back to day one of a student’s time in your institution.

Thirty-eight percent of districts say enrollment is often or always paper-based. Before a student has sat down in a new classroom, office staff have stacks of forms to get into three different systems. From there, every request is its own manual hunt of finding the file, printing it, mailing it, logging it, etc. Do that a hundred times a semester, and you've got a part-time job nobody budgeted for.

And some of it never even gets used. One district printed more than 15,000 transcripts in a year, and a good chunk were never picked up. Paper piles up with too little of it moving fast enough when someone needs it, and then too much of it sitting there when nobody does.

 

Where paper shows up

What it costs you

Transcripts

Each one means a manual hunt. You find the file, print it, mail it, and log it.

Printing

You print hundreds or thousands of records—how many aren’t even picked up?

Staff time

The budget doesn’t account for time, but tasks get pushed back when you’re physically managing records.

Families and alumni

A transcript that takes days instead of minutes can mean a missed deadline or blocked opportunity.

Physical risk

A fire or natural disaster can wipe out decades of records.

 

Nobody line-items "staff time spent hunting for a file." But it's there, buried in every other task that got pushed to next week because paper ate the afternoon. Families and alumni feel it when a transcript that takes days instead of minutes can mean a missed deadline or a stalled application. And there's the risk that physical records face. One fire or natural disaster can wipe out decades of records.

 

Let’s un-complicate this, shall we?

Paper records feel familiar, but they bring complications, many of which aren’t necessary in a digital world. Is it time to redefine the relationship?

Find out if paper records are holding your district back and see how you can break up with paper with our quick and free quiz!

title: Connecting the Classroom, Practical, and Continuing Ed in Fire Training
intro: Fire training records are often fragmented across classroom, practical, and continuing ed. Discover how to centralize compliance and streamline tracking with Canvas Career.

body.text: Verisk evaluates municipal fire-protection efforts in communities throughout the United States, and their Public Protection Classification (PPC®) program is used a benchmark for measuring the effectiveness of their fire-protection services. Their Fire Suppression Rating Schedule is a comprehensive list of what they consider when reviewing a community’s training for firefighters: 240 hours per recruit in the first year, 16 hours of company training per member per month, a six-hour hazardous materials session per member per year, and 12 hours of continuing education for every officer. One caveat, clearly at the bottom of the schedule: when no records exist for training, there's no credit for it . Training can happen exactly as required, but the record needs to be somewhere an evaluator can see it (and a training officer can track it down) for credit. Since training requirements are spread out over a firefighter's entire career, and across the very different settings where fire training happens, it means that, in most departments, training and certifications end up across different systems, too. The three phases don't share a system Classroom. In Iowa, a Firefighter I candidate sits for a 100-question written exam and needs at least 70% to pass, per the Fire Service Training Bureau's certification guide. That's cognitive knowledge, delivered in a classroom or an online course, and it produces the kind of record most training systems handle well, like enrollments, completions, and test scores. Practical. The same Iowa candidate has to pass every skill station assigned to them, drawn from a list of 26 possible stations, with two attempts allowed at each. That happens on a drill ground with an evaluator standing there watching. Verisk expects departments to maintain a drill tower, a live fire structure with a smoke room, and a two-acre training area, and to use those facilities 18 hours per year per firefighter for maximum credit. These hands-on evaluations don’t generate a completion record on their own, but an evaluator-signed skill sheet. Continuing ed. The day a recruit graduates, a completely different set of clocks starts. An EMT recertifying through the National Registry of Emergency Medical Technicians needs 40 credits over a two-year cycle, split into 20 national, 10 local, and 10 individual. Paramedics need 60 on the same 50/25/25 structure. Officers need their 12 hours. Drivers and operators need theirs. Hazmat comes back around every year. Three phases usually means three places to look for and keep track of documentation. The recruit file closes at graduation and a personnel file opens, with different formats and different owners. The readiness question If you ask a training officer if a specific firefighter is current on everything their assignment requires, it might mean opening a spreadsheet and then a filing cabinet to get an answer. Reporting to command, reporting to the state certifying body, and preparing for an ISO evaluation can require assembling the same underlying facts from different sources in different formats, but they’re all necessary to answer the question, “Who’s ready?” That question keeps coming up as the workforce keeps turning over. The National Volunteer Fire Council counts 1,018,100 firefighters across 29,452 U.S. departments, 635,100 of them volunteer, or roughly 62% of the total. Volunteer numbers hit a recorded low in 2023, and the NVFC reports that call volume has more than tripled over the last 40 years. Fewer people are covering more calls, and the certification standard doesn't bend to accommodate that. Iowa's Firefighter I process, for one, draws no distinction between career and volunteer candidates: same written exam, skill stations, and 12-month window to finish. So departments run more academies and certify more people just to hold the line, and every additional cohort adds skill sheets, exam scores, and certification dates. What connecting the three actually looks like Modern training for fire departments doesn’t require drastic changes to how the department trains, but changing how training is delivered and how evidence of mastery is recorded can help connect the three critical phases to standardize training and centralize compliance. One record per person, opened when they apply and never closed. Standards mapped to content once, so a change to a state requirement updates in a single place instead of in every cohort's materials. Practical evaluation captured digitally where the evaluation happens, on a phone at the drill ground, so the skill sheet joins the record the same day. Continuing education that adds to that same record rather than starting a parallel one. Reporting that reads across all three phases without anyone rebuilding it by hand the week before an audit. Where Canvas Career fits Canvas Career by Instructure was built for training that runs on standards, evaluation, and recurring requirements rather than one-time course completions. For fire academies and departments, that means a few specific things. Role-specific pathways deliver the same training to every recruit across every shift and station, in the right order, so a cohort in March and a cohort in September come out of the academy against the same standard. Training scales across stations, shifts, and regional academies in one system, with notifications sent directly to recruits and officers, so growth doesn't mean adding more spreadsheets to track. Real-time dashboards show command who's trained, what's current, and where the gaps are, which is the same view a state evaluator or an ISO reviewer is going to ask for. Existing training content moves into Canvas Career rather than being rebuilt from scratch, which matters when a department has 10 or 15 years of curriculum it doesn't want to re-author. See how Canvas Career supports recruit training and ongoing crew certification.

title: Finding the Sensible Middle: AI Literacy, Cognitive Offloading, and Student Voice in the Classroom
intro: Explore how educator Matt Miller, creator of "Ditch That Textbook," applies a "sensible middle" approach to AI in the classroom. Learn how to foster AI literacy, navigate cognitive offloading, and empower student voice by prioritizing human connection over technology.

body.text: In his junior year English class, Matt Miller sat watching a lesson drag and quietly redesigned it in his head. This would be so much better if she did this. This would be better if she did that. He never said anything to his teacher, but he did go home and tell his mom about it. Years later, after he'd switched out of a journalism major and into teaching, she brought that afternoon back up, reminding him, “You've been thinking like a teacher since you were a student all the way back in high school.” The lecture that emptied the room First, though, he had to become the teacher. Matt was wrapping up a lecture on reflexive verbs, and by his own account it was an absolutely riveting one, described in detail, fantastically, he's sure. His Spanish students had gone glassy. With five minutes left he did what he thought was the generous thing and told them to start their homework. When nobody moved and no notebooks opened, he walked to the front of the room. "You're not working on your homework, I see. That must mean that you got it all done and that I didn't give you enough. So let me give you some more homework." He owns it now without flinching: "Yes, I went there. Unfortunately, I went there." The bell rang and every student in that room sprinted for the door. Matt stood alone in a space he had just emptied, holding one thought: babies learn how to speak a language without verb conjugation drills and long vocabulary lists. There has to be a better way to do this. What Ditch That Textbook actually means The name gets misread constantly, so Matt corrects it himself. "Contrary to popular belief, Ditch That Textbook wasn't created because I hate textbooks or I think that they're evil or terrible or anything," he told us. "I was just like, if we can do better than them, then we should." The blog came before the mission. Going from journalism major to classroom educator, he already liked to write, and once he had his sea legs in the classroom he started publishing what he was trying, including the parts that flopped. Alongside that, he kept hunting for better things to do than the questions at the end of the chapter. One at a time, little by little. As he added more of them he reached for the textbook less, until he looked at the shelf one day and wondered why the things were still there. That test, if we can do better than this, then we should, is also the test he applies to AI. Why he's still in the room Matt taught Spanish full time for 11 years, then left in 2015 to do workshops and keynotes, which he did for eight years. Seven books later, he's back in a classroom teaching one period of Spanish a day at the high school his own kids attend, then turning back into Ditch That Textbook Matt for the rest of the day. "I'm going through the creative struggle of trying to engage them every single day," he said. He's in the hallway. He's with colleagues. Problems confront him and he has to solve them on the spot, which means he never runs out of material, because the classroom hands it to him. The roller coaster That's his description of AI in the classroom . "You have the highs and the lows, you know, all of a sudden things are going great and then you go down a terrifying hill and you're screaming." The promise, for him, is arithmetic. He has 31 kids in one Spanish 1 class and one of himself. He's good at whole-group direct instruction and he'll tell you so. He's equally clear that 31 students in that arrangement are not all getting meaningful, personalized feedback, and that they can't. Immediate feedback has been one of the real barriers to the results teachers want for decades. If safe, reliable tools start closing that gap, that isn't a small thing. And then there’s the tedium. Plenty of what fills a teacher's day adds nothing a human uniquely brings, and it's part of why good people keep leaving a profession that can't afford to lose them. The concerns are also specific. Cognitive offloading, and students who ask before they think. Hallucinations, bias, and data privacy. The energy, water, and resources that data centers consume. And the version of this that families are actually voicing: Matt presented recently to parents in a district that had surveyed them about their beliefs on AI , and in a lot of different words, the answers came back the same. We're afraid it's going to make our kids stupid. They won't be able to solve problems . They won't be able to think critically. "There's no easy answer," he said, "and it's complicated for people who understand it, let alone for teachers who are just getting to know it." Why this one feels different Two things make AI unlike the technology waves teachers have absorbed before. The first is order of arrival. Jody described the pattern every veteran teacher knows: you get the tool first, you get comfortable with it, then you introduce it to students. That’s by and large not what happened with generative AI. A lot of students had it before their teachers did, or at the exact same moment, so the usual runway for getting comfortable never existed. Ryan Lufkin heard from educators recently that some students say they trust AI more than they trust their teacher. Others won't touch the tools their school provides, because they assume they're being watched or recorded. The second is that the thing itself doesn't behave like software. "Traditional software has a repeatable process where you can expect the same thing out of it over and over again," Matt said. "And if you ask an AI model the same question 10 times, you might get 10 different answers." So it’s no wonder plenty of teachers are struggling with navigating the “idea” use and impact of AI. The sensible middle The loudest voices sit at the edges: Technology is the savior and you have to use all of it, or technology is the devil and you should never touch it. "I feel like the ones of us that are in schools on a regular basis, we live in the sensible middle," he said, "where we go, if it'll help me, I'll use it. But if it doesn't, I won't." The edges are exhausting precisely because they contradict each other and both point at teachers. As he put it, it's easy to wag a finger and ask why you aren't keeping up with the times, then turn around and ask why in the world you're using something so harmful and dangerous. He has no patience for the nostalgia either. When people propose turning the screens off and going back to paper, pencil, and textbooks, his answer is that we're looking at it through rose-colored glasses.A textbook isn't responsive. A textbook gets outdated. A textbook is one shot to get it right at one moment in time, and if it doesn't engage a kid, that kid can simply switch off. What actually holds teachers back Matt has worked with hundreds of schools and districts, so we asked what stops teachers from making the shifts he made. The first answer is the obvious one: time. We take professional development time and pack it full of presentations about things, instead of giving teachers time to plan. Add the obligations that eat prep periods and the hours before and after school, and the room to actually build something new never appears. His second answer is the one nobody talks about: comfort, noting he knows plenty of teachers who say, "I've done it this way for a while and it's predictable and I know how it's gonna be." And plenty of the teachers using settled methods get genuinely good results. His point is about ceilings, not competence. "We're sort of fooling ourselves if we think, okay, I've arrived. This is it. This is the curriculum that I will teach until I retire." Then he turned the harder question back on us: do we have teachers who really want to take it to the next level? He left it open. Ask your students When asked for one concrete thing a teacher could try tomorrow without needing anyone's permission, Matt answered, “Ask your students” with the conviction of the kid in that English class who was never asked. He lays out the kind of conversation (think: not a survey) in his recent book, AI Literacy in Any Class . Start wide with general concerns about AI. Narrow to specific fields, medicine, law, and creative work, and press on what's unfair, what's acceptable, and how they can tell the difference. Narrow again to schools in general. Should it be allowed, in what ways, and why? Only after all of that do you get to how this class is going to handle it. Open with "how should we use this in Spanish class" and students answer to protect their own access. They're calculating which answer keeps the door open, which is human nature, but also useless data. Build down from the wide questions instead, and by the time you reach your own room, they've put a lot on the record that they now have to reconcile. They see the implications of the whole thing, and the norms belong to them rather than to you. Teachers have been taught for decades to build classroom norms with students rather than for them. The reason it matters more here is that the alternative isn't a rule students resent. It's a rule they route around. Everything that was going to replace us Matt has a list. YouTube and Khan Academy were going to make teachers obsolete. So were Wikipedia, encyclopedias, and printed books. He can take it back to the printing press and mentioned ancient Greek philosophers worrying that written text would ruin memory. Printed books are now the hallmark of a good education. So maybe AI won’t replace teachers, like all tech before it didn’t, but it’s important to think about the evolution of modern teaching and learning. Start at the one-room schoolhouse, where the curriculum lives in the teacher's brain plus whatever handful of books they have, and the teacher is the source of all information. Then printed books, then the internet. Each step decentralizes knowledge away from the teacher and toward the student. AI is another couple of big leaps in that same direction. So the question he thinks every educator should be asking about the next decade is what remains uniquely ours. Part of his answer is about relationships and experience, the adult in the room with real adult life behind them. Part of it is stranger and better than that. "Our brains are still wired to engage with other humans because, you know, as humans, we are we're unpredictable," he said. "We're unique and complex and messy and unhinged sometimes. And it is fascinating and entertaining." The rest of his answer is a list of places rather than features. The hallway. The lunchroom. The principal's office, when you didn't make great decisions. Indiana is a year into a statewide phone ban, and what they're noticing at Matt's school is that kids are talking to each other, and that there's suddenly serious demand for decks of cards so they can play Euchre at lunch. "Let's center that and preserve it," Matt said. "It's sacred. We've got to protect it at all costs." He ditched textbooks because they weren't engaging, and AI can very much be the same way, because it isn't real human to human connection either. Every episode of the Educast 3000 show opens by asking the guest for a favorite learning moment. Not one guest has ever named a piece of technology. Every answer has been about a person. Listen to the full conversation with Matt Miller on our latest episode of Educast 3000, “Planet of the Apps: Every Technology That Was Going to Replace Teachers, and Why None Did”.

Build down from the wide questions instead, and by the time you reach your own room, they've put a lot on the record that they now have to reconcile. They see the implications of the whole thing, and the norms belong to them rather than to you.

Teachers have been taught for decades to build classroom norms with students rather than for them. The reason it matters more here is that the alternative isn't a rule students resent. It's a rule they route around.

Everything that was going to replace us

Matt has a list. YouTube and Khan Academy were going to make teachers obsolete. So were Wikipedia, encyclopedias, and printed books. He can take it back to the printing press and mentioned ancient Greek philosophers worrying that written text would ruin memory. Printed books are now the hallmark of a good education. 

So maybe AI won’t replace teachers, like all tech before it didn’t, but it’s important to think about the evolution of modern teaching and learning. Start at the one-room schoolhouse, where the curriculum lives in the teacher's brain plus whatever handful of books they have, and the teacher is the source of all information. Then printed books, then the internet. Each step decentralizes knowledge away from the teacher and toward the student. AI is another couple of big leaps in that same direction.

So the question he thinks every educator should be asking about the next decade is what remains uniquely ours. Part of his answer is about relationships and experience, the adult in the room with real adult life behind them. Part of it is stranger and better than that. "Our brains are still wired to engage with other humans because, you know, as humans, we are we're unpredictable," he said. "We're unique and complex and messy and unhinged sometimes. And it is fascinating and entertaining." 

The rest of his answer is a list of places rather than features. The hallway. The lunchroom. The principal's office, when you didn't make great decisions. Indiana is a year into a statewide phone ban, and what they're noticing at Matt's school is that kids are talking to each other, and that there's suddenly serious demand for decks of cards so they can play Euchre at lunch. 

"Let's center that and preserve it," Matt said. "It's sacred. We've got to protect it at all costs." He ditched textbooks because they weren't engaging, and AI can very much be the same way, because it isn't real human to human connection either.

Every episode of the Educast 3000 show opens by asking the guest for a favorite learning moment. Not one guest has ever named a piece of technology. Every answer has been about a person.

Listen to the full conversation with Matt Miller on our latest episode of Educast 3000, “Planet of the Apps: Every Technology That Was Going to Replace Teachers, and Why None Did”.

title: LMS as the Learning Analytics Hub: Early Alert Systems in Higher Ed
intro: Discover why integrating early alert systems directly into your LMS is crucial for improving student retention. Learn how predictive analytics can help faculty and advisors identify at-risk students and intervene before it's too late.

body.text: Penn State generates close to two terabytes of raw learning activity data every day across 89,000 students and 24 campuses, and until recently, almost none of it reached instructors while a course was still running. "Our faculty is hungry for data to support students," said Ben Hellar, manager of data empowered learning, explaining why the university built Course Insights to surface engagement signals during the term rather than after it. The pilot launched in Fall 2021 and now runs in more than 4,000 courses for over 250 instructors. Every institution running an LMS sits on data like that, but they’re not all able to turn their data into actionable insights that support student progress and improve retention. Helping students decide to stay The National Student Clearinghouse Research Center tracked the nearly 2.62 million students who started college in fall 2024. A year later, 77.1% were still enrolled somewhere, but only 69.1% were still enrolled at the institution where they started. Most of the students an institution loses at that rate are leaving while still academically eligible to stay, having decided somewhere in the first year that the place wasn't working for them. There are lots of reasons that students point to for leaving a higher ed program, from academics to cost of attendance to work to other responsibilities outside of academia. Regardless of the reason, the signals that students might leave are there before they make the decision, and early alert systems can help institutions find ways to keep them enrolled and on track. Early alerts should live in the LMS, not beside it Tyton Partners surveyed more than 3,000 students, advisors, faculty, and administrators across 825-plus US institutions for Driving Toward a Degree 2025 and found two things. First, the demand side: "Less than half of students are aware of academic advising, and only 29% report using it." Second, the supply side: staffing shortages are pushing more than 70% of large and public institutions to increase advisor caseloads, and nearly 40% of four-year publics anticipate budget cuts to student support services over the next three years. So the traditional channel for catching struggling students reaches fewer than a third of them, and might be getting thinner. But the LMS is also the primary hub of information, not just a content delivery system. It’s a communication tool across all parts of campus, connecting and exchanging data across systems like the SIS, assessment tools, publisher content, proctoring and accessibility services, analytics platforms, and the credentialing, which is why early alert systems need to function inside of and as an extension of the LMS. Predictive analytics that work across higher education Early alert systems and learning analytics tools need to work for everyone at the institution, and at all the intersections of instruction and administration. The adjunct in week two. She teaches one section of 34 students. On Thursday she notices a student with no submissions and no page views since the second day of class. She has no advising relationship with him, and no idea whether anyone else has noticed. The advisor with a Monday flag list. His caseload is 340 students. The dashboard shows 61 flags this week. Nothing tells him which three matter most, and by Wednesday afternoon he’s only worked through 12. The administrator with a Friday deadline. The provost office wants a retention dashboard. Course activity lives in the LMS, credit history lives in the student information system, financial holds live somewhere else. He can build the dashboard by Friday. Getting four offices to agree on which system is authoritative might take a whole semester. The provost reading a year-end summary. The report says the institution generated 4,200 alerts last year, up 18%, but it’s harder to say how many produced a conversation, or whether flagged students did better than comparable students who weren't flagged. Most teams in higher education need learning analytics data for different things, but the right tool can surface the right information, help the right people across functions get in sync, and make it clear what needs to come next. The capabilities that make early alerts work Vendors describe this category in wildly different language, which makes comparison hard. Here are the capabilities that determine whether an early alert program actually functions, and what each one contributes. Capability Who works in it How it contributes Course-level engagement view Instructors Shows who has gone quiet while the course is still running, so the person closest to the student can act earlier Participation measured as specific actions Instructors and administrators Separates students who are present from who are just logging in Assignment status reporting Instructors and advisors Turns missing and late work into a working list, the earliest reliable predictor in most courses Messaging from inside the analytics view Instructors and advisors Closes the gap between noticing and reaching out Institution-level dashboards Administrators and leadership Aggregates the same signals across courses and terms, so patterns surface at the program level and not just the section level Institution-defined risk criteria Administrators Puts the rules in your hands and makes them explainable to faculty governance and adjustable mid-semester Plain-language querying Advisors, deans, and leadership Lets the people doing outreach ask their own questions instead of queuing behind a data team Raw data export with a documented schema Data and IT teams Supports institutions building their own models, and keeps the analysis portable if systems change Adoption measurement Administrators Shows whether anyone acted on the flag to help distinguish a working program from a busy one Data freshness measured in hours Everyone Determines whether the dashboard supports intervention or just records history Three questions can get you started on early alert functionality conversations with vendors: Which specific student actions count as participation, and can you see the full list? Do instructors get the course-level view by default, or does it take an administrator request? Can you inspect and change the risk criteria yourself, mid-semester, without filing a ticket? What the LMS can see, and how early: An analytics approach across 3 states A study published in Big Data and Cognitive Computing on November 20, 2025 worked with 22,437 students and built a model that predicts at-risk status using only data observable within the first two weeks of a course, then tuned it to a flag rate instructors could handle. At their recommended threshold, the model "flags 15% of students with 84% precision and 35% recall, creating actionable alert lists instructors can manage within normal teaching duties." What drove the predictions are metrics that every institution can use: “ assessment completion and activity patterns dominate demographic factors, providing transparent evidence that behavioral engagement matters more than student background ”. Basically, what a student does in week two tells you a lot. San Diego University Sean Hauze, senior director of instructional technology at San Diego State University , describes what plain-language querying changed for a campus of more than 37,000 students: it opened up tools "democratizing access to the data, not just for the technical team members that know how to write SQL and other technical languages for looking at data, but actually just asking in natural language: Which students are at risk?" His example of the follow-through was simple: ask the data which students haven't logged in for two weeks, then share that list with advisors. Penn State For most schools, the data is available, but it lives in different places. To be truly useful, most faculty know they need the data where they already work, not another tool, and so the most effective early alert systems can pull all the relevant information into one place. That's the path Penn State took , pulling LMS data alongside Kaltura, Top Hat, Starfish, and the student information system into Course Insights. Indiana University Sometimes the first step is to start with the calendar, not the software. Writing for the Association for Institutional Research in February 2026, a team from Indiana University and Indiana University Indianapolis described what their own data told them about timing. Engagement roster notifications submitted by the end of week three turned out to be, in their words, "highly predictive of end-of-semester grades." Campus policy had required faculty reports by week six. The provost reset the expectation for all lower-level courses to the start of week four so that actionable insights were available earlier. The whole intervention was a revision to the reporting calendar, costing nothing. That's the cheapest test available to almost any institution, and it's a good way to start small with your own data. Pick one lower-level course sequence. Pull engagement and grade data from the first four weeks of the last three terms, and check whether it predicts final grades on your campus. If it does, you'll know exactly which signals your early alert criteria should use. title: Are Your Paper Records Holding You Back?
intro: Paper records are slow to fulfill, easy to lose, costly to store, and hard to track. This free quiz helps you decide if it's time to break up with paper for good.

body.text: Still chasing down transcripts by hand, one paper file at a time? Paper has been the default for K-12 records for decades. It's familiar… but familiar isn't the same as working. Paper records are slow to fulfill, easy to lose, costly to store, and hard to track. And every request stuck in a pile is a student, family, or staff member left waiting. After this quick quiz, you’ll see to what degree paper is holding your district back, and what breaking up with it could look like. What this quiz reveals about your records process. Six questions lead to four possible outcomes, and the next steps for your district to get your records ready for the years ahead. The quiz measures: How fast you fulfill a records or transcript request How much staff time your current process takes How well your records are protected against damage or disaster How easily students, alumni, and families can get their records How much of your diploma and credential processes still run on paper How confidently you can track requests and prove compliance A modern records process saves time as it cuts costs. Parchment by Instructure helps you protect your student records so you can break up with paper for good.

title: AI Changed the Math for Education, Including Security
intro: How has AI changed security in education? Discover why schools are increasingly targeted and how shifting to speed and resilience is the new gold standard.

body.text: I opened my session at InstructureCon 2026 with a number that still stops me. In 2019, the average time for an attacker to exploit a known vulnerability was 63 days. Today it's just seven. Attackers are moving roughly nine times faster than they were a few years ago, and the pace is still climbing. Since ChatGPT arrived in 2022, most of the conversation in our field has been about how AI changed the math for teaching and learning. While the rest of the world used the new tools to generate dad jokes and cat memes, educators were immediately handed hard questions about assessment, honesty, and what teaching looks like now. Those questions won't ever be fully "answered," because the tools and the learners keep changing. The same disruption is happening in security. Education is now one of the most attacked sectors online This isn't an Instructure story or even an LMS story. It's an industry-wide one. Microsoft's Cyber Signals report found that education is among the most targeted industries online, with the average institution facing roughly 2,507 attack attempts every week. Ransomware follows the same curve. Comparitech tracked a 23 percent year-over-year rise in ransomware attacks on education in the first half of 2025, and the sector now ranks fourth for ransomware targeting, behind only business, government, and healthcare. Schools and universities make appealing targets for reasons that won't change soon. They hold enormous amounts of personal and research data, they run on tight budgets and lean IT teams, and they can't simply take systems offline when a semester is in progress. AI hasn't created these conditions, but it’s made them far cheaper to exploit. Good security is now measured in speed I've been at Instructure for almost 15 years, and for most of that time, our security program looked the way you'd expect from an enterprise software company: phish-resistant authentication at the perimeter, annual penetration tests and a researcher-led bug bounty program to surface gaps, and certifications like SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 to validate the work. That model was designed for a world where an attack took real resources and deep knowledge of the platform. Finding and exploiting a vulnerability was slow, skilled work. The cost of that work has dropped by a factor of nine. The perimeter still matters, but a strategy that assumes attackers are slow and few is already out of date. The question I care about isn't how we recover from any single event. It's how we design for a world where attacks are more frequent, cheaper to launch, and harder to see coming. That reframes what "good security" even means. The advantage goes to whoever can detect, decide, and respond fastest while an attack is still taking shape. We've built toward that. We consolidated and expanded the protections in Canvas by Instructure against cross-site scripting and similar attacks so gaps are easier to find and fix. We added step-up authentication and a second identity layer that shrinks the blast radius if any one account is compromised. And we sharpened real-time detection with better logging, monitoring, and blocking tools. AI is on our side of this too. We use it to validate changes faster and close the gap between finding a weakness and fixing it. But as we do this, our principle remains clear: AI is a tool, not a pilot. A human developer still reviews, signs off on, and takes ultimate ownership of every single change we push to production. Resilience is becoming its own discipline The encouraging part is that the sector is already learning this. Sophos, in its State of Ransomware in Education 2025 report , found that 53 percent of education institutions hit by ransomware recovered within a week, up from 35 percent the year before. Recovery is getting faster because more institutions treat continuity as something to plan for in advance rather than improvise mid-crisis. Hardening reduces risk, but it never eliminates it. Trees with deep roots still have to sway when the storm comes. No honest vendor can promise a world with zero incidents, so the more useful promise is a different one: if something disrupts teaching and learning, you won't be left in the dark, and you'll have options. We build what you need, and nothing you don't The principle I keep coming back to: We could ship a long list of continuity features. Instead we're building what institutions have told us they need first. Backing up a course shouldn't require a strong engineering team, and it shouldn't be a software project. It should be a setting. So we're making scheduled exports something any admin can turn on, starting with the gradebook data that ranked as most important, available to every Canvas customer without an upgrade. We're also building self-service tools to remove data you don't need us to keep, because good stewardship means holding only what's necessary. The next questions are the interesting ones We're thinking further ahead than the next release. We’ve heard requests from customers and started exploring what we can do to increase resilience: read-only access so instructors and learners can reach content during an outage, offline grading in our mobile apps, a partnership with AWS to explore failover to a secondary instance. None of these are committed roadmap items yet, but continuity is a shared responsibility, and I'd rather decide what's worth building with our community than for it. Securing and strengthening these platforms is never finished, for the same reason the work of teaching never is. The tools change, the challenges change, and staying ahead means treating prevention and resilience as living systems rather than boxes to check. We'll keep building in the open, because the collaboration that made edtech what it is will be what keeps it secure. Where this goes next InstructureCon was where we started this conversation, but we’re excited to show off where we’re headed next at our New & Next Showcase in October. You can see what else we launched this summer and announced at InstructureCon 2026 here .

title: Looking Back: Musings from the Instructure Learning Strategy Team on InstructureCon 2026
intro: InstructureCon 2026 takeaways: our Learning Strategy Team on the AI, accessibility, and credentialing trends shaping education right now. See the highlights.

body.text: I’m still trying to catch my breath from my first InstructureCon. While I imagined what the week might be like, it really took me being there to fully understand the energy that you feel when seeing so many passionate educators convene and share ideas (not to mention Louisville is such a charming city). While it was just a few weeks ago, many of the sessions I attended and conversations I had with educators are still buzzing around in my head. What an amazing experience, and I’m glad I had the foresight to bring a few notebooks, as each of them is completely filled. However, I couldn't attend every session and therefore asked our wonderful Learning Strategy Team to share some highlights of their InstructureCon experience and the big topics from their discussions with attendees that educators and learners are facing today. Melissa Loble: Chief Academic Officer Educators are looking for ways to deliver experiential education at scale in traditional AND non-traditional programs. AI is unlocking content replicability through scenarios and simulations, but doing this meaningfully across various programs is still new and a challenge we need to work together to solve. We cannot discount the social aspect of learning, especially in a world where social capital unlocks pathways for employment, growth, and personal development. Educators can be powerful combaters of isolation as long as we, too, actively and positively engage with one another and our communities. Caring for each other should not go underrated. Change doesn’t just come from reinvention; it comes from our ability as education leaders to build the right amount of resilience and an experiential mindset. Too much resilience can lead to disengagement. Tackling too big a project can cause it to stall. Tiny experiments allow us to engage our human sides in inspiring and impactful change. Ryan Lufkin: VP, Global Learning Strategy Simply purchasing enterprise-wide AI licenses isn’t enough for universities or school districts. Lack of training for educators in applying AI has led to widely inconsistent adoption and levels of trust in these innovative tools and, hence, wildly inconsistent expectations and experiences for students. Innovation is happening in pockets by educators experimenting on their own. As we move into the “Agentic AI” phase, moving beyond the simple focus on AI as a threat to academic integrity, educators are hungry for examples of applying AI in the classroom to improve student engagement, evolve the learning experience, and positively impact learning outcomes. Student data privacy remains a primary concern for educators and administrators in an environment where students may not be as concerned about, or fully understand, the threats to that privacy. Jody Sailor: Sr Academic Strategy and Innovation Director Accessibility and Universal Design for Learning (UDL) drive better outcomes for all learners. Institutions are shifting from compliance-driven accessibility to design-first inclusion while also using UDL principles. They're building predictable, consistent course templates that reduce cognitive load and work better for every student. Assessment systems drive real instructional change. Institutions are moving from data collection to data action. They're using integrated assessment systems and formative data to drive targeted interventions, show student growth, and engage in professional conversations centered on impact rather than activity. Effective technology is about depth, not breadth. Institutions are consolidating tools and maximizing existing platforms. They're auditing for ROI, eliminating redundancy, and going deeper with fewer systems. In K-12, districts are moving away from the quantity of screen time and toward the impact of technology use. Rather than asking "How much time are students spending on devices?" districts are asking "When students are on devices, are they learning better?" Their focus is on the right tool, at the right time, for the right purpose to drive real outcomes. Tracy Weeks: Sr Education Policy & Strategy Director Educators aren’t waiting for approval to innovate in their classrooms. Through our Academic Excellence Awards, we celebrated three colleagues who saw the need to evolve learning processes and tools to ensure all learners had the best opportunity to succeed. They identified gaps, built pilot programs, and found success within their institutions; all based on the belief that students learn best when they have the right access to tools and are able to express themselves. Experimentation isn’t stopping either, but we need better means to implement at scale. Similarly, many educators are experimenting with new methods to better prepare today’s learner for the jobs of tomorrow. What we still fundamentally lack is a means to share successful experiments so more educators become aware. Simone Ravaioli: Principal, Global Learning Ecosystem The real issue is trust. It's tempting to think the fix is a better-looking transcript or a richer badge, but the design session with registrars, credentialing leads, and employers pointed somewhere else. Records fail because they're self-asserted, unofficial, or missing the basics that make them believable: a clear issuer, real metadata, and a working link to what the credential actually means. Until a record carries that, it's just a claim. The unit of value is a verified credential that a decision-maker can trust at a glance, and everything else we build has to serve that. Shared language has to come before the technology. When one campus calls a skill "project management" and another calls the same thing "Agile," transferability breaks and trust go with it. Attendees were clear-eyed about AI's role here. Its best job is mapping a described skill to an existing, agreed-upon one, not inventing new skills on the fly. Educators want us to build a foundation that explains to AI why a skill has value, rather than asking AI to decide. The learning and employment record is a process and a digital wallet. A comprehensive learner record has real standards and schemas. The LER is the container that pulls everything into one place. That distinction reframes our role: institutions remain the trusted issuers, and the network's job is to translate value between systems so a record can travel from a campus to an employer's hiring system. Mary Styers: Director, Evidence & Learning Strategy Evidence increasingly matters in procurement. Accessibility and Data Security agreements are “table stakes” in edtech procurement across K-12 and Higher Ed right now. Administrators won’t support tools that do not meet this basic criterion. Additionally, both requested that companies share usage data and participate in pilot/research programs, showing evidence of both usage and positive impact, to receive continued funding and adoption. For AI tools, they had additional criteria and words of caution. Both sectors desire transparency in how teachers remain in the loop, particularly as it relates to AI grading/feedback. Administrators also cautioned companies about AI fatigue, noting that companies need to name and provide evidence for specific outcomes tied to their solutions, or risk losing educators' interest in trying these new solutions. AI research, in particular, is a popular topic. Given the lack of rigorous AI research studies ( Fesler, Martinez Claeys, Agnew, Loeb, 2026 ) and educator concerns around AI in classrooms, particularly around critical thinking loss, overreliance, and academic integrity issues ( Instructure, 2026 ), it was not surprising to see a packed room eager for the research basis behind Instructure’s AI solutions. Our session on Ignite AI research studies had standing room only. Educators, parents, and communities are increasingly demanding proof that AI positively supports teaching and learning and are eager to use research frameworks (e.g., ESSA tiers ) when reviewing and comparing research studies. If you were at InstructureCon, I’d love to hear your thoughts on what you found compelling, surprising, or even controversial. Follow us on social media and share your experiences there. See you in Cleveland in 2027!
