I’m still trying to catch my breath from my first InstructureCon. While I imagined what the week might be like, it really took me being there to fully understand the energy that you feel when seeing so many passionate educators convene and share ideas (not to mention Louisville is such a charming city). While it was just a few weeks ago, many of the sessions I attended and conversations I had with educators are still buzzing around in my head. What an amazing experience, and I’m glad I had the foresight to bring a few notebooks, as each of them is completely filled. 

However, I couldn't attend every session and therefore asked our wonderful Learning Strategy Team to share some highlights of their InstructureCon experience and the big topics from their discussions with attendees that educators and learners are facing today.

 

Melissa Loble: Chief Academic Officer

  1. Educators are looking for ways to deliver experiential education at scale in traditional AND non-traditional programs. AI is unlocking content replicability through scenarios and simulations, but doing this meaningfully across various programs is still new and a challenge we need to work together to solve.
  2. We cannot discount the social aspect of learning, especially in a world where social capital unlocks pathways for employment, growth, and personal development. Educators can be powerful combaters of isolation as long as we, too, actively and positively engage with one another and our communities. Caring for each other should not go underrated.
  3. Change doesn’t just come from reinvention; it comes from our ability as education leaders to build the right amount of resilience and an experiential mindset. Too much resilience can lead to disengagement. Tackling too big a project can cause it to stall. Tiny experiments allow us to engage our human sides in inspiring and impactful change.

 

Ryan Lufkin: VP, Global Learning Strategy

  1. Simply purchasing enterprise-wide AI licenses isn’t enough for universities or school districts. Lack of training for educators in applying AI has led to widely inconsistent adoption and levels of trust in these innovative tools and, hence, wildly inconsistent expectations and experiences for students. Innovation is happening in pockets by educators experimenting on their own.  
  2. As we move into the “Agentic AI” phase, moving beyond the simple focus on AI as a threat to academic integrity, educators are hungry for examples of applying AI in the classroom to improve student engagement, evolve the learning experience, and positively impact learning outcomes. 
  3. Student data privacy remains a primary concern for educators and administrators in an environment where students may not be as concerned about, or fully understand, the threats to that privacy. 

 

Jody Sailor: Sr Academic Strategy and Innovation Director

  1. Accessibility and Universal Design for Learning (UDL) drive better outcomes for all learners. Institutions are shifting from compliance-driven accessibility to design-first inclusion while also using UDL principles. They're building predictable, consistent course templates that reduce cognitive load and work better for every student.
  2. Assessment systems drive real instructional change. Institutions are moving from data collection to data action. They're using integrated assessment systems and formative data to drive targeted interventions, show student growth, and engage in professional conversations centered on impact rather than activity.
  3. Effective technology is about depth, not breadth. Institutions are consolidating tools and maximizing existing platforms. They're auditing for ROI, eliminating redundancy, and going deeper with fewer systems. In K-12, districts are moving away from the quantity of screen time and toward the impact of technology use. Rather than asking "How much time are students spending on devices?" districts are asking "When students are on devices, are they learning better?" Their focus is on the right tool, at the right time, for the right purpose to drive real outcomes. 

 

Tracy Weeks: Sr Education Policy & Strategy Director

  1. Educators aren’t waiting for approval to innovate in their classrooms. Through our Academic Excellence Awards, we celebrated three colleagues who saw the need to evolve learning processes and tools to ensure all learners had the best opportunity to succeed. They identified gaps, built pilot programs, and found success within their institutions; all based on the belief that students learn best when they have the right access to tools and are able to express themselves. 
  2. Experimentation isn’t stopping either, but we need better means to implement at scale. Similarly, many educators are experimenting with new methods to better prepare today’s learner for the jobs of tomorrow. What we still fundamentally lack is a means to share successful experiments so more educators become aware. 

 

Simone Ravaioli: Principal, Global Learning Ecosystem

  1. The real issue is trust. It's tempting to think the fix is a better-looking transcript or a richer badge, but the design session with registrars, credentialing leads, and employers pointed somewhere else. Records fail because they're self-asserted, unofficial, or missing the basics that make them believable: a clear issuer, real metadata, and a working link to what the credential actually means. Until a record carries that, it's just a claim. The unit of value is a verified credential that a decision-maker can trust at a glance, and everything else we build has to serve that.
  2. Shared language has to come before the technology. When one campus calls a skill "project management" and another calls the same thing "Agile," transferability breaks and trust go with it. Attendees were clear-eyed about AI's role here. Its best job is mapping a described skill to an existing, agreed-upon one, not inventing new skills on the fly. Educators want us to build a foundation that explains to AI why a skill has value, rather than asking AI to decide.
  3. The learning and employment record is a process and a digital wallet. A comprehensive learner record has real standards and schemas. The LER is the container that pulls everything into one place. That distinction reframes our role: institutions remain the trusted issuers, and the network's job is to translate value between systems so a record can travel from a campus to an employer's hiring system.

 

Mary Styers: Director, Evidence & Learning Strategy

  1. Evidence increasingly matters in procurement. Accessibility and Data Security agreements are “table stakes” in edtech procurement across K-12 and Higher Ed right now. Administrators won’t support tools that do not meet this basic criterion. Additionally, both requested that companies share usage data and participate in pilot/research programs, showing evidence of both usage and positive impact, to receive continued funding and adoption. For AI tools, they had additional criteria and words of caution. Both sectors desire transparency in how teachers remain in the loop, particularly as it relates to AI grading/feedback. Administrators also cautioned companies about AI fatigue, noting that companies need to name and provide evidence for specific outcomes tied to their solutions, or risk losing educators' interest in trying these new solutions.
  2. AI research, in particular, is a popular topic. Given the lack of rigorous AI research studies (Fesler, Martinez Claeys, Agnew, Loeb, 2026) and educator concerns around AI in classrooms, particularly around critical thinking loss, overreliance, and academic integrity issues (Instructure, 2026), it was not surprising to see a packed room eager for the research basis behind Instructure’s AI solutions. Our session on Ignite AI research studies had standing room only. Educators, parents, and communities are increasingly demanding proof that AI positively supports teaching and learning and are eager to use research frameworks (e.g., ESSA tiers) when reviewing and comparing research studies.

 

If you were at InstructureCon, I’d love to hear your thoughts on what you found compelling, surprising, or even controversial. Follow us on social media and share your experiences there. See you in Cleveland in 2027!

title: AI, Equity, and Agency: The 3 Big Areas Education Leaders Are Focused on Right Now
intro: Explore how education leaders are integrating AI, equity, and student agency to improve academic strategy, foster human-centered learning, and prepare students for life beyond the classroom.

body.text: At InstructureCon 2026, more than 100 of the 275 breakout sessions touched artificial intelligence. That number might have been easy for most people to predict. What’s maybe more interesting than a straight number session count on a topic, though, is what sat next to AI on the agenda. Session after session paired it with two concerns that have lived on the desks of superintendents and provosts alike for years: reaching every learner, and helping learners take ownership of their own progress. The same pairing showed up at ISTELive 26 , where ISTE built a pavilion around a Portrait of an AI-Ready Graduate, named "Ignite Agency" as a core learning principle, and gave equity its own track under "Opportunity, Inclusivity, and Cultural Competency." ISTE's program focuses on K–12, but the three themes really matter for educators everywhere because they all address preparing every student for life outside the classroom. So whether you run a district or a campus, the conference programs make a strong case for three areas that deserve your planning time this year: AI, equity, and agency. None of them is a decision you make once. Each one requires the judgment to weigh options well, the flexibility to adjust as conditions change, and the footing to act with confidence when the evidence is still coming in. Here's why each one matters across K–12 and higher ed, and why it might influence high-level academic strategy. The focus on AI centers on responsibility Two years ago, AI sessions were mostly demos, focused mostly on “Look what this tool can do.” The rooms that filled up in 2026 were about judgment: how to teach students to check AI output, how to design an assignment that decides where AI belongs, and how to build AI literacy into what a teacher is expected to know . One session, "From Pilots to Proof: AI That Boosted College Admissions Success," showed the same shift playing out on the higher ed side, where the interest has moved from pilots to evidence of what actually worked. The pressure looks a little different depending on where you sit. In K–12, one ISTE session ("Keeping Gen Alpha Human") reported that 86% of children ages 9 to 17 already use AI, according to research from Dr. Yi Zhang. In higher ed, it’s more about protecting academic integrity and what a degree really certifies when a chatbot can draft the essay. Students are going to use AI, but what do educators believe that AI should never replace? Dr. Zhang's framework identifies four capacities worth protecting: the ability to self-regulate, to listen inward, to build identity beyond achievement, and to relate to others. Richard Culatta, CEO of ISTE+ASCD, made a parallel point from the main stage, arguing that the next chapter is using AI to strengthen human skills rather than substitute for them. Culatta framed it on the Edtech Insiders podcast this way: schools should model "using AI to help students be better at being human." Instructure's position lines up with that thinking. AI works best when it's built into the tools educators already use and pointed at instruction, not bolted on as a separate destination. IgniteAI , the AI built into Canvas by Instructure, follows that principle by keeping the instructor in the lead rather than just in the loop on both K-12 and higher-ed campuses. The strategic implication is the same at either level: write policy around purpose before you write it around tools. Name the friction you're trying to relieve, whether that's faculty capacity, feedback quality, or integrity, then judge vendors against that goal. Equity is now an access-and-design question Equity showed up in roughly 48 InstructureCon sessions, with fewer sessions treating it as a standalone initiative. More treated it as a design requirement built into everything else. Titles like "Crafting Stories for All: A UDL Pathway to Engagement" show equity moving into instructional design and universal design for learning; that language travels well into higher ed, where completion and persistence gaps are versions of that same equity and accessibility story. At ISTE, Gregory Trieste's session on neurodiversity landed on a line worth repeating in any leadership meeting: if you're in education, you're in special education. In a district, that means serving more students in general education settings. On a campus, it means disability services and accommodations can't be a separate office that content routes around. Instead of asking which learners receive accommodations, more educators are considering whether the core tools and materials work for everyone by default, including first-generation students, multilingual learners, and students with disabilities. This is where AI and equity meet, and where it’s important to consider the potential risks. A session titled "Mirror or Mirage? What AI Images Reveal About Hidden Bias" notes that the same tools that can personalize learning can also encode bias at a speed and volume no human review can catch. For strategy, equity can't be a downstream cleanup step. It belongs in procurement questions , in how you test tools for bias and developmental fit, and in whether accessibility is a real requirement or a checkbox. Agency is the outcome Agency , student voice, and ownership appeared in more than 30 InstructureCon sessions, from "Choice Boards That Drive Student Agency" to "From Consumers to Creators: Amplifying Student Voice with Design Thinking." In higher ed, we call it self-direction, and it's a key predictor of persistence and completion. One ISTE session, "Beyond Engagement: How AI and Hope Ignite True Student Agency” explained that hope is a psychological state that predicts achievement and resilience, and it can be taught. Their claim: the best use of AI helps a learner find another route when they get stuck, rather than handing over the answer. Because, as in all things AI in education, there is caution. A separate ISTE session on learned helplessness listed over-scaffolding and over-prompting among its root causes. AI that does the thinking for a learner produces the opposite of agency. So the design goal is narrow: tools should widen the paths a learner can take toward a goal, not shorten the distance to a finished product. What this means for your strategy The conference programs are a mirror that reflects what thousands of educators chose to spend their limited time learning about. What they show is a field, from kindergarten through college, that’s moved beyond asking whether AI technology belongs in education to a harder (and better) question: how do we make it work for every student, and how can a growing focus on AI, equity, and agency help prepare students for lifelong learning and life beyond the classroom? Leaders who work these three areas together end up building something none of them delivers alone: an institution that can take in new information and change course without losing its footing. For leaders, there are a few edtech-specific steps to support the shift. Define the human capacities you want to protect before adopting any AI tool, and write them into your evaluation rubric. Make accessibility and bias-testing part of procurement, not a review you run after the contract is signed. Judge every tool by one question that cuts across all three areas and both segments: Does this help a learner do something they couldn't do before, or does it just do it for them? Check out the resources below to get more insight into AI, equity, and agency for learners across K12 and higher education.

title: The Disease and the Cure: Technology and Academic Fraud in the Generative Age
intro: Diploma fraud has gone digital, and so has the fight against it. Learn how credential verification is evolving to keep pace with billion-dollar fraud.

body.text: Reflections following the UNESCO capacity-building webinar "Combatting academic fraud through technology and international cooperation," under the Global Convention on the Recognition of Qualifications concerning Higher Education. Marshall McLuhan warned that we shape our tools, and thereafter our tools shape us. Fifteen years ago, digital technology was the cure for diploma fraud. Today it's also the disease—and, built carefully, the cure again. That spiral framed UNESCO's recent webinar on academic fraud, which brought together perspectives from the Groningen Declaration Network, the Norwegian Directorate for Higher Education and Skills, and the technology and standards community. The occasion was serious: estimates cited by UNESCO put the fake degree market at more than $22 billion ( University World News , 2023). Behind that figure sits an industry now estimated to generate $7 billion a year—in one recent US federal case alone, three schools sold more than 7,600 fake nursing diplomas, and some 2,800 buyers went on to pass national licensing exams—and the human cost the panel insisted on naming, real learners, employers, and patients absorbing the consequences . The war on paper is over but the battle on digital is still on The original work of credential evaluation was forensic. Evaluators examined paper under magnifying glasses and blue light, hunting for inconsistent fonts, blurred seals, and missing signatures. Digital issuance was supposed to end that war, and for a while it did. Then the tools turned. Generative AI now produces forged documents of a fidelity no lightbox can catch, at a cost approaching zero, at a scale no evaluator's office can match. Industry telemetry tells the story plainly: digital forgeries have overtaken physical counterfeits as the leading form of document fraud. The scan and the PDF, which are the primary formats much of the world's recognition machinery still runs on, are precisely where the new fraud thrives. Yet there is a twist that should give the sector confidence rather than despair. The technologies built over the past decade, such as cryptographic signatures, independent verification, revocation, and verifiable credentials, carried features that were ahead of their time. They were harder to implement than the moment seemed to require. That moment has arrived. The features once difficult to justify are now exactly what the sector needs. Three generations of trust It helps to see verification as a sequence of paradigms, each removing a dependency that the last one couldn't shake. Generation one: phoning home. The verifier contacts the issuing institution, whether by post, phone, or email. It works when the institution answers. The arithmetic is unforgiving: Norway's recognition authority alone assesses some 30,000 foreign qualifications a year, and verifying each at source is impossible. Generation one depends entirely on someone picking up the phone, and much of the world still lives here. Generation two: trusted depositories and networks of networks. Instead of calling the institution, the verifier checks against a trusted hub—a national database, a sector-owned network, a hub-and-spoke federation of the kind the Groningen Declaration Network convenes. The logic, as the Norwegian experience shows, is precise: what a verifier actually needs is not the diploma but the connection between a serial number, an identity, and a result in an authoritative record. The document becomes almost incidental. This generation is not theoretical. Canada's MyCreds, the sector-owned national network, has reached majority adoption across the country's public institutions—and, as its founding leadership recounted in the session, five years of operation without a single case of fraud passing through the network. Across the world, My eQuals connects all 47 universities of Australia and New Zealand, with some ten million credentials issued and records shared into more than 130 countries; documents that once took over a month to deliver now reach learners in 24 to 48 hours. Generation two is today's workhorse, and it works. Generation three: the learner as the source of truth. The emerging paradigm inverts the architecture. The learner holds their credentials in a digital wallet and shares them directly with whoever needs to verify—no phone call, no central database query. The trust travels inside the credential itself: cryptographically signed by the issuer, tamper-evident, machine-verifiable in seconds. This is sovereignty in the fullest sense—personal agency over one's own record, trust established peer to peer rather than brokered through an intermediary. The standards are the same ones generation two already runs on, which means the handover requires no rebuild. When the sector is ready to trust the holder as the source of truth—and the technology increasingly warrants it—the rails are already laid. The tense matters. Generation three is motion, not arrival. The networks connecting national information centers, depositories, and evaluators remain the most efficient verification instrument the world has today. But the direction is set. Leave no one behind (including the paper) A caution, before the technology runs ahead of the world it serves. Institutions sit on a wide spectrum of readiness. Some are moving from paper to PDF; some from PDF to structured data; some are aligning to competence frameworks. No single technology dropped uniformly across that spectrum will serve everyone, and in parts of the world, the digital divide is not a metaphor but a bandwidth reading. The elegant answer is that generation-three trust doesn't require generation-three infrastructure. A cryptographically signed QR code printed on a paper document—not the decorative QR scanned for menus, but one embedding a verifiable signature—lets a paper credential be checked offline, in low-bandwidth and no-bandwidth contexts. It is the newest trust technology carried by the oldest medium: the digital and the physical closing the loop. Equity is not what gets added after the architecture is finished. Reflections following the UNESCO capacity-building webinar "Combatting academic fraud through technology and international cooperation," under the Global Convention on the Recognition of Qualifications concerning Higher Education.

Marshall McLuhan warned that we shape our tools, and thereafter our tools shape us. Fifteen years ago, digital technology was the cure for diploma fraud. Today it's also the disease—and, built carefully, the cure again.

That spiral framed UNESCO's recent webinar on academic fraud, which brought together perspectives from the Groningen Declaration Network, the Norwegian Directorate for Higher Education and Skills, and the technology and standards community. The occasion was serious: estimates cited by UNESCO put the fake degree market at more than $22 billion (University World News, 2023). Behind that figure sits an industry now estimated to generate $7 billion a year—in one recent US federal case alone, three schools sold more than 7,600 fake nursing diplomas, and some 2,800 buyers went on to pass national licensing exams—and the human cost the panel insisted on naming, real learners, employers, and patients absorbing the consequences.

 

The war on paper is over but the battle on digital is still on

The original work of credential evaluation was forensic. Evaluators examined paper under magnifying glasses and blue light, hunting for inconsistent fonts, blurred seals, and missing signatures. Digital issuance was supposed to end that war, and for a while it did.

Then the tools turned. Generative AI now produces forged documents of a fidelity no lightbox can catch, at a cost approaching zero, at a scale no evaluator's office can match. Industry telemetry tells the story plainly: digital forgeries have overtaken physical counterfeits as the leading form of document fraud. The scan and the PDF, which are the primary formats much of the world's recognition machinery still runs on, are precisely where the new fraud thrives.

Yet there is a twist that should give the sector confidence rather than despair. The technologies built over the past decade, such as cryptographic signatures, independent verification, revocation, and verifiable credentials, carried features that were ahead of their time. They were harder to implement than the moment seemed to require. That moment has arrived. The features once difficult to justify are now exactly what the sector needs.

 

Three generations of trust

It helps to see verification as a sequence of paradigms, each removing a dependency that the last one couldn't shake.

Generation one: phoning home. The verifier contacts the issuing institution, whether by post, phone, or email. It works when the institution answers. The arithmetic is unforgiving: Norway's recognition authority alone assesses some 30,000 foreign qualifications a year, and verifying each at source is impossible. Generation one depends entirely on someone picking up the phone, and much of the world still lives here.

Generation two: trusted depositories and networks of networks. Instead of calling the institution, the verifier checks against a trusted hub—a national database, a sector-owned network, a hub-and-spoke federation of the kind the Groningen Declaration Network convenes. The logic, as the Norwegian experience shows, is precise: what a verifier actually needs is not the diploma but the connection between a serial number, an identity, and a result in an authoritative record. The document becomes almost incidental.

This generation is not theoretical. Canada's MyCreds, the sector-owned national network, has reached majority adoption across the country's public institutions—and, as its founding leadership recounted in the session, five years of operation without a single case of fraud passing through the network. Across the world, My eQuals connects all 47 universities of Australia and New Zealand, with some ten million credentials issued and records shared into more than 130 countries; documents that once took over a month to deliver now reach learners in 24 to 48 hours. Generation two is today's workhorse, and it works.

Generation three: the learner as the source of truth. The emerging paradigm inverts the architecture. The learner holds their credentials in a digital wallet and shares them directly with whoever needs to verify—no phone call, no central database query. The trust travels inside the credential itself: cryptographically signed by the issuer, tamper-evident, machine-verifiable in seconds. This is sovereignty in the fullest sense—personal agency over one's own record, trust established peer to peer rather than brokered through an intermediary. The standards are the same ones generation two already runs on, which means the handover requires no rebuild. When the sector is ready to trust the holder as the source of truth—and the technology increasingly warrants it—the rails are already laid.

The tense matters. Generation three is motion, not arrival. The networks connecting national information centers, depositories, and evaluators remain the most efficient verification instrument the world has today. But the direction is set.

 

Leave no one behind (including the paper)

A caution, before the technology runs ahead of the world it serves. Institutions sit on a wide spectrum of readiness. Some are moving from paper to PDF; some from PDF to structured data; some are aligning to competence frameworks. No single technology dropped uniformly across that spectrum will serve everyone, and in parts of the world, the digital divide is not a metaphor but a bandwidth reading.

The elegant answer is that generation-three trust doesn't require generation-three infrastructure. A cryptographically signed QR code printed on a paper document—not the decorative QR scanned for menus, but one embedding a verifiable signature—lets a paper credential be checked offline, in low-bandwidth and no-bandwidth contexts. It is the newest trust technology carried by the oldest medium: the digital and the physical closing the loop. Equity is not what gets added after the architecture is finished. It is a design requirement of the architecture.

 

Prepared to be hacked

The session closed with a prediction that deserves to be wrong: diploma fraud will not keep looking like fake institutions. People will fake themselves. Instead of forged certificates, verifiers will receive generated applications, synthetic portfolios, and inflated representations of real people—plausible, polished, and hollow. That will be the new normal.

Cryptography answers part of this. What it cannot answer is the question that follows: once a credential is provably real, what is it actually telling us? The center of gravity in a credential is moving from authenticity to four harder properties—equivalence, transparency, expressiveness, and actionability. Equivalence: what is this qualification worth against that one, across borders and systems? Transparency: what learning actually sits beneath the label? Expressiveness: does the credential say enough about itself—skills, context, evidence—to be interpreted at all? Actionability: Can an admissions officer, a licensing board, or an employer make a defensible decision on it? Authenticity is becoming the floor. The judgment work above that floor—the work credential evaluators, national information centers, and recognition authorities have always done—is becoming the whole game.

 

The move

This is why the Global Convention on Higher Education matters, and why it's not primarily a technology instrument. Fraud is a coordination problem wearing a technology costume. The concrete steps are known: establish national information centers where none exist, so there is someone to answer when the world calls; connect them across regions through the convention's networks; treat verification as shared public infrastructure rather than each country's private burden; and keep educating across borders, because a network no one understands is a network no one trusts.

We shaped these tools. They are shaping us back. The task of the next fifteen years is to make sure that what they shape is a system where every learner's record is verifiable, every verifier's judgment is informed, and no one—no institution, no country, no learner—is left on the wrong side of trust.

title: Using AI to Streamline Course Management in Higher Education
intro: Streamline course management in higher education with IgniteAI Agent for Canvas. Learn how to automate administrative tasks, personalize student support, and keep course data secure, all without leaving your learning management system.

body.text: Four students in an intro environmental science course scored below 15 on the same assignment. Their instructor wanted to act before the pattern hardened: find those four, group them, build a shorter reinforcement assignment aimed just at them, and message each one before the next class. Done by hand, that's a trip through the gradebook, the People page, the assignment editor, and the Inbox, with a lot of clicking in between. With IgniteAI Agent in Canvas, the instructor did all of it in one conversation, without opening a separate AI tool. Getting AI-powered help with your course used to mean going outside Canvas. It doesn't anymore. The workaround has been leaving Canvas For a couple of years, the standard move has been to open a general-purpose chatbot like ChatGPT in another tab, describe what you need, and paste the result back into Canvas by hand. It works, but your course context doesn't travel with you, so you spend the time you saved toggling between tabs or re-explaining your syllabus along the way. IgniteAI keeps AI inside Canvas IgniteAI Agent is a conversational assistant built into Canvas. It works across more than 500 Canvas APIs, so it can take real action on your behalf rather than just suggesting text. You describe what you want in plain language, and it can pull data, create content, and make changes across your course just by prompting the Agent. Because it lives in Canvas, it answers both problems with workarounds at once. It's grounded in your actual course context, so a request like “the students who scored below 15 on the last assignment” resolves to real people in your roster, with no re-explaining. It runs inside your institution's environment so: access is admin-controlled and opt-in at the course, department, or institution level interactions stay within your instance instead of training an outside model every AI feature carries an “AI Nutrition Facts” label that spells out the model, the data it touches, and how privacy is handled It also asks before it acts. The Agent shows you its planned steps and waits for your approval, so nothing in your course changes until you say go. You get the reach of an agent that can operate in Canvas, without sending your work to one that operates outside it. From a list of names to a sent message Here's the sequence that ran in that environmental science course, start to finish, in one chat. We start with a question: “Can you pull a list of all students who scored below 15 points on the High Impact on the Environment assignment?” The Agent retrieved the submissions and returned the four students and their scores. Next came grouping. The instructor asked the Agent to create a tag called “Supplemental” and assign those four students to it. The Agent laid out its plan, the instructor approved it, and the differentiation tag was created and applied in a single step. As the Agent pointed out, that tag could then drive targeted assignment overrides, group messages, or extra instruction for exactly those students. With the group in place, the instructor asked for a new assignment to reinforce the original learning outcomes. The Agent asked the useful clarifying questions first: title, submission type, point value, due date, and whether to assign it to the Supplemental group or the whole class. Once the instructor answered, it built the assignment, scoped to the four tagged students, and left it in draft mode to publish when ready. Then communication. The instructor asked the Agent to draft a message telling those students about the new assignment and inviting them to reach out or review the week's reading. The Agent wrote it, confirmed before sending, and delivered it to each student's Canvas inbox. Four routine tasks that normally span across four corners of Canvas, done in one place, with the instructor approving each step. What the Agent handles across your course That scenario touched student data, assessment, and communication. Here's the fuller picture of the administrative work the Agent can take on, grouped the way instructors already think about their courses. Course management Create and organize modules, assignments, quizzes, and discussions Set up and manage course content and structure Export course content for backup or transfer Create and edit wiki pages Student management View student progress and performance data Find students in your courses Create and manage groups and differentiation tags View outcome results and learning progress Communication Create announcements for your courses, including the same announcement across several courses at once Draft and send messages to students Manage discussions and conversation threads Assessment Create and manage assignments with due dates Set up quizzes with various question types Manage assignment extensions and overrides Track submissions and grades You stay in control The Agent can do anything you're already able to do in Canvas, and nothing you can't. It acts only when you prompt it, and it checks in at key moments, so you approve the work rather than hand it over. That approval step keeps a person accountable for every change. It’s always worth reviewing what the Agent proposes before you confirm, especially on actions that overwrite content you've already built. Try it in your own course IgniteAI Agent is currently available with Canvas Next . If you see the IgniteAI sparkle icon on your Canvas dashboard, the Agent is ready for you. Open it and start with something small from your own to-do list, like drafting an announcement or pulling a list of students who missed the last quiz. The AI landscape feels huge and, in many ways, unknowable; the headlines are full of new tools, new models, new protocols, best practices, the risks of using or not using AI a certain way . Instructure believes that AI doesn’t need to be complicated to be powerful. IgniteAI Agent already lives where you teach, inside the system that already holds your course, so the work you were going to do anyway takes fewer steps. See more examples of how instructors are changing how they work with the IgniteAI Agent in the Instructure Community .

title: New Tools to Elevate Teaching, Learning, and Student Success: July 2026 Product Updates
intro: Explore top updates from InstructureCon’s New & Next Super Session, including new Canvas tiers, IgniteAI course tools, Parchment features, and more.

body.text: It was standing room only at our New & Next Super Session held at InstructureCon late last month. And with good reason, because we rolled out a host of new features across the Instructure portfolio of solutions. What we’re most proud of is that each of these features was driven by feedback from our customer community, and all are designed to help educators teach better, students learn more confidently, and institutions measure and demonstrate learner growth. Here are just a few of the highlights from our presentation. For the full rundown of all of the new announcements, you can learn more about each here in our Instructure Community. 1. Canvas news Three tiers to fit your needs Recently, we announced Canvas is now available in three distinct tiers , so you can choose the features and support that match your institution's needs: Canvas Core: Provides the accessible LMS foundation that powers essential teaching workflows for content, communication, and assessment. Canvas Plus: Adds enhanced tools for expanded analytics, AI, assessment insights, and content collaboration. Canvas Next: Delivers the full power of Canvas, including advanced AI capabilities and next-generation features. This approach means you're not paying for features you don't need, and you can upgrade as your institution grows. Available now in North America and rolling out globally by August 15th, these tiers give you flexibility to match Canvas to your institution’s roadmap. Meet your AI-powered course assistant We created IgniteAI for the sole purpose of giving educators the opportunity to spend time where it matters, in front of students, and less time on administrative tasks. One of the most useful features of IgniteAI is the Agent, which serves as an AI assistant. Ignite AI Agent is built into Canvas and helps faculty design better courses, respond to student needs faster, and make data-driven decisions about instruction. Ignite AI Agent also empowers learners by providing intelligent support and personalized guidance within the course itself. It elevates course content by helping instructors develop stronger learning materials and course structures. But that’s not all! Here are just some of the valuable Agent updates to features we're rolling out. Portfolio enhancements: Showcase student learning Portfolios are powerful tools for demonstrating what students have learned, and we’ve made them even stronger. Instructors can now comment directly on shared evidence, making feedback more meaningful and collaborative. Student work submitted to assignments automatically populates in their portfolios, eliminating manual data entry. And students can easily share their portfolios outside Canvas with a secure link, which is perfect for job applications, transfer applications, or showing family and mentors what they've accomplished. These enhancements are available with all Canvas tiers and will be generally available in September 2026. Whether you're using Canvas Core or Canvas Next, your students will have access to these tools. Block Content Editor: A smarter way to create course content Course design just got easier. The new Block Content Editor uses modern, flexible blocks to help instructors build rich, engaging course pages without needing technical skills or HTML knowledge. It's intuitive, fast, and puts creative control back in faculty hands. Block-based authoring is available in all Canvas tiers, making course development intuitive and fast for every instructor. For Canvas Plus and Next users, the editor includes AI-powered efficiencies with intelligent suggestions for content and layout. This means less time wrestling with formatting and more time focusing on pedagogy. Canvas Plus and Next users can join our Early Adopter Program in September 2026 to start building with blocks right away and help shape the future of the tool. 2. Canvas Career news Canvas Career is a complete learning and career development ecosystem. With peer-to-peer communities, cohort management, and AI-powered dashboards, organizations can better align their training to delivering programs that more closely resemble the outcomes that their workforce is ultimately seeking. Dashboard Builder with IgniteAI Canvas Career admins can now build custom dashboards using AI assistance to visualize learner progress, engagement, and outcomes without needing to write queries or know data structures. This allows you to build the exact data view that you need and can easily share with your customers. Learner Cohorts We know that you handle many different people structures within your organization. Now, you can leverage those structures within Canvas Career. Institutions can organize learners into managed groups (by program, department, or interest) with granular permissions and member tracking, making it easy to run cohort-based programs at scale. Peer-to-Peer communication Canvas Career now includes community forums where learners can connect, ask questions, and build networks with peers and mentors—creating the social layer that keeps alumni engaged long after graduation. 3. Parchment news The learning landscape continues to find new avenues for learners to attain the insight and knowledge they demand. With that, the ability to access the courses they need, the ability to share their learning journey, and receipt of their course completion has never been more crucial. We have added new features to Parchment to address these elements, ensuring all learners can continue their path forward. Identity verification When students order transcripts, you need to know they are who they say they are. Parchment is adding identity verification, letting students confirm their identity through multiple simple methods like scanning a QR code or getting a text link—no complicated processes, just quick and secure. It's coming in November 2026. Dual enrollment Dual enrollment opens doors for students, but the paperwork between high schools and colleges can be a nightmare. Parchment is building tools that streamline the whole process—from application through parent consent to college approval—keeping everyone on the same page and moving students forward faster. The Early Adopter Program kicks off in Q4 2026. Expanded analytics Digital badges are great, but institutions need to know if they're actually working—are students earning them, sharing them, and getting value from them? Parchment's expanded analytics show you everything from how many badges you've issued to how many times they've been viewed or shared, plus insights into what makes badges stick. It's available now. Teaching and learning tools are designed to make instruction more effective and give teachers time back. Assessment and growth features provide deeper insights into how students are progressing and where they need support. And credentials and opportunity tools help students document their learning and prepare for what's next—whether that's a job, further education, or a new career. Ready to learn more? Our team is ready to walk you through how these features fit your institution's roadmap, help you get the most value from Canvas, and guide you through the right decision about which tier is right for your needs. Start today by getting a tour of what Instructure has to offer your institution.

title: Why Your Edtech Tools Need to Talk to Each Other
intro: Learn why edtech interoperability is vital for your district. Discover how to evaluate vendors, save teachers time, and improve student data insights effectively.

body.text: On a Monday morning, a seventh-grade science teacher opens her laptop. She pulls up her learning management system (LMS) to make sure the day's assignment is ready, and switches to the district's assessment platform to see who needs to make up last week's quiz. Then, she opens another tab for the curriculum tool her department adopted in the fall, followed by a fourth tab to prep attendance. Each one requires a different login, and none of them shows the same student data. She's not doing anything wrong. Her tools just don't know about each other. Poor interoperability doesn’t show up in the classroom as a server error, but as small, daily hurdles to jump over. It eats into instruction or planning time and makes it harder for teachers to see the full picture of how students are doing. The good news: interoperability isn't magic. It's a tool standard you can ask for, evaluate, and require. What exactly does interoperability mean? Interoperability means your tools share data without someone in the middle having to manually make it happen. In practice, that means a student roster updated in your student information system (SIS) automatically updates in your LMS. It means a teacher can pass grades back from an assessment tool without exporting a spreadsheet. It means a student logs in once and gets where they need to go without another password or portal. Single sign-on (SSO) is the part most people picture first, but it's only one piece. Full interoperability also covers rosters (syncing who's in which class), grade passback (sending results back to the gradebook), assignment sync (seeing work across platforms), and data portability (being able to move your data out when you need to). Interoperability 101 Learning tools interoperability (LTI) — the standard that lets external tools plug into an LMS and exchange data. LTI 1.3 is the current version; if a vendor is still on LTI 1.1, that's worth flagging. OneRoster — the standard for syncing rosters, grades, and course data between systems. Ed-Fi — a broader data framework used mostly at the state and district level to connect systems across the ecosystem. SAML/SSO — the authentication standard that handles secure single sign-on. You should also know the term "platform agnostic." Vendors use it to mean their tool works with anything. Sometimes that's true, but sometimes it means they'll build a custom integration for your specific setup… that nobody else can maintain. That's more of a workaround than true interoperability. What does poor interoperability actually cost? A 2024 Clever survey of over 1,500 K–12 teachers found that 68% say their LMS doesn't integrate well with many or all of their applications. Time is lost manually entering data and checking multiple places to piece together a picture of student progress that should be automatic. The less visible cost is what districts lose when data stays stuck in separate platforms. If curriculum, assessment, and LMS data are all separated, no one has a holistic view of how a student is doing. Teachers are forced to make instructional decisions on partial information. Sometimes, an IT team member builds the workaround. They learn the quirks, maintain the custom sync, and fix it when something breaks. But when that person leaves, the workaround often goes with them, and whoever inherits it has to start from scratch. Finally, there's an equity dimension worth naming. If some schools in your district have working integrations and others don't, students don't have equal access to the tools their district paid for. And when some tools are evidence-backed while others aren’t, that can create differences in student growth. Most of this is preventable. The two most common culprits? Vendors who implement open standards inconsistently, and procurement processes that don’t ask the interoperability questions. What does good integration look like? Start with the standards. Before you sign a contract, ask vendors: Do you support LTI 1.3? OneRoster 2.0? What does roster sync look like in a district our size? If your district runs a lot of tools, a rostering platform like Clever or an Ed-Fi implementation can act as one place to manage how your SIS talks to everything else. On the LMS side, look for an API-first architecture and a published integration catalog. Canvas by Instructure maintains an open ecosystem of LTI-certified partners , so districts can evaluate integration quality before purchasing a tool. The burden is on vendors to demonstrate interoperability. In the next renewal and procurement cycle, treat interoperability as a requirement . If a tool is in classrooms and the integration is failing, you’ve lost time and leverage. Ask the questions before you sign, and make sure your IT team is in the room during the demo. Start asking better questions A well-integrated stack gives something back to everyone in the district. The IT team gets time back from fewer help tickets. Teachers get a cleaner daily experience and can focus more on instruction over technology barriers. Students get consistent access to their tools and fewer logins. And district leaders get a more complete picture of how those tools are actually performing. That last part matters more than it might seem. If your systems don't talk to each other, your data doesn't either, and you're back to making renewal decisions based on login counts and vendor pitches instead of evidence. Interoperability alone can’t fix a stack with too many tools . But it’s a lot easier to tell what's working and what isn't when your tools all speak the same language. Each one requires a different login, and none of them shows the same student data.

She's not doing anything wrong. Her tools just don't know about each other.

Poor interoperability doesn’t show up in the classroom as a server error, but as small, daily hurdles to jump over. It eats into instruction or planning time and makes it harder for teachers to see the full picture of how students are doing.

The good news: interoperability isn't magic. It's a tool standard you can ask for, evaluate, and require.

 

What exactly does interoperability mean?

Interoperability means your tools share data without someone in the middle having to manually make it happen.

In practice, that means a student roster updated in your student information system (SIS) automatically updates in your LMS. It means a teacher can pass grades back from an assessment tool without exporting a spreadsheet. It means a student logs in once and gets where they need to go without another password or portal.

Single sign-on (SSO) is the part most people picture first, but it's only one piece. Full interoperability also covers rosters (syncing who's in which class), grade passback (sending results back to the gradebook), assignment sync (seeing work across platforms), and data portability (being able to move your data out when you need to).

Interoperability 101

  • Learning tools interoperability (LTI) — the standard that lets external tools plug into an LMS and exchange data. LTI 1.3 is the current version; if a vendor is still on LTI 1.1, that's worth flagging.
  • OneRoster — the standard for syncing rosters, grades, and course data between systems.
  • Ed-Fi — a broader data framework used mostly at the state and district level to connect systems across the ecosystem.
  • SAML/SSO — the authentication standard that handles secure single sign-on.

You should also know the term "platform agnostic." Vendors use it to mean their tool works with anything. Sometimes that's true, but sometimes it means they'll build a custom integration for your specific setup… that nobody else can maintain. That's more of a workaround than true interoperability.

 

What does poor interoperability actually cost?

A 2024 Clever survey of over 1,500 K–12 teachers found that 68% say their LMS doesn't integrate well with many or all of their applications. Time is lost manually entering data and checking multiple places to piece together a picture of student progress that should be automatic.

The less visible cost is what districts lose when data stays stuck in separate platforms. If curriculum, assessment, and LMS data are all separated, no one has a holistic view of how a student is doing. Teachers are forced to make instructional decisions on partial information.

Sometimes, an IT team member builds the workaround. They learn the quirks, maintain the custom sync, and fix it when something breaks. But when that person leaves, the workaround often goes with them, and whoever inherits it has to start from scratch.

Finally, there's an equity dimension worth naming. If some schools in your district have working integrations and others don't, students don't have equal access to the tools their district paid for. And when some tools are evidence-backed while others aren’t, that can create differences in student growth.

Most of this is preventable. The two most common culprits? Vendors who implement open standards inconsistently, and procurement processes that don’t ask the interoperability questions.

 

What does good integration look like?

Start with the standards. Before you sign a contract, ask vendors: Do you support LTI 1.3? OneRoster 2.0? What does roster sync look like in a district our size?

If your district runs a lot of tools, a rostering platform like Clever or an Ed-Fi implementation can act as one place to manage how your SIS talks to everything else. On the LMS side, look for an API-first architecture and a published integration catalog. Canvas by Instructure maintains an open ecosystem of LTI-certified partners, so districts can evaluate integration quality before purchasing a tool. The burden is on vendors to demonstrate interoperability.

In the next renewal and procurement cycle, treat interoperability as a requirement. If a tool is in classrooms and the integration is failing, you’ve lost time and leverage. Ask the questions before you sign, and make sure your IT team is in the room during the demo.

 

Start asking better questions

A well-integrated stack gives something back to everyone in the district. The IT team gets time back from fewer help tickets. Teachers get a cleaner daily experience and can focus more on instruction over technology barriers. Students get consistent access to their tools and fewer logins. And district leaders get a more complete picture of how those tools are actually performing.

That last part matters more than it might seem. If your systems don't talk to each other, your data doesn't either, and you're back to making renewal decisions based on login counts and vendor pitches instead of evidence.

Interoperability alone can’t fix a stack with too many tools. But it’s a lot easier to tell what's working and what isn't when your tools all speak the same language.


Curious what's actually getting used?

The EdTech Top 40 from LearnPlatform by Instructure ranks the most-accessed K-12 tools of the 2024-25 school year, drawn from 64 billion-plus interactions. It's a national benchmark for the same question this post asks about your own stack: what's working, and what's just installed?

title: Educators Need an AI Skills Map, Not Another Tool
intro: Discover RMIT University’s Gen AI Skills Continuum, a framework for navigating the rapidly shifting AI landscape and building purposeful, expert practice.

body.text: Twenty stations, with close to 5,000 educators moving through them over the course of a day. At nearly every single stop, the same sudden, audible “oh.” That's how Dale Leszczynski describes RMIT University's make-and-take session, a room built for one purpose: get educators playing with generative AI instead of talking about it. Some built a game with AI. Others polished up a slide deck. At each station, Leszczynski watched the same two-beat moment repeat itself: first someone saw a colleague try something with the technology and went wide-eyed, then, about five minutes later, tried it themselves and wore the same look. “If we could bottle all those aha moments into one little place and sell it,” he said, “that’s the magic of education right there.” Leszczynski is head of AI education at RMIT University in Melbourne, Australia, where he leads the Generative AI Lab for Education, known internally as GAILE. Under his direction, GAILE launched a new AI skills framework for university educators. Every aha moment in that room came from a different starting point. Some educators walked in having never touched a large language model. Others had already built AI-powered simulations for their classrooms. That gap, and what to do about it, is the work that Leszczynski is doing in education. With a field changing this fast, giving 5,000 people at wildly different starting points a way to know where they actually stand matters more than teaching them another tool. Find your starting point on the AI skills continuum The tool GAILE built to answer that gap wasn't really a tool at all. Leszczynski and colleague Toni Jones (RMIT's lead education gen AI specialist) built the Gen AI Skills Continuum, published at aiskontinuum.com and on RMIT's own site . Rather than a single bar educators either clear or don't, the Continuum lays out a progression. Leszczynski describes it in three stages: introducing, adapting, and mastering. RMIT's published version breaks that arc into five stages nested across three broader phases, moving from basic AI awareness through to leading strategic adoption within a department or discipline. It was built as a continuum instead of a fixed benchmark on purpose. In this field, nobody stays right for long. “Everything that’s right today is wrong tomorrow,” he said. The framework was built for educators first, but something unplanned started happening in classrooms almost immediately. Educators began flipping the Continuum around, using it to decide which AI skills to teach their own students directly, sometimes turning it into an informal assessment: can a student explain why they picked one AI tool over another before they lean on it? Leszczynski is candid about the limits of a map, though. “The honesty about the Skills Continuum is that we've given people the map, and there's a bit of a sigh of relief that someone has the map,” he said. “And then maybe they put it down.” A map only does its job, he added, once someone actually picks it up and asks what the terrain means for their own classroom. Match your confidence to your actual practice There's a cultural backdrop to why RMIT is this comfortable naming what it doesn't know yet. Leszczynski likes to point out that Australia, by his own admission a small country, punches above its weight in behavioral science and educational psychology, and RMIT leans on that local expertise rather than importing someone else's playbook. He also says the most popular phrase in the room lately isn't some AI buzzword. It's “I was wrong, and I don't know.” That's the temperament he brought to a roundtable GAILE convened in June 2026 with senior leaders and digital experts from every Victorian university , in partnership with Amazon Web Services, to discuss the new framework and where the sector actually stood. Leszczynski ran an exercise using the Continuum: sticky notes, mapped against the stages, showing where each institution believed it sat. He expected the room to cluster around the middle of the scale. Instead, the sticky notes piled up at the introducing stage, even in cases where the practices people described suggested they were much further along. “Some of the sticky notes that we're seeing appear around the introducing stage, we're actually probably more faced towards that reinforcing or that mastery stage even,” he said. “There's some really good practices coming through. But the reality is that people don't have the confidence yet, because they're kind of looking at others and going, actually, I think this is what we're doing here. Is this good? Do we know this?” Part of the problem, Leszczynski said, is that no shared benchmark exists yet for what an AI-expert educator even looks like. Anyone claiming that title in public is doing so without much to measure it against, and the ground underneath that claim keeps shifting. The room was full of chief information officers and other technology leaders with a clear interest in the tools themselves, which made the session's dominant theme notable. Attendees kept returning to pedagogy before technology. “The tail isn't wagging the dog,” Leszczynski said. “The dog is leading here.” His caveat: the balance won't hold on its own. “Always more work to go on that one, because the pendulum will swing the other way as technology gets more and more exciting,” he conceded. Give students the consistency they keep asking for GeneratED also gave students a formal seat in the conversation. A student panel drew a standing-room-only crowd, including RMIT's vice chancellor, who showed up to find people sitting on the floor. GAILE followed that panel by launching an AI student advisory board, made up of students spanning business, design, ethics, and STEM disciplines, from undergraduate through postgraduate. What Leszczynski heard in that room surprised him. Students raised concerns about their own learning unprompted, specifically around what researchers call metacognitive offloading, the tendency to hand off planning, monitoring, and self-checking to an AI tool rather than doing that reflective work themselves. It's an active area of study: a 2025 framework published in Frontiers in Education examines how AI tools can either erode or support self-regulated learning depending on how they're designed into a course, and a 2026 scale published in the Journal of Educational Computing Research gives the phenomenon a formal name: metacognitive laziness. Across every discipline represented on the advisory board, one request cut through everything else: not more rules, just consistency, even while the guidance underneath those rules keeps shifting. “There's a desire for clarity around what is right, what is wrong,” Leszczynski said. “That is always going to be a gap. It's going to be difficult to fill. People want the clarity. Everyone wants the understanding.” One thread students raised: some students are consciously choosing not to use AI tools at all, tied to concerns about unequal access. It's a documented pattern beyond RMIT, too. Researchers writing on AI equity in higher education point to gaps in who can afford premium AI tools and who arrives at university with prior AI exposure at all, disparities that existing access gaps in higher education can easily deepen rather than close. The focus in higher ed should be purposeful AI use: using a tool deliberately, for a reason he could explain out loud, rather than reaching for it by default. That's the throughline underneath the make-and-take session, the sticky notes, the debate stage, and the advisory board. AI keeps expanding what it can do. Leszczynski's real question is what humans choose to keep doing themselves. What do humans get to keep when AI takes on more and more? Partway through the recording, his dog started barking at the door. An inherited Samoyed the family calls Aunt Lillian needed letting in, and Leszczynski excused himself for a few seconds to handle it himself. Nobody suggested an AI agent for that job. Some things, purposeful or not, still need a human at the door. Hear the full conversation on the No Country for Fast Answers: Safeguarding Critical Human Logic in a World of Instant AI Responses episode of the EduCast3000 podcast.

title: ansrAccess®️: The Spellcheck for Accessibility
intro: ansrAccess gives instructors and support staff the tools they need to handle accessibility quickly and without stress. It is integrated with Canvas via LTI. It is right there, within Canvas, for faculty and staff to use.

body.text: When was the last time you published something with a typo in it? Probably not recently. Spellcheck more or less solved the problem of typing errors so long ago that most of us don't even think about it anymore. Unless we are dealing with autocorrect on our phones. Now a more difficult question, geared toward my online instructors and instructional designers: when was the last time you published an online course page with a missing alt tag, a skipped heading level, or a video that accidentally didn’t have captions? I had the pleasure of speaking with an accessibility expert from a large public university last week, and something he said resonated with me. A course, or course page, with "small" errors like missing alt tags and skipped headings isn't just less accessible; it's less usable. In the same way that a page full of typos is less usable for anyone who sees it, a content page lacking alt tags or headings is less usable for anyone who needs them to have a pleasant online course experience. This gap in understanding has always been present among individuals who are just learning about accessibility (me in 2016). What's new is how much attention the gap is getting among everyone. Due to deadlines set by the U.S. DOJ, priorities have been shifting for online course content teams, ed tech teams, instructors, and support staff. In the product world, companies have been shifting their roadmaps and product offerings to ensure accessibility by adding new features and layouts, beefing up existing accessibility tools, or creating new tools and automations focused on accessibility. Just as institutions were moving toward the 2026 deadlines, it was announced that the deadlines were extended to 2027. Some institutions let out a sigh of relief, while others felt like the wind had been taken out of their sails. For me, it was a mix of both. There was a brief pause, a “what happens now?” moment. Maybe that summer vacation I had been postponing until Fall could actually happen! Independent of whatever reaction anyone had, most institutions began looking at the extension like extra time given on an assignment. Some went back to treating the extension as a reprieve, or taking it as a sign that the accessibility deadline will never actually happen. I like to think of the extension as an opportunity to define sustainable accessibility workflows, review tools more thoroughly, and give more time for training staff. Or maybe it’s time to review a tool that is like a spellchecker for accessibility within Canvas. Meet ansrAccess ansr Access, a new accessibility tool on the rise that can be leveraged within Canvas, aims to be that spellchecking friend. Created by the team at ansr source , ansr Access is a one-stop shop for accessibility remediation. It checks every portion of course content for accessibility errors, much like the grammar or spell check tool in Microsoft Word that flags grammar and spelling errors. ansr Access does more than just check for errors. It also: Assists instructors, instructional designers, and technologists in fixing the errors in their courses. Audits the existing courses in Canvas and provides users with a dynamic and useful dashboard for tracking accessibility concerns. Provides a reporting function for Canvas LMS admins. ansr Access walks the user through the critical fixes needed in their course, one item at a time. It reviews headings, links, images, and files across the course and surfaces guidance for the issues it finds. As the user learns what is inaccessible, they also learn how to make the content accessible. ansr Access tells the user what WCAG requirement is in question and gives them guidance on how to correct the issue. With this model, creating accessible content in the future gets easier for instructors, instructional designers, and technologists - they are learning as they go. Planning for accessible content For some institutions, WCAG compliance is brand new territory, which can feel scary and daunting. In addition to having to learn about the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG), instructors, instructional designers, and support staff also need to figure out what it means to implement the guidelines and then roll out a plan for training. Speaking from personal experience, getting everyone on board to make course content accessible is not an easy task. It's a job in and of itself, and requires time, money, and the right people to make it happen smoothly. ansr Access is designed to lessen the burden of the resources needed. When was the last time you published something with a typo in it? Probably not recently. Spellcheck more or less solved the problem of typing errors so long ago that most of us don't even think about it anymore. Unless we are dealing with autocorrect on our phones. 

Now a more difficult question, geared toward my online instructors and instructional designers: when was the last time you published an online course page with a missing alt tag, a skipped heading level, or a video that accidentally didn’t have captions? 

I had the pleasure of speaking with an accessibility expert from a large public university last week, and something he said resonated with me. A course, or course page, with "small" errors like missing alt tags and skipped headings isn't just less accessible; it's less usable. In the same way that a page full of typos is less usable for anyone who sees it, a content page lacking alt tags or headings is less usable for anyone who needs them to have a pleasant online course experience. This gap in understanding has always been present among individuals who are just learning about accessibility (me in 2016). What's new is how much attention the gap is getting among everyone. 

Due to deadlines set by the U.S. DOJ, priorities have been shifting for online course content teams, ed tech teams, instructors, and support staff. In the product world, companies have been shifting their roadmaps and product offerings to ensure accessibility by adding new features and layouts, beefing up existing accessibility tools, or creating new tools and automations focused on accessibility. 

Just as institutions were moving toward the 2026 deadlines, it was announced that the deadlines were extended to 2027. Some institutions let out a sigh of relief, while others felt like the wind had been taken out of their sails. For me, it was a mix of both. There was a brief pause, a “what happens now?” moment. Maybe that summer vacation I had been postponing until Fall could actually happen! 

Independent of whatever reaction anyone had, most institutions began looking at the extension like extra time given on an assignment. Some went back to treating the extension as a reprieve, or taking it as a sign that the accessibility deadline will never actually happen. I like to think of the extension as an opportunity to define sustainable accessibility workflows, review tools more thoroughly, and give more time for training staff. Or maybe it’s time to review a tool that is like a spellchecker for accessibility within Canvas. 

Meet ansrAccess

ansrAccess, a new accessibility tool on the rise that can be leveraged within Canvas, aims to be that spellchecking friend.   • It leverages AI to make remediation as efficient as possible, cutting down on human hours spent remediating troublesome content. 
  • It is affordable so that institutions can stay within their technology budgets. 
  • It is intuitive and user-friendly.

Being able to see the accessibility items that need to be corrected in one place and being able to click through them to fix them is amazing. Seeing an accessibility score that increases when a broken link has been fixed? Even more rewarding. 

What is cool about this tool is that it combines the efficiency of AI with human oversight. You can review the AI generated alt tag to make sure it’s accurate. title: The K-12 LMS Migration Checklist: What Has to Happen Before Go-live
intro: Preparing for a K-12 LMS migration? Use this step-by-step checklist to manage data, integrations, and communication for a seamless, successful rollout.

body.text: An August LMS go-live is really a project that should be in ramp-up mode by February. Here’s why: on rollout day one, the first breaks are going to show up at the operational layer the platform is built on, like gradebook columns that didn't carry over, parent observer accounts that were never provisioned, principals who can't see their own staff. These issues aren’t going to pop up during a demo, but they all trace back to work that should have started months earlier. After deciding on a vendor, the migration work starts in earnest. The K-12 LMS migration checklist helps teams running transitions for districts moving to Canvas by Instructure. It draws on the same work done with districts moving from Schoology to Canvas and districts managing a Blackboard migration to Canvas. This list lays out the steps that will help a launch to hold up. Before: the four to six months ahead of go-live Most of a clean migration happens before anyone logs in. Four workstreams run in parallel during this window, and the district owns all four. Run the data audit first. Before any vendor touches any file, get a clean inventory of the current system. Inventory course shells, assignments, grade history, user accounts, parent observer relationships, third-party integrations, and custom roles. The vendor can't tell you what matters here. This is a district deliverable. Make data-retention decisions up front, while there's still time to act on them. Five-year-old course shells no teacher uses don't need to come over. Migration scope drives cost and timeline, so be focused and decisive about what travels. Lock the integration architecture before signing. Each integration is its own project with its own data owner, and this is where a launch starts to slip. Settle the full list before contract signature: SIS (PowerSchool, Infinite Campus, Skyward), identity provider (Clever, ClassLink, native SAML), assessment tools, content platforms, and family communication tools. Build the communication calendar. Each audience hears about the change on a different schedule. Districts that under-communicate pay for it in helpdesk volume at launch. Staff: first communication four to six months out Families: start three months out Students: start two months out Board: updates on the regular board cycle, not a one-time announcement Design the training program in spring, not July. An August launch needs its training built months ahead, across three tracks. A teacher onboarding LMS rollout track built around what teachers actually do in the first month of school, not a general feature tour An admin track for principals and instructional coaches who support teachers from day one An asynchronous library for teachers who skip the live sessions or need to revisit material after launch The Canvas implementation team can share a sample training calendar from past district rollouts. Use it as a starting point and shape it to your district. During: the launch window For the launch window itself, the work narrows to execution and triage. Run a parallel period. This is a deliberate cutover timeline. Keep the old and new systems live together for two to four weeks so teachers can confirm their courses are intact before they lose access to the old one. Set up a launch command center. For the first couple of weeks of school, it helps to have a small group focused on the launch: district IT lead, district instructional technology lead, the vendor implementation contact, and a rotating set of building tech coaches. A short daily standup, one channel for issue triage, and a running resolution log give them a single place to catch problems while they're still small. It's one of the higher-payoff things to put in place, since launch support that's folded into everyone's regular duties tends to surface issues later. Watch three numbers daily. Active teacher accounts (who has logged in and posted content in the last seven days), SIS sync health (whether rosters match enrollment in real time), and helpdesk tickets by category (what's breaking, and whether the same thing breaks twice). Everything else is context, but those three metrics are foundational. After: the first 90 days By the end of the launch window the work shifts from getting the platform up to getting it used. That's a different mode, and it has its own checklist. Run a 30-day retrospective with the implementation team and a representative group of teachers and admins. Og over what worked, what broke, and what surprised you; the output is the punch list for the next 60 days. Resource the second wave of training. Day-one training answers "where's the login button”, but day-45 training answers "how do I use this to teach better." Most districts under-resource the second wave. Peers matter a lot here; teachers pick up the practical moves fastest from other teachers, so point them to the Instructure Community and Canvas user groups, and give your early-adopter teachers a channel to share what's working with the rest of the staff. Audit the migration at 90 days. Reconcile gradebook records against the SIS, confirm archived course content is present for compliance retention, and check that parent observer accounts mapped correctly. Find the gaps while institutional memory still exists. Plan year two. Analytics use cases, advanced feature rollout, the integrations you deferred from launch scope, and the start of the next budget cycle conversation. Where the outcome is actually decided The data audit, the integration tests, and a strong comms plan will help decide how the first month of migration goes. A Canvas LMS migration guide scoped to your district is the kind of plan the Instructure team builds during the planning phase of a transition. If you're getting close to launch, request Canvas migration support .
