title: How to Get Teacher and Staff Buy-In Before Rolling Out a New LMS
intro: Secure teacher buy-in for your new LMS rollout. Explore this five-phase model to prioritize training, feedback, and peer support for successful, long-term classroom adoption.

body.text: Calcasieu Parish School Board serves more than 28,000 students across 60 school sites in and around Lake Charles, Louisiana. By 2021, the district faced a problem most K-12 leaders will recognize. Teachers were juggling a stack of disconnected edtech tools, and a run of COVID and hurricane-related closures had pushed the old learning management system past its limit. A committee of stakeholders evaluated the options and chose Canvas by Instructure. Choosing the platform was the easy part. Anissa Fontenot, a technology facilitator for the district, is direct about what came next: "Transitioning to Canvas was the right move, even though it felt a little overwhelming at first." Overcoming teacher resistance to new technology depends on how a district sequences everything around the decision: who helps make it, how teachers learn the platform, and what support reaches their buildings once the rollout begins. Calcasieu Parish treated that sequence as the actual project, and the buy-in followed. Why teacher buy-in is the variable that matters most Districts spend enormous time on platform evaluation and meaningfully less on adoption planning. The ratio is backwards. Teacher training and support are what most reliably determine whether new classroom technology gets used. A 2026 RAND review of EdTech trials found that teacher training and support consistently "made or broke" the success of those rollouts, and that the programs that worked were the ones with ongoing, built-in professional development. A teacher who doesn't trust the new platform uses it for the bare minimum the district can see (think a posted syllabus and maybe a grade column) and keeps the real work where they've always kept it: a spreadsheet updated by hand, maybe even the paper system that got them through last year. The platform turns into a box to check rather than the connected learning hub it was bought to be. In a national RAND survey of K–12 educators , those working in coherent, aligned instructional systems reported stronger confidence in their teaching, while those dealing with inconsistent systems reported frustration and anxiety. A shared platform that every teacher actually uses is one of the pieces that keeps instruction consistent across a district. The five-phase model for teacher buy-in The five phases below map to the year around a launch: evaluation roughly nine to twelve months out, the pilot cohort the semester before go-live, training over the summer, structured feedback through the first month teachers are live, and ongoing measurement after that. Phase one: bring teachers into the evaluation, not the announcement Teacher voice in the LMS evaluation is important work in the vetting process, not a courtesy tacked onto the end of it. A district evaluation committee should include classroom teachers from at least three grade bands, special education, and a content area with high digital tool use (typically science or math). The committee meets through the evaluation. Teachers sit in vendor demos, run scenarios in sandbox environments, and contribute to the scoring rubric. This can be done in parallel to other evaluation processes, so it doesn't have to slow the decision. But it does change who feels accountable to the decision after it's made. Phase two: build the early adopter cohort Before any district-wide rollout, identify 15 to 30 teachers to run an extended pilot. The right people here aren't necessarily the most tech-fluent teachers in the district, but they should have credibility in their buildings and be someone other staff turn to with a question, because what they say about the platform will move adoption further than any message from leadership. The cohort needs three commitments from the district: real classroom use of the platform for a full semester instead of a two-week trial, a direct channel to the implementation team so their feedback actually shapes the rollout, and a stipend or course-release that makes clear the district counts this as work. Phase three: design the training around what teachers actually do Most LMS training is built around the platform. It walks through features, navigation, and configuration. Widespread LMS adoption is more effective when it's built around the teacher's actual work: how do you set up the first week of school in this platform, how do you build a unit, how do you handle a struggling student. A working LMS training plan for teachers has three layers: A short, role-specific live session that gets teachers through the first two weeks of school An asynchronous library they can return to as they encounter new needs Building-level coaching, ideally from the early adopter cohort, in the first 60 days The third layer is the one most districts cut for budget reasons, but it has a high impact on adoption. Teachers might not reach out to the IT team if they have a question, but they are likely to ask the person down the hall if they need help. Phase four: respond to the feedback you actually get Teachers will surface things during rollout that the evaluation didn’t anticipate. Some of what they raise will be real platform constraints, some will be training gaps, and some will be configuration choices the district can change on its own. The work after that is sorting them quickly and reporting back. A weekly digest sent to all staff for the first month, one that says plainly "here's what we heard, and here's what we're doing about it," is a high-impact communication for a district to provide in this stretch and proves the feedback channel is real. Phase five: measure adoption, don't assume it To a central office, a teacher can post a syllabus, log in once a week, and show up as "active", and this looks like success, but usage data is the only way to confirm genuine adoption. Canvas LMS has analytics that show which features teachers and students actually engage with, so a district can find the classrooms where use is thin and find ways to bring in support before the gap widens. The work also doesn't end at launch. The RAND review is explicit that the rollouts that succeed are the ones with ongoing professional development, and every August brings a fresh group of teachers who missed the original training entirely. Adoption holds up when a district builds a standing onboarding path for new hires and a yearly refresh for everyone else, rather than treating training as a one-time event tied to go-live. A district doesn't have to carry all of that alone, either. The Instructure Community gives teachers and coaches a standing place to ask questions, share what's working, and learn from other districts running Canvas, which extends peer support well past what any single district's training calendar can cover. What not to do Don't lead with mandates. Districts that frame the rollout as compliance ("by November 1, all teachers will be using the new LMS for assignments") get compliance. They don't get use. The teachers who weren't on board on October 31 are probably not on board on November 2. Don't pretend the change is small. When leadership communication minimizes the workload of switching platforms, teachers stop trusting the rest of the communication. The changes, and the workload, are real. Acknowledging that doesn't weaken the case for the change, but it can build trust with your users. Don't skip the coaches. Instructional coaches and building-level technology coaches are the layer between the district decision and the classroom. If they're not bought in, teachers might see a rocky rollout in the classroom. At Shakopee Public Schools in Minnesota , the district's instructional and digital learning coaches ran the professional learning that carried Canvas into classrooms, using a workshop model to show teachers how to use it day to day. The teacher champion program A formal teacher champion for edtech programs is an easy, cost-effective adoption investment. Two to four teachers per building, with a clear charter, a small stipend, and protected time. They model use, they coach peers, they surface issues, and they bring the rest of the staff with them. The champion model works because it routes change through the people teachers already trust, instead of through the people who made the purchasing decision. That distinction can do a lot of work. How buy-in spread at Calcasieu Parish Calcasieu Parish didn't chase adoption through mandates. The district met teachers where they were, literally. Technology facilitators visit campuses every nine weeks, and teachers can book extra help whenever they hit a wall. Support comes as model lessons, coteaching, virtual sessions, and quick microtraining moments, and the district moved its professional development out of conference-room "sit and get" sessions into teachers' own classrooms, on their own equipment, aimed at what they were actually trying to do that week. Calcasieu Parish School Board serves more than 28,000 students across 60 school sites in and around Lake Charles, Louisiana. By 2021, the district faced a problem most K-12 leaders will recognize. Teachers were juggling a stack of disconnected edtech tools, and a run of COVID and hurricane-related closures had pushed the old learning management system past its limit. A committee of stakeholders evaluated the options and chose Canvas by Instructure.

Choosing the platform was the easy part. Anissa Fontenot, a technology facilitator for the district, is direct about what came next: "Transitioning to Canvas was the right move, even though it felt a little overwhelming at first."

Overcoming teacher resistance to new technology depends on how a district sequences everything around the decision: who helps make it, how teachers learn the platform, and what support reaches their buildings once the rollout begins. Calcasieu Parish treated that sequence as the actual project, and the buy-in followed.

Why teacher buy-in is the variable that matters most

Districts spend enormous time on platform evaluation and meaningfully less on adoption planning. The ratio is backwards. Teacher training and support are what most reliably determine whether new classroom technology gets used. A 2026 RAND review of EdTech trials found that teacher training and support consistently "made or broke" the success of those rollouts, and that the programs that worked were the ones with ongoing, built-in professional development.

A teacher who doesn't trust the new platform uses it for the bare minimum the district can see (think a posted syllabus and maybe a grade column) and keeps the real work where they've always kept it: a spreadsheet updated by hand, maybe even the paper system that got them through last year. The platform turns into a box to check rather than the connected learning hub it was bought to be. 

In a national RAND survey of K–12 educators, those working in coherent, aligned instructional systems reported stronger confidence in their teaching, while those dealing with inconsistent systems reported frustration and anxiety. A shared platform that every teacher actually uses is one of the pieces that keeps instruction consistent across a district. 

The five-phase model for teacher buy-in

The five phases below map to the year around a launch: evaluation roughly nine to twelve months out, the pilot cohort the semester before go-live, training over the summer, structured feedback through the first month teachers are live, and ongoing measurement after that. 

Phase one: bring teachers into the evaluation, not the announcement

Teacher voice in the LMS evaluation is important work in the vetting process, not a courtesy tacked onto the end of it. A district evaluation committee should include classroom teachers from at least three grade bands, special education, and a content area with high digital tool use (typically science or math). The committee meets through the evaluation. Teachers sit in vendor demos, run scenarios in sandbox environments, and contribute to the scoring rubric.

This can be done in parallel to other evaluation processes, so it doesn't have to slow the decision. But it does change who feels accountable to the decision after it's made.

Phase two: build the early adopter cohort

Before any district-wide rollout, identify 15 to 30 teachers to run an extended pilot. The right people here aren't necessarily the most tech-fluent teachers in the district, but they should have credibility in their buildings and be someone other staff turn to with a question, because what they say about the platform will move adoption further than any message from leadership.

The cohort needs three commitments from the district: real classroom use of the platform for a full semester instead of a two-week trial, a direct channel to the implementation team so their feedback actually shapes the rollout, and a stipend or course-release that makes clear the district counts this as work.

Phase three: design the training around what teachers actually do

Most LMS training is built around the platform. It walks through features, navigation, and configuration. Widespread LMS adoption is more effective when it's built around the teacher's actual work: how do you set up the first week of school in this platform, how do you build a unit, how do you handle a struggling student.

A working LMS training plan for teachers has three layers:

  • A short, role-specific live session that gets teachers through the first two weeks of school
  • An asynchronous library they can return to as they encounter new needs
  • Building-level coaching, ideally from the early adopter cohort, in the first 60 days

The third layer is the one most districts cut for budget reasons, but it has a high impact on adoption. Teachers might not reach out to the IT team if they have a question, but they are likely to ask the person down the hall if they need help.

Phase four: respond to the feedback you actually get

Teachers will surface things during rollout that the evaluation didn’t anticipate. Some of what they raise will be real platform constraints, some will be training gaps, and some will be configuration choices the district can change on its own. The work after that is sorting them quickly and reporting back.

A weekly digest sent to all staff for the first month, one that says plainly "here's what we heard, and here's what we're doing about it," is a high-impact communication for a district to provide in this stretch and proves the feedback channel is real.

Phase five: measure adoption, don't assume it

To a central office, a teacher can post a syllabus, log in once a week, and show up as "active", and this looks like success, but usage data is the only way to confirm genuine adoption. Canvas LMS has analytics that show which features teachers and students actually engage with, so a district can find the classrooms where use is thin and find ways to bring in support before the gap widens.

The work also doesn't end at launch. The RAND review is explicit that the rollouts that succeed are the ones with ongoing professional development, and every August brings a fresh group of teachers who missed the original training entirely. Adoption holds up when a district builds a standing onboarding path for new hires and a yearly refresh for everyone else, rather than treating training as a one-time event tied to go-live.

A district doesn't have to carry all of that alone, either. The Instructure Community gives teachers and coaches a standing place to ask questions, share what's working, and learn from other districts running Canvas, which extends peer support well past what any single district's training calendar can cover. 

What not to do

  • Don't lead with mandates. Districts that frame the rollout as compliance ("by November 1, all teachers will be using the new LMS for assignments") get compliance. They don't get use. The teachers who weren't on board on October 31 are probably not on board on November 2.
  • Don't pretend the change is small. When leadership communication minimizes the workload of switching platforms, teachers stop trusting the rest of the communication. The changes, and the workload, are real. Acknowledging that doesn't weaken the case for the change, but it can build trust with your users.
  • Don't skip the coaches. Instructional coaches and building-level technology coaches are the layer between the district decision and the classroom. If they're not bought in, teachers might see a rocky rollout in the classroom. At Shakopee Public Schools in Minnesota, the district's instructional and digital learning coaches ran the professional learning that carried Canvas into classrooms, using a workshop model to show teachers how to use it day to day.

The teacher champion program

A formal teacher champion for edtech programs is an easy, cost-effective adoption investment. Two to four teachers per building, with a clear charter, a small stipend, and protected time. They model use, they coach peers, they surface issues, and they bring the rest of the staff with them.

The champion model works because it routes change through the people teachers already trust, instead of through the people who made the purchasing decision. That distinction can do a lot of work.

How buy-in spread at Calcasieu Parish

Calcasieu Parish didn't chase adoption through mandates. The district met teachers where they were, literally. Technology facilitators visit campuses every nine weeks, and teachers can book extra help whenever they hit a wall. Support comes as model lessons, coteaching, virtual sessions, and quick microtraining moments, and the district moved its professional development out of conference-room "sit and get" sessions into teachers' own classrooms, on their own equipment, aimed at what they were actually trying to do that week. Canvas training runs through the district's existing IMPACT program, targeted by grade level and content area.

The spread came on its own from there. As Fontenot puts it: "Once we get teachers to see how Canvas LMS will make their lives easier, we get the buy-in. And once you get the buy-in from the teachers, then it spreads like wildfire amongst the other teachers." Canvas now runs from kindergarten through high school across the district, and because students use it for dual enrollment courses with SOWELA, the local community college, the platform follows them past graduation.

title: Art in Motion with Louisville’s Next Generation of Artists at InstructureCon
intro: 58 student artists, a fashion show, and outfits made entirely of trash. Discover the InstructureCon Louisville story behind Art in Motion and its impact.

body.text: The first day of InstructureCon is in the books, and the day closed out in high fashion. Well, high “trashion,” may be more like it. Literally. Let me explain: one of the best parts of hosting InstructureCon in different cities is the opportunity to partner with each community to develop a program, via our Impact in Action initiative, that leaves a lasting benefit after the event week. This year, we partnered with Louisville Visual Art , a staple in the Louisville art community for over a century, to develop a mentorship program matching young (and incredibly talented) artists with professional artists, supporting their growth, development, and encouragement in pursuing art along their life journey. LVA education director Annette Cable explained that the four-week summer program counters the typical drop-off in high school arts participation. The initiative, “Art in Motion,” involved 58 students (selected among local Louisville schools), who participated in a four-week workshop with local established artist Richard Sullivan and other professional artists . The project theme was “Trashion: Recycled Wearable Art,” in which the young artists were tasked with creating fashion sourced from items that would otherwise have been seen as refuse. A novel, and dare I say a sustainable, objective, and these students really delivered. InstructureCon attendees were treated to a fashion show during Tuesday’s welcome reception, where select artists from their program modeled their designs, and it truly was an amazing sight to see. I wasn’t alone in my awe, many attendees snapped photos and cheered as each student showcased their creation. It really was art in motion. This initiative is so important to validating the need for art in the community, as well as the developmental role art plays in young people’s lives. Chief Learning Officer Melissa Loble highlighted that investing in Art in Motion expands access to creative learning experiences that build critical problem-solving skills, offering the ultimate example of education in the making to end day one.

title: Is Your Edtech Stack Getting Stagnant? Going Beyond a K–12 Edtech Audit
intro: Is your K-12 edtech stack growing stagnant? Learn how to evaluate usage data, identify redundant tools, and ensure your technology truly supports student outcomes.

body.text: The renewal notice lands in your inbox in early June. It's a six-figure district-wide license for a supplemental reading tool that auto-renews in 30 days. You open a spreadsheet and find the login count, but realize you don't actually know if it reflects usage and if the tool is worth keeping. A new tech director inherits an old stack, licenses auto-renew, tools get duplicated, and regular responsibilities dominate the day-to-day. And these commonplace occurrences can prevent slowing down to ask a central question: Does our technology actually help teachers and students? A license report helps, but you need a more comprehensive framework to assess if your stack is helping or hindering your district and its goals. What can you measure? You might want to start with renewal dates and budget lines, but pause and consider usage data instead. Pull four numbers for every tool in your stack: active users, purchased licenses, how often they’ve been used over the past 90 days, and which roles are actually logging in, whether teachers, students, or mostly admins running reports. From there, sort your tools by instructional category, like formative assessment, supplemental curriculum, communication, or productivity, for example. You'll almost certainly find doubles: two tools that do the same job for different grade levels, or a legacy platform still running alongside its more widely used replacement. Platform redundancy means twice the cost and the possibility of inequitable outcomes if one platform has more evidence on student outcomes. If your district doesn't have a clean way to map this out, the Building Efficient Edtech Ecosystems guide shows how districts inventory their tech stack without overwhelming their teams. If usage tells you what's being opened, the next step is figuring out what story that data is telling. What can’t the data tell you? Login counts don't tell you the problems your students or teachers face once inside the platform. Look at your help desk and sort your support tickets by tool over the last school year. Look for red flags like high ticket volume on a specific platform. That won’t show up in a vendor's renewal pitch, but if a tool consistently causes problems, it eats up your team’s time on higher-value work while frustrating end users. This can also give you a data point to consider when deciding which to keep among redundant tools. Integration quality gives you another data point. Consider these questions that reveal deeper problems: Does the tool connect cleanly with your SIS and LMS, or does someone have to manually enter data or create custom workarounds? You can work through poor interoperability for a while, but what if the person who knows how to do that work leaves the district? Or if a data import breaks in the middle of the year? Vendor lock-in is the final piece to look at. You might be working against proprietary data formats and have limited export options. High switching costs are another flag worth documenting before renewal season. If you can't easily move your data out of a platform, the vendor may hold more power than you’d like. Once you've mapped usage and have qualitative data points to work with, it’s time to score your stack. How do tools score? A scorecard doesn't have to be complicated to be useful. Four criteria cover most of what you need to make a defensible case to district leadership. Score each tool on adoption rate, support burden, integration quality, and evidence of student impact . Not every tool will score high on all four—a niche assessment tool might have low adoption but strong outcome data, and that's worth knowing. When a tool scores low on three or four, it’s time to consider if it’s worth the low score in the other categories. If a tool is impactful and integrates well but has low adoption, you may look at training options. If a platform is widely adopted but lags in the other three areas, it may be time to look at alternatives. That's your shortlist for consolidation conversations. Keep in mind that getting trustworthy evidence of student impact requires instructional leaders or professional researchers in the conversation. A tool your tech team can't evaluate for learning outcomes shouldn't get scored without curriculum and instruction input. Tools like LearnPlatform by Instructure help districts run evidence-based evaluations at the tool level, so those conversations are grounded in data, not opinions or anecdotes. Even if no tools get cut this cycle, you'll have a baseline for next year's renewals and a record that makes future decisions easier. Bad tool or bad rollout? Before you decide to consolidate or not renew a tool, ask one more question: Did staff actually get a fair shot at using it? Low adoption doesn't always equate to a bad product. The rollout might have happened during testing season, or training was optional (and thus, largely skipped). If a tool scores low on adoption but hits the other criteria, look at the rollout history before writing it off . Talk to a few teachers and check whether and when professional development was offered. This distinction matters because cutting a tool your district didn't fully implement doesn't solve the underlying problem; it just restarts the procurement cycle and wastes more time and resources, while student outcomes could be better supported with stronger tools. "Is this tool being used?" is a necessary question. "Does the district have the capacity and conditions to use it well?" is just as important. If the answer’s no, that's still useful information. It could be the right tool at the wrong time. Or teachers need more structured training . Or your stack is too big for your team to reasonably support. Either way, the conversation moves from cut-or-keep to invest-or-exit, and gets you closer to the right tech stack . Start (don’t finish) with an audit Assessing your K–12 edtech stack won't fix everything by next school year. It’s an interactive, ongoing process. A tool may be acquired, but now comes at a higher price; state requirements around accessibility or privacy shift; your district goals change focus; and the budget forecast could turn. So your process needs to be flexible, too. But you still gain a little more clarity into what's being used, what’s collecting digital dust, which tools are evidence-backed, and how much support they require from your IT team. That clarity means renewal conversations start with workable data, and that’s worth working towards.

Start (don’t finish) with an audit

title: The Student Journey Doesn’t End at Graduation: Simplifying Transfers, Mobility, and Student Records
intro: Modernize your school's records management. Improve transcript retrieval, ensure FERPA compliance, and support student mobility with digital solutions that simplify the student journey.

body.text: Somewhere right now, a 34-year-old is sitting in a parking lot on her lunch break, on hold with a college she left in 2011. Her manager told her the promotion is hers if she can show a completed degree. She has 58 credits sitting at a school two states away, and the person on the phone has just told her the registrar who would know where her file is retired years ago. She's not going to get that promotion this quarter. Maybe not this year. Last year, more than 1 million adults who had left college without a credential went back to finish, the most the National Student Clearinghouse Research Center has ever recorded. Every one of those comebacks depended on something small: someone, somewhere, had to find an old record and get it to a new school. When that record lives in a filing cabinet, on a reel of microfilm, or in the inbox of a person who no longer works there, "finding it" can take weeks. Sometimes it just never happens, and a person quietly gives up. As of the 2023-24 school year, 43.1 million Americans had left higher education with some college credit and no credential to show for it . The million who made it back are the lucky ones. For a lot of the other 42 million, a hard-to-find transcript isn't the only thing standing between them and the finish line. But it's a real one, and it's one we know how to fix. That's the thing about student records that's easy to miss when you're deep in a school year: a person's record has to outlive their time with you. It travels when a family moves in the middle of March or a when a kid switches districts. And it has to still be findable a decade later, when that same kid, now grown, decides they're ready to go back and finish what they started. The record has a longer life than the relationship that created it. Most schools aren't set up that way. The cost of doing it by hand Paper is not the enemy; print magazines can be a luxurious reading experience (or a way to pass time on a plane); a card in the mail is an almost universally welcomed experience (probably); a sticky Post-it is still an excellent way to leave a note, mark up a white board during a meeting, or scribble down a quick grocery note. The US stationery market was valued at almost 60 billion dollars in 2025. People love paper, and it has always loved them back. But records are almost always easier when handled digitally. There is a time and a place for paper, but schools records aren’t one of them. A few of the ways that plays out: Space . Records take up rooms. Real rooms, with real square footage, that could hold a counselor or a program or almost anything more useful than boxes. Most schools are still paying to keep them dry, secure, and eventually scanned anyway. The scavenger hunt . A paper file can't be searched. Tracking down one transcript can eat an afternoon, and that's if the file is where it's supposed to be. AACRAO ran the number s on this and found schools typically save 25 to 35 percent by moving from paper to electronic transcripts once you count the paper, the postage, the matching, and the re-keying. That afternoon in the storage room has a price tag. The one person who knows. Every office has them: the staff member who can find anything because the system lives in their head. Then they retire; goodbye, system. The privacy near-miss. When you can't track who touched a record or control who sees it, FERPA is a risk. Sometimes the clock isn't yours to set FERPA gives schools a hard ceiling: respond to a records request within 45 days . Plenty of states are stricter; California gives you 5 days, and you can't hold a record hostage over an unpaid fee. Connecticut gives districts 10 days from the moment they learn a student enrolled somewhere new. Now picture meeting a five-day deadline with a process that depends on the right person being in the building, remembering the right drawer, and getting to the post office. What it feels like when it just works Move those same records into a system built to hold them, and the day changes for the people doing the work in an "I found it in ten seconds and got to go home on time" way. Anyone with the right permissions can pull a record in seconds, not spelunk through cabinets and inboxes. The data sits somewhere secure, with real access controls, so FERPA compliance is just how the system works instead of one more thing to stay on top of. Registrars can actually see their own data, answer real questions, and catch patterns, rather than spending the week playing file clerk. That storage room? You get it back. Where to start (you don't have to boil the ocean) If you're reading this thinking "great, and where exactly would I find the time," fair. Nobody's suggesting you digitize thirty years of paper by Friday. Here's a sane order of operations, roughly in the sequence that tends to pay off fastest. Take inventory. Spend some part of a week just figuring out where your records actually live. How much is paper only? How much got scanned but still can't be searched? And the honest one: last time someone needed a record fast, how long did it really take? That number is your baseline. Hold your turnaround time up against your state's deadline. If the law says five days and your reality is closer to three weeks, congratulations! You've just found the most persuasive line item in your next budget conversation. Third, digitize the stuff that moves the most. The highest-stress requests in any records office are the time-sensitive ones: a student applying somewhere, a transcript a job offer is waiting on, a mid-year transfer. Start there. Decide who owns FERPA before you decide who owns the project. Moving records changes who can see what and how you prove it. That's a compliance call as much as a tech one, and it's a much friendlier conversation to have before anything moves than after something leaks. Each of those steps maps to a piece of how Parchment by Instructure thinks about the same problem. Instead of treating every records request as its own little fire drill, Parchment keeps a learner's record moving with them, through every transition, for as long as they need it. Many parts, one journey Parchment treats learner records as a set of connected jobs, not a pile of separate tools you have to duct-tape together. Document Management gives your records one real home. Old files, current student documents, everything your credentialed staff reach for, all of it searchable, secure, and access-controlled. The filing room, and the anxiety that comes with it, retires. District Transfer handles the moment a student changes schools. No more mailing a record and crossing your fingers. It moves electronically, school to school, which closes the gap where transcripts vanish and helps you actually hit the deadline your state is counting. Award Transcript Services covers the request itself, whether it comes the week after graduation or ten years into a career. A former student orders an official transcript and sends it wherever they're headed next. The Parchment Learner Dashboard hands all of this to the person it's actually about. One place for learners to see and send their own transcripts, diplomas, and credentials. The record follows them, instead of staying locked up at a school they left a lifetime ago. Records should outlive the classroom Transcripts might matter most long after the student walks out the door: when they transfer, when they apply somewhere new, when they finally come back to finish. Keeping a record findable, safe, and ready to travel is how a school keeps showing up for people it stopped teaching years ago. Not all 42 million at once. Just one at a time, starting with whoever's sitting in that parking lot, on hold, hoping someone picks up. Find out more about how Parchment opens doors across a lifetime-long learning journey in K-12, higher education, and beyond (and makes life easier for admins along the way).

She has 58 credits sitting at a school two states away, and the person on the phone has just told her the registrar who would know where her file is retired years ago. She's not going to get that promotion this quarter. Maybe not this year.

Last year, more than 1 million adults who had left college without a credential went back to finish, the most the National Student Clearinghouse Research Center has ever recorded. Every one of those comebacks depended on something small: someone, somewhere, had to find an old record and get it to a new school. When that record lives in a filing cabinet, on a reel of microfilm, or in the inbox of a person who no longer works there, "finding it" can take weeks. Sometimes it just never happens, and a person quietly gives up.

As of the 2023-24 school year, 43.1 million Americans had left higher education with some college credit and no credential to show for it.  The million who made it back are the lucky ones. For a lot of the other 42 million, a hard-to-find transcript isn't the only thing standing between them and the finish line. But it's a real one, and it's one we know how to fix.

That's the thing about student records that's easy to miss when you're deep in a school year: a person's record has to outlive their time with you. It travels when a family moves in the middle of March or a when a kid switches districts. And it has to still be findable a decade later, when that same kid, now grown, decides they're ready to go back and finish what they started. The record has a longer life than the relationship that created it. Most schools aren't set up that way.

The cost of doing it by hand

Paper is not the enemy; print magazines can be a luxurious reading experience (or a way to pass time on a plane); a card in the mail is an almost universally welcomed experience (probably); a sticky Post-it is still an excellent way to leave a note, mark up a white board during a meeting, or scribble down a quick grocery note. The US stationery market was valued at almost 60 billion dollars in 2025. People love paper, and it has always loved them back. 

But records are almost always easier when handled digitally. There is a time and a place for paper, but schools records aren’t one of them. A few of the ways that plays out:

  • Space. Records take up rooms. Real rooms, with real square footage, that could hold a counselor or a program or almost anything more useful than boxes. Most schools are still paying to keep them dry, secure, and eventually scanned anyway.
  • The scavenger hunt. A paper file can't be searched. Tracking down one transcript can eat an afternoon, and that's if the file is where it's supposed to be. AACRAO ran the numbers on this and found schools typically save 25 to 35 percent by moving from paper to electronic transcripts once you count the paper, the postage, the matching, and the re-keying. That afternoon in the storage room has a price tag. 
  • The one person who knows. Every office has them: the staff member who can find anything because the system lives in their head. Then they retire; goodbye, system. 
  • The privacy near-miss. When you can't track who touched a record or control who sees it, FERPA is a risk.

Sometimes the clock isn't yours to set

FERPA gives schools a hard ceiling: respond to a records request within 45 days. Plenty of states are stricter; California gives you 5 days, and you can't hold a record hostage over an unpaid fee. Connecticut gives districts 10 days from the moment they learn a student enrolled somewhere new. Now picture meeting a five-day deadline with a process that depends on the right person being in the building, remembering the right drawer, and getting to the post office. 

What it feels like when it just works

Move those same records into a system built to hold them, and the day changes for the people doing the work in an "I found it in ten seconds and got to go home on time" way.

  • Anyone with the right permissions can pull a record in seconds, not spelunk through cabinets and inboxes.
  • The data sits somewhere secure, with real access controls, so FERPA compliance is just how the system works instead of one more thing to stay on top of.
  • Registrars can actually see their own data, answer real questions, and catch patterns, rather than spending the week playing file clerk.
  • That storage room? You get it back.

Where to start (you don't have to boil the ocean)

If you're reading this thinking "great, and where exactly would I find the time," fair. Nobody's suggesting you digitize thirty years of paper by Friday. Here's a sane order of operations, roughly in the sequence that tends to pay off fastest.

  1. Take inventory. Spend some part of a week just figuring out where your records actually live. How much is paper only? How much got scanned but still can't be searched? And the honest one: last time someone needed a record fast, how long did it really take? That number is your baseline. 
  2. Hold your turnaround time up against your state's deadline. If the law says five days and your reality is closer to three weeks, congratulations! You've just found the most persuasive line item in your next budget conversation. 
  3. Third, digitize the stuff that moves the most. The highest-stress requests in any records office are the time-sensitive ones: a student applying somewhere, a transcript a job offer is waiting on, a mid-year transfer. Start there. 
  4. Decide who owns FERPA before you decide who owns the project. Moving records changes who can see what and how you prove it. That's a compliance call as much as a tech one, and it's a much friendlier conversation to have before anything moves than after something leaks.

Each of those steps maps to a piece of how Parchment by Instructure thinks about the same problem. Instead of treating every records request as its own little fire drill, Parchment keeps a learner's record moving with them, through every transition, for as long as they need it.

Many parts, one journey

Parchment treats learner records as a set of connected jobs, not a pile of separate tools you have to duct-tape together.

Document Management gives your records one real home. Old files, current student documents, everything your credentialed staff reach for, all of it searchable, secure, and access-controlled. The filing room, and the anxiety that comes with it, retires.

District Transfer handles the moment a student changes schools. No more mailing a record and crossing your fingers. It moves electronically, school to school, which closes the gap where transcripts vanish and helps you actually hit the deadline your state is counting.

Award Transcript Services covers the request itself, whether it comes the week after graduation or ten years into a career. A former student orders an official transcript and sends it wherever they're headed next. 

The Parchment Learner Dashboard hands all of this to the person it's actually about. One place for learners to see and send their own transcripts, diplomas, and credentials. The record follows them, instead of staying locked up at a school they left a lifetime ago.

Records should outlive the classroom

Transcripts might matter most long after the student walks out the door: when they transfer, when they apply somewhere new, when they finally come back to finish.

Keeping a record findable, safe, and ready to travel is how a school keeps showing up for people it stopped teaching years ago. Not all 42 million at once. Just one at a time, starting with whoever's sitting in that parking lot, on hold, hoping someone picks up.

Find out more about how Parchment opens doors across a lifetime-long learning journey in K-12, higher education, and beyond (and makes life easier for admins along the way).

title: How Workforce Pell Grants Are Helping to Evolve Equity in Education
intro: Learn how the expansion of Federal Pell Grant eligibility to short-term, industry-aligned programs is fostering greater equity in education and opening new pathways for adult learners to achieve upward mobility.

body.text: The introduction of the Federal Pell Grant program in the 1970s was a major step forward in educational equity in higher education. By focusing on underserved communities, it provided non-traditional students (read: those not enrolling in a 4-year degree program straight from high school) with more accessible pathways to better employment and lifelong learning. In 2025, 48% of Pell Grant recipients were independent students, including adult learners, veterans, single parents, and students who had aged out of dependency status, and 45% of recipients were aged 23 or older. But as important as Pell Grants are to equity and accessibility in higher ed, they’re limited in their scope. While the program has served a lot of adult and low-income learners, these funds have still been most advantageous to a specific kind of learner: young enough to enroll full-time, flexible enough to follow a 16-week academic calendar, and committed enough to spend two to four years pursuing a degree before earning their first dollar using the skills they learned. Expanding Pell Grant access to short-term programs is an overdue step in serving students and expanding pathways to upward mobility. Workforce Pell is for the adult warehouse worker looking to move into advanced manufacturing, the GED holder who wants a certified nursing assistant credential, and the unemployed logistics coordinator with a mortgage and 90 days of savings who needs to re-enter the workforce quickly. What actually changed with the Federal Pell Grant program On July 1, 2026, Federal Pell Grant eligibility was extended to short-term, industry-aligned certificate programs. Federal aid can now flow to a kind of program it never supported before: programs between 8 and 15 weeks between 150 and 599 clock hours focused on high-skill, high-wage, or in-demand occupations identified by state workforce boards The equity implication here is as significant as the original Pell Grant motion was over fifty years ago. When federal aid only reaches degree-seeking students, the entire machinery of American higher education orients around degrees. Colleges prioritize programs that qualify for aid, and advisors push students toward them. Short-term, skills-based offerings are often priced at full cost to the learner and sometimes deprioritized when staff scheduling accommodations need to be made. Opening Pell to short-term programs tells institutions that the adult learner pursuing a 12-week certificate is a legitimate federal-aid recipient, not a second-class student. This evolution will change how colleges invest, how they design programs, and who they design them for. The 70/70 rule is an equity mechanism The part of Workforce Pell that sounds like red tape (the 70% completion rate, the 70% job placement rate within 180 days, the value-added earnings requirement) is actually the part that does the most equity work. The history of short-term, non-federal workforce programs includes plenty of examples of low-quality credentials that didn't produce economic mobility. Think bootcamps that charged adult learners thousands of dollars and placed a small fraction of graduates into further education, with certificates that didn't articulate. Adult learning programs often look like opportunities… that deliver little to no meaningful change. Adult learners paying out of pocket have often had limited ways to assess program quality in advance. Workforce Pell's accountability rules close that information gap. A program only keeps its Pell eligibility if 70% of students complete, 70% of completers find jobs within six months, and the earnings those completers see exceed 150% of the Federal Poverty Level after accounting for tuition. The value-added earnings requirement says federal aid won't flow to programs that charge more than they produce in economic mobility. For adult learners, some of whom have been burned by credentials that didn't pay, this is the first time the federal government has taken on the job of filtering out programs that don't deliver. It's not a perfect mechanism, but it shifts risk off the learner and creates more certainty when weighing their education options. Who does the new Workforce Pell actually reach? The adult learner population Workforce Pell is designed to serve looks different from the traditional Pell population in ways that matter for how institutions have to operate. These are people who may not have a standard academic transcript. Some finished high school, but some didn't. Many have GEDs; some have associate degrees that didn't lead to employment; some have work histories that should count for something but don't. Regardless of their backgrounds, all of these students are looking to continuing education to help them advance in work, but might find themselves facing an admissions system that wants to see 11th-grade algebra grades. They're not the same group of students who are shopping for a college experience. They're looking for the fastest credible route to a higher-paying job. Reaching them requires operational changes most institutions haven't fully made yet. Supporting these learners will require: an enrollment process that doesn't assume a traditional transcript course content that works on a phone in 20-minute pockets credentials that are usable the day a student completes the program a path from a short-term sprint back into a longer degree if the student wants one Qualifying for aid is one piece of increasing equity, but delivering on the full potential hinges on whether programs are actually built to serve the people the aid is meant for. Access without infrastructure is a promise, not an outcome This is the part that matters for institutional leaders reading this post. Workforce Pell has opened a door. Whether adult learners actually walk through it depends on whether the institutions closest to them—community colleges, workforce systems, regional employers—have built what it takes to serve them on the other side. This means: enrollment systems that don't turn non-matriculated adults away at the front door. instructional design that treats adult learners as the primary audience, not an edge case. verifiable digital credentials that a student can use the day she earns them, stackable toward future degrees if she decides to keep going. longitudinal data systems that prove, year after year, that the programs are working for the people they're supposed to work for. Institutions that build this infrastructure will capture Workforce Pell dollars. Adult learners will trust them with the next phase of their careers. And states, workforce boards, and federal regulators will look to them as the model for how publicly funded workforce development should function. The Alabama Community College System is one example. Alabama built a unified, statewide workforce development architecture, connecting more than 1,700 credentials directly to active job openings and creating a single operating model across the state. The work ahead Evolving equity in education through Workforce Pell isn't going to just happen because legislation was passed. It will happen because individual institutions decide, program by program, to do the operational work of serving adult learners the way the policy assumes they'll be served. These institutions will have a significant impact on how adult learner equity looks in the next decade of American higher education. Check out our Workforce Pell Checklist to find out how to meet the requirements to receive new Pell Grant funding and become a state-wide workforce engine that can upskill and train adult learners and provide more opportunities for every student. FAQ How do Workforce Pell Grants work? A Workforce Pell Grant is federal money for a short-term certificate program that you don't pay back. It works like a traditional Pell Grant, with one big difference in what it covers. Students apply through the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA), and the U.S. Department of Education uses that information to decide who qualifies and how much they receive, based on financial need, cost of attendance, and enrollment status. What's new, as of July 1, 2026, is the kind of program the aid can fund: certificate programs that run 8 to 15 weeks, span 150 to 599 clock hours, and train students for high-skill, high-wage, or in-demand jobs identified by state workforce boards. Workforce Pell draws from the same pool as the traditional grant, so for the 2026-27 award year the maximum award is $7,395. The grant is meant for undergraduates who haven't yet earned a bachelor's degree, and there's no age limit, so the 19-year-old and the 45-year-old changing careers qualify on the same terms. Programs also have to earn their eligibility by hitting completion, job placement, and earnings benchmarks, so the funds only flow to programs that actually pay off for the people taking them.

title: Rebuilding the Education Blueprint: How to Turn Innovation into a Shared Strategy
intro: Educational innovation is currently fragmented as institutions test AI in isolation. Discover why it’s time to move beyond pilot programs and collaborate on a unified, sustainable roadmap for the future of learning.

body.text: Part two of two. Visit here for part one . To recap the first part of my notes on education in the making, I talked about why the old model of learning has to prove itself again, and why so few of us have the AI playbook figured out yet. Today I want to talk about what's actually happening while we wait for that playbook: everyone is building at once, but how many of those plays become standards that we can all employ? Learners are experimenting with AI tutors and study tools faster than most institutions can write a policy about them. Faculty are quietly testing new ways to teach, grade, and give feedback. Institutions are piloting programs, partnerships, and platforms. System administrators are trying to keep all of it secure, compliant, and standing upright. These are all valid challenges and approaches, much happening without permission, and valuable IF they all lead to an end goal in which all parties feel like they know how their roles play within it. That's exactly what this moment calls for. When the ground is genuinely shifting, you don't want everyone waiting for a memo. You want people testing, failing fast, and learning in public. That instinct is healthy. It's what real innovation looks like from the inside, messy, uneven, and a little chaotic. But it can't stay unstructured forever Why experimentation needs direction To my earlier point, experimentation without direction turns into fragmentation. Here's the risk. Every learner, classroom, and institution figuring this out on its own, with no shared reference point, eventually stops looking like innovation and starts looking like drift. One school's AI policy contradicts the school down the road. One professor's approach to AI-assisted writing has nothing to do with the approach one floor up. Learners move between these environments and get a different set of rules every time. That's not agility. That's fragmentation wearing agility's clothes. Let’s continue to experiment, let’s learn, unlearn, and relearn . But, we have to keep our eyes on the horizon, and that’s to start building consensus around what's actually working, and turn that into a roadmap the whole field can use. Yes, there will be outliers, and nuance depending on the sector. But, it’s the formation of the backbone of the new learning model that allows for nuance, not for wide variation. We need action and we need it today. That takes all four groups in the room together: learners, who know firsthand what helps them learn; educators, who know what holds up in front of a real class; institution/organization leadership, who have to think about outcomes and accreditation and trust; and system administrators, who have to make sure whatever gets built is actually secure and sustainable at scale. Where the roadmap gets built This is exactly why InstructureCon exists, and exactly why this year's theme, "Education in the Making," isn't just a clever line. It's a description of the work. More than 200 sessions, workshops, and meetups will bring together the people actually doing this work: testing, comparing notes, and figuring out what's real versus what's just noise. My ask is simple. Come to be inspired. But, also come to compare what you're testing against what a thousand other people in the room are testing, and leave with a clearer sense of where the field is actually heading, not just where your institution is headed alone. "Education in the making" isn't a slogan we picked because it sounded good. It's the honest state of things right now. The system is being rebuilt while we're standing inside it, by learners, educators, institutions, and administrators who are all, in their own way, refusing to wait for permission. The next stage of that rebuild doesn't have to be built by any one of us alone. Let's build it together, starting in Louisville.

title: Rebuilding the Education Blueprint: We’re All in This Together
intro: The traditional education model is becoming obsolete. Discover why institutions need to reset, rethink the needs of modern learners, and embrace AI to collaboratively build the future of education.

body.text: Part one of two. Ask anyone in education today their view on the current landscape, and while the answers may be different, you can bet they’re all leading back to a single source of truth; the old learning model is gone, and few have a solid handle on what today’s model actually is. And, while that may appear concerning on the surface (and truth be told, it is), if you look at the larger picture, it’s a tremendous opportunity to collectively rewrite the new model; penned by both educators and learners. But, first we need to look at the reality of things. We are facing significant headwinds across the board. Institutions are facing enrollment and retention challenges, the value of technology in classrooms is being misunderstood or underused. Employers keep saying the same thing: graduates show up with credentials but not always with the judgment the job requires. Most institutions can see all of this. What they don't have is an answer. Here's the part that should be reassuring: no one does. Not yet. This isn’t due to anyone being stuck in their ways, it’s just the reality of today. The model most of us grew up with, sit in a room, absorb information, prove you absorbed it, get a credential, was built for a world where knowledge was scarce and hard to reach. That world is gone. Learners today can get an explanation, a tutor, a study plan, and instant feedback from a phone in their pocket. The scarcity that justified the old model doesn't exist anymore. So the model has to earn its place again. It can't just point to tradition. This isn’t new news, but bears repeating, and often. Institutions know something has shifted, but may be reticent to stop and rebuild in public. It feels safer to keep running the same race a little faster: tighten the curriculum, add a workshop, update the syllabus language. Stopping altogether feels like standing still while everyone else moves, or worse, like walking off a cliff no one can see the bottom of. As long as there isn’t a widely adopted new model, the old model will continue to be THE model. I understand the fear, but I question if it’s warranted. I’m blessed to be given opportunities to regularly speak with many different folks within the education community, and what I can tell you: there's solid ground on the other side of that reset. You don't have to build the parachute alone. But, we all can’t build different parachutes and expect to land on the ground at the same time. Three honest moves to reset Pushing reset starts with three honest moves, and they're not sequential. They happen together. First, institutions need the confidence to actually hit reset, not just adjust around the margins. That means naming what's not working instead of defending it. And, they have to be brave to acknowledge there is a need for them to revisit their approach and ask for guidance on a new one. Second, we have to get serious about who today's learner actually is. Not the learner in the strategic plan. The one sitting in the class right now, who's already using AI to study, already comparing a degree against a bootcamp or a certificate, already asking what any of this is for. title: How to Pilot a New LMS Before Your District Commits
intro: Learn how to run a successful LMS pilot program in your district. Validate platform functionality in your own environment to make evidence-based decisions before you commit.

body.text: A district is three weeks into vendor evaluation, deep in feature matrices, pricing, and reference calls, when the assistant superintendent for instruction asks the question none of those things is really answering: will this actually work in our buildings, on our network, with our teachers and our students? Every reference district she called says it works for them. But none of them run her network, teach her kids, or hand devices to her staff, so hers is the only district where the answer counts. Testing new LMS before full rollout is the difference between buying a platform on the strength of a polished demo and buying one on the strength of evidence from your own classrooms. Vendor demos are useful, but they’re not evidence like a pilot is. When Oconomowoc Area School District in Wisconsin moved off Google Classroom, the case wasn't made from a deck. Their own instructional-technology coaches worked out what teachers and students could do with assignments, submission types, and feedback in Canvas, then brought the rest of the district along. Learning how to pilot a new LMS in schools is how anxious district leaders answer the real question: Is this thing actually going to work in our buildings, or are we about to sign a three-year contract on a hunch? The job a pilot actually does A pilot does three things no other evaluation activity can. First, it shows you the platform under real conditions: your teachers, your network, your devices, your students. Your bandwidth at 8 a.m. when every class logs in at once, your SIS sync, your oldest Chromebooks, your multilingual learners. A vendor sandbox can’t simulate as many of your specific circumstances. Second, it generates the evidence the decision actually rests on. When the contract goes to the board, someone will ask "why this one?” Teacher voices, classroom data, and observed adoption from your own buildings answer that question more fully than any set of references. That same evidence does double duty later, when you have to defend the line item in an edtech budget conversation . Third, it builds the early-adopter cohort the rollout depends on. The teachers who run the pilot become the people who help support full adoption during rollout. How to design the pilot Pick the right schools Most districts pick pilot schools by who volunteers, but the schools that should pilot aren't necessarily the most enthusiastic or the highest-performing. They need to represent the range of conditions across your district: a building with strong tech leadership, one with average tech leadership, one with weaker home connectivity, one with a heavy multilingual-learner population, and a building at each grade band you serve. Three to five schools is usually enough to ensure variation that represents enough district conditions (Smaller district? This guide to choosing an LMS walks the same logic at your size). Define the duration honestly A real pilot needs to run a full semester, because a semester-long full learning cycle is how long it takes to surface questions that need to be answered: does it hold up under unit-assessment season, does it handle the gradebook close, does it integrate cleanly across a full marking period. Districts compress pilots because the board wants a decision by spring, but this compression can mean hitting a huge operational snag during rollout. Build the evaluation criteria up front Pilot success metrics have to exist before the pilot starts, not after. And districts increasingly demand this kind of evidence before they buy: in the 2026 EdTech Top 40 report from LearnPlatform by Instructure, 52.5 percent of the most-used tools carried at least ESSA Level IV evidence (the entry tier of the Every Student Succeeds Act framework). A pilot is how you generate that evidence for your own context instead of waiting for a vendor to hand it to you. A working set of pilot program metrics that education teams can use includes: Teacher use: Active teachers per week, and what they're actually doing (assignments, discussions, gradebook, feedback). Student experience: Submission patterns, time on platform, qualitative feedback. Family experience: Parent observer enrollment, use of family-facing communication. Operational health: SIS sync errors, helpdesk tickets per teacher, integration uptime. Pedagogical quality: What teachers can do in this platform that they couldn't do before, captured through structured interviews. Capture that explicitly, ideally against the same evidence tiers your eventual RFP will ask vendors about. How to capture the evidence Teacher voice Structured interviews with pilot teachers at three points: week four, mid-semester, and the end. The same questions each time, so you can watch the answers change. Recordings or detailed notes are more helpful than hallway conversations in this instance. Classroom observation A small set of observations during the pilot, run by instructional leadership rather than IT. Observe what the teacher is doing with students, and whether the platform supports that or gets in the way. Whether they're "using the LMS" is the wrong thing to count. Quantitative data You should have access to platform usage analytics, either in a self-serve dashboard in a report from the vendor. Cross-reference it with your SIS data and your helpdesk logs. The gap between what teachers say is happening and what the data shows is happening is often the most useful finding of the whole pilot. Student and family input A short survey to pilot students and families at the end (this five questions, not 30; you want insight, not overwhelm). How to evaluate the pilot results A working pilot evaluation answers four questions. Did teachers end up doing more of what they wanted to do, or less? This is the one that matters most. If teachers finished the pilot feeling the platform expanded what they could do, it passed. If the same tasks are harder or take longer than before, it doesn’t. Did the operational integrations hold up? SIS sync, identity provider, gradebook passback, parent observer creation. If any of the infrastructure fails during the pilot, it’s important to consider what that failure would look like a district level. Did the vendor show up? Think about the evolution of your vendor relationship during the pilot and get feedback on their response times, escalation paths, and overall problem-solving partnership. A pilot is a vendor evaluation as much as a platform one. What does year one look like across the district? Use the pilot to build the full-rollout plan: training hours required, helpdesk volume to budget for, integration projects to scope. The pilot is a big part of the data set the rollout is built from. What this looks like in practice Run that vendor evaluation scenario forward. The district pilots for a full semester at four buildings, two on Canvas by Instructure and two on a competing platform. By the end, the assistant superintendent has her answer about what instruction looks like in her schools, and she has it from the teachers in her own buildings rather than from a vendor reference. The decision the board approves rests on evidence the district generated itself, and the rollout the next year moves faster because the pilot already trained the people involved in helping to roll it out. Real districts follow the same pattern. If you're in evaluation now and Canvas is on your list, the Instructure team can help you scope a pilot that produces evidence instead of talking points. Request a Canvas LMS demo and ask, what a pilot would look like for your district: which buildings, how long, what the vendor commits to. Those answers are some of your first data point

title: How to Think About Open Standards for AI in the Classroom
intro: Learn how agentic AI is reshaping edtech interoperability. Discover why maintaining open standards and building a connective context layer is key to responsible, effective AI integration in the classroom.

body.text: Zach Pendleton's 10-year-old son wants to be a stuntman. The current plan involves a bike ramp, which is how Pendleton, the chief architect at Instructure, recently ended up at the hardware store buying wood, screws, and fasteners, then teaching his son how to assemble them so the ramp would actually hold. The boy was motivated, mostly because he was a little afraid the whole thing might collapse out from under him on the first jump. How do you let something powerful build on everything already in place without the structure giving way? That question is also a useful way to talk about agentic AI in edtech, and it's the one Pendleton brought to a conversation with fellow technologist Mike Mast on Educast 3000. Mast is principal group program manager for Microsoft Education and a board member at 1EdTech , the consortium behind many of the open standards connecting edtech tools today. Here's how they think about it, starting with what's shifting underneath edtech and ending with the question that should govern how anyone deploys this. The agent changes what interoperability is for For years, interoperability meant getting two systems to agree on the same vocabulary, the same data schema, and the same API definitions. If you can get them to speak the same language, they could talk. An AI agent rewrites that requirement. Given a clear enough description of a system, an agent can work with a new vocabulary, interpret an unfamiliar schema, and call an API it hasn't encountered before. How far that goes depends on how well each system describes itself. It matters less that every system conforms to one identical rulebook, and more that each system can describe itself to an agent well enough to be used. At the same time, that doesn't make older standards optional, and it doesn't replace them. Ask whether an agent should learn to speak LTI or OneRoster directly and the answer is mostly no. Those specifications were built for specific jobs that haven't gone away: LTI governs how a learning tool launches inside a platform and fits into a person's path through a course. OneRoster moves roster and enrollment data from one system to another. Caliper carries the activity and event data that tells you what actually happened. What changes when an agent is introduced is the question sitting on top of it: not "how do we make the systems agree," but "how does each system explain itself to something that can adapt?" The goal used to be making the systems agree. Now it's describing each system well enough that something adaptive can use it. The vocabulary stops having to match. As Mast put it, "it doesn't matter if it calls an entity a course offering or a section, as long as that can be described to the agent." The standards still carry the load underneath. The connective layer that gives an agent context Even with an agent’s ability to reason, there is a gap; namely, context. A Canvas course often doesn't store its content directly. It stores links out to other learning tools built to carry a person from the platform into the tool. Hand one of those links to an agent and it might stall, because an LTI link isn't a readable web address. It's a launch handshake, built to sign a specific person into a specific tool and drop them where they need to be. There's nothing to fetch: no page at the other end, and whatever content exists is locked behind a login meant for a human. A person clicks through, signs in without thinking about it, and sees in a second whether they've hit a reading, a quiz, or a video call. The agent just sees an address it can't open. So getting in is only half of it. To actually help, an agent needs a semantic understanding of the course, the ability to find related pages, assignments, and content by meaning rather than by exact label. If a student is working on photosynthesis, the agent has to pull what's relevant from across the course and reason over it. Mast pointed to the Smart Search beta in Canvas by Instructure as one of the few examples of that already shipping in a product, calling it "really forward looking." The industry doesn’t need to rebuild the standards that already work. What’s needed is the connective layer that gives agents context, turning a link an agent can't use into content an agent can work with. Why vendors build walls first, and why the walls come down All of that assumes vendors want to be read. Early in any technology shift, they don't. They retreat into their own gardens, because building inside your own ecosystem is the fastest way to ship. The pressure to open up tends to follow on its own, because no platform's AI can do much with the tools around it, and no surrounding tool can see into the course, until each side opens to the other. As the need for increased connectivity grows, Mast’s worry is that this will lead to accidental inoperability: everyone shipping their own MCP (the Model Context Protocol, an emerging open standard for connecting agents to tools) servers and clients without coordinating, and the field waking up to a pile of tools that don't fit together. A bad annotation here, an odd authentication choice there, and it means there might be very little interoperability at all. That's the work a consortium exists to do, and 1EdTech is spinning up a group to work through how MCP could fit edtech now. The hard part, Mast admitted, is human, not technical: getting vendors to focus on the unglamorous, high-return question of making their tools work together, instead of chasing the theoretical moonshots that are more fun to talk about. When agentic action drifts from human goals In an agentic world, in edtech and otherwise, the action drifts away from the person who asked for it. "The actions that are taking place become increasingly distant from the human who expressed the intent or set the goal," Pendleton said. Most of our systems assume the user is a rational human acting in their own interest. We built flows on the logic that nobody would delete their own course roster, because why would they? AI agents don’t have that instinct, so the behavior changes. An agent pointed at a goal finds the most direct path to it, even when the most direct path is the one a person would never take (picture an agent who’s been directed to manage someone’s email inbox, but decides the best path towards organizing messages to “inbox zero” is to just delete all the emails. And hey, it’s not wrong. Zero emails IS fewer emails to manage). Mast reframed the concern as something familiar. We've always had non-deterministic actors in our systems, he said. We just called them users. People make mistakes when they grade and when they assess. Which points to the one design principle worth holding onto: treat agents as users, and build for their access, security, and accountability the same way you would for a person. The protections built up over years to handle people map directly onto agents: Consent through OAuth, so the user logs in and authorizes the agent rather than handing over credentials. Least-privilege access, so an agent can reach only what its task requires. Token scoping, so permissions are narrow and specific. Real audit trails, expanded to capture not just the account but the application ID and user agent behind each action. MCP writes consent into the specification: an agent needs permission to connect to a system and permission to act on someone's behalf. When the agent gets it wrong, who pays? This is a question that should shape how districts and institutions deploy any of this, because if you strip away the architecture, you're left with a fairness problem. An automated grading assistant gets an essay wrong. The instructor chose the tool, but the student carries the consequence. AI detection tools run the same way: the institution adopts them, and a student can be wrongly flagged for something they didn't do. The burden lands on the person with the least power in the exchange. Both technologists drew the same line, and it's a practical one for anyone piloting these tools: Add, don't replace. Pendleton's approach is to use AI for a second, optional assignment that gives students extra feedback, clearly labeled as AI-graded, rather than handing over the grading he already does. More chances to learn, no new risk to the student's standing. Keep grades human. Microsoft has drawn a similar line, Mast said: it helps educators draft feedback they can edit and approve, but it does not automate grading. Make AI involvement visible and contestable. If AI touches a grade, students should know, and they should be able to challenge the result. Two bets on the next 10 years At the end of a 50-minute technical deep dive, Pendleton and Mast were asked to think about AI in edtech over the next decade. What’s one principle to hold the field together and drive it forward? The two answers fit together like a handshake. Mast’s focus is on the design rule that gives this piece its frame. Treat agents as users. When you think about accessibility in your application, think about accessibility for agentic users, and ask what they need: the same care you'd extend to a person navigating your system. He sees a near future where students and educators carry personal assistants across their lives, and he thinks the conversation about how that consumer AI meets institutional systems is already overdue. Pendleton's pointed at control. The version of "human in the loop" the field imagined three years ago is already breaking down, he said, so the work now is building frameworks that keep people in authority no matter where an action happens. And it starts off the screen, with educators and students deciding how they want to teach and learn, then holding technology providers accountable to delivering it. Which brings it back to the bike ramp. You hand a kid real tools and real lumber, you teach him how it all fits together, and you build it so it holds before he points it downhill. Same job here. Just bigger jumps. Hear the full conversation with Mike Mast and Zach Pendleton on the Educast 3000 podcast .
