title: 48 Hours of Building, Breaking, and Figuring it Out Together
intro: Discover how the Instructure CX team moved beyond AI discussion to action during a 48-hour hackathon, building real, impactful tools to solve customer challenges and drive deeper connections.

body.text: Honestly, we weren't sure what would happen. There’s no shortage of discussions around AI these days. How learners are using it, how educators are employing it, and even how we leverage it to improve our customers’ experience. However, many times discussions lead to more discussions. What if we pulled back on the talk and focused more on the act? So we tried something different. We cleared two days, assembled the entire Customer Experience team in our HQ, gave them real problems to solve, and said: just build something. Make mistakes. Ask for help. See what happens. Put yourselves in the shoes of our customer community and see what we can build that drives even stronger connections. What happened was kind of remarkable. People who'd never thought of themselves as builders shipped actual working tools — not prototypes, but things their teammates could use the next week. Ideas that had been stuck in the "we should really do something about that" pile finally got unstuck. And somewhere in the middle of all the chaos and debate, people started teaching each other things they'd figured out on their own. That cross-pollination was the part nobody planned for. Someone in one corner of the room had already solved a problem that someone else had been fighting for months. It just took getting everyone in the same place to find out, and the opportunity to try an idea, build it, present it, defend it, and move it forward. An inspiring sight to witness, I have to say. We think this says something about where AI actually lives, in the hands of people who deeply understand the problems they're trying to fix. Our CX team knows your pain points better than almost anyone. Watching them build tools around those pain points, from scratch, in two days, was genuinely exciting. We're still learning. We'll keep sharing what we find.

Ask for help. See what happens. Put yourselves in the shoes of our customer community and see what we can build that drives even stronger connections. 

What happened was kind of remarkable.

People who'd never thought of themselves as builders shipped actual working tools — not prototypes, but things their teammates could use the next week. Ideas that had been stuck in the "we should really do something about that" pile finally got unstuck. And somewhere in the middle of all the chaos and debate, people started teaching each other things they'd figured out on their own.

That cross-pollination was the part nobody planned for. Someone in one corner of the room had already solved a problem that someone else had been fighting for months. It just took getting everyone in the same place to find out, and the opportunity to try an idea, build it, present it, defend it, and move it forward. An inspiring sight to witness, I have to say.

We think this says something about where AI actually lives, in the hands of people who deeply understand the problems they're trying to fix. Our CX team knows your pain points better than almost anyone. Watching them build tools around those pain points, from scratch, in two days, was genuinely exciting.

We're still learning. We'll keep sharing what we find.

title: Stop Typing, Start Thinking:  The Power of Digital Ink in Canvas
intro: Mr. Maggart, a high school math teacher in Oklahoma, spent last year on a focused mission: to eliminate paper worksheets and consolidate student note-taking into a single, organized space inside Canvas.

title: From Compliance to Career Growth: Unlocking the Full Potential of Your LMS
intro: A great LMS goes beyond compliance, driving engagement, skill development, and long-term growth for your workforce.

body.text: Learning and development programs are essential for building a skilled, adaptable workforce. But if your LMS is only focused on compliance training, you're missing a huge opportunity. Checking the box on mandatory training isn't enough. An effective platform should foster engagement, knowledge retention, and career growth, helping employees thrive and organizations succeed. Compliance gets people through the door. It doesn't keep them growing. Compliance training ensures employees meet legal and safety requirements, but it rarely creates a real learning experience. When training is treated as a box to check, engagement suffers. Employees rush through modules without retaining much, and the opportunity for meaningful skill development gets lost along the way. A platform built around interactive, engaging content, scenario-based learning, video, quizzes, helps employees actually absorb and apply what they learn. But an effective learning program goes further than better content. It becomes a platform for continuous growth. From training event to career growth engine Canvas Career supports upskilling, leadership development, and professional training, so learning doesn't stop once the required modules are done. Courses on soft skills, technical expertise, and management prepare employees for roles they haven't stepped into yet. That investment pays off in ways that show up on the balance sheet, not just the org chart: Employees who see a clear link between training and career progression stay engaged instead of disengaging halfway through a program. Organizations that excel at internal mobility, enabled by real skills visibility, retain employees twice as long. Role-based pathways mean a new hire, a technician, and a rising manager each get development that's actually relevant to where they're headed, not the same generic course Recognition turns learning into something visible Sustaining engagement takes more than good content. Gamification, digital badges, and personalized learning paths keep employees motivated and invested in their own growth. Two pieces work together here: Within Canvas Career, Skillspace lets learners track their own skill progress in real time, so growth feels visible instead of abstract. Parchment Award Digital Badges turns that progress into portable, verifiable proof, credentials employees can carry with them and share, and that employers can actually trust. That combination, skills built at scale and proof employers recognize, is what separates a learning program that motivates people from one they're just trying to get through. It also gives L&D teams something concrete to show leadership: not just who finished a course, but who's actually building capability. Proof this works Organizations are already putting this into practice. At USA Swimming, more than 20,000 coaches use a centralized hub for certifications, hybrid courses, and continuing education. Their team put it simply: Canvas Career allows their team to equip learners with the skills they need to move their careers forward. At Ent Credit Union, extending the platform with Parchment Award Digital Badges gave the team an efficient way to monitor completions, validate skills, and generate reporting for internal stakeholders, keeping leadership informed and decisions data-driven, not guesswork. Ready to move past the checkbox? A learning program built only for compliance will always feel like a requirement. One built for engagement, recognition, and career growth becomes something employees actually want to be part of. Discover how Canvas Career can turn your training program into a driver of real workforce development.

title: Thinking about adding AI to your curriculum? Guess what? Your students already are
intro: As education grapples with AI, how do we rethink learning? In part one of this series, we explore the behavior, expectations, and motivations of today's AI-driven learners.

body.text: Over the past six months, I’ve had conversations with educators across the globe about AI. How they’re using it, how and why they’re not using it, and how they’re thinking about it. Those conversations have been incredibly important to understanding the perceptions around the value of AI in the education space. But they’ve also been oddly consistent. The questions keep circling the same territory: Which models are safe to use? How are they using our data? What policies do we need? How do we make sure everyone—students, faculty, and staff alike—understands what they’re dealing with? But there’s a question we’re mostly not asking, and I think it’s the one that matters most: Who is our AI learner right now, and what does good design actually look like for them? That’s what this series is about. Part one starts with what we already know. Part two will look at what it means to shift from transferring knowledge to building capability. Part three will get into how we design learning experiences that actually prepare students for what’s ahead. Let’s start with the data, because it’s not subtle. The numbers aren’t a warning sign; they’re a description of now Microsoft’s 2025 AI in Education Report found that 93% of US students have used AI for school-related work. That number jumped 26 percentage points in a single year. A separate 2025 survey by Studiosity and YouGov found 82% of US students have turned to AI for assignments or study tasks. The Digital Education Council’s Global AI Student Survey reports that more than half of students use AI weekly, and a quarter use it every day. That’s an illuminating truth; AI use among students is the baseline now, not the exception. Meanwhile, the 2026 Lumina Foundation-Gallup State of Higher Education study tells a different story on the institutional side. About half of US college students say their school discourages AI use, and another 11% say it’s outright prohibited. Only about four in 10 say they’re actually encouraged to use it. That gap is real and it’s growing. Learners have moved on while many institutions haven’t. And while that distance stays open, the chance to teach AI use thoughtfully, based on judgment and genuine skill-building, keeps slipping. Three shifts worth sitting with Let’s look at three deeper shifts happening among student AI adoption, and explore what it means to be a learner today. Behavior. Students aren’t asking permission. They’ve already woven AI into how they read, write, study, and prepare. When we design assignments without acknowledging that, we’re not stopping AI use. We’re just losing visibility into it. The work is still getting done. We’ve just taken ourselves out of the conversation about how. Expectations. Learners now expect personalization, speed, and relevance as a given. If a textbook explanation doesn’t click, an AI tutor will try five different ways until one does. If a draft needs feedback, they don’t wait for office hours. The bar for instruction has quietly shifted to adaptive, on-demand, and tailored—and anything that feels generic by comparison feels like a step backwards. A degree is no longer the only path learners see as credible. Micro-credentials, bootcamps, and self-directed AI-assisted study are all on the table. Motivation. This is the deepest one. For a long time, the logic of academic work was clear: do the assignment, earn the grade, get the credential. Effort was evidence of learning. That logic falls apart when AI can complete the assignment in 30 seconds. And students know it. The honest question a lot of them are sitting with is: what’s the point? The answer can’t be that the assignment matters because it always has. That won’t hold. The answer has to be that the work demonstrates something AI can’t: real capability, sound judgment, the ability to adapt. Those are exactly the things employers say they need most, and they’re what education has to actually deliver. This is a presence problem, not a technology problem If 93% of learners use AI and most institutions either ban it or ignore it, what we’re looking at isn’t a technology gap. It’s a presence gap. We’re still designing learning for a student who doesn’t really exist anymore. Not because learners have changed who they are, but because the context they’re operating in has shifted completely, and our design hasn’t followed. The work isn’t about banning a tool or bolting one on. It’s about actually seeing the learner in front of us. That takes presence. It takes being willing to sit with what’s true before reaching for a policy or a solution. In part two, I’ll dig into what that presence makes possible: a genuine rethinking of what education is actually for, when knowledge is everywhere and execution can be automated.

In part two, I’ll dig into what that presence makes possible: a genuine rethinking of what education is actually for, when knowledge is everywhere and execution can be automated.

title: A Better Target for the Screen Time Debate
intro: Shift the classroom screen time debate. Focus on evidence-backed edtech that improves outcomes, rather than just limiting device minutes, using the ESSA framework.

body.text: Schools spent years working to put a device in every student's hands. Now a growing number of leaders are asking whether students are on those devices too much — during the school day and for homework alike. The phone debate may have started the conversation, but it hasn't stayed there. The unease has moved to the laptops and tablets schools deployed themselves, and to the screen time that comes with digital assignments. States are starting to act on it. Utah, Missouri, Alabama, and Tennessee are among those exploring policies on the safety and effectiveness of educational technology. The question is shifting from how much technology schools can get to how, and whether, it should be used during instructional time. If we're going to measure something, though, minutes on a device is the wrong number. The better measure is whether the tools and methods students use — digital or not — are backed by evidence, and whether they're improving outcomes. What we should measure instead Screen time is easy to measure, easy to compare, and easy to argue about. But skepticism toward classroom technology is fairly new. For most of my years in state education leadership, we were working to get more technology into schools. Research on student equit y and outcomes showed that at-risk students made measurable progress in one-to-one laptop programs, so the goal was one device for every student. The pandemic pushed districts there almost overnight as learning moved home. Then came the rush for content. In a single year, as classrooms went remote, the number of digital tools the average district used jumped from about 900 to more than 2,200 . Some of it worked well. A lot of it was never built to teach. So it's understandable to ask how many hours a student spends on a device. But the better question is whether the tool has evidence that it improves learning, and how strong that evidence is. The Every Student Succeeds Act already gives us a shared way to answer. ESSA sorts evidence into four levels, from strong studies showing a tool actually caused better outcomes down to a clear, research-based rationale for why it should. The system isn't perfect, but it's widely understood, and it gives a board something steadier to weigh than gut feeling and brand recognition. The 2026 EdTech Evidence Report applied that lens to the tools districts actually use. It found that about 40% of purpose-built edtech carries research evidence aligned to an ESSA tier. For the general consumer tools that show up in classrooms anyway, that figure drops to 2%. What matters is where the time goes. A tool built to teach, with evidence behind it, does more for a student than one that simply holds attention. The K–12 leaders who understand that distinction are already a step ahead on the argument forming right behind it: the one about AI. AI is where minute-cutting backfires One of the clearest responsibilities they have right now is preparing students for workplaces being rebuilt around AI, and that readiness doesn't come from keeping students away from the tools — it comes from guided, supervised practice with them. This is where cutting minutes for its own sake starts to work against schools. A blunt push to reduce device time collides head-on with the skills these students will be expected to have. The way through isn't more minutes or fewer minutes. It's measuring the right thing: whether students are learning to use AI safely and with judgment, where it genuinely helps their work, where it gets misused, and how to tell the difference. This is supervised, responsible use, not a free-for-all, with clear guardrails around student privacy and age-appropriate practice. It takes clear instructional goals and teachers who know how to bring AI into their practice. And because AI is moving into classrooms faster than the research that would tell us what works, it's judgment we have to teach deliberately, not something we can wait on. That makes discipline more important, not less. Before adopting an AI tool, ask what you'd ask of anything: what claims can it actually support, how does it protect student data, and will it work with the systems you already run? Districts that build this habit on today's tools won't start from zero when the harder AI questions arrive. And they will arrive. What we'll work through at ISTELive 26 Whether learning happens digitally, on paper, or with AI, the real question is whether the strategy is evidence-based and improves student outcomes. That's what I'll dig into at ISTELive 26 in Orlando on Tuesday, June 30, from 10 – 11 a.m. We'll work through the evaluation framework from the Evidence Report, the one districts and states can actually apply, and turn it into plain talking points you can use the week you get home: how to read an evidence claim, what to ask a vendor before you sign, and how to make the case for a well-researched tool. If you want the underlying data first, the full report is worth reading before you come. And if you'd rather just talk it through, the Instructure team will be at the booth with updates across the ecosystem, or you can join us offsite on June 28 for the Cuba Libre reception, where these conversations tend to get more honest anyway. The point is to walk into your next board meeting or vendor pitch with better questions and a way to weigh the answers.

A tool built to teach, with evidence behind it, does more for a student than one that simply holds attention. The K–12 leaders who understand that distinction are already a step ahead on the argument forming right behind it: the one about AI.

AI is where minute-cutting backfires

One of the clearest responsibilities they have right now is preparing students for workplaces being rebuilt around AI, and that readiness doesn't come from keeping students away from the tools — it comes from guided, supervised practice with them. This is where cutting minutes for its own sake starts to work against schools. A blunt push to reduce device time collides head-on with the skills these students will be expected to have.

The way through isn't more minutes or fewer minutes. It's measuring the right thing: whether students are learning to use AI safely and with judgment, where it genuinely helps their work, where it gets misused, and how to tell the difference. This is supervised, responsible use, not a free-for-all, with clear guardrails around student privacy and age-appropriate practice. It takes clear instructional goals and teachers who know how to bring AI into their practice. And because AI is moving into classrooms faster than the research that would tell us what works, it's judgment we have to teach deliberately, not something we can wait on.

That makes discipline more important, not less. Before adopting an AI tool, ask what you'd ask of anything: what claims can it actually support, how does it protect student data, and will it work with the systems you already run? Districts that build this habit on today's tools won't start from zero when the harder AI questions arrive. And they will arrive.

What we'll work through at ISTELive 26

Whether learning happens digitally, on paper, or with AI, the real question is whether the strategy is evidence-based and improves student outcomes.

That's what I'll dig into at ISTELive 26 in Orlando on Tuesday, June 30, from 10 – 11 a.m. We'll work through the evaluation framework from the Evidence Report, the one districts and states can actually apply, and turn it into plain talking points you can use the week you get home: how to read an evidence claim, what to ask a vendor before you sign, and how to make the case for a well-researched tool.

If you want the underlying data first, the full report is worth reading before you come. And if you'd rather just talk it through, the Instructure team will be at the booth with updates across the ecosystem, or you can join us offsite on June 28 for the Cuba Libre reception, where these conversations tend to get more honest anyway.

The point is to walk into your next board meeting or vendor pitch with better questions and a way to weigh the answers.

title: The 3 Technology Priorities Every Education Leader Needs to Balance
intro: Stuck between incremental improvement and bold transformation? Learn how education leaders can balance optimization, experimentation, and influence for a future-ready strategy.

body.text: I've spent years in education asking one question in district meetings, budget reviews, and technology audits: are the systems, tools, and cultures we're building ready for where education is heading, while still serving the leaders and learners in front of us right now? That question often splits the room. Half the table wants to fix what’s broken. The other half wants to build toward something bigger. Both halves are right, and the institutions that pick only one pay for it. Unreadiness is expensive in ways that don’t show up in the original budget: emergency procurement, rushed implementations, workarounds that turn into less-than-ideal permanent processes. Institutions that plan only for today tend to pay twice, once to survive the moment they’re in, and again to catch up to the one they didn't see coming. There's a quieter cost, too, and it’s the one most leaders miss. The window to shape what comes next closes faster than most leaders realize. The institutions that show up early to conversations about AI , credentialing models, and policy shifts help write the rules. They're on advisory boards. They're piloting early enough to have a real voice. The institutions that arrive late inherit decisions other people made and have a harder time adapting. Most educational leaders feel this tension. Jyotveer Singh Gill, associate director of education technology at Oxford's Saïd Business School, put it plainly in Times Higher Education : technology strategy in higher education keeps getting pulled between two extremes, incremental improvement and bold transformation. Picking one and committing feels like decisive leadership. It’s usually where institutions get stuck. Consider what each extreme looks like when it runs unchecked. When an institution leans too hard into optimization, it gets very good at running the system it already has leaner, faster, more efficient. The metrics improve, but none of them tell you whether you're still pointed in the right direction. By the time the gap between your tools and your learners’ needs is obvious, you've built substantial infrastructure on the wrong foundation, and changing course gets harder over time. Swing too far toward transformation and you chase bold change without a stable enough base to support it. Educators absorb the disruption. Learners absorb it too. Bold ideas rarely survive on an unstable system, which is a tension that the 2025 EDUCAUSE Horizon Report on teaching and learning traces across institutions. Hold all three at once A better approach replaces "evolution or revolution?" with three questions asked at the same time: Optimize. Are we making what we have work better? Using data well , reducing friction, building tools that actually fit how teachers actually teach. It's the least glamorous horizon, and often the most neglected. Experiment. Are we testing what's new to us? Intentional pilots, sandbox thinking, learning from what doesn't work before it breaks something that matters. Experimentation with accountability built in. Influence. Are we helping shape what comes next? Sitting on advisory boards, contributing to community conversations, pushing vendors and policymakers toward what educators actually need. These aren't steps in a sequence. They run in parallel, and each one requires deliberate investment. Technology is easy to track. You can measure adoption, uptime, and utilization. Culture is harder. The habits and expectations that make steady progress possible don’t show up on a dashboard. So many leaders wait for certainty before acting, wanting to see a proven solution, a clear roadmap, or a peer institution that went first. The pace of change in education won't hold for that kind of certainty. AI, shifting credential models , workforce demands, and widening equity gaps don't pause while we build consensus. The leaders who serve their institutions best are building readiness and managing the present at the same time. What this looks like in practice If you're evaluating your technology strategy, here are three reframes worth sitting with: From "Does this tool work for us right now?" to "Does this partnership give us room to grow in a direction we haven't fully defined yet?" From evaluating technology by feature count to evaluating it by whose voice shaped the roadmap From treating stability and innovation as opposites to treating stability as the prerequisite that makes real innovation possible That last reframe is the whole argument. Stability isn't the cautious choice you make instead of being bold. It's the ground bold work stands on. Getting readiness right means building the capacity to keep choosing well both for today, and for whatever today becomes.

title: Show-and-tell: How Educators Are Putting Agentic AI to Work in the Classroom
intro: AI agents in education are moving fast. See how Sydney, ASU, and InstructureCon are sharing real classroom practice, and why show-and-tell might be AI's most useful phase yet.

body.text: We're entering the show-and-tell phase of agentic AI in education, and it might be the most useful phase yet. After three years of predictions, frameworks, and policy drafts, the most valuable work is now happening in the open. Educators building AI agents, deploying them in actual courses, gathering evidence, and walking peers through what worked and what didn't. Why this phase matters Show and tell isn't a new idea in education. What's new is the speed at which classroom practice is now ahead of institutional policy. While committees draft guidance documents, individual educators are running pilots that move quickly enough to learn something every term. The bottleneck has shifted. It used to be "what is this technology capable of." Now it's "what actually works in front of students." Closing that gap is going to take more visible, shared practice across institutions. The kind of detail that lives in classroom stories, not in slide decks. A few events from the past year show what this can look like at scale. The Cogniti mini symposiums at the University of Sydney Cogniti is a platform built at the University of Sydney that lets educators create custom, steerable AI agents for teaching. It now has a community of educators across multiple universities, and once a year that community gathers to share what they've built. The Cogniti mini symposium runs in hybrid format, hosted by Sydney's Educational Innovation team, with the most recent edition held in November 2025 . What stands out is the specificity of what gets presented. Not "how to think about AI in higher education," but "here is the agent I built to help my pharmacy students practice teamwork." Recent sessions have included AI agents for oral assessment preparation, scaling formative feedback in large cohorts, simulated patient interactions for clinical assessment skills, AI voice chat designed to reveal student thinking, and feedback at scale in radiology education. The contributors come from Sydney, Monash, Murdoch, Newcastle, the University of Saskatchewan, and others. The format is simple: build something, run it with students, gather what you learned, and share it with peers facing similar problems. I recently sat down with Danny Liu, Professor in Educational Technologies and leader of the Cogniti.ai initiative at University of Sydney, and there are more exciting things to come from that team in the near future. ASU's Agentic AI and the student experience. Arizona State University ran a three-day summit in Tempe in October 2025 called Agentic AI and the Student Experience. It sold out at 500 attendees. The agenda was built around hands-on workshops as much as keynotes. Participants got a live demonstration of ASU's CreateAI toolset and tested adaptive tutoring prototypes and multi-step advising agents. ASU student workers presented an AI-powered chatbot they had designed and built to support prospective students through the admissions process. The signal in that programming is worth naming. A major research university with the resources to host any kind of AI conference chose to center the event on what its own students and staff had actually built. The closing message from the organizers was that the community is on its way to navigating the era of agentic AI, but success depends on doing it together. That's a show-and-tell ethic, applied at the level of a flagship event. Call for submissions has closed for the event to be held on October 20-22, 2026, but registration is open , and the event promises to sell out again. InstructureCon: education in the making This pattern is also coming to InstructureCon, our user conference in Louisville this July. The theme is Education in the Making, which is the right theme for this moment. Zach Pendleton, our Chief Architect, and I will host a super session focused on exactly this question: how are colleges, universities, and K-12 institutions putting AI to work in ways that genuinely change teaching and learning? The sessions in this year's catalog make the answer concrete. The University of Auckland is presenting on how they've scaled Cogniti — the same platform anchoring the Sydney symposiums — across their teaching environment in a pedagogy-first partnership between learning design and product teams. The University of Michigan's Perry Samson is presenting Coach Mode, an AI teaching assistant grounded in his own course's lectures and materials, designed to prompt students to explain their reasoning rather than hand them answers. The University of Illinois Gies College of Business is showing how a single course can run in personalized versions for each student, with adaptive explanations and AI feedback on every submission. Dozens of other sessions span K-12 districts, community colleges, and large research universities, all built around the same question of how to put AI in service of learning. Show-and-tell. What show and tell asks of the rest of us The pattern across the Cogniti symposiums, the ASU summit, and InstructureCon is the same. Show your work. Let other educators see the specifics. Talk about what didn't work as openly as what did. Make practice visible across institutional lines. That ethic puts a useful kind of pressure on leadership. If the most valuable knowledge about AI in education is being generated in classrooms and shared at events like these, then the leadership question isn't "what is our AI strategy" in the abstract. It's "what are we doing to support, surface, and learn from the practice that's already happening on our own campuses, and what are we doing to connect it to the practice happening on others." Funding educators to attend these events. Giving them time to write up what they're learning. Treating cross-institutional sharing as a core capability, not a nice-to-have. The show-and-tell phase won't last forever. At some point this practice will settle into curricula, into platforms, into established models. The window we're in right now, where the field is still figuring itself out in public, is the one where the most generous contributions get made and the most learning happens. The educators leading these efforts are already doing their part. The rest of the work is showing up, paying attention, and bringing what we learn back to our own institutions. If you're working on something interesting in this space, the most useful thing you can do is share it. Submit to a symposium. Apply to speak. Write up what you're trying. Talk with colleagues at other institutions about what they're seeing. Heck, shoot me an email with what you’re doing - rlufkin@instructure.com . The conversation gets better the more voices contribute.

The University of Michigan's Perry Samson is presenting Coach Mode, an AI teaching assistant grounded in his own course's lectures and materials, designed to prompt students to explain their reasoning rather than hand them answers. The University of Illinois Gies College of Business is showing how a single course can run in personalized versions for each student, with adaptive explanations and AI feedback on every submission. Dozens of other sessions span K-12 districts, community colleges, and large research universities, all built around the same question of how to put AI in service of learning. Show-and-tell.

 

What show and tell asks of the rest of us

The pattern across the Cogniti symposiums, the ASU summit, and InstructureCon is the same. Show your work. Let other educators see the specifics. Talk about what didn't work as openly as what did. Make practice visible across institutional lines.

That ethic puts a useful kind of pressure on leadership. If the most valuable knowledge about AI in education is being generated in classrooms and shared at events like these, then the leadership question isn't "what is our AI strategy" in the abstract. It's "what are we doing to support, surface, and learn from the practice that's already happening on our own campuses, and what are we doing to connect it to the practice happening on others." Funding educators to attend these events. Giving them time to write up what they're learning. Treating cross-institutional sharing as a core capability, not a nice-to-have.

The show-and-tell phase won't last forever. At some point this practice will settle into curricula, into platforms, into established models. The window we're in right now, where the field is still figuring itself out in public, is the one where the most generous contributions get made and the most learning happens. The educators leading these efforts are already doing their part. The rest of the work is showing up, paying attention, and bringing what we learn back to our own institutions.

If you're working on something interesting in this space, the most useful thing you can do is share it. Submit to a symposium. Apply to speak. Write up what you're trying. Talk with colleagues at other institutions about what they're seeing. Heck, shoot me an email with what you’re doing - rlufkin@instructure.com. title: What a Skills-First Labor Market Means for Educators and Employers
intro: Explore how a "skills-first" labor market is transforming hiring. See how educators and employers can bridge the gap in credentialing language to make on-the-job learning visible and portable.

body.text: A few months ago, Glenda Quintini set out to learn more in an industry she knew almost nothing about. "I hardly could tell critical minerals from rare earths," she admits. So she read, and she called people who knew more than she did, and within weeks she could hold her own. Quintini leads the OECD's Skills and Future Readiness Division in Paris, and getting up to speed fast on unfamiliar fields is the job. She earned no certificate for any of her new geological prowess, and if you read her resume, you'd never know it happened. But this skills building and knowledge growth still matters. That's the whole problem in miniature. "I feel quite lucky because I'm in a role where I learn something new almost every day," she told us on the latest Educast 3000 episode. Most adults learn the way Quintini just did, in the middle of the work, with nothing to hand an employer at the end. The skill is real, but it’s also largely invisible; it’s not a tangible, documented “learning” the way that a degree, diploma, or certificate is. What would it take to make that learning visible, and to let it travel? Start with the degree (because that's where the panic lives) When people hear "skills-first," some brace for the end of the diploma. Quintini doesn't. "I don't think that degrees are dead," she says. A skills-first approach widens the pool of who gets a serious look, and a degree does more than bank job skills. The College Board's Education Pays 2026 report finds that adults with more education don't just earn more and work more steadily; they're also more likely to report good health and to take part in civic life. A degree is a broad education with effects that outlast any single job, and it's one of the most dependable routes into that kind of learning. It just isn't the only one . What needs a closer look is what a credential can tell you over time On graduation day, it's a strong signal. Two decades later, it might say less about what someone can actually do, especially after years of on-the-job training, industry conferences, and informal knowledge transfer. Quintini offers herself as the example: her first qualification barely describes the work she does now. Her fix is to stop treating a credential as a single stamp and start treating it as a bundle of specific skills you can open up and inspect. Once you can see what's inside, an employer, a learner, and a training provider can finally mean the same thing when they describe what a graduate knows. Everyone's describing the same skill in a different language Educators write learning outcomes in one vocabulary, while employers write job postings in another. Quintini has watched managers inside a single company describe the same role four different ways. She puts the cost plainly: when a skill learned in one place can't be read in another, it blocks the movement of workers and learners about as effectively as a visa does. People are building the shared dictionary now. The UK launched its Standard Skills Classification through Skills England on April 30, a common framework for the skills, tasks, and knowledge behind every occupation. George Washington University's LAiSER project comes at it from the other side, using AI to link existing taxonomies into what its researchers call a taxonomy of taxonomies. And the OECD is working with the International Labour Organization on a global version, because right now two countries can't reliably agree on what a given job even requires. What happens when a skill can finally be read Once a skill is legible, it starts to behave like currency. In fact, tools like France's Compte Personnel de Formation try to make the exchange literal, putting a training budget directly in a worker's hands so they can turn money into skills on their own terms. A currency only works if people trust it, though, and Quintini's caution lands hardest here. For an adult already working three jobs, more training has to clearly pay before they'll trade an evening for it. "How do you justify to them the value of training?" she asks. Nobody has a clean answer yet, which is why the question keeps coming back to her. Until it does, a legible skill is just a coin the worker can't be sure anyone will take. Dropping the degree requirement isn't the finish line Simone Ravaioli, Senior Director of Global Learning Innovation at Instructure, brought up something noteworthy in the upcoming OECD report that Quintini helped spearhead: while the number of job postings that drop the degree requirement has shot up, but the number of non-degree candidates those same employers actually hired has barely moved. Quintini points to what already works. Eli Lilly's Skills First apprenticeship pays adults without a four-year degree a real wage while they train and puts a full-time job on the other side. It works because it pairs the open door with a way through it, rather than removing one barrier and hoping the rest sort themselves out. A program like that matters because employers rarely make the leap on their own, and Quintini is blunt about why. Ask them if they're struggling to hire and they say yes. Ask whether they've looked past the usual profile and they admit they haven't. The picture in their head is specific. "For a mechanic, they look for a middle-aged man," she says. "For a nurse, they will look for a woman." Why the next 15 years belong to recognition All of it points the same direction. Reading a skill, pricing it, and hiring on it fall apart without the shared infrastructure underneath: the common language, the skills passports, the recognition of learning that happened somewhere other than a classroom. That's work for governments as much as employers, and there’s an obvious catch; a program can't take eighteen months to two years to get approved when the skills themselves turn over in a season. Guest co-host Simone Ravaioli made a prediction. If the past 15 years were about lifelong learning, he said, the next 15 will be about lifelong recognition. The full conversation goes further than we can here, into why New Zealand regulates micro-credentials while platforms like Coursera let the market sort them out, and why Quintini wants to stand up an observatory just to track how employers actually hire. Listen to Lost in Translation: Getting Employers and Educators to Speak the Same Language , and read the OECD report A Skills-First Labour Market for the full picture.

Nobody has a clean answer yet, which is why the question keeps coming back to her. Until it does, a legible skill is just a coin the worker can't be sure anyone will take.

Dropping the degree requirement isn't the finish line

Simone Ravaioli, Senior Director of Global Learning Innovation at Instructure, brought up something noteworthy in the upcoming OECD report that Quintini helped spearhead: while the number of job postings that drop the degree requirement has shot up, but the number of non-degree candidates those same employers actually hired has barely moved.  

Quintini points to what already works. Eli Lilly's Skills First apprenticeship pays adults without a four-year degree a real wage while they train and puts a full-time job on the other side. It works because it pairs the open door with a way through it, rather than removing one barrier and hoping the rest sort themselves out. A program like that matters because employers rarely make the leap on their own, and Quintini is blunt about why. Ask them if they're struggling to hire and they say yes. Ask whether they've looked past the usual profile and they admit they haven't. The picture in their head is specific. "For a mechanic, they look for a middle-aged man," she says. "For a nurse, they will look for a woman." 

Why the next 15 years belong to recognition

All of it points the same direction. Reading a skill, pricing it, and hiring on it fall apart without the shared infrastructure underneath: the common language, the skills passports, the recognition of learning that happened somewhere other than a classroom. That's work for governments as much as employers, and there’s an obvious catch; a program can't take eighteen months to two years to get approved when the skills themselves turn over in a season.

Guest co-host Simone Ravaioli made a prediction. If the past 15 years were about lifelong learning, he said, the next 15 will be about lifelong recognition.

The full conversation goes further than we can here, into why New Zealand regulates micro-credentials while platforms like Coursera let the market sort them out, and why Quintini wants to stand up an observatory just to track how employers actually hire. Listen to Lost in Translation: Getting Employers and Educators to Speak the Same Language, and read the OECD report A Skills-First Labour Market for the full picture.

title: The Last Mile of AI Literacy
intro: AI literacy frameworks keep multiplying, but adoption remains low. Find out why machine-readable standards are the missing step between a published PDF and real-world use.

body.text: On 18 June, in Brussels and online, the European Commission and the OECD launch the final version of their AI Literacy Framework. It's a common, global account of what young people need in order to understand, create with, manage, and question artificial intelligence. Supported by Code.org and feeding into the PISA 2029 assessment, it's serious work. And it arrives in a crowded field. A single research tool at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology already catalogues 20 AI literacy frameworks , spanning K–12 standards, higher-education competency models, workforce programs, and clinical training. The reason that tool had to be built is the tell: different frameworks name the same skills differently, so someone had to construct a translator before the documents could speak to each other. The content questions are largely settled. The open question is which of these frameworks actually gets used. In a field this crowded, what separates a framework that travels from one that sits on a shelf is rarely its quality. It's how easily the systems where learning and hiring happen can pick it up and put it to work. Those systems (learning management systems, credentialing platforms, job boards, and hiring tools) run on structured data: stable identifiers, importable taxonomies, and machine-readable formats. A framework published only as a document asks every institution and vendor to do that integration itself, one interpretation at a time. Publish the same framework as structured data, and the work is done once, for everyone. The new framework targets schools. But the competencies a student builds there only matter if they stay legible as that learner moves into higher education and work, and that hand-off is exactly where mismatched frameworks break down. A PDF is a photograph of a framework. You can read it. You can't run it. Where machine-readability already works. Europe has the clearest example in its own infrastructure. ESCO, the EU's multilingual classification of skills and occupations, covers 27 member states and was published from the start as linked open data: stable identifiers for every element, downloadable in standard formats, free for any platform to integrate. Labor platforms, learning systems, and credential systems across Europe adopted it, not because anyone required them to, but because integration was easier than building from scratch. The content mattered. The format made the content usable. The United States built the same thing for occupations. O NET, the federal Occupational Information Network, maps skills, tasks, and knowledge across hundreds of jobs, and it's published as linked open data, too. The result is that O NET is embedded across job boards, workforce tools, and labor-market analytics nationwide. No mandate. Just a format that made adoption the path of least resistance. This is the fork every framework reaches. Without a machine-readable layer, a framework depends on manual interpretation across thousands of institutions and vendors, which produces fragmented alignment at best. At worst, it becomes a "standard" that each platform reads differently, until comparability, the entire point, is gone. Where adoption actually happens. Once a framework is structured, the systems that reach learners can do something with it. In a learning management system, native alignment means an instructor doesn't re-interpret the framework for every course. Outcomes get tagged the same way across programs, analytics become comparable, and when the framework updates, connected courses update with it. The work of alignment happens once, in the platform, instead of thousands of times, by hand. In a credentialing system, the identifier is what makes a credential portable. A badge that carries the framework's competency identifiers is legible to employers and recognizable to hiring systems anywhere. A badge that carries only a label, "AI Literacy Certificate," means something different at every issuer, and the shared understanding the framework promised dissolves into noise. None of this requires a framework to be complex. It requires it to be structured: each competency assigned a stable identifier, the full taxonomy available in importable formats, and explicit crosswalks to the infrastructure that already exists, ESCO and O*NET, plus the other frameworks already in use. The cost of skipping this is quiet fragmentation. Without machine-readability, the pattern is predictable. Institutions implement by hand, or not at all. Vendors build their own interpretations. Credentials multiply without comparability. Employers stop trusting the signal. The framework becomes a reference the field cites but doesn't systematically use. With this many frameworks already in circulation, each new PDF doesn't reduce the confusion. It adds another dialect to it. This isn't a failure of content or intent. It's a failure of format, and it lands hardest where capacity is thinnest. Well-resourced universities and large employers can interpret dense guidance by hand, and they will. Community colleges, workforce programs, and apprenticeships, which serve the learners who most need a portable AI literacy credential, are left to improvise. Machine-readability is what turns a document the strong can implement into infrastructure everyone can adopt. What the next step looks like. The ask is concrete and well within reach. Every framework author, the EU-OECD initiative first among them given its reach, should publish a structured implementation package alongside the PDF: a machine-readable version in which each competency carries a stable identifier, the full taxonomy is available in standard formats, and explicit crosswalks connect it to ESCO, O*NET, and the major frameworks already in use. This needs no new program and no significant funding. It means treating a framework as public data infrastructure, which is exactly what ESCO and O*NET already are. We don't need another framework. We need the ones we already have to be usable by the systems that decide whether a learner's AI literacy ever counts. The content is written. The infrastructure step is next.

title: How Data Helps Teachers Identify Disengaged Students Before They Fall Behind
intro: Learn how teachers use LMS data to identify at-risk students early, apply interventions, and improve student success with actionable analytics.

body.text: Student engagement is a critical measure of student success, and early warning systems for disengagement are an important way to identify students most likely to fall behind. One of the most studied works on identifying at-risk students with data comes from Robert Balfanz and the Everyone Graduates Center at Johns Hopkins. Their decade-plus of research established the "ABC" framework that most state-level early warning systems are built on today: Attendance, Behavior, and Course performance. Students showing warning signs in at least one of these in the first months of high school have an elevated dropout risk, sometimes showing up years before other formal indicators that many schools track. The researchers at the University of Chicago Consortium on School Research (CCSR) have done parallel work showing that ninth-grade course performance is one of the strongest predictors of high school graduation, more powerful than test scores or family income variables on their own. Two patterns from this research are important here. The signs are usually visible early. Students who eventually disengage almost always show measurable changes in attendance, work completion, or behavior weeks or even months before the formal warning systems catch them. The patterns are visible in the data the school already has. Districts don't need a new platform to do this work. They need the data that existing platforms are producing to land in front of teachers in usable form, in time to act on it. What changes when LMS data enters the picture The granularity of available data can overwhelm educators at times, but it can play a crucial role in identifying engagement. A modern LMS produces a continuous stream of student stats: which students are submitting work, which are opening course materials, which are participating in discussions, and which are just showing up on the platform. That LMS data maps well to existing engagement guidelines for identifying at-risk students, such as Balfanz’s ABC framework. Canvas LMS can measure how students engage with learning because it sees engagement behavior: whether a student is posting in discussions, submitting work on time, going quiet, or completing work. Each of these can count as a participation event. A sustained decline is often the first observable sign a student is pulling back, and it tends to appear before the conduct side of behavior reaches anyone's desk. The Canvas grade trendline shows that same trajectory while it's still forming. A teacher can see an average slide across two or three missing assignments, pull the missing-submission report to see exactly which ones are missing, and step in weeks before the slide hardens. Practical, predictive analytics in K-12 education is not a model that predicts dropout three years out, but a dashboard that shows a teacher what's happening this week. A teacher who sees that a student isn’t submitting work or even opening the course materials is seeing disengagement happen in real time. What teachers actually need There is a possible downside to all of this data, though; too many edtech tools can produce more data than teachers can act on. The most useful learning analytics tools for teachers share a small set of design choices. Visible at a glance. A teacher with 130 students should be able to see who needs attention this week in 30 seconds. It’s important that a dashboard doesn’t require drilling into individual student profiles to surface something useful. Tied to actionable indicators. "Engagement score" as a single composite metric is less useful than separate indicators (assignment completion rate, last login, current grade trajectory) that teachers can read and act on. The teacher needs to know specifically what has changed so they can decide what to do about it . Recent enough to matter. Data that's a week old is much less useful than data from this morning. The systems that produce real classroom impact are the ones that surface a signal fast enough for intervention to still be available. Integrated with where the teacher already is. An LMS with analytics, reporting, and even assessment data built directly into the platform the teacher uses for everything else helps surface both insights into student engagement and appropriate intervention for at-risk students. Canvas student insights dashboards are designed around these principles, but the broader principle holds for any platform: the data has to land in front of the teacher in time and in a form that doesn't require an analyst to interpret. The risk of data without judgment Important caveat: data can identify a student who's disengaging, but it can’t tell a teacher why. Districts that treat data-driven instruction K–12 as the answer often skip the part where a human looks at the data, holds the broader context, and decides what to do. The data can just flag a student. The teacher (and the counselor, and the family) produces the intervention. This is also where the equity conversation lives. Algorithmic systems that identify "at-risk" students can replicate the same patterns of who-gets-attention that the broader system has always produced, if nobody is checking. Schools that use early warning systems well have explicit equity checks built into how the data is used: who is being flagged, who is not, and whether the patterns align with the structural inequities the school is supposed to be working against. Research from organizations like the Data Quality Campaign on equity in education data emphasizes that data is a tool, but the real impact comes from people who exercise sound judgment and decide what comes next. What this looks like in a classroom that's getting it right You don’t need specialized initiative to take steps in the right direction. Teachers can get the most out of this kind of data by building a routine. A 10-minute check at the start of the week to see which students have new patterns of concern. A five-minute look on Wednesday to see who's still slipping after the Monday outreach. A note in the gradebook system or the LMS to track which intervention was tried with which student, so the data is there next time. A handoff to counselors or to family-engagement staff when the pattern crosses into territory the teacher can't address alone. About 20 minutes a week can produce the kind of early intervention that research consistently ties to meaningful outcomes. For districts considering how their LMS supports this kind of teacher routine, Canvas offers strong reporting and analytics integrations that provide insight into student performance and other metrics . You can also go deeper on turning that signal into action: Using Actionable, Comprehensive Data to Impact Student Success walks through how attendance, assessment, and grade data come together to show a teacher exactly where to step in.

Districts that treat data-driven instruction K–12 as the answer often skip the part where a human looks at the data, holds the broader context, and decides what to do. The data can just flag a student. The teacher (and the counselor, and the family) produces the intervention.

This is also where the equity conversation lives. Algorithmic systems that identify "at-risk" students can replicate the same patterns of who-gets-attention that the broader system has always produced, if nobody is checking. Schools that use early warning systems well have explicit equity checks built into how the data is used: who is being flagged, who is not, and whether the patterns align with the structural inequities the school is supposed to be working against. Research from organizations like the Data Quality Campaign on equity in education data emphasizes that data is a tool, but the real impact comes from people who exercise sound judgment and decide what comes next. 

What this looks like in a classroom that's getting it right

You don’t need specialized initiative to take steps in the right direction. Teachers can get the most out of this kind of data by building a routine. 

  • A 10-minute check at the start of the week to see which students have new patterns of concern. 
  • A five-minute look on Wednesday to see who's still slipping after the Monday outreach. 
  • A note in the gradebook system or the LMS to track which intervention was tried with which student, so the data is there next time. 
  • A handoff to counselors or to family-engagement staff when the pattern crosses into territory the teacher can't address alone.

About 20 minutes a week can produce the kind of early intervention that research consistently ties to meaningful outcomes. For districts considering how their LMS supports this kind of teacher routine, Canvas offers strong reporting and analytics integrations that provide insight into student performance and other metrics. 

You can also go deeper on turning that signal into action: Using Actionable, Comprehensive Data to Impact Student Success walks through how attendance, assessment, and grade data come together to show a teacher exactly where to step in.

title: “Adult-ify” Programs into 8-Week Skill Sprints
intro: Workforce Pell requires 8 to 15 weeks. A step-by-step method for cutting a semester course to a skills sprint without losing what employers actually hire for.

body.text: Instructional designers trying to make a certificate program Workforce Pell eligible are hitting the same wall: the program is too long. Federal rules cap an eligible program at 15 weeks, and most community college certificates are built on a 16-week semester. The instinct is to compress the calendar. Same content over a shorter timeline, with more hours per week, but you can't cram 16 weeks of material into a shorter calendar without shortchanging the learner. Successful short-term workforce programs aren't just compressing their existing courses, but redesigning them from the competency up. Here's what to focus on. What follows is a step-by-step way to rebuild a semester course into an 8-week skill sprint, a full worked example using an entry-level welding program, and short answers to the questions higher ed program teams raise most often. 1. Start with the job, not the syllabus The first question should be "what does the employer on the other end need this graduate to be able to do on day one?" Pull the job postings for the roles your program is supposed to feed into. Talk to the regional workforce board, and look at what the employers in your state actually hire for. You're looking for the five to eight competencies that actually matter for employment; a small number of hireable skills that a graduate can demonstrate in an interview and use in week one on the job 2. Cut what isn't hireable Once you have the competency list, run every topic in your existing 16-week course against it. Two questions per topic: Does this directly build one of the five-to-eight competencies? Can the student get hired without it? A disproportionate amount of what lives in a semester-length course might be there because of academic convention, not employer demand. This is one of the hardest parts of "adult-ifying" a course, and it usually requires a conversation with faculty who built the original curriculum. The goal is to name what the sprint is for: not a substitute for a two-year degree, but a focused on-ramp to a specific job. 3. Rebuild for the phone, not the lecture hall Working adults don't consume learning in two-and-a-half-hour evening blocks. Widely-cited research from Bersin/Deloitte found that the typical employee has just 1% of their workweek — roughly 24 minutes total — to focus on professional development. Adult learning happens in the pockets of time between shifts, at lunch, in the pickup line at school, after the kids are asleep, on the phone. If your module requires a long uninterrupted block, she'll put it off. Design accordingly: Modules should run 10 to 20 minutes, with each video lesson not exceeding 6 minutes Video should be short-form, captioned, and watchable at 1.5x without losing meaning. Every module should have a clear completion point. "You've just learned to do X. Here's how to practice it right now." The mobile experience has to be the primary experience 4. Collapse assessment into the work Measuring learning is a load-bearing beam in education. Traditional courses batch assessment: midterms, finals, maybe a capstone. Sprints can't afford to wait that long to know whether a learner is on track. The Workforce Pell requires an average of 70% completion rates per course. If a certificate program only runs 8 weeks, you need to understand student engagement and mastery early. The sooner you know a learner is slipping, the sooner you can intervene. And the sooner a learner knows she's demonstrated a competency, the sooner she can move to the next one without second-guessing herself. This means: Embedding assessment inside the modules Short practical demonstrations Skills checks at the end of each unit Portfolio artifacts that accumulate into the credential itself, so "finishing the course" and "earning the credential" become the same act It also means building in the data to catch dropoff early. If a learner hasn't logged in by Wednesday of week three, someone should know by Thursday. For those schools running their programs from Canvas LMS, insights available in Canvas Plus and Canvas Next does real work as an early-warning system that helps schools meet their 70% completion requirement. Similarly, Canvas Career has data and insights dashboards that offer visibility into progress, making development tangible and measurable. 5. Design with employer partners, not just for them One of the steps that often gets underweighted in program design is building validation into the process. Workforce boards, regional employer councils, and industry advisory committees can be useful partners here. They can weigh in on which competencies are showing up in regional job postings, review draft course structures, and flag gaps that a classroom-only design process might miss. A program that's been stress-tested against regional labor market data and reviewed by employers in the field tends to be a stronger program before students enroll. From there, a pilot cohort can function as a feedback loop. Employer partners might review the skills demonstrations students produce as part of the program, sit in on a practical assessment, or weigh in on the portfolio artifacts learners are building. Some of that feedback will be about content and some will surface readiness signals that the original curriculum didn't address. This is also where the 70% job placement requirement can start to feel more manageable. Programs designed in partnership with regional employers , reviewed by workforce boards, and piloted with employer touch points tend to have stronger relationships to draw on for placement. For example: an entry-level welding certificate The process gets concrete fast when you run one occupation through it. Take an entry-level structural welding certificate feeding into shop and fabrication roles. Pull the postings and the hireable competencies come down to a short list: read basic weld symbols and shop drawings, set up and safely operate stick (SMAW) and MIG (GMAW) equipment, prep joints through fit-up and tacking, lay sound fillet welds in the flat and horizontal positions to AWS D1.1 visual standards, spot and correct common defects like porosity and undercut, follow shop safety and hot-work practices, and pass a fillet weld test for the target role. A 16-week program teaches far more than that list. The redesign keeps what gets a graduate hired and moves the rest to a follow-on credential. The graduate walks into an entry-level welding job able to do the work on day one, and can stack pipe, TIG, and all-position certifications later without repeating the fundamentals. When the institution doesn't have the bandwidth Most community colleges trying to stand up multiple Workforce Pell programs simultaneously don't have the internal instructional design capacity to run this process across a dozen programs. The faculty who built the original courses already have full teaching loads. Instructional designers are supporting existing semester programs. Overall, there’s not a lot of room on most staff’s plates for a from-scratch redesign effort. Partnering with Instructure Professional Services gives you access to instructional designers who have done this kind of work: condensing semester-length curricula into skills sprints, rebuilding academic content for mobile-first delivery, and mapping programs to the competencies regional workforce boards have actually identified as high-skill and high-wage. More importantly, we build templates your institution can reuse, so the design investment compounds across every Workforce Pell program you stand up instead of starting over each time. If you're looking at your existing certificate programs and trying to figure out which ones can be sprinted, compressed, and delivered to adult learners, check out our professional services offerings and learn more about how we support instructional design projects. FAQ How do you shorten a 16-week course to 8 weeks? You rebuild the course around the five to eight competencies an employer hires for, then cut the topics that exist for academic convention rather than employment. In practice that means keeping the skills a graduate demonstrates in an interview and uses in week one, moving content into 10-to-20-minute mobile modules, folding assessment into the work, and removing advanced or specialized units that belong in a follow-on credential. Can existing certificate programs qualify for Workforce Pell? Yes. An existing certificate program can qualify for Workforce Pell, but length is usually the first thing standing in the way. A program has to run between 8 and 15 weeks, meet the completion and job-placement thresholds, and map to a high-skill, high-wage occupation your state has identified as in demand. A lot of 16-week certificates are already pretty close, so the work is redesigning them to fit rather than building something new. How long can a Workforce Pell program be? A Workforce Pell program has to run between 8 and 15 weeks. Programs shorter than 8 weeks or longer than 15 aren't eligible, which is why schools need to condense their existing 16-week semester courses.

title: Future-proofing Academic Integrity with Canvas and Turnitin
intro: Turnitin and Instructure bring academic integrity into Canvas, reducing friction and making it part of everyday instructional workflows.

body.text: Achieving assurance of student learning shouldn’t be a logistical marathon. But as AI becomes a staple in the modern classroom, the act of grading has evolved into a complex ‘investigation’ for original thought and authentic composition. To move forward, we need to stop treating academic integrity as an administrative burden and start treating it as an instructional insight. What you need to know Use AI writing and Similarity Reports to shift from reactive detection to proactive coaching, giving students the AI mentorship they crave. Eliminate educator fatigue in a tech-heavy world by using Turnitin and Canvas together seamlessly through their improved integration. Empower educators to assess their way by customizing integrity checks according to the Canvas assignment type. Why are fragmented AI workflows causing educator fatigue? Disconnected tools create a ‘friction tax’ on teaching. The core challenge for most educators isn't the AI itself, but the fragmented way they are forced to manage it. This is reflected in the data: while 90% of teachers believe student AI proficiency is critical, 80% feel overwhelmed by the technology*. This overwhelm is often the result of a bloated tech stack ; when integrity checks sit outside the daily grading workflow, instructors are trapped in a cycle of ‘context switching’. Senior leaders are working to align policies, governance, and tech to support responsible AI use across the instruction, but with growing class sizes and disjointed workflows, even well-intentioned systems can cause educator fatigue and student frustration. On a single submission, educators might have to: Open submissions in their Learning Management System (LMS). Run integrity checks in a separate window or platform. Toggle to a third interface to provide student feedback. When this ‘investigation’ is repeated across dozens of students, the cognitive load becomes unsustainable. Without a seamless, integrated environment, a significant efficiency gap emerges. Rather than having the space to mentor students on responsible AI usage (only 42% of students feel their instructors are currently equipped to help them use AI effectively*) , educators are forced into a reactive, time-consuming detective role that leads to fatigue. Students (already anxious about an unfair playing field and accusations of cheating) are left feedback hungry and left to navigate AI on their own, often resulting in the very misuse that threatens academic integrity. Tool sprawl places an invisible burden on IT teams. Behind the scenes, IT carries additional burdens, too. Every separate tool requires configuration, integration, permissions management, security review, and ongoing maintenance and user support. As tools grow and fragment, multiple teams and individuals feel the strain – and student and institutional success are put at risk. How does the Turnitin Advantage Integration optimize the Canvas LMS experience? Integration removes the need for context switching. To solve this, Turnitin is deepening and streamlining the partnership with Instructure. By making the full suite of Turnitin tools available within Canvas, the Turnitin Advantage Integration (built on the LTI 1.3 standard) addresses the challenge of fragmented tech and ensures that academic integrity isn't just another task on a to-do list, but a natural part of the instructional workflow. This isn't just a technical upgrade; it’s a much-needed workflow transformation for education in an AI world. When educators are now looking to achieve assurance of learning, they need tools that simplify that effort without having to export assignments and switch between platforms. Recognizing that every instructor has their own preferences and methodology for assessing, the Turnitin Advantage integration in Canvas allows educators an array of flexible options and assignment types to assess their way. To prevent overkill and educator overwhelm, educators can choose the depth of integrity checks per assignment: Major essays: Full similarity and AI checks. Drafts: A lighter review for progress tracking. Reflective assignments : No additional checks, preserving the student’s personal voice. This choice and flexibility ensures Turnitin solutions support educators, rather than weigh them down with unnecessary oversight or admin. What is the institutional value of integrated academic integrity tools? Integrated workflows shift the narrative from detection to proactive education. By embedding advanced integrity capabilities into everyday Canvas workflows, institutions prepare for the next phase of AI in education without overstretching IT teams or confusing students. It shifts the narrative from reactive detection to proactive education. For educators: Smoother workflows and less ‘context switching’. Achieving assurance of student learning shouldn’t be a logistical marathon. But as AI becomes a staple in the modern classroom, the act of grading has evolved into a complex ‘investigation’ for original thought and authentic composition. To move forward, we need to stop treating academic integrity as an administrative burden and start treating it as an instructional insight.

What you need to know

  • Use AI writing and Similarity Reports to shift from reactive detection to proactive coaching, giving students the AI mentorship they crave.
  • Eliminate educator fatigue in a tech-heavy world by using Turnitin and Canvas together seamlessly through their improved integration.
  • Empower educators to assess their way by customizing integrity checks according to the Canvas assignment type.

Why are fragmented AI workflows causing educator fatigue?

Disconnected tools create a ‘friction tax’ on teaching.

The core challenge for most educators isn't the AI itself, but the fragmented way they are forced to manage it. This is reflected in the data: while 90% of teachers believe student AI proficiency is critical, 80% feel overwhelmed by the technology*. This overwhelm is often the result of a bloated tech stack; when integrity checks sit outside the daily grading workflow, instructors are trapped in a cycle of ‘context switching’.

Senior leaders are working to align policies, governance, and tech to support responsible AI use across the instruction, but with growing class sizes and disjointed workflows, even well-intentioned systems can cause educator fatigue and student frustration. On a single submission, educators might have to:

  • Open submissions in their Learning Management System (LMS).
  • Run integrity checks in a separate window or platform.
  • Toggle to a third interface to provide student feedback.

When this ‘investigation’ is repeated across dozens of students, the cognitive load becomes unsustainable. Without a seamless, integrated environment, a significant efficiency gap emerges.

Rather than having the space to mentor students on responsible AI usage (only 42% of students feel their instructors are currently equipped to help them use AI effectively*), educators are forced into a reactive, time-consuming detective role that leads to fatigue. Students (already anxious about an unfair playing field and accusations of cheating) are left feedback hungry and left to navigate AI on their own, often resulting in the very misuse that threatens academic integrity.

Tool sprawl places an invisible burden on IT teams.

Behind the scenes, IT carries additional burdens, too. Every separate tool requires configuration, integration, permissions management, security review, and ongoing maintenance and user support. As tools grow and fragment, multiple teams and individuals feel the strain – and student and institutional success are put at risk.

How does the Turnitin Advantage Integration optimize the Canvas LMS experience?

Integration removes the need for context switching.

To solve this, Turnitin is deepening and streamlining the partnership with Instructure. By making the full suite of Turnitin tools available within Canvas, the Turnitin Advantage Integration (built on the LTI 1.3 standard) addresses the challenge of fragmented tech and ensures that academic integrity isn't just another task on a to-do list, but a natural part of the instructional workflow.

This isn't just a technical upgrade; it’s a much-needed workflow transformation for education in an AI world. When educators are now looking to achieve assurance of learning, they need tools that simplify that effort without having to export assignments and switch between platforms.

Flexible settings allow educators to assess their way.

Recognizing that every instructor has their own preferences and methodology for assessing, the Turnitin Advantage integration in Canvas allows educators an array of flexible options and assignment types to assess their way.

To prevent overkill and educator overwhelm, educators can choose the depth of integrity checks per assignment:

  • Major essays: Full similarity and AI checks.
  • Drafts: A lighter review for progress tracking.
  • Reflective assignments: No additional checks, preserving the student’s personal voice.

This choice and flexibility ensures Turnitin solutions support educators, rather than weigh them down with unnecessary oversight or admin.

Integrated workflows shift the narrative from detection to proactive education.

By embedding advanced integrity capabilities into everyday Canvas workflows, institutions prepare for the next phase of AI in education without overstretching IT teams or confusing students. It shifts the narrative from reactive detection to proactive education.

  • For educators: Smoother workflows and less ‘context switching’.
  • For students: Timelier, more constructive feedback on their writing process.
  • For IT teams: Simplified configuration, permissions management, and maintenance.
