title: Building for the Future: The Role of a Scalable LMS in Workforce Learning
intro: Businesses need an LMS that grows with them, adapts to evolving needs, and doesn't require costly replacements down the line. Learn why Canvas Career is the scalable, flexible solution built for long-term success.

body.text: Skills gaps aren't a future problem. They're already here. 87% of companies say they're facing, or expect to face, significant skills gaps within the next five years. At the same time, employees want development that's tied to real career progression, not generic, one-size-fits-all training. And leaders are under growing pressure to prove that learning investments actually move the business forward. That's a lot to ask of a learning management system built for compliance checkboxes. It's exactly what Canvas Career was built to solve. A skills-based foundation, not a compliance one As organizations grow, training needs change with them: A company might start with basic onboarding but quickly need compliance training, leadership development, and skills-based certifications as roles get more specialized. A large workforce with mission-critical roles, healthcare, credentialed technical positions, needs training that proves competency, not just attendance. A hybrid or distributed workforce needs learning that stays accessible and consistent across shifts, locations, and time zones. Traditional corporate LMS platforms weren't built to flex across all three. They were built to track completions, not capabilities, which leaves leaders without real visibility into what their workforce can actually do. Canvas Career changes that foundation. Organizations use it to deliver: Onboarding and compliance training: Structured programs that get new employees up to speed while automating the tracking mandatory training requires. Role-specific, skills-based training: Interactive modules and real-world scenarios that build job-relevant skills, not just check a box. Leadership and career development: Pathways that help employees see how today's training connects to tomorrow's role. With Canvas Career , organizations aren't limited to one type of training. Instead, they can evolve their learning programs seamlessly, ensuring long-term impact. Learning that connects to career growth Generic training doesn't motivate anyone. Employees want to see how a program connects to where they're headed, and when they don't, engagement drops fast. Organizations that get this right see the payoff directly in retention: companies that excel at internal mobility, enabled by skills visibility, retain employees twice as long. Canvas Career gives employees a clear, personalized path. Role-based pathways and AI-driven recommendations through IgniteAI keep development relevant to each person's actual job and goals, so training feels like an opportunity instead of a task to complete. AI that removes the administrative drag Building and maintaining training programs at scale used to mean hours of manual content creation and reporting. IgniteAI automates the repetitive parts, content creation, workflow updates, reporting, so teams can spend their time on strategy instead of spreadsheets. Proof, not just promises The hardest part of running an L&D program isn't delivering training. It's proving it worked. Only 8% of CEOs say they see a clear return on their learning investments, and 59% of learning leaders report real pressure to measure impact without having the tools to do it. title: Why Traditional Teaching Methods are Losing Students' Attention
intro: Traditional lectures are struggling to hold student attention in today's landscape. Discover why active-learning strategies and rethinking instructional design, not 'short attention spans', are the key to boosting student engagement.

body.text: In 2012, the learning scientist Manu Kapur ran a study in a Singapore public school. Two classes of ninth-graders, taught by the same teacher, worked through the same statistics concept. One class got the standard sequence: instruction first, then practice. The other got the order reversed. Those students spent about 40 minutes wrestling with a problem nobody had taught them how to solve, and only then sat through the instruction. The students who struggled first, and mostly failed to reach a correct answer, went on to outperform the instruction-first group on conceptual understanding and on transferring what they'd learned to new problems. Kapur named the approach “productive failure”. The students had a reason to listen to the explanation because they'd already hit a wall while trying to solve the problem. This, among other studies, is an important piece of the story about student attention because it shows that students can pay attention… if the lesson structure gives them a reason to. The research on attention is not what you think it is The "human attention span has dropped to eight seconds, less than a goldfish" claim that went around in the mid-2010s was misattributed to Microsoft research that never said that. When Karen Wilson and James Korn reviewed the underlying studies in 2007 , and when Neil Bradbury revisited them in 2016 , both found little primary evidence for a fixed attention limit. The biggest sources of variation in student attention are the teacher and the lesson design. Sustained attention to a single passive task is bounded, but the ceiling isn't a clock you can set. It moves with how engaging the input is and how much spare working memory the listener has left. A significant factor in sustained attention is also the cost-benefit math the student is doing. In 1995, the alternatives to a 50-minute lecture were more limited than they are today, when the top alternatives are engineered to capture attention. It's not a fair fight if the lecture is the only option. The structural problems with traditional teaching vs modern teaching Three structural patterns make lecture-heavy models hard to sustain. The cognitive load problem Cognitive load theory , most associated with John Sweller's work, holds that working memory has hard limits. Lectures that present a lot of new material quickly, without scaffolding, push past those limits. Students don't fail to learn because they aren't trying, but because the material is being delivered faster than working memory can encode it. The fix is breaks for processing, retrieval practice, and active engagement at intervals short enough to keep working memory from overloading. The intrinsic vs extrinsic motivation problem The research on intrinsic vs extrinsic motivation posits that students who feel they have autonomy, competence, and relatedness in their learning sustain engagement. Students who feel they're being managed through compliance structures (assignments to complete, points to accumulate, deadlines to meet) sustain engagement only as long as the compliance pressure holds. When the pressure drops (over a long weekend, during a substitute teacher's class, in the final stretch of senior year), engagement collapses. Lecture-heavy models lean heavily on extrinsic structure. The student agency problem There’s a substantial and growing body of research work connecting student agency, voice, and choice to engagement. Students who have meaningful choices in their learning, can pursue questions they care about, and can produce work with an audience beyond the gradebook show stronger engagement across every measure. Lecture-based learning problems can be linked to a lack of agency: in a lecture-only classroom, the student's role is to receive. That's a hard role to sustain attention in. Why "kids these days" is the wrong frame The most common explanation for student disengagement in schools, in casual conversation, is usually some version of "screens are ruining the children.” But there might be a better (or at least more nuanced) framing of the issue: the methods that worked well enough when the attention competition was less intense are now competing with attention engineering that is just better at its job (The Social Dilemma is just one of many, many documentaries about this kind of attention engineering). But students aren't inherently “more broken” than previous cohorts; the instructional designs that previous classrooms tolerated are now actively losing. This shifts what intervention looks like. Asking students to be more disciplined is asking them to do something most adults have not asked of themselves. Redesigning the instruction to be the kind of thing that holds attention is, if not easy, at least more attainable. You can check out a K-12 example of what that looks like here . What works for engaging reluctant learners Research on active learning in K-12 points to a relatively short list of approaches that consistently improve engagement and outcomes. Retrieval practice. Frequent low-stakes opportunities to recall information without notes. Quick quizzes, partner explanations, and exit tickets. The cognitive science of retrieval practice is strong in education research. Problem-first instruction. The Singapore teacher's experiment is a version of this. Students attempt a problem before being taught the solution method. The struggle motivates listening to the explanation. This is sometimes called " desirable difficulty ". Discussion-based formats. Sustained classroom discussion, structured carefully, sustains attention and engagement at higher levels than a lecture in most settings. Methods like the Harkness method in literature classrooms and Socratic seminars in social studies have produced consistent results for decades. Project-based learning (done well). Where it's well-designed (with strong content alignment, clear assessment, and real audiences for student work), it produces a strong engagement signal. Gamification. Game mechanics can elevate ordinary classwork: whether it’s points, badges, or some kind of challenge structure, any narrative that frames a unit as something other than a worksheet raises engagement and motivation. An escape room is an engaging tool to teach problem-solving, for instance. None of these approaches requires a specific LMS or device (though those can do some heavy lifting as tools); they do require classroom design that gives students something to do beyond strictly listening. What technology can and can't do here It would be untrue so say that the right platform “fixes” engagement problems. An edtech platform can support better pedagogy or get in the way of it, but it doesn't determine the pedagogy. What good platforms do support is the operational work and make it easier to track and encourage engagement: Making formative assessment easier to deploy and review: Mastery Connect lets a teacher build a standards-aligned check, send it to a class, and read the results without hand-scoring a stack of papers. The Mastery Tracker turns those results into a color-coded view of who has a standard and who doesn't, student by student. Because it passes data back to Canvas, the quiz given on Tuesday is shaping instruction on Wednesday instead of sitting in a grading pile. Giving teachers visibility into who's engaging in real time: The course analytics in Canvas show a teacher which students have opened the materials, who's behind on submissions, and where participation is thinning, then let them message everyone who hasn't started an assignment in a couple of clicks. Organizing materials so a teacher can focus on instruction instead of file management: Canvas Modules let a teacher lay out a course the way students actually move through it, by unit or by week, so no one is digging through a folder named "Lectures" to find a reading due tomorrow. When the same course runs across several sections or campuses, Blueprint Courses push a single source version to all of them and keep them in sync. Creating space for the kind of student work that benefits from more than a paper turn-in: Canvas Studio lets students submit a video or audio recording as the assignment itself. For work that spans a year rather than a single due date, Canvas Portfolio provides students with a place to collect and showcase their growth, with options for both student-led showcases and teacher-assessed, competency-based portfolios. The lecture is not coming back as the default for most secondary classrooms. But what’s replacing it? It’s less likely to be one specific tool and more about rethinking how time in the room is spent.

title: The Instructure Community is Writing the IgniteAI Playbook, One Prompt Party at a Time
intro: See how the Instructure Community uses IgniteAI to build study guides, improve courses, and support student success through shared prompts.

body.text: The best ideas about how to use the Instructure IgniteAI Agent during the last few months haven't come from a product team or a webinar. They came from a Thursday call where 19 educators showed up, opened their real courses, and started building on each other's prompts in the chat. Someone tried a course review. Someone else asked whether the same prompt could find at-risk students. By the end, the room had done what Community does best; they showed up curious and left inspired. What a Prompt Party actually is A Prompt Party is a live, low-key session inside the Instructure Community where educators open their real Canvas by Instructure courses and show the prompts they're using with the IgniteAI agent. We skip slides and scripts and focus on two or three demos and a lot of questions. It's a standing invitation for educators to bring their own prompt and test it in front of people who are figuring it out right alongside them. The premise is simple: hand the mic to the people doing the work, and see what happens. The room keeps showing up In practice, a Prompt Party looks like a string of demos worth stealing. Some weeks the crowd is bigger and the demos run long. Some weeks it's smaller and the conversation goes deeper. As such, the Community Prompt Library has filled up just as fast. Rick Upchurch from Belhaven University challenged all 10 instructional designers on his team to post a prompt, and most already have. May's top-voted prompt went to Christopher Gaudreau from Bay Path University for a one-sentence fix that adds proper headers to layout tables, clearing an accessibility issue that used to eat whole afternoons. What presenters said about the prompts they built Brandon Mitchell, Director of Instructional Design and Technology at Hinds Community College, handed the agent an entire course and asked it to review the whole thing the way an experienced instructor would mentor a first-timer. The report came back long and specific: missing rubrics, unclear submission guidelines, and places to strengthen discussion. "The amount of time that a designer would have to go through with a checklist to go through this course line by line, page by page. Saves an amazing amount of time." Brandon Mitchell, Hinds Community College Kyle Cole, a senior solutions engineer at Instructure who also teaches as an adjunct, built a prompt he runs every semester: find students scoring below 70 percent, identify the concepts they're struggling with, and draft personalized outreach to each group. What he took from it wasn't only about the students. "It's a great way to call yourself out and give yourself a pulse check. Sometimes it's not a student problem, it's a Kyle problem." Kyle Cole, Instructure Paula Eure, a Canvas admin at Belhaven University, shared the smallest change with the biggest payoff. She'd been starting prompts with "can you," and the agent kept handing the work back to her. So she switched it up. "Things have been working a lot better since I'm now saying 'help me' instead of asking it if it can do something." Paula Eure, Belhaven University Try the IgniteAI Agent free through June 30 The free period for the IgniteAI agent ends June 30, 2026 for customers in the US and September 30, 2026 for customers outside the US. Until then, you can open your own course and run the kinds of prompts these educators demoed, including: the full course reviews study guides differentiated reading passages outreach to students who are falling behind You can check out our prompt library here to get started. Everything you create with the Agent before the free trial ends stays yours. You can also join us and get in on the action live; we’ve got sessions scheduled on June 11 and June 18 , with more sessions on the books through July. Bring a prompt you're proud of, or one that flopped and you can't figure out why; both are welcome. Come curious, and leave with something you'll use in your own classroom. See you in the Community !

title: The Role of Gamification and Interactive Learning in K-12 Classrooms
intro: Instructure shares how gamification drives K-12 engagement and what educators should prioritize when selecting learning tools.

body.text: Quest to Learn opened in New York City in 2009 as a public school that supports a dynamic curriculum using game design principles to create academically challenging, immersive, game-like learning experiences for students. Today, it's one of the most-documented real-world examples of game-based learning in K–12, focused on answering the question about if “gamification works”. Students at Quest engage with academic content at a high level. On standardized tests, they perform in roughly the same range as students at comparable NYC public schools, not dramatically above them. That result usually gets read one of two ways: proof that game-based learning is overhyped, or proof that it just needs more runway. But gamification was never meant to stand in for all curriculum or replace all instruction methods. Still, in the right places, it does real work; in some of those places, it does a specific job better than the conventional approach it replaces. What gamification in K-12 education actually means The word "gamification" gets used for at least three different things. The first is points-and-badges gamification. This is the version most districts encounter first: a layer added on top of existing instruction that awards students points for completion, badges for milestones, and a leaderboard position for accumulation. Karl Kapp's foundational work on gamification notes that points-and-badges layers need to be applied to well-designed instruction to produce the strongest engagement and academic results. The second is game-based learning in the stricter sense. Students play a designed game that directly teaches the content. DragonBox Algebra , Minecraft Education Edition , iCivics games, and similar titles fit here. The research on well-designed educational games is positive: a 2022 meta-analysis in the International Journal of STEM Education pooled 33 studies covering nearly 3,900 students and found a moderate overall effect on learning achievement when digital games were compared to other instructional methods, and games built with clear learning objectives and tight assessment loops produce measurable gains. The third is interactive learning more broadly, which includes simulations, branching scenarios, and student-driven exploration. This category overlaps with game-based learning but reaches wider. PhET Interactive Simulations from the University of Colorado Boulder offer free science and math simulations built for K-12 and college classrooms. ExploreLearning Gizmos runs a library of more than 550 math and science simulations for grades 3 through 12, aligned to NGSS and Common Core. The Concord Consortium builds inquiry-based STEM tools that let students model phenomena like genetic inheritance and climate change. None of these are games in the formal sense, but they share a design principle with games: the student takes active control of a learning system instead of receiving content passively. When a district says it's doing "gamification," it could mean any of these. The implementation choices and expected outcomes differ for each. What the research actually says The most useful summary of educational gamification research comes from a 2020 meta-analysis published in Educational Technology Research and Development , which reviewed effect sizes across 30 studies. The headline finding: gamification, on average, produces a small positive effect on learning outcomes. The more interesting finding underneath: the effect varies enormously by implementation quality. Studies of well-designed implementations (with clear learning objectives, alignment between game mechanics and content, and meaningful student choice) showed more positive effects. In Greg Toppo's book The Game Believes in You , he documented gamification across multiple K-12 implementations in the mid-2010s. The schools where gamification worked didn’t purchase the most game-like software, but worked to build game-design thinking into the curriculum. Where gamification works Five patterns show up in the implementations that produce results. Tight feedback loops. Students get rapid feedback onwhether they're on the right track, without having to wait for a teacher to grade something. This is one of the most consistently supported findings in game-based learning research. The cognitive science here connects to retrieval practice and formative assessment more broadly. Failure that doesn't carry permanent consequences. In games, failure is information. In most school assignments, failure is a number that goes in a gradebook and stays there. Game-based and interactive designs work in part because they let students fail, learn from the failure, and try again without paying a permanent grade cost. This connects to the research on growth mindset, but the operational design point is more concrete: build assessment structures that let students improve performance over time, not just measure it once. Meaningful choice. Students have real agency over how they pursue a goal, and the choices are not cosmetic. They affect what the student learns and how. Minecraft Education Edition implementations work in part because the student has to make consequential design decisions to complete the assigned task. Visible progress. Students can see where they are in a sequence of work and what's ahead. This sounds small, but it can make a difference in classrooms where students need support in sustaining engagement. It helps if the student knows the shape of the thing they're climbing. Aligned challenge. The work is hard enough to be interesting and not so hard that it's defeating; using formative assessment data helps adjust the challenge level for individual students. Where gamification fails Treating gamification as a delivery wrapper for content that hasn't itself been redesigned is less likely to produce change. In these cases, the game layer just sits on top, and the underlying content stays exactly as it was. The lesson doesn't change, but a leaderboard goes around it, or the assessment doesn't change, but a badge gets attached to a passing score. In these cases, the gamification layer is just another kind of compliance, like hitting “submit” on an assignment. Students who would have been engaged anyway accumulate points. Students who were disengaged still are, just with a lower leaderboard ranking attached. This pattern is well documented. Hanus and Fox found that a course gamified with a leaderboard and badges produced lower student motivation and satisfaction over time than the same course without them. The most consistent risk in gamification or game-based learning decisions is overestimating what the wrapper can do. Practical guidance for districts and teachers If you're a K-12 leader thinking about interactive learning tools for students, here’s how to track what’s important. Does the tool change what students do, or only how their work gets tracked? Tools that change the underlying student activity (a simulation that lets students model a system they couldn't model on paper, a game that requires applying a concept under pressure) have more leverage than tools that wrap existing activity in a new interface. Does the tool produce information that teachers can use? Game-based and interactive tools generate a lot of data. The tools that have a meaningful effect on classroom learning are usually the ones where that data lands in front of the teacher in time to inform the next instructional decision. body.html:
Quest to Learn opened in New York City in 2009 as a public school that supports a dynamic curriculum using game design principles to create academically challenging, immersive, game-like learning experiences for students. Today, it's one of the most-documented real-world examples of game-based learning in K–12, focused on answering the question about if “gamification works”. Students at Quest engage with academic content at a high level. On standardized tests, they perform in roughly the same range as students at comparable NYC public schools, not dramatically above them.

That result usually gets read one of two ways: proof that game-based learning is overhyped, or proof that it just needs more runway. But gamification was never meant to stand in for all curriculum or replace all instruction methods. Still, in the right places, it does real work; in some of those places, it does a specific job better than the conventional approach it replaces.

 

What gamification in K-12 education actually means

The word "gamification" gets used for at least three different things.

The first is points-and-badges gamification. This is the version most districts encounter first: a layer added on top of existing instruction that awards students points for completion, badges for milestones, and a leaderboard position for accumulation. Karl Kapp's foundational work on gamification notes that points-and-badges layers need to be applied to well-designed instruction to produce the strongest engagement and academic results. 

The second is game-based learning in the stricter sense. Students play a designed game that directly teaches the content. DragonBox Algebra, Minecraft Education Edition, iCivics games, and similar titles fit here. The research on well-designed educational games is positive: a 2022 meta-analysis in the International Journal of STEM Education pooled 33 studies covering nearly 3,900 students and found a moderate overall effect on learning achievement when digital games were compared to other instructional methods, and games built with clear learning objectives and tight assessment loops produce measurable gains. 

The third is interactive learning more broadly, which includes simulations, branching scenarios, and student-driven exploration. This category overlaps with game-based learning but reaches wider. PhET Interactive Simulations from the University of Colorado Boulder offer free science and math simulations built for K-12 and college classrooms. ExploreLearning Gizmos runs a library of more than 550 math and science simulations for grades 3 through 12, aligned to NGSS and Common Core. The Concord Consortium builds inquiry-based STEM tools that let students model phenomena like genetic inheritance and climate change. None of these are games in the formal sense, but they share a design principle with games: the student takes active control of a learning system instead of receiving content passively. 

When a district says it's doing "gamification," it could mean any of these. The implementation choices and expected outcomes differ for each.
 

What the research actually says

The most useful summary of educational gamification research comes from a 2020 meta-analysis published in Educational Technology Research and Development, which reviewed effect sizes across 30 studies. The headline finding: gamification, on average, produces a small positive effect on learning outcomes. The more interesting finding underneath: the effect varies enormously by implementation quality. Studies of well-designed implementations (with clear learning objectives, alignment between game mechanics and content, and meaningful student choice) showed more positive effects.

In Greg Toppo's book The Game Believes in You, he documented gamification across multiple K-12 implementations in the mid-2010s. The schools where gamification worked didn’t purchase the most game-like software, but worked to build game-design thinking into the curriculum.
 

Where gamification works

Five patterns show up in the implementations that produce results.

  • Tight feedback loops. Students get rapid feedback onwhether they're on the right track, without having to wait for a teacher to grade something. This is one of the most consistently supported findings in game-based learning research. The cognitive science here connects to retrieval practice and formative assessment more broadly.
  • Failure that doesn't carry permanent consequences. In games, failure is information. In most school assignments, failure is a number that goes in a gradebook and stays there. Game-based and interactive designs work in part because they let students fail, learn from the failure, and try again without paying a permanent grade cost. This connects to the research on growth mindset, but the operational design point is more concrete: build assessment structures that let students improve performance over time, not just measure it once.
  • Meaningful choice. Students have real agency over how they pursue a goal, and the choices are not cosmetic. They affect what the student learns and how. Minecraft Education Edition implementations work in part because the student has to make consequential design decisions to complete the assigned task.
  • Visible progress. Students can see where they are in a sequence of work and what's ahead. This sounds small, but it can make a difference in classrooms where students need support in sustaining engagement. It helps if the student knows the shape of the thing they're climbing.
  • Aligned challenge. The work is hard enough to be interesting and not so hard that it's defeating; using formative assessment data helps adjust the challenge level for individual students.
     

Where gamification fails

Treating gamification as a delivery wrapper for content that hasn't itself been redesigned is less likely to produce change.  In these cases, the game layer just sits on top, and the underlying content stays exactly as it was. The lesson doesn't change, but a leaderboard goes around it, or the assessment doesn't change, but a badge gets attached to a passing score. 

In these cases, the gamification layer is just another kind of compliance, like hitting “submit” on an assignment. Students who would have been engaged anyway accumulate points. Students who were disengaged still are, just with a lower leaderboard ranking attached. This pattern is well documented. Hanus and Fox found that a course gamified with a leaderboard and badges produced lower student motivation and satisfaction over time than the same course without them.

The most consistent risk in gamification or game-based learning decisions is overestimating what the wrapper can do.
 

Practical guidance for districts and teachers

If you're a K-12 leader thinking about interactive learning tools for students, here’s how to track what’s important.

  • Does the tool change what students do, or only how their work gets tracked? Tools that change the underlying student activity (a simulation that lets students model a system they couldn't model on paper, a game that requires applying a concept under pressure) have more leverage than tools that wrap existing activity in a new interface.
  • Does the tool produce information that teachers can use? Game-based and interactive tools generate a lot of data. The tools that have a meaningful effect on classroom learning are usually the ones where that data lands in front of the teacher in time to inform the next instructional decision. 
  • Does the tool integrate with the broader instructional environment, or does it sit on the side? Single-purpose game tools that don't connect to the gradebook, SIS, or LMS create operational drag that might outweigh engagement value. Canvas LMS offers customization that enables gamification features and integrates with other vendors. This gives schools an approach to addressing the integration problem, but the broader principle applies regardless of platform: tools that don't fit the rest of the stack aren’t going to be as impactful.

A district pairs DragonBox Algebra with a structured weekly classroom routine: students play the game in 15-minute segments at the start of class, then work conventional problem sets that draw on the same concepts. Students who'd been disengaged in earlier math classes sustained engagement in algebra readiness. Pairing the game with traditional practice allows the game to generate the cognitive readiness that the practice consolidates.

High school civics. iCivics' Drafting Board, an argument-building tool, was used across three Florida districts. After just two or three class days using it, students scored measurably higher on argumentative essays than a control group. The gain showed up in how students built and defended a position, not in how many facts they could recall. The tool didn't transfer civic content into students' heads, but it gave them structured practice in something that civics actually asks of a citizen, like taking a defensible position and arguing. 

These stories are about tools that don’t replace instruction but help change its texture in ways that engage students. If you're evaluating an interactive K-12 LMS that includes built-in gamification features and integrations with game-based learning tools, Canvas for K-12 is one starting point. But the north star of gamification is answering the question: Does this change what students do, or only how their work gets tracked?

title: Skills-Based Learning for Professional Associations: 5 Strategic Shifts
intro: Legacy content libraries weren't built for career growth. See how associations are using skills-based learning to deliver programs members can actually use to stay competitive.

body.text: The data from our The State of Learning and Readiness B-Sides report tells a specific story: 72% of professionals trust that a certification leads to advancement, but 37% say they lack the career planning tools or guidance to get there. For professional associations, the lesson is clear. Your members demand career currency: learning that has immediate, recognizable value in the labor market. To provide it, you must move from being a content warehouse to a career navigator. Visibility as a motivator A significant part of the readiness gap is a visibility problem. Professionals often feel they are working in a vacuum, unsure if their efforts are being recognized or if they are actually closing their own skill gaps. Using a centralized LMS allows associations to make progress visible in real time. When members can see exactly what they have accomplished and what remains to reach their next career milestone, your programs become their most valuable professional asset. You are not just selling a membership; you are providing the infrastructure for their professional survival. The shift from "course catalogs" to "skill pathways" Most associations have a deep inventory of learning materials, but they are often trapped in legacy systems built for compliance, not growth. When resources are presented as a flat list of off-the-shelf webinars and PDFs, they contribute to the very burnout that 47% of workers say is stalling their growth. To move members from "stagnant" to "ready," organizations need to deliver skills-based learning at scale. This means organizing learning into personalized, role-based programs where every credential maps to a specific competency employers are actively hiring for—not just a course a member had to complete to renew their membership. A solution like Canvas Career makes that possible by connecting program design to the skills and roles members are actually trying to grow into. Modernizing your learning strategy If you are moving away from a traditional "webinar warehouse" model, here are three strategic shifts that turn legacy content into career currency. 1. Transition from topics to outcomes A prospect looking to modernize should start by reviewing their top-performing courses through the lens of employability. Traditional titles like "Advanced Project Management" are often too broad to serve as currency in a modern job market. By utilizing AI-powered skill extraction, you can identify the specific competencies your existing courses already validate, such as "Risk Mitigation" or "Agile Budgeting." When you tag content with these specific skills, you help members build a portfolio of capabilities that translates directly to job descriptions. This turns a standard transcript into a map of professional value, making it easier for members to see exactly how your association helps them remain competitive. 2. Visualize progress to sustain motivation One of the biggest contributors to learner fatigue is the feeling of "infinite scrolling." If a member sees a long course with no intermediate markers, they are more likely to drop out. This is a critical risk, considering 34% of professionals cite "lack of time" as their primary barrier to learning. Associations can counter this by breaking larger certifications into microlearning short, focused learning experiences centered around a single skill. Using a dedicated environment like Skillspace allows learners to see their growth in real time. When a learner sees they are only a few steps away from a specific milestone, the psychological barrier of "not having time" shrinks. It transforms the experience from completing a mandatory task to attaining a tangible capability. 3. Create a frictionless path to discovery The discovery process is where many associations lose their members. If the path to find and purchase a course is difficult, participation quietly erodes. This transition requires organizing your branded storefront—using a tool like Canvas Catalog —to mirror how members actually think about their careers. When you group offerings by "Role" or "Career Goal" rather than internal department codes, you align your storefront with market demand. This proves your association is the most efficient route to staying relevant. Once a member completes a pathway, bridging the gap to the market with Parchment Digital Badges provides the verifiable, portable "gold standard" they can share with employers, completing the loop from learning to career advancement. 4. Remove structural friction with AI Administrative bloat is a silent killer of member engagement. Sixty percent of associations say limited staff capacity is a top barrier to improving the learning experience. That's a systems problem, and it compounds fast. Canvas Career addresses this through an AI Creation Agent that accelerates content development and automated reporting that eliminates manual data pulls. Your team stops managing spreadsheets and starts focusing on curriculum strategy, community building, and member relationships. That's where associations create value. The back end should run itself. 5. Visibility as a motivator A significant part of the readiness gap is a visibility problem. Professionals often feel they are working in a vacuum, unsure if their efforts are being recognized or if they are actually closing their own skill gaps. A centralized learning environment changes that by making progress concrete and continuous. When members can see exactly what they've completed, which skills they've built, and what stands between them and their next milestone, your programs stop feeling like obligations and start functioning as a career asset. That shift matters beyond motivation. When a member can point to a clear record of demonstrated competency—verified through digital credentials they can share with employers—your association isn't just a professional home. It's part of how they prove their value in the market. That's a reason to stay current, stay enrolled, and stay engaged. The opportunity in the gap Workers are ready to engage. They believe in the power of development, but they are making rational decisions about where to spend their attention. Associations that provide clear, skill-aligned guidance will become the essential partners their members are looking for. Ready to see how Canvas Career helps you guide your members? Request a demo to see our skill-based LMS in action.

title: 5 Ways Canvas Career Can Help Schools Unlock Workforce Pell Grant Funding
intro: Track clock hours, enforce 8-to-15-week windows, and flag disengaged students before completion rates slip. Five Canvas Career capabilities for Workforce Pell.

body.text: Workforce Pell is one of the most prescriptive federal aid programs colleges have ever had to implement, but the opportunities for both institutions and students who participate in Workforce Pell programs are massive. Some institutions are facing a looming operational question about whether their existing systems can actually track compliance metrics, enforce milestone thresholds, and report against federal mandates without building new infrastructure. How do you track Workforce Pell compliance? It starts by knowing exactly what has to be tracked, and Workforce Pell asks for a lot. Each program has to document clock hours at the learning-object level so they roll up to a defensible total in the 150-to-599 range. Beyond that, institutions have to track per-student engagement throughout the term, enforce a fixed 8-to-15-week cohort window, hit a 70% completion rate and a 70% job placement rate, and eventually connect all of it to value-added earnings data that the federal government reviews year after year. If completion data lives in one system, enrollment in another, and placement in a third, every reporting cycle turns into a manual reconciliation project. The Government Accountability Office has listed financial aid regulations as among the most burdensome category of federal requirements colleges face, and Workforce Pell's demands add to the existing load. A compliant approach keeps the data in one place, tied to a clean cohort structure, and visible while a program is still running rather than assembled after the fact. That means clock hours documented at the object level, engagement tracked per student in real time, hard start and end dates on every cohort, completion visible in the interface, and skills tagged to learning objects so outcomes can be traced back to what was taught. Canvas Career is built for exactly this kind of program. Here are five specific ways it helps institutions move from "Pell-aware" to "Pell-ready." 1. Codify time-to-complete at the learning-object level Workforce Pell programs have to fall within the 150-to-599 clock hour range. That sounds simple until you try to prove it for a program built from dozens of discrete modules, videos, and assessments. Canvas Career lets instructors specify expected time-to-complete on every learning object: a video, a module, a reading, an assessment. When those values roll up across a program, you have a defensible, documentable hour count that matches the federal specification. Instead of an estimate or a post-hoc calculation, you can deliver a program-level hours total, built from the objects that actually make up the program. For compliance purposes, this matters twice: once when the program is being submitted for Pell eligibility, and again every reporting cycle when auditors want to see that what students actually completed matches what the program was approved for. 2. Track engagement per student, per course, in real time The 70% completion rate can’t just be a number you measure at the end of the cohort. It needs to be managed throughout the cohort, which requires visibility into whether students are actually engaging with the program while there's still time to intervene. Canvas Career tracks time-in-course at the student level, giving instructors and advisors a clear view of how long each learner has spent inside the course environment. It's not a perfect measure (no system can guarantee every minute logged is a minute actually learning), but it's a strong proxy, and it's the closest thing to an early-warning system most institutions will have for adult learner engagement. Importantly, it lets staff act on the data. When a learner in week three hasn't logged in since week one, someone knows, and someone can reach out. That intervention window makes a difference when in if the 70% completion rate is actually earned or lost. 3. Enforce the 8-to-15-week program length with date-restricted courses Workforce Pell programs have to run at least 8 weeks and no more than 15 . For institutions accustomed to flexible-start, self-paced, or rolling-enrollment courses, this is a structural change. Canvas Career lets administrators set hard start and end dates on courses, ensuring every cohort runs within the federally required window. It also means the data you report on, such as enrollment, completion, and placement, is tied to a clean cohort structure, which makes longitudinal tracking dramatically simpler and federal audit responses dramatically faster. 4. See course completion directly in the UI, with audit-ready confidence One of the most time-consuming parts of federal compliance reporting is assembling the numbers: pulling completion data from one system, cross-referencing enrollment from another, reconciling against a third, and building a report that auditors will accept. Federal compliance reporting is already one of the most time-consuming parts of running a financial aid-eligible program. A Boston Consulting Group study estimated that faculty and staff at higher ed institutions spend between 4 and 15 percent of their time on regulatory compliance. Workforce Pell's reporting requirements — longitudinal tracking, completion and placement rates, value-added earnings calculations — sit on top of that. Canvas Career surfaces completion data directly in the interface. Staff can see, at a glance, what percentage of a cohort has completed every course or program. That visibility does two things: It makes ongoing program management faster, because leadership can spot underperforming cohorts before they become reporting problems. It makes the federal reporting process dramatically more efficient, because the underlying data is already in the system, tied to a program, and attached to the right cohort. If the plan is for an institution to efficiently (key word!) run a full portfolio of Workforce Pell-eligible programs across a system of schools, this is the move. 5. Align skills to learning objects and start to see what's actually driving outcomes This one is more strategic than immediate, but it's the capability that matters most over the long arc of a Workforce Pell program. Canvas Career lets institutions tag learning objects with the specific skills they're designed to teach. Over time, as students complete programs, move into jobs, and produce the employment outcomes federal reporting tracks, that skills-tagging layer gives the institutions a connection between which skills were taught and which outcomes followed. An institution running a welding certificates, a CNA program, and an advanced manufacturing sprint can start to see which specific competencies correlate with higher job placement rates, which correlate with faster time-to-hire, and which correlate with higher value-added earnings. Over several cohorts, this turns into the kind of evidence base institutions can use to refine programs, defend federal funding renewals, and build the next generation of Workforce Pell offerings around what actually works. The federal government requires the outcomes, and Canvas Career helps institutions understand the inputs that produced them. From feature list to federal readiness Canvas Career delivers capabilities that map to specific Workforce Pell requirements. Together, they're the operational foundation for running Workforce Pell-eligible programs. It has to be managed while the cohort is still running, when there's time to act on it. It also tracks time-in-course at the student level, which gives advisors an early read on who's falling behind. When a learner hasn't logged in since week one, someone knows, and someone can reach out. What data does Workforce Pell reporting require? Reporting sits on top of the program's core thresholds and asks institutions to prove them, cohort after cohort. You're accounting for clock hours in the 150-to-599 range, program length between 8 and 15 weeks, a 70% completion rate, and a 70% job placement rate. On top of that, Workforce Pell adds longitudinal tracking and value-added earnings calculations, so enrollment, completion, and placement all have to be tied to a specific cohort and program. When that data lives in one place and stays attached to the right cohort, the reporting process is far less painful than when it's scattered across different systems that have to be reconciled. A program built from dozens of modules, videos, readings, and assessments makes the 150-to-599 clock hour requirement harder to prove than it sounds. That gives you a documented total rather than an estimate. This is especially important when the program is submitted for Pell eligibility and then at every reporting cycle after, when auditors want to confirm that what students completed matches what the program was approved for.

Workforce Pell programs have to run at least 8 weeks and no more than 15. For institutions accustomed to flexible-start, self-paced, or rolling-enrollment courses, this is a structural change.

Canvas Career lets administrators set hard start and end dates on courses, ensuring every cohort runs within the federally required window. It also means the data you report on, such as enrollment, completion, and placement, is tied to a clean cohort structure, which makes longitudinal tracking dramatically simpler and federal audit responses dramatically faster.

4. See course completion directly in the UI, with audit-ready confidence

One of the most time-consuming parts of federal compliance reporting is assembling the numbers: pulling completion data from one system, cross-referencing enrollment from another, reconciling against a third, and building a report that auditors will accept.

Federal compliance reporting is already one of the most time-consuming parts of running a financial aid-eligible program. A Boston Consulting Group study estimated that faculty and staff at higher ed institutions spend between 4 and 15 percent of their time on regulatory compliance. Workforce Pell's reporting requirements — longitudinal tracking, completion and placement rates, value-added earnings calculations — sit on top of that.

Canvas Career surfaces completion data directly in the interface. Staff can see, at a glance, what percentage of a cohort has completed every course or program. That visibility does two things:

  • It makes ongoing program management faster, because leadership can spot underperforming cohorts before they become reporting problems.
  • It makes the federal reporting process dramatically more efficient, because the underlying data is already in the system, tied to a program, and attached to the right cohort.

If the plan is for an institution to efficiently (key word!) run a full portfolio of Workforce Pell-eligible programs across a system of schools, this is the move.

5. Align skills to learning objects and start to see what's actually driving outcomes

This one is more strategic than immediate, but it's the capability that matters most over the long arc of a Workforce Pell program.

Canvas Career lets institutions tag learning objects with the specific skills they're designed to teach. Over time, as students complete programs, move into jobs, and produce the employment outcomes federal reporting tracks, that skills-tagging layer gives the institutions a connection between which skills were taught and which outcomes followed.

An institution running a welding certificates, a CNA program, and an advanced manufacturing sprint can start to see which specific competencies correlate with higher job placement rates, which correlate with faster time-to-hire, and which correlate with higher value-added earnings. Over several cohorts, this turns into the kind of evidence base institutions can use to refine programs, defend federal funding renewals, and build the next generation of Workforce Pell offerings around what actually works.

The federal government requires the outcomes, and Canvas Career helps institutions understand the inputs that produced them.

From feature list to federal readiness

Canvas Career delivers capabilities that map to specific Workforce Pell requirements. Together, they're the operational foundation for running Workforce Pell-eligible programs.

FAQ

How do institutions track Workforce Pell completion rates?

Workforce Pell requires programs to hit a 70% completion rate, and that number can't be something you check at the finish line. It has to be managed while the cohort is still running, when there's time to act on it. Canvas Career surfaces completion data directly in the interface, so staff can see at a glance what share of a cohort has finished each course or program. It also tracks time-in-course at the student level, which gives advisors an early read on who's falling behind. What data does Workforce Pell reporting require?

Reporting sits on top of the program's core thresholds and asks institutions to prove them, cohort after cohort. You're accounting for clock hours in the 150-to-599 range, program length between 8 and 15 weeks, a 70% completion rate, and a 70% job placement rate. On top of that, Workforce Pell adds longitudinal tracking and value-added earnings calculations, so enrollment, completion, and placement all have to be tied to a specific cohort and program. When that data lives in one place and stays attached to the right cohort, the reporting process is far less painful than when it's scattered across different systems that have to be reconciled.

A program built from dozens of modules, videos, readings, and assessments makes the 150-to-599 clock hour requirement harder to prove than it sounds. This is especially important when the program is submitted for Pell eligibility and then at every reporting cycle after, when auditors want to confirm that what students completed matches what the program was approved for.

title: The Readiness Gap: What the Data Says About Member Engagement
intro: 73% of workers don't feel prepared for what's coming. For professional associations, that number has a direct implication. Here's what the data says—and what to do with it.

body.text: Three out of four workers. That's how many American professionals told us they don't feel prepared for career changes or disruptions coming their way. The State of Learning and Readiness B-Sides covers a lot of ground, but that number is where we want to start. For professional associations and credentialing bodies, there's a specific thread worth pulling: your members are in that 73%. They're navigating real uncertainty about which skills matter, whether their credentials carry weight with employers, and how to stay relevant in roles that keep changing. When your learning programs feel disconnected from those concerns, participation quietly erodes. And that can lead to the potential for your organization to lose relevancy. That's worth taking seriously. Not as a crisis, but as a useful signal about where the opportunity is. Workers believe in learning; they're just not sure it's working for them Start here, because it matters: the workforce is not checked out. Workers believe in learning as a step towards career growth, and they're actively looking for development opportunities. Some illuminating survey stats: 88% of workers say additional training would help them advance in their careers 72% trust that earning a certification would lead to real career advancement 60% are actively interested in upskilling opportunities These strong results reflect a workforce that understands development is part of staying competitive, and that credentials carry real value. But, that desire to learn is mired in uncertainty. Half of workers (50%) say they aren't sure which credentials, certifications, or skills employers actually value. For an association, that gap deserves attention. Your members trust the idea of credentialed learning. Whether they trust that your specific programs lead to the outcomes they're after is a different question, and one worth asking honestly. When learning stops feeling relevant, people stop showing up We know what pulls professionals away from continuing education. It's rare that they've lost interest in growing. More often, it's that the learning they've been asked to complete feels like it belongs to a job description from five years ago. Over 70% of workers surveyed said they've felt professionally stagnant at some point. When asked what contributed to that feeling, the answers land in familiar territory for anyone who has worked in professional learning: 47% cited low motivation or burnout 37% lacked career planning tools or guidance 30% had outdated skills with no clear path forward 29% saw their roles reduced or altered by automation, with no corresponding development offered For associations, the implication is direct. Programs built around seat time, checkbox requirements, or credentials that don't clearly map to career relevance are competing poorly for member attention. The fix isn't adding more content to the catalog. It's making the connection between learning and real career progress more visible and more credible. The barriers are real, and they're fixable When the survey asked workers what's getting in the way, the answers were practical, not philosophical. Structural friction. Gaps in support. Schedules that don't leave room. Nearly three-quarters of workers cited at least one obstacle to success in their current role: Lack of opportunities for upward mobility (26%) Heavy workloads or insufficient support (20%) Lack of employer-provided upskilling opportunities (17%) Lack of proper training for current responsibilities (15%) On future readiness, the picture is similar. The top barriers workers cited were lack of time for learning (34%), uncertainty about future career paths (30%), and feeling overwhelmed by changing technology (30%). None of those are solved by adding another webinar to the lineup. What workers are describing is a need for learning that fits how they actually work. That means flexible delivery, clear skill alignment, and visible outcomes they can point to. Associations that can deliver on those dimensions have a genuine advantage. Those running on legacy platforms and manual workflows will keep bumping up against the same ceiling. What professional associations can do with this The research report puts it plainly: the readiness gap is not a learner problem. It's a challenge within the learning systems responsible for developing skills at scale. That's a useful framing, because it points to where the leverage is. Organizations that are successfully building readiness in their member communities tend to share a few common practices: They align programs directly to the skills and roles their members are trying to grow into, not just the continuing education requirements they need to fulfill They make learner progress visible so members can see what they've built and where to go next They've removed friction from the participation experience, meeting members in formats and schedules that work They track what's actually driving engagement and outcomes, and adjust when something isn't landing That’s the kind of work Canvas Career is built to support. Not as a content library or a compliance tracker, but as a platform that connects learning to the career outcomes members are actually chasing — and gives your team the visibility to prove it's working. The demand is already there Workers believe in credentials. They want development that leads somewhere real. They're ready to engage with organizations that make the path forward clear. Associations that build programs with that in mind are the ones members will keep coming back to. Want the full picture? See what the data says about where professional learning is headed. Or see how Canvas Career helps professional associations keep learning essential.

The research report puts it plainly: the readiness gap is not a learner problem. It's a challenge within the learning systems responsible for developing skills at scale. That's a useful framing, because it points to where the leverage is.

  • They align programs directly to the skills and roles their members are trying to grow into, not just the continuing education requirements they need to fulfill
  • They make learner progress visible so members can see what they've built and where to go next
  • They've removed friction from the participation experience, meeting members in formats and schedules that work
  • They track what's actually driving engagement and outcomes, and adjust when something isn't landing

That’s the kind of work Canvas Career is built to support. Not as a content library or a compliance tracker, but as a platform that connects learning to the career outcomes members are actually chasing — and gives your team the visibility to prove it's working.

The demand is already there

Workers believe in credentials. They want development that leads somewhere real. They're ready to engage with organizations that make the path forward clear. Associations that build programs with that in mind are the ones members will keep coming back to.

title: An Edtech Roadmap (Without the Sprawl) for the Future-ready K-12 District
intro: Bring simplicity and strategy to your K-12 technology ecosystem with a multi-year roadmap. Learn how an edtech audit reduces tool sprawl and technical debt.

body.text: If you want to understand modern K-12 technology planning, a teacher’s web browser reveals more than the district's strategic IT roadmap. On a Tuesday morning, a middle school math teacher has a tab open for attendance, a quiz app, a supplemental digital curriculum, a behavior tracker, and an assessment platform that doesn’t talk to their LMS. Over the last several years, school districts have adopted—and in many cases, absorbed hidden costs of—educational technology. Urgent digital needs prompted leadership teams to fast-track new tools in 2020. Rooted in survival, it (mostly) worked for the time. But now the dust has settled, and many district decision-makers find themselves with a tech stack of applications and data streams that don’t speak to one another. Worse, leaders often have zero insight into tool usage rates or true impact on learners. This administrative headache for your IT department works against your district’s operational efficiency and budget. When you consider that the average school district accesses over 3,000 unique digital tools in a single school year, more isn’t better. Shiny new apps and big promises have been around since the beginning of edtech. But post-pandemic, leaders are savvier and necessarily more critical than ever of what tech is being used (and why). Consolidation has become the financial and efficient go-to move. And as districts face tough funding changes, the smartest best edtech strategy for the years to come may be less, but better . Step 1: Assess your K–12 edtech stack First, start with your baseline. You can’t optimize what you haven't mapped! Many K–12 leadership teams have focused on deployment. They ask questions like, “Did the software get installed? Do the accounts work?” But future-ready schools are evolving from "What software do we own?" to "What tools actually help us give the best educational experience possible to our staff and students?" When a district evaluates school technology tools, they often uncover a gap between purchased licenses and what classroom teachers actually use. A district might pay for a thousand-user site license for a supplemental tool, just to discover through an audit that teachers prefer a different, free tool. Platform redundancy means you pay double or triple for tools that serve the exact same instructional purpose. But logins don’t tell the full story. No one wants to scale an application that doesn’t show any real impact on student learning. Consider how this looks in practice for a district facing six-figure renewal decisions. Faced with evaluating a major six-figure software tool, Edmonds School District teamed up with Instructure’s researchers to run rapid-cycle evaluations . Used in tandem with anecdotal feedback, they used an iterative, evidence-based approach to analyze whether the tool was genuinely supporting positive student outcomes. This gave them the objective data necessary to confidently justify and protect that massive financial investment. Modernization isn’t a one-and-done process. Like Edmonds, you iterate, evaluate, wonder, and reassess, so every dollar in your budget planning goes directly towards tools that are both used and effective. Step 2: Move to a unified learning platform infrastructure Once you audit your stack, your tools that actually deliver value to staff and students need an environment in which they can succeed (together). If your technology infrastructure relies on patchworked software, your IT department ends up acting as an emergency response crew. Modernization means previously siloed data can talk, and your team is freed up to support staff and learners with more meaningful work. Two pillars hold up this infrastructure: The central core Built-in extensibility Instead of managing half a dozen entry points for different digital tools, future-ready districts anchor their digital environment in an LMS, where instructional delivery and administrative oversight come together. But it shouldn’t box you in. Extensible means it connects cleanly with your existing student information systems (SIS) and critical IT frameworks through standardized LTIs that don’t require custom code or manual work. When students complete high-quality lessons or formative assessments within the unified learning environment, you create predictability and safeguard screentime for when it can make the most impact on teaching and learning. Though not an extensible piece, AI-native features get a lot of hype. But those features should support workflows teachers actually use, not just be added on for AI’s sake. When your core platforms are consolidated and communicating with one another, your IT team can help staff across the district get the most out of an integrated platform. You dramatically reduce technical debt and can focus on scaling it as your needs and goals evolve. Step 3: Build a future-ready learning architecture The ultimate metric of any technology ecosystem is the human experience it creates. Should your tech stack create efficiency? Definitely, but it’s ultimately about every individual user’s experience, from the central office administrator down to the student in the classroom. Teachers and students bear the biggest burden of systems with disjointed platforms. They’re forced to navigate different apps, remember what lives where, manually input data in some cases, and if some students experience any kind of friction just getting to the assignment, they’re out. Their focus shifts away from instruction, and teachers have to wear the hat of tech support. LTIs purpose-built for education are more often used in an LMS than non-purpose-built tools. That matters because every minute of screentime should be intentional, so every minute spent troubleshooting in a classroom is a minute lost. A modern learning architecture simplifies the experience for teachers and learners. Technology takes its rightful place supporting learning rather than distracting from it when your core cloud-based platforms are consolidated and fully integrated. The budget benefits from this kind of structural harmony, to be clear. But it also shows up daily in classrooms. Teachers see data flow from one app to another, so they spend that previously lost time analyzing the results and planning their next steps. Students see assignments and assessments in the same digital environment, allowing them to focus on the content. And what’s more innovative in the age of distraction than focused instructional time? Step 4: Plan your multi-year roadmap Modernizing your IT systems is a marathon, not a sprint. From the procurement process to balancing near-term financial pressures with long-term change management, there’s plenty to consider when building your long-term edtech strategy. A multi-year technology plan helps leaders strategically sunset outdated or redundant tools, align contract renewal dates, anticipate consolidation efforts, and give your staff the time they need to adjust to structural changes. Here are three questions to consider as you build your roadmap. 1. Who should sit on our cross-functional technology committee? Tech modernization is not solely an IT responsibility, nor is it purely an academic one. A successful committee bridges central office staff, technology directors, curriculum and instruction leaders, building administrators, and classroom teachers. Some districts even include students and parents to get a 360-degree view of tools, so every procurement or sunsetting decision balances backend technical weight with frontend instructional needs, usage reports, and user experience. 2. How does the budget impact the timeline? Map out every software contract expiration for the next three, four, and five years, so you can smoothly offboard and consolidate tools instead of getting surprised by an automatic renewal that got lost in the shuffle. It also aligns your edtech budget planning with the resources you expect to become available once certain legacy funds open, as well as with the larger strategic investments your district is making. 3. How will you make training accessible and equitable over time? A smaller district handles technology adoption differently than a massive metropolitan system. Regardless of your district's size, your roadmap must account for your localized rollout capacity. Overwhelming educators with massive software drops won’t help students learn. Prioritize continuous professional development on your core, consolidated systems so teachers are confident with the foundation you’re building. A long-game K–12 edtech strategy Rome wasn’t built in a day, and neither are modern K–12 tech ecosystems. When K-12 leadership teams commit to auditing their environments for redundancy or lack of impact, anchoring their infrastructure around an LMS they can build upon, prioritizing the human experience in the classroom, and aligning the budget and tech roadmaps, they’re better prepared for whatever lies ahead. The smartest technology governance strategy serves your administrators, your staff, your students, and your families, and ultimately reflects two central values of many K–12 districts: unity and preparedness.

title: Rethinking Higher Ed Assessment in the Age of AI
intro: Did AI break higher ed assessment, or was it already cracked? Discover how Giorgio Lagna's 'Crucible' course uses AI tutors, some designed to intentionally lie, to promote durable learning and equity.

body.text: An undergraduate from a well-established Bay Area university was working in Giorgio Lagna's cardiovascular research lab at UCSF. She could design a control experiment most postdocs would have struggled with. Lagna, a research scientist and biologist by training, asked her what classes had helped her learn to do that. "Not in class," she told him. She'd attended lectures and taken exams. The things she actually knew, she'd learned in internships, where people had asked her hard questions and made her defend her answers. That conversation crystallized something Lagna had already started to suspect. The students with the strongest transcripts sometimes struggled at the bench, and he saw students with unremarkable transcripts outperform their peers in certain exercises. Whatever the transcript credential was measuring, it was not the biggest priority in his classroom. An assessment crisis that started before ChatGPT Lagna started teaching in 2018. By spring of 2020, he was getting batches of student essays that were essentially the same essay. Lightly edited, but functionally identical. This was before any current AI tools existed. Students were copying from each other and from the same online sources. "AI didn't break assessment," he said. "Assessment was already broken." The standard response to AI in higher ed has been to retreat to lower-tech assessment methods. Recent reporting notes that Penn, Cornell, NYU, and others have been moving back to oral exams and handwritten in-class work because they're worried about AI cheating. Lagna agrees oral exams are a better measure of what a student actually knows. He just doesn't think going back to a number two pencil is the move. "You are not testing their knowledge," he says of the locked-room, paper-and-pencil exam. "You are preparing them for the last century's jobs." The Crucible is built on a different bet. If students remember the questions they had to defend and forget the lectures they sat through, the design job is to put those questions back in the classroom. AI is the only tool Lagna has seen that can do that for every student, every week.
