title: How IgniteAI Does More Than Just Save Instructors Time
intro: IgniteAI for SpeedGrader helps educators grade faster with consistent standards, reduce fatigue, and deliver meaningful, personalized feedback at scale.

body.text: It’s almost impossible to have a discussion about using AI at work and in the classroom that doesn’t end with "AI will save you time." And it does, to a significant degree. A new Gallup report notes that while only three out of every ten classroom teachers are using AI weekly, those who do are saving up to 6 weeks of time a year. B ut focusing only on the clock misses the point. For most educators, the heaviest burden of grading isn’t just the minutes spent, but the mental exhaustion, the worry over fairness, and the struggle to provide meaningful feedback to every single student. IgniteAI Grading Assistance for SpeedGrader can shave hours off your work week, but when you integrate IgniteAI into your SpeedGrader workflow, you aren't just getting time back. You’re getting your creative and cognitive energy back. Here is how IgniteAI changes the spirit of grading, not just the speed. 1. Defeating the "decision fatigue" wall Grading is a series of a thousand tiny decisions. Does this thesis meet the criteria? Is this citation format close enough? By the time you reach student #25, your "decision muscle" is exhausted. Decision fatigue is why the last paper often feels much harder to grade than the first. IgniteAI can act as a cognitive buffer. By providing an initial alignment between the student’s submission and your Canvas rubric, it handles the "low-level" identification tasks. This leaves your mental energy intact for high-level mentoring and the kind of nuanced feedback that only a human educator can provide. 2. Eliminating "grading drift" One of many quiet truths in education: we are different graders at 8:00 AM than we are at 11:00 PM. Because it applies your rubric with clinical consistency across every submission in SpeedGrader, it acts as an anchor for fairness. It’s a creative hurdle that can slow down even the best and most experienced educators and drain inspiration along the way. IgniteAI solves the "blank page" problem by generating a draft of rubric-aligned feedback based on the student's actual work. This shifts your role from a generator of text to an editor. It is much easier to refine and personalize a draft than to build one from scratch. You get to step into the role of "Editor-in-Chief," adding your unique voice and classroom context to a solid foundation. 5. Standardizing excellence for every student In the rush of a heavy grading load, we often focus our best feedback on the students who are struggling, while the high-achievers get a "Great job!" and a checkmark. But those top-tier students deserve to know why they succeeded just as much as others need to know why they missed the mark. Because IgniteAI helps scale the feedback process, you can provide deep, rubric-specific commentary to every single student on your roster. You can finally offer a "VIP feedback experience" to the quiet "B+" student who might get overlooked, ensuring that every learner in your Canvas course feels seen and supported. The bottom line benefit for educators: reclaiming mental clarity and instructional integrity IgniteAI for SpeedGrader isn't all about doing less work; it's about helping instructors focus on the most high-impact work. Over the past six years, charter schools have seen enrollment grow year over year, with no signs of slowing down. In 2025, charter schools hit their highest enrollment numbers ever at nearly 4 million students attending the institutions. That same year, Charter School Growth Fund invested in more than 50 charter school networks and projected that their series of charter networks will serve 1 million students by 2030.

This growth means more options for students and families; it also puts lot more weight on the systems behind the schools. Every new campus adds more transcripts, more enrollment records, and more credential requests.

When a network expands, the administrative friction usually starts in the registrar's office. As it grows, it often inherits a collection of disjointed "back-office" identities. There are also resources to contend with; charter schools are known for specialized educational environments, run by lean teams. Come spring, these things add up quickly. A registrar at a growing charter network in 2026 might spend 15 hours a week just verifying graduation dates for alumni across three different campuses. Families who choose a charter school for its modern approach to education often find the administrative experience feels like 1995.

The cost of manual record management

Most charter networks operate with small teams where the registrar often wears three other hats. During the spring window, those teams spend hours on tasks that should be automated:

  • Identity verification: Spending 20 minutes on the phone to verify a graduation date for a background check company.
  • Manual data entry: Typing the same student information into a print-shop portal for diplomas and again into a mailing label program.
  • Physical triaging: Hunting down a cumulative folder in a filing cabinet at a different campus because the record hasn't been digitized.

A 3-day delay in sending a transcript can be the difference between a student securing a summer internship or losing the opportunity.
 

3 ways consistency strengthens charter school networks
 

1. Student mobility without the data lag

In a charter network, a student moving from a middle school in one zip code to a high school in another shouldn’t create more work for students or their families. When grading scales and credit recovery protocols are consistent, a consistent "administrative engine" means a student’s academic history follows them instantly. This keeps the focus on creating the best possible individual student outcomes instead of hunting down digital paper trails.

2. Operational breathing room for staff

Consistency is the antidote to the data entry work that eats up charter school staff’s days. When leaders standardize how records are managed across every campus, they eliminate the need for their teams to juggle extra work every June. A streamlined experience can help balance a workload among already stretched campus staff. 

3. Protecting the charter purpose

Charter schools have a reputation for innovation, flexibility, and performance. Their purpose is to provide a more personalized, agile approach to public education. A modern, secure digital records experience can help charter networks more readily deliver on that purpose. It not only improves compliance and sharpens accountability, but can also remove a bureaucratic friction that slows down schoolwide innovation. 

Standardizing the network identity

Standardizing records across a network ensures that a student’s achievement is treated with the same professional speed regardless of which campus they attended. Moving to a digital-first system like Parchment allows a network to replace fragmented workflows with a single, secure process.

  • Self-service ordering: Families and alumni place orders through a 24/7 digital storefront, removing the front office from the initial transaction.
  • Secure compliance: The platform includes built-in controls for FERPA and identity verification, ensuring audit trails are automatically generated.
  • Standardized quality: Every diploma and transcript looks and feels like it belongs to the same prestigious network.
  • Cost recovery: Schools can implement a service or processing fee to offset the cost of the platform to help drive sustainable operation.

Planning for next-year readiness

A charter network is a promise of a specific kind of educational experience. Standardizing records across all campuses protects your network's good reputation and ensures students don't lose momentum during transitions or graduation audits.

title: 5 Ways to Reduce Admin Work and Reclaim Time with IgniteAI
intro: Reduce admin load with IgniteAI for Canvas. Discover 5 AI use cases—from rubric drafting to quiz generation—to save time and support student focus.

body.text: The administrative load in a modern classroom feels like a second, unpaid job. While teaching is about connection and discovery, many educators spend hours each week on data entry, formatting rubrics, and auditing discussion threads. Premium IgniteAI features are currently available at no cost for United States Canvas customers through June 30, 2026, and it’s designed to handle these repetitive tasks so you can focus on students. Here are five actionable ways to reduce your administrative time using the tools already in your Canvas environment. 1. Draft rubrics in 30 seconds Building a detailed rubric is a time sink that requires aligning specific learning outcomes with performance levels. The IgniteAI Generator for Rubrics takes your assignment description and creates a full draft for you to review. Edit instead of author : You can regenerate specific criteria or manually adjust the wording to match your expectations. Maintain quality standards : The tool provides a structured baseline that you can refine, ensuring you don't miss a key requirement in a rush to finish your planning. How to use IgniteAI Generator for Rubrics : To start a draft, navigate to the Assignments or Outcomes tab in your course. Select IgniteAI Generator for Rubrics and provide a brief description of your assignment or paste your learning outcomes. The tool will suggest criteria and performance levels that you can manually edit, delete, or regenerate until the draft matches your specific grading standards. 2. Automate question generation for assessments Creating a fresh quiz for every unit might mean hours of manual drafting. IgniteAI Question Authoring Assistance for Quizzes allows you to generate items directly from your existing course materials. Direct source alignment : Upload a PDF or select specific modules to ensure your questions are actually testing the content you taught. Diverse question types : You can prompt the tool to generate different formats and difficulty levels, reducing the time you spend staring at a blank screen while helping create quality quizzes. How to use IgniteAI Question Authoring Assistance for Quizzes: Open the Quizzes tool and select IgniteAI Question Authoring Assistance. You can upload a specific PDF or select existing course modules as the source material. Choose the number of questions and desired difficulty levels based on Bloom’s taxonomy, then review and refine each item before adding them to your quiz bank. 3. Identify the signal in discussion threads Manually checking a thread with 30 or more participants for quality is exhausting. IgniteAI Insights for Discussions scans student replies to identify who is contributing substantively and who might be drifting off topic. Actionable intervention : Instead of reading every post to find the struggling student, use the insights to flag participants who need immediate feedback. Thread summaries : Use the summary feature to get a high-level view of the common questions or emerging themes without scrolling through 100 entries. How to use IgniteAI Insights for Discussions : Navigate to a specific Discussion thread and select Summaries for discussions to get a recap of main points and emerging questions. For a deeper dive into student participation, use Insights for discussions to scan replies for substance and relevance. 4. Use the IgniteAI Agent for complex workflows Adjusting course logistics, such as due dates or module organization, usually requires clicking through multiple menus. The IgniteAI Agent acts as an orchestrator that can handle these multi-step tasks from a single prompt. Bulk updates : You can ask the Agent to adjust all due dates in a module at once. Resource coordination : Prompt the Agent to find specific files or organize content based on your instructions, saving you from navigating deep folder structures. How to use IgniteAI Agent : Locate the IgniteAI Agent icon within your Canvas environment to open the prompt interface. Enter a single, descriptive command, such as "Adjust all due dates in Module 3 to be one week later" or "Organize my new modules based on this syllabus". The Agent coordinates these multi-step updates across your course settings automatically. 5. Search with context instead of just keywords Finding a specific assignment or discussion prompt from a previous semester can be a frustrating hunt. IgniteAI Search uses semantic algorithms to understand what you are actually looking for, even if you don't remember the exact title. Natural language queries : You can search using everyday language to surface content across all your modules, assignments, and announcements. In-place translations : If you are working with multilingual teams or students, you can use the translation feature to communicate in the Canvas Inbox or discussions without switching to external tools. How to use IgniteAI Search and Translation : Use the IgniteAI Search bar to enter natural language queries, like "find that assignment about plate tectonics from last spring". The semantic algorithm searches across your pages, assignments, and announcements to find the specific content. For multilingual communication, select the Translation icon in the Canvas Inbox or discussions to view original and translated text side by side. Making teaching, not tasking, the priority Most educators have the same goal: to spend less time on admin tasks and more time on students. These tools, from rubric generation to automated quiz authoring, are designed to save time (and reduce an already heavy cognitive load) by handling the repetitive tasks that don't require your specific expertise. You can test which features actually save you the most time by using IgniteAI free as a Canvas user until June 30, 2026. Find out how here .

body.text: Today's learning leaders face a paradox: they can clearly describe the forces reshaping their organizations, whether it’s AI adoption, skills-based hiring, or shifting workforce expectations; yet knowing what's changing isn't the same as knowing what to do about it. The real challenge lies in making high-stakes decisions without a clear picture of what comes next and then proving it worked. According to Brandon Hall Group research, 75% of organizations identify improving alignment between learning strategy and business goals as their top priority. Without the proof, even well-reasoned decisions become difficult to defend, and L&D loses credibility with the business. In this webinar, Melissa Loble, Chief Learning Officer at Instructure, and David Wentworth, Brandon Hall Group’s Managing Director of Learning and Talent will cut through the awareness gap to focus on what resilient learning functions actually do differently. They will share: The judgment frameworks that help leaders evaluate options and move forward with confidence Practical approaches to adopting new tools, including AI, without losing organizational footing What it takes to build proof that connects learning to outcomes the business can't argue with. Whether you're navigating technology decisions, justifying program investments, or trying to keep your function effective as conditions keep shifting, this session offers the patterns and habits that separate organizations that absorb disruption from the ones that adapt through it. Attendees will come away with: An understanding of how to develop the decision-making framework to move forward with confidence when the future isn't clear A governance model for new technology Insight into how to connect learning investment to skills application and business outcomes. The habits of resilient L&D teams and how to build the flexibility to adapt without losing what already works

Beginning with short-term, high-value workforce programs, institutions have an unprecedented opportunity to expand access for adult learners while strengthening regional workforce pipelines. But success will require far more than launching new certificates. You'll learn how to: Understand the latest Workforce Pell requirements and institutional implications Build stackable credential pathways Use digital badges and learner records Design employer-aligned programs Develop a sustainable strategy supporting enrollment growth and workforce impact What to expect To qualify and thrive under Workforce Pell, institutions must build the infrastructure to recruit learners, deliver employer-aligned programs, verify skills, measure outcomes, and demonstrate strong completion, employment, and earnings results. Join higher education and workforce leaders as they explore what it takes to become a Workforce Pell-ready institution. You'll hear how institutions are designing stackable credential pathways, using digital credentials and learner records to document skills, partnering with employers to improve job placement, and creating scalable systems that position students—and institutions—for long-term success.

And how do we use AI to build for where learning is going, helping you to accelerate outcomes and transform learning? What we were really asking was what does it mean to provide the industry leading LMS today given the pace of change we're all experiencing? And it became clear that the opportunity wasn't just AI. It was a chance to simplify Canvas overall from the way it works day to day to how you access its value. Starting this year, not only will we be refreshing the user experience, but also the purchasing experience to bring Canvas into the future. To put it simply, the future of Canvas is modern and accessible, easy to adopt and implement, and AI forward while keeping AI transparent and optional. Let's start by sharing with you how Canvas will be packaged to meet institutions where they are. Rachel? We've heard your feedback over the years. Too many add ons make budgeting and procurement complex. So we're excited to introduce three Canvas tiers for our institutional customers: Canvas Core, Canvas Plus and Canvas Next. This approach allows you to purchase the Canvas tier that makes sense for your institutional needs and appetite for AI. If you're a Canvas customer today, you're already on Canvas Core. It just has a new name. I want to be very clear, you won't be forced to make a switch. Nothing about your contract or functionality is changing, and there's no migration required. The Canvas core tier includes our core LMS functionality for consistent and accessible teaching and learning.

We also previewed the shift to more modern, connected workflows within the Canvas experience itself, and shared exciting advancements in our Impact product. These updates reflect a broader commitment to delivering more connected experiences, greater flexibility, and long-term partnership built for the accelerated evolution of learning. You can learn more about our new Canvas tiers and request a quote from our team here.

Practical Takeaways Leave with clear actions your institution can take to strengthen verification, protect credentials, and reduce fraud risk across key workflows. Helpful Resource Strengthening Trust Through Smarter Fraud Prevention for Transcripts Fraud attempts targeting transcript requests are becoming more sophisticated, often using stolen student data to obtain legitimate credentials. This blog explores how institutions can strengthen identity verification and protect academic records while maintaining a smooth experience for legitimate learners.

After leading a successful transition to Canvas across all nine of its campuses in early 2024, the University of Louisiana System quickly turned its attention to the next frontier: transforming the way it accessed and used data. With increasing pressure to drive data-informed decision-making and reduce manual reporting burdens, the UL System needed a solution that could:

  • Deliver near real-time data across its enterprise systems

Join this Instructure-hosted webinar to hear how the UL System team, alongside leaders from Instructure and K16 Solutions—successfully tackled data fragmentation and built a foundation for long-term innovation, and learn how your institution can do the same.

body.heading: What the research reveals about Canvas
body.text: What the research reveals about Canvas Across 250 surveyed educators, here are four findings that stand out. 94% of K–12 educators and 97% of higher education educators log into Canvas every day or every week An average of 4.6 hours per week freed up for instruction instead of paperwork Educators who use Canvas 8+ hours a week report double the time savings and higher effectiveness ratings than lighter users Announcements, Ignite AI features, and SpeedGrader rank among the strongest drivers of better student and educator outcomes The full report breaks this down by usage level and feature, so you can see exactly where Canvas fits into your own strategy. (And you can read how the study meets ESSA Level III (Promising Evidence) requirements, giving districts and institutions research-backed support for a Canvas investment!)

title: 2026 EdTech Evidence Report
snippet: A district-ready framework and market findings from a review of 150 widely used
intro: A district-ready framework and market findings from a review of 150 widely used tools, so teams can evaluate what belongs in classrooms with confidence.

body.text: Screen time questions are turning into screen time policy. Boards, families, and now states want proof that classroom technology actually helps students learn, not just a promise that it might. The 2026 EdTech Evidence Report reviewed 150 widely used tools and found a clear gap: research, privacy, and accessibility standards cluster in purpose-built edtech, not the consumer apps that end up in classrooms anyway. Read on to learn where the gaps are widest.
body.html:
Screen time questions are turning into screen time policy. Boards, families, and now states want proof that classroom technology actually helps students learn, not just a promise that it might.

The 2026 EdTech Evidence Report reviewed 150 widely used tools and found a clear gap: research, privacy, and accessibility standards cluster in purpose-built edtech, not the consumer apps that end up in classrooms anyway. Read on to learn where the gaps are widest.

body.heading: What the 2026 EdTech Evidence Report covers
body.text: What the 2026 EdTech Evidence Report covers Instructure and InnovateEDU reviewed 150 of the most-used K-12 classroom technologies from fall 2025, sorting them into purpose-built edtech and general consumer technology, then checking each against research and quality benchmarks districts increasingly require. The report lays out the following: Maps every tool against Every Student Succeeds Act (ESSA) evidence levels I through IV, showing how much classroom technology actually has evidence behind it Compares data privacy and interoperability certifications, including iKeepSafe, 1EdTech, and Project Unicorn, across edtech and consumer technology Reviews accessibility and usability standards, including Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) alignment and Voluntary Product Accessibility Templates (VPATs) Lays out a four-phase path for consumer technology companies to build the evidence and certifications schools expect Gives states and districts eight procurement questions to use immediately when evaluating a new tool Districts are formalizing procurement, and the tools that can show their work are the ones that will hold up under review. (And for inquiring minds: Canvas by Instructure remains the only learning management system with ESSA Level III research behind it!)
body.html:
Instructure and InnovateEDU reviewed 150 of the most-used K-12 classroom technologies from fall 2025, sorting them into purpose-built edtech and general consumer technology, then checking each against research and quality benchmarks districts increasingly require. The report lays out the following:

  • Compares data privacy and interoperability certifications, including iKeepSafe, 1EdTech, and Project Unicorn, across edtech and consumer technology
  • Reviews accessibility and usability standards, including Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) alignment and Voluntary Product Accessibility Templates (VPATs)

snippet: Instructure’s research team recently evaluated the predictive validity of

body.heading: Do Mastery Predictive Assessments align with End-of-Course state assessments?
body.text: Do Mastery Predictive Assessments align with End-of-Course state assessments? Instructure’s research team recently evaluated the predictive validity of Mastery Predictive Assessments (MPAs) across Tennessee, South Carolina, and Mississippi during the 2022–2023 school year. Analyzing data from over 54,000 students from nine school districts and a diverse range of locales, the study found strong correlations between students' performance on MPAs and their state end-of-course assessments in math, ELA, science, and social studies. Key findings: High predictive correlations : Correlation analysis between the Mastery Predictive Assessment (MPA) cumulative benchmark and the End-of-Course state assessments demonstrated strong concurrent and predictive validity evidence, with all correlations exceeding the .70 standard. Strong classification accuracy : MPAs correctly identified student proficiency on state tests 84% of the time in grades 3–8 and 82% in high school, exceeding the 75% benchmark. Broad representation : Results held across states, reinforcing MPAs as a reliable benchmark tool for identifying students needing intervention.
body.html:
Instructure’s research team recently evaluated the predictive validity of Mastery Predictive Assessments (MPAs) across Tennessee, South Carolina, and Mississippi during the 2022–2023 school year. Analyzing data from over 54,000 students from nine school districts and a diverse range of locales, the study found strong correlations between students' performance on MPAs and their state end-of-course assessments in math, ELA, science, and social studies.

Key findings:

  • High predictive correlations : Correlation analysis between the Mastery Predictive Assessment (MPA) cumulative benchmark and the End-of-Course state assessments demonstrated strong concurrent and predictive validity evidence, with all correlations exceeding the .70 standard.
  • Strong classification accuracy : MPAs correctly identified student proficiency on state tests 84% of the time in grades 3–8 and 82% in high school, exceeding the 75% benchmark.
  • Broad representation : Results held across states, reinforcing MPAs as a reliable benchmark tool for identifying students needing intervention.

title: 100+ Student Voices: State of Student Success & Engagement in North Carolina Higher Education
snippet: Explore the perspectives of 100 North Carolina students on success and
intro: Explore the perspectives of 100 North Carolina students on success and engagement. Discover why career readiness and mental health are the new priorities for higher ed.

body.text: Students in North Carolina know what it takes to engage and succeed, and they are clear about the support mechanisms that can help them do so. Download the 100+ Student Voices report for insights on the state of student success and engagement in North Carolina higher education. "100 Student Voices: The State of Higher Ed in North Carolina" is a qualitative research report that brings a human face to the data of student success and engagement. By capturing direct feedback from 100 students across various North Carolina institutions, the report identifies a significant shift in student priorities: success is no longer defined solely by degree completion, but by a holistic sense of career preparedness and emotional well-being. The findings suggest that for North Carolina’s higher education system to remain resilient, it must prioritize flexibility, accessibility, and a student-centric "Ed-cosystem" that mirrors the needs of a modern, diverse workforce. The report highlights four key themes derived from student experiences: The Career-Ready Mindset: North Carolina students increasingly view their education through a professional lens, seeking tangible skills and internships that directly correlate to employment. Flexibility as a Necessity: Whether attending a community college or a major research university, students across the state demand hybrid and asynchronous learning options to balance their education with work and family commitments. The Importance of Personal Connection: Despite the move toward digital learning, students emphasize that their success is deeply tied to feeling seen and supported by their instructors and the campus community. Mental Health and Whole-Student Support: Students in North Carolina are vocal about the need for better integration of mental health resources and financial transparency within the digital learning environment. This report reflects Instructure’s empathetic, authoritative, and student-focused brand voice. By centering the actual voices of students, Instructure positions itself not just as a technology provider, but as a strategic advocate for the North Carolina academic community. It serves as a call to action for institutional leaders to build a more inclusive and responsive future where technology bridges the gap between student aspirations and institutional support.

title: Building Transferable Skills for the Workplace of Tomorrow
snippet: Building Transferrable Skills for the Workforce of Tomorrow is a new report to
intro: Building Transferrable Skills for the Workforce of Tomorrow is a new report to help leaders and learners identify and close skills gaps, starting with the transformation to competency-based and skills-based learning approaches.

body.text: Futurists are predicting that by 2030, almost 50% of jobs will become obsolete. Stack that on top of an already present skills gap and declining trends in enrollment for undergraduate and graduate programs due to perceived Return on Investment. These two circumstances alone should serve as a critical wake-up call not only for organizations but for academia preparing the future of the workforce. A shift in upskilling and reskilling is imperative to match the labor demand of the coming era. The focus now requires a competency-based and skills-based learning approach to validate and demonstrate the mastery of skills achievement in a meaningful and equitable way. How can leaders and learners start on this transformation journey to help identify and close skills gaps? No need to start from scratch. This report has the answers. title: The State of Teaching and Learning in K- 12 Education
snippet: Explore the global research on K-12 student success. Learn why high-quality
intro: Explore the global research on K-12 student success. Learn why high-quality content, teacher efficiency, and digital equity are the top priorities for educators.

body.text: The last few years have been unprecedented in K-12 education, and the K-12 community faces an opportunity for meaningful change. Our 2022 K-12 research study uncovers vital stats and key trends that are top of mind for educators and parents nationwide, including measures of student success, the role of technology in student learning, and considerations for the future. "The State of Teaching and Learning in K-12 Education" is a research-intensive report based on a global survey of educators, parents, and students. The study identifies the primary drivers of student success in an increasingly digital landscape, arguing that technology’s role has shifted from a temporary pandemic solution to a foundational element of the modern "Ed-cosystem." The report positions the Instructure Learning Platform (Canvas, Mastery, and Elevate) as the catalyst for creating more equitable, efficient, and engaging K-12 environments. The report identifies several key pillars that define the current state of K-12 education: The Importance of High-Quality Content: Research shows that access to engaging, standards-aligned digital content is the #1 factor in driving student success. The Equity Mandate: Addressing the "digital divide" remains a top priority, with a focus on ensuring mobile-friendly access and inclusive design to support all learners regardless of socioeconomic status. Streamlining Teacher Workflows: Highlighting that teacher burnout is a major threat, the report advocates for unified technology that integrates instruction, assessment, and grading into a single "pane of glass" to save time and reduce stress. Holistic Student Success: A growing emphasis on Social-Emotional Learning (SEL) and mental health, recognizing that academic mastery is only possible when a student's basic well-being and sense of belonging are met. The Shift to Formative Assessment: Moving away from high-stakes testing toward frequent, low-stakes "checks for understanding" that allow for immediate feedback and personalized interventions. Instructure’s authoritative, data-driven, and empathetic brand voice is likewise delineated in this guide. It frames the current challenges in K-12 not as obstacles, but as a unique opportunity for districts to intentionally design a more resilient and student-centric future.

title: The State of Student Success & Engagement in Higher Education
snippet: Bridge the gap between pedagogical theory and practice. Discover how to foster
intro: Bridge the gap between pedagogical theory and practice. Discover how to foster active learning, community, and student success with the Canvas engagement guide.

body.text: 2021 presented a unique set of challenges. One trend remained: the resiliency of students and educators. In partnership with Hanover Research, we revisited the state of student sucess and engagement in our Global Student engagement and success study. Uncover vital stats and key trends to help higher education institutions like yours thrive through today's education challenges. "Higher Education Student Engagement: Bringing Theory to Life" is a comprehensive guide that bridges the gap between pedagogical theory and the practical application of technology. The document argues that high-impact student engagement is not a byproduct of technology itself, but of how technology is used to foster active learning, community, and belonging. It positions the Instructure Learning Platform (Canvas) as the essential infrastructure for moving beyond "passive" digital learning toward an "Ed-cosystem" where students are co-creators of their educational journey. The guide explores several strategic pillars for turning engagement theory into practice: Active Learning in Digital Spaces: Applying established theories (like Bloom’s Taxonomy and Constructivism) to online environments, encouraging faculty to design courses that require critical thinking and hands-on application. The "Human Element": Strategies for building social presence and community through interactive discussions, peer review, and video-based feedback to reduce the isolation often felt in online or hybrid learning. Data-Informed Support: Utilizing learning analytics to identify engagement gaps in real-time, allowing instructors to provide proactive, personalized interventions before a student falls behind. Universal Design for Learning (UDL): Ensuring that course content is accessible, inclusive, and flexible, meeting the needs of a diverse student population with varying backgrounds and abilities. The Power of Feedback: Emphasizing the role of timely, specific, and actionable feedback in maintaining student motivation and driving academic persistence. This resource posits Instructure’s authoritative, visionary, and supportive brand voice. It also highlights student engagement as the "heartbeat" of the modern university, providing educators with the theoretical foundation and practical tools needed to create meaningful learning experiences at scale.

title: The State of Assessment in K-12 Education: Study & Trends
snippet: Explore the latest trends in K-12 assessments and school district priorities
intro: Explore the latest trends in K-12 assessments and school district priorities. Learn how formative data and integrated technology drive student growth and teacher efficiency.

body.text: Assessment is critical. It serves as essential check in on the student's learning journey for educators and students alike. In 2022, we surveyed educators across the county to weigh in on the state of assessment. We asked if it was time to reassess K-12 assessment. The result? The time for an overhaul to our approach to assessment is now. Review their insights and research findings below. The "K-12 School Districts, State Assessments, & Education Trends Study" is a comprehensive research report that examines the evolving landscape of assessment and instructional technology in U.S. school districts. The study highlights a significant shift away from high-stakes, end-of-year summative testing toward a more continuous, formative approach to measuring student growth. By leveraging the Instructure Learning Platform—specifically MasteryConnect—the report argues that districts can bridge the gap between assessment and instruction, ensuring that data is used to drive student success in real-time. The study identifies several key trends and challenges facing K-12 leaders: The Rise of Formative Assessment: A growing consensus among educators that frequent, low-stakes "checks for understanding" are more effective at improving student outcomes than traditional annual state tests. Addressing Learning Loss: Using data-driven insights to identify specific learning gaps caused by pandemic-related disruptions and implementing targeted interventions to bring students back to grade-level mastery. Teacher Burnout and Tool Fatigue: The urgent need for a unified "Ed-cosystem" that integrates assessments directly into the LMS (Canvas), reducing the administrative burden on teachers and allowing them to focus on instruction. Parent and Community Engagement: The increasing importance of providing transparent, easy-to-understand data to parents to foster a collaborative support system for students. Standardized Testing Evolution: A call for state assessments to become more flexible and aligned with the daily classroom experience, rather than serving as isolated, stressful events. The reports fortifies Instructure’s authoritative, data-driven, and advocate-oriented brand voice in the industry. It positions Instructure as a thought leader that understands the complexities of the K-12 environment and provides the necessary tools to transform assessment from a bureaucratic requirement into a powerful engine for equity and student achievement.

title: Formative Assessment: A Research Summary
snippet: Explore the research behind formative assessment. Learn how real-time feedback
intro: Explore the research behind formative assessment. Learn how real-time feedback and data-driven instruction improve student mastery and teacher effectiveness.

body.text: The cancellation of summative assessments in the spring of 2020 coupled with the variability of the spring 2021 testing season has significantly impacted the K-12 assessment landscape, making formatives essential. Formative assessments provide teachers with immediate, meaningful feedback about student mastery so they can adjust instruction in the moment and design targeted interventions. The "Formative Assessment Research Summary" is a research-backed white paper that clarifies the critical role of frequent, low-stakes assessment in driving student growth. The document synthesizes educational research to argue that formative assessment is not a "test," but a continuous instructional process that provides immediate feedback to both teachers and students. By leveraging the Instructure Learning Platform—specifically tools like MasteryConnect—educators can move away from "autopsy-style" summative testing (evaluating learning after it’s over) toward "check-up" style formative assessment that allows for mid-stream course corrections. The research summary highlights several evidence-based benefits of this approach: Immediate Feedback Loops: Research shows that timely feedback is one of the most powerful influences on achievement, helping students identify gaps in their understanding while there is still time to improve. Informing Differentiated Instruction: By collecting real-time data on student mastery, teachers can group students based on specific needs, providing targeted interventions for those struggling and enrichment for those ready to move ahead. Student Agency and Ownership: Formative practices encourage students to reflect on their own learning goals, fostering metacognitive skills and a "growth mindset." Reducing Assessment Anxiety: Shifting the focus from high-stakes grades to continuous improvement creates a safer, more supportive "Ed-cosystem" where students feel empowered to take risks and learn from mistakes.

title: American Universities and the Case for Lifelong Learning
snippet: Discover why American universities must embrace lifelong learning. Explore how
intro: Discover why American universities must embrace lifelong learning. Explore how flexible pathways and micro-credentials help institutions meet modern workforce demands.

body.text: In collaboration with The Stanford Center on Longevity, this research examines how educational institutions can better meet the needs of adult learners in the wake of the pandemic. Dive into the concerns adult learners have surrounding transparency, portability, certainty, the role of the university, and explore a practical case study from ASU. "American Universities and the Case for Lifelong Learning" is a strategic white paper that examines the shifting landscape of US higher education as it moves toward a model of continuous, life-cycle learning. The document argues that traditional four-year degree paths are no longer sufficient to meet the demands of a rapidly evolving workforce. Instead, it positions American universities as potential hubs for "lifelong learning," utilizing the Instructure Learning Platform (Canvas) to support non-traditional students, professional development, and micro-credentialing. The paper outlines the critical drivers for this institutional shift: The "60-Year Curriculum": A move away from the "one-and-done" degree toward a sustained relationship with learners that spans their entire professional careers. Economic and Workforce Alignment: Highlighting the urgent need for universities to partner with industries to provide short-term, high-impact certifications that close the skills gap. Serving the "New Traditional" Student: Recognizing that adult learners, career-switchers, and part-time students now make up a significant portion of the learner population, requiring flexible, mobile-first digital environments. Diversifying Revenue Streams: Positioning lifelong learning programs (like those managed via Canvas Catalog) as essential for the financial sustainability of universities facing declining traditional enrollment. Micro-credentialing and Portability: The role of digital badges and verifiable credentials in providing immediate value to learners and employers alike. The document highlights Instructure’s authoritative, visionary, and partner-oriented brand voice. It frames the adoption of lifelong learning not as a threat to traditional academia, but as a vital evolution that allows American universities to remain relevant and indispensable in the 21st-century global economy.

title: State of Student Success & Engagement in Higher Education
snippet: Explore the 2021 State of Higher Education Global Report. Discover how hybrid
intro: Explore the 2021 State of Higher Education Global Report. Discover how hybrid learning, career readiness, and student well-being are redefining success worldwide.

body.text: Higher education faced immense challenges in 2020. In partnership with Hanover Research, we fielded a survey in 13 countries with over 7,070 students, admin, and faculty surrounding the impact of COVID-19 on student success and engagement. This global study on the state of student success and engagement gives institutions vital insights for thriving through challenges in 2020 and beyond. The "State of Higher Education 2021 Global Report" is a landmark research study that examines the lasting impact of the pandemic on the global academic community. Based on a survey of thousands of students and educators across 18 countries, the report identifies a fundamental shift in how "success" is defined—moving away from traditional academic metrics toward a more holistic view that encompasses career readiness, student well-being, and social equity. It argues that the "new normal" in higher education is not a return to the past, but a permanent move toward a hybrid, flexible, and student-centric future. The report identifies six key trends driving the global higher education landscape: The Redefinition of Success: While grades still matter, work readiness and the acquisition of tangible skills have become the top priorities for students and employers alike. The Mental Health Imperative: Student well-being and a sense of belonging are now recognized as critical drivers of persistence, forcing institutions to integrate support services more deeply into the digital experience. The "Mobile-First" Reality: Accessibility is no longer optional. Students increasingly rely on mobile devices to access their learning, making a high-quality mobile LMS experience a requirement for equity. The Rise of the Hybrid Model: A majority of students and faculty now prefer a blend of in-person and online learning, viewing flexibility as a core component of a high-quality educational experience. Narrowing the Socioeconomic Gap: The report highlights that the pandemic widened existing inequities, placing a greater burden on institutions to provide inclusive technology and support for marginalized learners. The Need for Data-Informed Interventions: Institutions are increasingly turning to analytics to identify "at-risk" students earlier, allowing for more proactive and personalized support. This report finally reflects Instructure’s authoritative, research-driven, and visionary brand voice. By providing a global perspective, Instructure positions itself as a thought leader and strategic partner, advocating for an "Ed-cosystem" that is resilient, inclusive, and fundamentally focused on the success of the modern learner.

title: No Country for Fast Answers: Safeguarding Critical Human Logic in a World of Instant AI Responses Educast 3000 July 28, 2026 36 min 0:00 / 36:23 ▶

body.text: Dale Leszczynski leads RMIT University's Generative AI Lab for Education (GAILE), where he's spent the past year building a skills continuum (instead of a single checklist) for roughly 5,000 educators , on the theory that nobody stays an expert in this field for long. Hosts Ryan Lufkin and Melissa Loble talk with Dale about what happened when other Australian university leaders mapped their own institutions against that continuum, and about the debate RMIT staged at its first education conference: are AI tools morally neutral, or does responsibility for them rest entirely on the people using them? And now that AI can do almost anything, what should humans still do themselves? In this episode: RMIT's AI Skills Continuum treats AI skill-building as a moving target, not a fixed benchmark, since what counts as expert practice keeps changing faster than anyone can master it. When Victorian university leaders mapped their own institutions against that continuum, most landed at the earliest stage, a sign of a confidence gap more than a competence gap. Efficiency is the wrong goal for AI in education, since it's made his own work more expansive, not faster, which means the work itself has to change instead of just speeding up. Students at RMIT's new AI advisory board raised concerns about their own learning unprompted, and the thing they asked for most, across every discipline, was consistency, not more rules. title: Lost in Translation: Getting Employers and Educators to Speak the Same Language Educast 3000 June 16, 2026 35 min 0:00 / 35:05 ▶

body.text: What makes a skill count, and how does it travel from a classroom or a kitchen table into a job? Ryan Lufkin puts that question to Glenda Quintini, who runs the OECD's Skills and Future Readiness Division in Paris, with Simone Ravaioli sitting in for Melissa. Glenda's answer starts with a confession: a few months ago she couldn't tell critical minerals from rare earths, taught herself by reading and talking to people, and never enrolled in anything. That's how most adults actually learn, and almost none of it shows up on a resume. The conversation works through what it takes to fix that. Degrees aren't dead, Glenda argues, they're bundles of skills nobody has unpacked. The harder problem is language: employers and educators describe the same skills in completely different words, a gap she says blocks worker mobility as much as visa rules do. From there the three of them get into micro-credentials, individual learning accounts, the data behind dropped degree requirements, and why governments have to move faster than a two-year accreditation cycle. In this episode: Why eliminating degree requirements barely moves non-degree hiring on its own The difference between regulating credentials like New Zealand and letting the market sort it out Why the next 15 years will be about lifelong recognition, not just lifelong learning For further reading: A Skills-First Labour Market (opens in a new tab) What is Educast 3000? body.text: In this episode, Melissa and Ryan are joined by Katherine Burton-Jones. Katherine discusses the intersection of museum studies and technology, sharing her journey from archaeology to teaching at Harvard Extension School. She highlights the evolution of museums over the past few decades, emphasizing the importance of human-centered learning and the challenges museums face in modernizing. The group explores how technology, including AI, can enhance the museum experience and foster social connections. Takeaways: The role of museums has evolved to become more user-centric and inclusive. Data collection is crucial for understanding visitor needs and behaviors. Technology can enhance the museum experience and make it more accessible. AI has potential applications in museums, but ethical considerations are important. Personal stories behind objects can create deeper connections with visitors. Museums can serve as spaces for social connection and community building. Curators of the future need to be data-aware and conceptually prepared. The future of museums lies in embracing technology while remaining inclusive. body.text: We’re kicking off a new season of Educast 3000! In this episode, hosts Ryan Lufkin and Melissa Loble welcome back Professor Martin Bean to discuss the future of education. They explore the importance of lifelong learning, the evolution of credentials, and the need for educational institutions to adapt to the changing workforce landscape. Martin shares his personal learning moments and emphasizes the significance of recognizing prior learning. Together they discuss the need for equity in education and the vision for a connected learning system by 2026. Takeaways Lifelong learning is essential for success in the modern world. Credentials must evolve to reflect continuous learning and skills acquisition. Recognition of prior learning can enhance educational pathways. Equity in education is crucial for inclusivity and relevance. Educational institutions need to adapt to the needs of adult learners. The future of education requires dynamic and flexible pathways. Assuming competence rather than deficit can transform learning experiences. Collaboration between educators and employers is necessary for relevance. Shared skill descriptors can help align education with workforce needs. Investing in a connected learning system is vital for future success. What is Educast 3000? Conferences

ISTELive 26 and the ASCD Annual Conference were held June 28–July 1, 2026, in Orlando, Florida. ISTE reports 15,201 participants from 86 countries and all 50 states, and announced its renaming to the International Society for Transforming Education at the event. Source: ISTE, "Second Annual ISTELive and ASCD Annual Conference Convenes Global Education Leaders Around the Future of Learning".

InstructureCon 2026 was held July 21–23, 2026, at the Kentucky International Convention Center in Louisville, Kentucky, under the theme "Education in the Making." Attendee reports from Instructure show 2,700+ attendees from all 50 states and 24 countries. Source: Instructure, "InstructureCon 2026 Brings Educators and Innovators Together to Advance Future-Ready Teaching and Learning".

 

Session analysis

Session counts for ISTELive 2026 come from an analysis of the published conference program conducted by Instructure. The program listed 1,438 unique sessions; 561, or 39%, referenced artificial intelligence in the session title or description. Artificial Intelligence was also the largest single program strand, with 317 sessions.

Counts for InstructureCon 2026 come from the published K–12 session list.

 

Trend 1: AI is the pressure test.

Student AI use: Common Sense Media, The Common Sense Media Census: AI Use by Tweens and Teens, 2026, March 2026. Nationally representative survey of 1,204 children ages nine to 17, fielded March 18–26, 2026; margin of error ±3.8 percentage points. Read the report.

Teacher opposition to student AI use: EdChoice, Spring 2026 Teacher Survey, conducted with Morning Consult. Nationally representative survey of 1,030 K–12 teachers, fielded April 1–9, 2026. Read the findings.

District AI guidelines: Consortium for School Networking (CoSN), U.S. State of EdTech 2026, March 2026. Survey of 607 education technology leaders across 44 states, fielded January 14–March 1, 2026; margin of error ±4% at 95% confidence. Read the report.

Educator AI training: Instructure, The Future of Edtech: Building Better AI for Schools, 2026 research.

Remarks by Melissa Loble, Michael Horn, and Richard Culatta are summarized from their sessions at InstructureCon 2026 and ISTELive 2026.

 

Trend 2: Screen value replaced screen time.

Screen time guidance: American Academy of Pediatrics, Center of Excellence on Social Media and Youth Mental Health. The AAP recommends "considering the quality of interactions with digital media and not just the quantity, or amount of time." Read the guidance.

Edtech quality and student benefit: ISTE+ASCD, From Screentime to Learning Time: Edtech Evidence. Read the research.

ESSA evidence levels across classroom technology: Instructure and InnovateEDU, 2026 EdTech Evidence Report, February 2026. Reviews the 150 most-used K–12 classroom technologies, based on de-identified LearnPlatform data collected August 1–December 31, 2025, and a synthesis of publicly available research compiled in January 2026. State policy activity on edtech safety and effectiveness is also reported here. Read the report.

Outcomes-based contracting: The Center for Outcomes Based Contracting, 2025 Impact Report. Read the report.

Remarks by Brittany Miller, Holly Clark, and Adam Sparks are summarized from their sessions at ISTELive 2026.

 

Trend 3: Rebuilding assessment.

EdChoice, Spring 2026 Teacher Survey (see Trend 1).

Remarks by Stevie Frank, Melissa Loble, and Michael Horn are summarized from sessions at ISTELive 2026 and InstructureCon 2026.

 

Trend 4: The teacher capacity problem.

Teacher AI use and time saved: Gallup and the Walton Family Foundation, Three in 10 Teachers Use AI Weekly, Saving Six Weeks a Year, June 2025. Survey of 2,232 U.S. public K–12 teachers from the RAND American Teacher Panel, fielded March 18–April 11, 2025. Read the findings.

Remarks by Jeannette Tejeda, Susan Bostick, and Shiren Vijiasingam are summarized from their sessions at ISTELive 2026 and InstructureCon 2026.

 

Educator interviews

Quotations from Mark Griffith, Carrie Schurman, and Jenna Eastham are drawn from interviews recorded at InstructureCon 2026 in Louisville, Kentucky, July 2026. Quotations have been lightly edited for length and clarity.

title: Are My Benchmark Assessments Predictive or Descriptive? A Checklist for District Leaders
snippet: Evaluate your district's tools with our benchmark assessment checklist. Learn
intro: Evaluate your district's tools with our benchmark assessment checklist. Learn the difference between descriptive and predictive data to improve student outcomes, and how Mastery Predictive Assessments can help you confidently look ahead.

body.text: Most benchmark assessments function as a rearview mirror, reporting on a student’s past performance. Predictive benchmark assessments, however, act as a GPS. They use high-validity data to forecast how students will perform on end-of-course assessments while there’s still time to adjust instruction and help students close gaps. Descriptive benchmarks show you what students know today. However, they don’t always fully align with the rigor of state tests, making it harder for educators to confidently predict how students will perform on the state test. Predictive benchmarks show you what students know today and project how they’ll perform months from now on high-stakes assessments. Teachers know which students need support and on which standards, allowing for proactive Tier 2 and Tier 3 interventions.

intro: Validate your impact. Learn how the Instructure Research Certification helps edtech providers meet ESSA evidence standards and build trust with K-12 leaders.

body.text: The "Research Certification One Pager" by Instructure (LearnPlatform) outlines a strategic program designed to help edtech providers validate the effectiveness of their products. In an increasingly crowded market, this certification serves as a beacon of trust for K-12 district leaders, ensuring that digital tools are backed by rigorous, evidence-based research. By aligning with ESSA (Every Student Succeeds Act) tiers of evidence, the program helps providers bridge the gap between product development and proven classroom impact, ultimately strengthening the entire educational "Ed-cosystem." The document details how the certification process empowers both edtech companies and school districts: ESSA Alignment: Provides a clear pathway for products to meet ESSA Tiers IV (Demonstrates a Rationale) and III (Promising Evidence), which are increasingly required for district procurement and federal funding. Third-Party Validation: Offers an objective, expert review of a product's logic model and research base, providing the "seal of approval" that administrators need to make confident purchasing decisions. Standardized Evidence: Establishes a common language for edtech efficacy, making it easier for districts to compare tools based on documented pedagogical impact rather than marketing claims. Accelerated Adoption: Helps providers stand out in a competitive landscape by demonstrating a commitment to continuous improvement and student outcomes. Data-Informed Innovation: Encourages a culture of evidence where research insights are used to refine product features and better serve the needs of teachers and learners.

title: Navigate Your Evidence Journey
snippet: Learn how Instructure’s Evidence as a Service helps edtech partners build
intro: Learn how Instructure’s Evidence as a Service helps edtech partners build research portfolios and meet ESSA funding requirements through rigorous validation.

body.text: In an era where evidence-based decision-making is paramount, education technology providers must demonstrate the tangible impact of their solutions to satisfy stakeholders and unlock funding. Instructure’s "Evidence as a Service" offers a strategic pathway for partners to build a comprehensive research portfolio, ranging from foundational logic models to rigorous randomized controlled trials. By providing a starter pack of "Evidence Essentials" or customized research agendas, Instructure helps organizations validate their effectiveness and meet critical U.S. K-12 funding requirements, such as Every Student Succeeds Act (ESSA) alignment. This service bridges the gap between product development and academic validation by offering accessible, high-quality research at a fraction of the cost of traditional third-party evaluations. Partners can leverage a variety of study options—including correlational research briefs, quasi-experimental designs, and R&D evaluations—to identify how specific features impact user outcomes. By turning data into credible, badge-certified evidence, education providers can build deeper trust with administrators and demonstrate a clear return on investment, ensuring their tools are not just used, but are truly driving student success.

body.text: Geering brings two decades of privacy, risk and public policy experience to spearhead global data privacy and AI regulatory compliance SALT LAKE CITY — Sept. 14, 2026 — Instructure , the leading learning ecosystem and maker of Canvas LMS, today announced Stephan Geering as chief privacy officer. In this role, Geering will lead Instructure's global data privacy programs, working across legal, security and product teams to guide how the company builds and governs technology for educators and learners worldwide. He will define Instructure's data privacy strategy and ensure compliance with evolving AI regulations worldwide, overseeing how Instructure evaluates AI features for data privacy and safety risks before they reach customers, setting requirements for how new products handle learner and educator data, and leading the company's response to emerging AI regulation. He will work directly with product and engineering teams to build data privacy and AI governance requirements into the company's roadmap from the earliest stages of development. Most recently, he led the data privacy, AI governance, and compliance programs at a major education technology firm, where he helped secure key ISO certifications. Earlier in his career, he oversaw international data privacy compliance for global financial institutions and developed regulatory frameworks while serving at a government data protection authority. Geering holds Masters of Law from the University of Basel and University College London. He is a Certified Information Privacy Professional in both Europe and the United States, an IAPP board member and the London co-chair of the Future of Privacy Forum's Privacy Executives Network. “AI is changing education faster than most institutions can plan for, and getting data privacy and governance right is critical to how we build and support our products," said Steve Daly, CEO at Instructure. "Stephan will play a key role in that work, helping Instructure and our customers use AI responsibly as the pace of change keeps accelerating.”

title: Instructure Partners With Veriff to Give Institutions a New Defense Against Rising Credential Fraud
intro: Instructure is shaping the future of learning by delivering a future-ready ecosystem that helps learners thrive in tomorrow’s landscape. body.text: Identity verification built into the world's largest academic credential network, with registrars keeping final say over every order SALT LAKE CITY — Sep. 9, 2026 — Instructure , the leading learning ecosystem and maker of Canvas LMS, today announced a partnership with Veriff , a global identity verification provider, to build identity verification directly into Parchment by Instructure Transcript Services. The new capability allows institutions to require learners to verify their identity before a transcript request is fulfilled. Parchment runs the largest academic credential network in the world, connecting more than 6,200 colleges and universities with 6,700 K-12 schools and districts, and has exchanged more than 165 million credentials. Verification now happens inside that network, at the point where the credential is issued. The capability is currently being piloted with a small group of higher education institutions, with general availability planned for November 2026 in the United States. Fraud is outpacing manual review “Ghost student” schemes cost U.S. community colleges $180 million in a single year, according to Equifax , citing U.S. Department of Education findings. Fraudsters enroll under stolen or fabricated identities, collect financial aid and disappear. These bad actors then leverage academic records in their scheme by ordering transcripts under someone else's name, then use them to apply for admission and aid at other institutions. AI tools have made the problem worse by lowering the cost of producing convincing fake documents and scaling fraudulent requests. Many registrars have responded the only way they could, by reviewing orders one at a time. That work is slow, expensive and hard to sustain. "Fraud is evolving faster than the legacy systems that most institutions rely on were built to handle," said Brian Cully, senior vice president of finance and strategy at Instructure. "Registrars are spending hours reviewing orders by hand because they have no scalable way to confirm the person behind an account is real. With Parchment, that confirmation becomes part of the workflow itself, running inside the same trusted network they already use to send credentials. Institutions get proof that credential submissions are legitimate, and learners still get their transcripts fast." How identity verification works in Parchment Institutions turn on identity verification at the account level. Setup and administration happen inside Parchment, in the same system where registrars already process orders. When a learner creates an account or places an order, Veriff checks a government-issued ID against a live selfie. Parchment assigns a verification status and a confidence score, then routes the order. Trusted orders are approved automatically. Suspicious orders are held for staff review. Learners who sign in through single sign-on or an institution-issued token are verified automatically and skip the extra step. Veriff supports more than 12,500 document types from over 230 countries and territories, including passports, national ID cards, driver's licenses and residence permits. Parchment stores verification status and metadata only. It does not store biometric data. Institutions get the proof they need to act on an order while the sensitive images stay out of their systems. Registrars maintain final say over every approval. Parchment flags and routes orders against the thresholds an institution sets, and institution staff decide what happens to anything held for review. Institutions can block fraudulent orders at registration, before staff spends hours investigating them after the fact. Verification that protects access Identity verification in Parchment lets an institution raise its defenses without raising barriers for the learners it exists to serve. Every friction point meant to stop fraud carries a risk of excluding a real student. Learners who cannot produce a government-issued ID can defer verification, and orders that fall short of an institution's confidence threshold route to human review instead of automatic denial. Institutions set their own thresholds and document the policy behind them. “A transcript is a key to money, admission and employment, which is exactly why fraudsters have started going after them,” said Kaarel Kotkas, Founder and CEO of Veriff. “The right place to stop that is at the moment the credential changes hands. Instructure connects learners from the classroom through to the workforce, so verifying identity inside Parchment protects the whole chain rather than one institution at a time.” Availability Identity Verification for Parchment Transcript Services entered a pilot program in August 2026. General availability is planned for November 2026 in the United States. A later phase is expected to add step-up verification for high-risk account changes such as name and date of birth updates. Instructure leaders Brian Cully, Kristie Lindell and Steve Proud discussed how fraud patterns are changing across education, and what institutions can do about them, in the webinar The Growing Fraud Threat in Education: Risks, Responses, and Real Solutions , available on demand. About Veriff Veriff is a global AI-native identity platform that helps organizations build trust online. Leading companies across financial services, marketplaces, mobility, gig economy, and other digital sectors rely on Veriff’s technology to stay compliant, prevent fraud, protect users, and scale globally. Veriff’s trust infrastructure supports the full customer journey, from verification to ongoing authentication and fraud prevention, with the least friction for honest people. Built for global scale, Veriff helps businesses expand across borders without the complexity of managing identity verification, compliance, and fraud in multiple markets – creating a single source of truth for trusted identities.

intro: Instructure is shaping the future of learning by delivering a future-ready ecosystem that helps learners thrive in tomorrow’s landscape. body.text: New product runs on the Canvas platform and adds identity verification for every teacher who signs up SALT LAKE CITY — Sept. 9, 2026 — Instructure , the leading learning ecosystem and maker of Canvas LMS, today announced Canvas Lite, a new no-cost product that gives educators a simple way to build and deliver course content to learners. Canvas Lite is built on the Canvas platform that schools, colleges, and universities worldwide rely on every day. It goes live on September 30, 2026, at canvaslite.instructure.com. Educators can create a course, invite students and start teaching even if the institution doesn’t currently have a full license. Many teachers work outside a district or campus license. Canvas Lite provides homeschool educators, tutors, community instructors and teachers piloting a new course one place to organize materials, assign work, collect submissions and give feedback. Through Canvas Lite, teachers have complimentary access to the core Canvas tools at the course level without IT deployment or procurement. "Individual educators have been part of the Canvas story since the beginning,” said Melissa Loble, chief learning officer at Instructure. “Canvas Lite is how we keep showing up for them, with a free place to build a course and teach the way they want to teach. And there's a benefit for their students too. A learner who works in Canvas Lite this year will recognize Canvas when they walk into a high school, a college or a training program down the road." Canvas Lite includes the Canvas tools teachers use most, including: Building modules and pages with rich content Collecting file, text, and URL submissions Running quizzes and applying rubrics SpeedGrader with support for annotations, audio and video feedback, and grade exports Built-in messaging, discussions, and course announcements Course-level integrations with third-party tools such as Google Drive, Zoom, and Microsoft Teams Canvas Teacher and Canvas Student mobile apps Every teacher who signs up completes an identity check, using a government-issued ID and a selfie, through the verification partner Veriff . Students invited by a teacher do not complete that step. Canvas Lite runs on its own domain, separate from the Canvas environments that institutional customers use. ”We built privacy and security into Canvas Lite's core design,” said Zach Pendleton, chief architect at Instructure. “Canvas Lite ensures that independent educators get a safe, reliable environment without compromise.” Canvas Lite is available worldwide at canvaslite.instructure.com beginning September 30, 2026. All Canvas Lite data is hosted in the United States, and teachers can find self-serve guides in the Instructure Community. The Canvas Lite terms set a 500 MB storage limit per course. Teachers who need more, or who need course analytics, attendance tracking or API access tokens, can talk with Instructure about a full Canvas license. Learn more at canvaslite.instructure.com .

body.text: In its second year, the awards celebrate educators worldwide advancing student success through innovative courses, programs and tools SALT LAKE CITY — Aug. 11, 2026 — Instructure , the leading learning ecosystem and maker of Canvas LMS , announced the winners of its 2026 Academic Excellence Awards , recognizing exceptional educators, technologies and programs worldwide for remarkable achievements in teaching, learning and innovation. The awards spotlight individuals and teams who have demonstrated meaningful impact across three categories: Outstanding Course, Transformative Program and Innovative Technology. The Academic Excellence Awards are a key component of Instructure's commitment to supporting educators worldwide. The rigorous submission and review process highlights excellence. It also gives Instructure firsthand insight into how educators use its tools in teaching and learning. This feedback helps shape future product updates with the goal of improving how Instructure supports its customers. Finalists were selected from a competitive global pool of nominees from a wide variety of institutions and disciplines. The recipients were chosen based on their creativity, measurable impact and overall influence on education. Honorees received complimentary passes to attend InstructureCon 2026 and were recognized for their dedication, ingenuity and impact. All awardees will also be featured across Instructure’s social media channels. “We celebrate educators as often as we can because they show us what it means to give learners the space and grace to focus on human connection,” said Melissa Loble, chief learning officer at Instructure. “Their dedication to using evidence-backed tools to improve outcomes guides how we build, how we listen and how we keep evolving to support the new learner.” This year's winners show what that impact looks like in practice. Their work ranges from AI-powered interactive storytelling in higher education to bilingual language instruction in K-12 classrooms and accessible online course design in sociology. The 2026 winners are: Chris Rains (Innovative Technology Award): Chris Rains, instructional designer at Belmont University, has been honored with the Innovative Technology award for developing "AI-Generated Micro-Stories and Interactive Technologies." This pioneering platform leverages generative AI to transform traditional, static online activities into immersive, scenario-based learning experiences. By enabling instructional teams to easily build realistic branching scenarios complete with character dialogue, voice and visuals without needing advanced technical skills, the tool bridges the gap between classroom theory and professional practice. The result is a highly user-friendly, accessible and scalable solution that boosts student engagement, improves knowledge retention and prepares learners to confidently navigate real-world workplace challenges. Jasmin Muñoz (Transformative Program): Jasmin Muñoz, a third-grade bilingual teacher in Pasadena ISD, has received the Transformative Program award for her exceptional design and delivery of Language Arts 3. Muñoz demonstrates outstanding instructional innovation by building a vibrant, button-based digital program specifically tailored to support bilingual learners. She builds student independence through clear visual cues and accessible language, while meeting the Technology Applications standards within the Texas Essential Knowledge and Skills (TEKS) framework. Her forward-thinking approach ensures that young learners gain essential academic and digital literacy skills, confidently preparing them to navigate online environments and excel on STAAR assessments. Jaclyn A. Tabor, Ph.D. (Outstanding Course Award): Jaclyn Tabor, instructional designer and instructor of sociology at Lincoln Land Community College, is honored with the Outstanding Course award for her innovative online asynchronous course, SOC 101: Introduction to Sociology. body.text: AWS collaboration accelerates AI-powered migration tools and Canvas Career capabilities designed to expand access for underserved learners SALT LAKE CITY — August 4, 2026 — Instructure , the leading learning ecosystem and maker of Canvas LMS, powered by AWS, today announced it will build AI-powered tools to expand learning access for underserved communities worldwide, supported by the Amazon Web Services, Inc. (AWS) Education Equity Initiative. The effort advances two workstreams. intro: Instructure is shaping the future of learning by delivering a future-ready ecosystem that helps learners thrive in tomorrow’s landscape.
